Quantum Observable Universe

Frederick Carl Leitner

2026-03-21

Abstract

This paper develops the mathematical framework of the Quantum Observable Universe (QOU): a rigid braided monoidal category equipped with a Frobenius–Hopf object whose differential geometry is controlled by a substrate parameter \(q\). Part I (Chapters 1–3) establishes the categorical foundations and the Yekutieli brane tower. Part II (Chapters 4–8) develops the structural consequences: braiding and knot theory, models over various ground fields, the algebraic substrate, fluid dynamics, and information-theoretic perspectives. Part III (Chapters 9–10) specialises to the Descartes universe on Bring’s surface (\(\chi = -6\)) and collects physical predictions. Chapter 11 develops the \(q\)-geometric Langlands correspondence.

On the Mechanics of Quantum Observable Universes
Frederick Carl Leitner
2026-03-21

Introduction

Overview

We see colours — three of them mix to white. We rotate, translate, and boost, yet measurements remain invariant. Time flows forward. Multiple observers share one world, not private copies. We integrate, differentiate, and compute; the universe has volume. Free will — the ability to choose what to measure — produces outcomes not determined by initial conditions.

These observations, once stated precisely, determine a specific algebraic structure: a rigid monoidal category equipped with a fibre functor and a Frobenius trace \(\int_A\). We call this structure a quantum observable universe (QOU). Its axioms encode the features listed above and nothing more.

An assumption this paper does not make is that the constants of our universe are constant. We allow them to vary — in a controlled, algebraic way — and ask: what does that change?

We do not ask what the universe is; we ask what its mechanics do. Category theory is the natural language, because it describes transformation without committing to ontology. Noether’s principle converts observed symmetries into conserved quantities; the Frobenius trace \(\int_A\) is the categorical Noether current. The \(q\)-deformation of the substrate shifts conservation laws from exact identities to approximate ones, with anomalies that are themselves measurable.

What follows from these axioms is broad in scope and specific in detail. The symmetry group \(\mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) is not assumed; it emerges via Tannaka–Krein reconstruction. Particles are knots; interactions are braid relations. The capacity for computation is a consequence, not an input.

The paper is organised as follows.

Part I: Foundations. Chapter 1 introduces the quantum universe (QU): a rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\), a Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\), and a fibre functor \(\tau\). The Frobenius trace \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) provides categorical integration; combined with Kähler differentials on \(A\), it provides differentiation. Self-duality \(A \cong A^{\vee}\) ensures these operations are compatible. From these ingredients the chapter derives the Frobenius relation, the dagger involution, and the Tannaka–Krein reconstruction of the symmetry group.

Chapter 2 imposes three cohomological constraints — observability, measurability, and volume — that promote the QU to a quantum observable universe (QOU). These constraints remove unobservable hidden structures and bad behaviour. Self-duality within this constrained space forces the gauge group \(G = \mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) to emerge naturally, together with a natural coordinate \(q\), an ordering direction, and a strict genus limitation of four on the state space. The QOU is characterised by the archimedean tuple

\[(\mathbf{C},\; \theta,\; G,\; \mathcal{S}).\]

A categorical Dirac operator \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\), forced by the Frobenius–Hopf structure, decomposes into gravity (Ricci), gauge (Yang–Mills), and matter terms — yielding the categorical action

\[\mathcal{S}_q[\nabla, \textstyle\int_A, \psi] \;=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{tr}\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr)}_{\text{gravity}} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \!\circ\, \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl( F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla \bigr)}_{\text{gauge}} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A\!\bigl(\psi^{\ast} \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\,\psi\bigr)}_{\text{matter}},\]

from which quantum versions of the Einstein, Yang–Mills, and Dirac equations follow.

Chapter 3 addresses the obstructions that arise when local categorical data is extended globally. The Yekutieli lifting condition makes this precise: an object admits a lift if and only if its obstruction class \(\kappa(x) \in H^2(S, B)\) vanishes. A key result is the Descartes condition \(\chi(A) = -6\), forced by the lifting obstructions and the Archimedean constraint.

Part II: Structure. Chapter 4 replaces continuum path integrals with discrete braid-group computations. Fundamental particles — photons, electrons, protons — are defined purely mathematically as specific knots and words on the genus-\(4\) state space. Particle interactions are modelled through braid relations by computing the Gröbner–Shirshov basis normal form of knot words using Hecke relations, where the parameter \(q\) tracks the energy cost of each crossing. The topological mass formula

\[\mathfrak{m}(K) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K)}{\hbar_q^{\,2}}\]

acts as a Feynman path integral via the non-abelian Stokes formula, but because the space is finite-dimensional it naturally avoids standard infinities. The embeddability bound on \(\Sigma_4\) yields exactly \(7\) transfer matrices — six non-trivial force operators and the identity (interaction completeness).

Chapter 5 examines concrete realisations of the QOU axioms: archimedean, \(p\)-adic, and finite-field models.

Chapter 6 develops the spectral theory of the Frobenius–Hopf algebra. The local \(q\)-zeta function of Bring’s curve encodes the Frobenius eigenvalues, and the Hasse–Weil bound confines them to the critical line \(|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}\). The categorical machinery provides a natural framing for classical questions in analytic number theory — including the Riemann hypothesis, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture , and the Collatz problem — through the Kummer tower associated to the Frobenius–Hopf algebra.

Chapter 7 explores the correlation between the knot structures developed in earlier chapters and topological fluid dynamics, offering an obstruction-based perspective on Navier–Stokes regularity.

Chapter 8 examines the categorical framework through the lens of information theory and computational complexity. The Gröbner–Shirshov basis makes computation confluent; the Reeb flow generates a dynamical system whose boundary is a Julia-set fractal. The framework provides an interesting perspective on questions such as P versus NP in terms of categorical obstructions and event horizons for information flow. Crossing energy relates to categorical mass by \(E_{\mathfrak{H}} = \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot c_q^{\,2}\) where \(c_q = 1/(q - 1)\).

Part III: The Descartes Universe and Observations. Chapter 9 maps the genus-\(4\) constraint to Bring’s surface \(\Sigma_4\), a complex curve with Euler characteristic \(-6\) and maximal automorphisms (\(S_5\)). This surface serves as the foundational state space: its coral tubes — the exceptional divisors — provide coordinate systems for spacetime and the electromagnetic field, mapping exactly where vertex operators interact. Within this space, embeddable knots form a basis for homology and cohomology; specific knots and torus-knot words define the full particle spectrum. The geometric structure also provides a natural setting in which to examine Yang–Mills theory and the question of a mass gap.

Chapter 10 confronts theory with experiment. We use observed CODATA values for the muon and electron mass to determine \(q_0\) for our local patch of the universe:

\[(1 - q^{-1})^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)}{m_\mu / m_e} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q \;=\; q_0 \;+\; O\!\bigl(2.2 \times 10^{-8}\bigr).\]

From this single parameter we derive formulas for the masses of all atoms parametrised by \(q_0\), which align with observed values to good precision. The transfer matrices describe hadron half-lives that match observation.

Chapter 11 develops the \(q\)-geometric Langlands correspondence that connects the categorical framework to the geometric Langlands programme.

All algebraic groups and projective spaces in this paper are written with their base ring \(R\) explicit:

Object Notation Over \(\mathbb{C}\)
Special unitary group \(\mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)
Maximal torus / Reeb gauge group \(U_1(R)\) \(U(1)\)
Quantum group \(\mathrm{SU}_{q,2}(R)\) \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\)
Projective line \(\mathbb{P}^1(R)\) \(\mathbb{CP}^1 \cong S^2\)
Multiplicative group \(\mathbb{G}_m(R) = R^{\times}\) \(\mathbb{C}^{\times}\)

When the base ring is clear from context, we may write \(\mathrm{SU}_2\) for \(\mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) and \(\mathbb{P}^1\) for \(\mathbb{P}^1(R)\). The category-theoretic definitions (quantum universe, quantum observable universe) are formulated over an arbitrary commutative ring \(R\) and specialise to any base by substitution. A reader working over \(\mathbb{Z}_p\), \(\mathbb{F}_q\), or \(\mathbb{C}\) reads the same axioms and the same proofs — only the ground ring changes.

Preliminary: rigid monoidal categories

📄

Definition 1.1 ∀ stated (Algebra without quasi-zeros). \(\forall\) Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with unity and let \(A\) be an \(R\)-algebra. An element \(a \in A\) is called a quasi-zero if

\[bac = 0 \qquad \text{for all } b, c \in A \text{ not both } 1.\]

We say \(A\) is an algebra without quasi-zeros if no such element exists. Throughout this paper, whenever \(\mathbf{C}\) is \(R\)-linear we assume that \(R\) has no quasi-zeros.

This condition appears naturally in the theory of unital Gröbner–Shirshov bases , where it ensures that leading-term decompositions are well-defined and the division algorithm terminates correctly. In the categorical setting it guarantees that \(R\)-linear hom-spaces have no "phantom" morphisms annihilated by all compositions — a necessary condition for the Frobenius pairing to be non-degenerate.

📄

Definition 1.2 ∀ stated (Snake identity). \(\forall\) Let \((\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})\) be a monoidal category and let \(V\) be an object with dual \(V^{\vee}\), evaluation \(\mathrm{ev} \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1}\), and coevaluation \(\mathrm{coev} \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V\). The snake identities (also called zig-zag identities) are the two commutative diagrams:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:snake-identities} \begin{gathered} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em] V \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}"] \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_V"'] & V \otimes V^{\vee} \otimes V \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"] \\ & V \end{tikzcd} \\[-0.5em] \text{\small (left snake identity)} \end{gathered} \qquad\qquad \begin{gathered} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=2.5em] V^{\vee} \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev} \otimes \mathrm{id}"] \ar[dr, "\mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}}"'] & V^{\vee} \otimes V \otimes V^{\vee} \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{ev}"] \\ & V^{\vee} \end{tikzcd} \\[-0.5em] \text{\small (right snake identity)} \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

These identities express the fact that \((\mathrm{ev}, \mathrm{coev})\) exhibit \(V^{\vee}\) as a right dual of \(V\) (equivalently, that the pair forms an exact pairing in the sense of CategoryTheory.ExactPairing). The terminology "snake" comes from the graphical calculus, where the composites trace out an S-shaped curve that straightens to a vertical line.

📄

Definition 1.3 ∀ stated (Rigid monoidal category). \(\forall\)

A monoidal category \((\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})\) is a category equipped with a bifunctor \(\otimes \colon \mathbf{C} \times \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{C}\) (the tensor product), a unit object \(\mathbf{1}\), and natural isomorphisms expressing associativity and unitality:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:monoidal-axioms} \begin{gathered} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] (X \otimes Y) \otimes Z \ar[r, "\alpha_{X,Y,Z}", "\sim"'] & X \otimes (Y \otimes Z) \end{tikzcd} \\[-0.5em] \text{\small (associativity)} \end{gathered} \qquad \begin{gathered} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \mathbf{1} \otimes X \ar[r, "\ell_X", "\sim"'] & X & X \otimes \mathbf{1} \ar[l, "\rho_X"', "\sim"] \end{tikzcd} \\[-0.5em] \text{\small (unitality)} \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

The category is rigid if every object \(V\) has a dual \(V^{\vee}\) together with morphisms \(\mathrm{ev}_V \colon V \otimes V^{\vee} \to \mathbf{1}\) and \(\mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V^{\vee} \otimes V\) satisfying the snake identities.

We say \(\mathbf{C}\) is \(R\)-linear (for a commutative ring \(R\)) if every hom-set is an \(R\)-module and composition is \(R\)-bilinear. We require \(R\) to be without quasi-zeros.

The category is braided monoidal if it is further equipped with a natural isomorphism (the braiding) \(c_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X\) compatible with the associator and satisfying the hexagon axioms. When \(c_{Y,X} \circ c_{X,Y} = \mathrm{id}\) the braiding is symmetric; in general \(c^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\). Given a braiding, the exterior power \(\Lambda^k V\) is defined as the image of the antisymmetriser \(\mathrm{Alt}_k = \sum_{\pi \in S_k} \mathrm{sgn}(\pi)\,\pi\) acting on \(V^{\otimes k}\), where permutations act via \(c\).

Example 1.4 (\(\mathbb{C}[z]\) and \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

The polynomial ring \(\mathbb{C}[z]\) is the algebra of functions on the complex line \(\mathbb{C}\). The category \(\mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}\) of finite-dimensional complex vector spaces is the simplest \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear rigid monoidal category: the tensor product is \(V \otimes W\), the unit is \(\mathbf{1} = \mathbb{C}\), and the dual is \(V^{\vee} = \mathrm{Hom}(V, \mathbb{C})\) with \(\mathrm{ev}(v \otimes f) = f(v)\).

Similarly, the coordinate ring \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) is the algebra of polynomial functions on the group \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\), generated by the matrix entries \(\alpha, \beta, \bar\alpha, \bar\beta\) with \(\alpha\bar\alpha + \beta\bar\beta = 1\). The category \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) of finite-dimensional representations is \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear rigid monoidal. Its simple objects are the spin-\(j\) representations \(V_j\) (\(j = 0, \tfrac12, 1, \ldots\), \(\dim V_j = 2j+1\)). The fundamental object is \(V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\).

The Quantum Universe

📄

Definition 1.5 ∀ stated (Quantum Universe). \(\forall\)

Let \(R\) be a commutative ring. A quantum universe over \(R\) is a triple \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) where:

  1. \((\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})\) is an \(R\)-linear rigid braided monoidal category (rigid monoidal category) with braiding \(c_{X,Y} \colon X \otimes Y \xrightarrow{\sim} Y \otimes X\) — the braiding is required for exterior powers \(\Lambda^k V\) and need not be symmetric (\(c^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\) in general);

  2. \(A\) is a Frobenius–Hopf object in \(\mathbf{C}\): an object equipped with morphisms \[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=2.5em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"] & A \ar[r, "\int_A"] & \mathbf{1} & {\scriptstyle\text{(multiplication, Frobenius form)}} \\ \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\eta"] & A \ar[r, "\varepsilon"] & \mathbf{1} & {\scriptstyle\text{(unit, counit)}} \\ A \ar[r, "\Delta"] & A \otimes A & A \ar[l, "S"'] & {\scriptstyle\text{(comultiplication, antipode)}} \end{tikzcd}\] — multiplication \(\mu\), unit \(\eta\), comultiplication \(\Delta\), counit \(\varepsilon\), antipode \(S\), and Frobenius form \(\int_A\) — satisfying: (H) \((A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S)\) is a Hopf algebra object in \(\mathbf{C}\); (F) the Frobenius pairing \(\int_A \circ \mu \colon A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1}\) is non-degenerate, inducing an isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\);

  3. \(\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) is a fibre functor: an exact, faithful, \(R\)-linear monoidal functor;

  4. \(A\) admits a differential calculus: the module of K"ahler differentials \(\Omega^1(A)\) exists in \(\mathbf{C}\).

We denote the forgetful (fibre) functor by \(\tau\) rather than the more common \(\omega\) to avoid conflict with differential-form notation (\(\omega_i\) for left-invariant \(1\)-forms, \(\omega_V\) for the vertical curvature form) that appears throughout the paper. The choice of \(\tau\) carries several resonances:

  • Tannakian reconstruction. The letter \(\tau\) recalls the Tannaka–Krein theorem that reconstructs the gauge group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) from the functor alone.

  • Trace / integration. In von Neumann algebra theory, a faithful normal state is traditionally denoted \(\tau\) (the trace). Since the forgetful functor underlies the Frobenius integration \(\int_A\) (integral notation), this identification is more than notational.

  • Proper time. In the archimedean realisation, \(\tau\) can be read as the observer’s proper time: the functor parameterises the "emergence" of \(R\)-modules from the abstract category, turning the static quantum universe into a temporal observable one.

📄

Definition 1.6 ∀ stated (Frobenius pairing). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe with multiplication \(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A\) and Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\). The Frobenius pairing is the composite

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:frobenius-pairing} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"] & A \ar[r, "\int_A"] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

We say the Frobenius pairing is non-degenerate when this composite induces an isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\) to the dual object. Equivalently, the snake identities hold: there exists a coevaluation \(\tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A\) such that the two composites

\[A \xrightarrow{\rho^{-1}} A \otimes \mathbf{1} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{\alpha^{-1}} (A \otimes A) \otimes A \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} \mathbf{1} \otimes A \xrightarrow{\lambda_A} A\]

and its mirror are both equal to \(\mathrm{id}_A\).

📄

Example 1.7 ✗ no Lean (The Frobenius pairing on \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)).

Continuing the SU(2) example (quantum universe on SU(2)), we make the Frobenius pairing concrete.

Set \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with pointwise multiplication \(\mu(f \otimes g) = fg\) and Frobenius form \(\int_A f = \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(g)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(g)\) (the Haar integral). The Frobenius pairing is the composite

\[\langle f, g \rangle_A \;=\; \int_A \!\circ\, \mu(f \otimes g) \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} f(g)\,h(g)\,d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(g).\]

This is the \(L^2\) inner product on SU(2).

Non-degeneracy. The pairing is non-degenerate because Haar measure on a compact group has full support: if \(\langle f, g \rangle_A = 0\) for all \(g \in A\), then \(f = 0\) a.e., hence \(f = 0\) in \(A\). Equivalently, the Peter–Weyl theorem gives an orthonormal basis of matrix coefficients \(\{D^j_{mn}\}_{j \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}}\) satisfying

\[\langle D^j_{mn},\, D^{j'}_{m'n'} \rangle_A \;=\; \frac{1}{2j+1}\,\delta_{jj'}\,\delta_{mm'}\,\delta_{nn'}.\]

The isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\sim} A^{\vee}\) sends each basis element to its dual functional scaled by \(1/(2j+1)\).

Concrete calculation on \(\mathbb{C}^2\). The matrix generators of \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) are \(\alpha, \beta, \bar{\alpha}, \bar{\beta}\) with \(|\alpha|^2 + |\beta|^2 = 1\). The spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) matrix coefficients are \(D^{1/2}_{mn} \in \{\alpha, \beta, -\bar{\beta}, \bar{\alpha}\}\). We compute:

\[\langle \alpha, \alpha \rangle_A \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} |\alpha|^2\,d\mu \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}, \qquad \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_A \;=\; \int_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} \alpha\,\beta\,d\mu \;=\; 0.\]

The factor \(\tfrac{1}{2} = 1/(2 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2} + 1)\) confirms the Peter–Weyl normalisation for spin \(j = \tfrac{1}{2}\).

The snake identity (non-degeneracy in categorical language): the coevaluation \(\tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A\) sends \(1 \mapsto \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)\,D^j_{mn} \otimes \overline{D^j_{mn}}\). The composite \(A \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id} \otimes \tilde{\eta}} A \otimes A \otimes A \xrightarrow{(\int_A \circ \mu) \otimes \mathrm{id}} A\) acts as

\[f \;\longmapsto\; \sum_{j,m,n} (2j+1)\, \langle f,\, D^j_{mn} \rangle_A \cdot \overline{D^j_{mn}} \;=\; f,\]

by Peter–Weyl completeness. This is \(\mathrm{id}_A\), confirming non-degeneracy.

📄

Example 1.8 ∀ stated (\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) as a quantum universe). \(\forall\)

Continuing rigid monoidal Vect, we verify each axiom of quantum universe for \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\).

(i) Category. \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), the category of finite-dimensional complex representations. Objects are vector spaces \(V\) with a continuous \(G\)-action \(\rho_V \colon G \to \mathrm{GL}(V)\); morphisms are \(G\)-equivariant linear maps. This is an \(\mathbb{C}\)-linear rigid monoidal category (rigid monoidal Vect). The \(G\)-action on tensor products is diagonal: \(g \cdot (v \otimes w) = (g \cdot v) \otimes (g \cdot w)\); on duals it is the contragredient: \((g \cdot f)(v) = f(g^{-1} \cdot v)\).

(ii) Frobenius–Hopf object. \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), the coordinate ring of polynomial functions on the group. Its Hopf structure encodes the group operations:

Operation Formula Meaning
Multiplication \(\mu(f \otimes g)\) \(f \cdot g\) pointwise product of functions
Unit \(\eta(1)\) \(1_A\) constant function \(1\)
Comultiplication \(\Delta(f)(x, y)\) \(f(xy)\) pullback of group multiplication
Counit \(\varepsilon(f)\) \(f(e)\) evaluation at the identity
Antipode \(S(f)(x)\) \(f(x^{-1})\) pullback of inversion
Frobenius form \(\int_A(f)\) \(\int_G f\, d\mu\) Haar integration on \(G\)

The Frobenius pairing \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_A(\mu(f \otimes g)) = \int_G f(x)\, g(x)\, d\mu_{\mathrm{Haar}}(x)\) is positive definite (faithfulness of the Haar integral).

(iii) Fibre functor. \(\tau \colon \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2)) \to \mathrm{Vect}_{\mathbb{C}}\) is the forgetful functor: \(\tau(V, \rho) = V\) (forget the \(G\)-action, keep the vector space). It is exact (short exact sequences of representations split), faithful (a non-zero equivariant map is non-zero as a linear map), and monoidal (\(\tau(V \otimes W) = \tau(V) \otimes \tau(W)\)). By Tannaka–Krein duality, \(G\) can be recovered from \(\tau\): \(G \cong \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\), the group of monoidal natural automorphisms of the fibre functor.

(iv) Differential calculus. The left-invariant calculus on \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) provides \(\Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}\), the left-invariant \(1\)-forms dual to the Lie algebra basis \(\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}\) of \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) (with \([e_a, e_b] = \epsilon_{abc}\, e_c\); SU(2) basis). The universal derivation \(d \colon A \to \Omega^1(A)\) acts by \(df = \sum_i (\partial_i f)\, \omega_i\), recovering the Lie derivative along each generator.

📄

Definition 1.9 ∀ stated (Higher differential forms). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe with differential calculus \(\Omega^1(A)\) (quantum universe). The higher differential forms are the graded \(A\)-bimodule

\[\Omega^k(A) \;=\; \bigwedge\nolimits_A^k \Omega^1(A), \qquad k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\]

(exterior powers of the \(A\)-bimodule \(\Omega^1(A)\) in \(\mathbf{C}\)), with \(\Omega^0(A) = A\). For an object \(V\) in \(\mathbf{C}\), \(\Lambda^k V\) denotes the \(k\)-th exterior power of \(V\) in the sense of rigid monoidal categories. The differential \(d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)\) extends the universal derivation by the graded Leibniz rule, and satisfies \(d^2 = 0\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:de-rham-complex} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] A = \Omega^0(A) \ar[r, "d"] & \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "d"] & \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "d"] & \cdots \end{tikzcd} \qquad (d^2 = 0) \end{equation}\]

📄

Example 1.10 ∀ stated (Higher forms on \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing quantum universe on SU(2), the left-invariant calculus on \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) has \(\Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}\) (three left-invariant \(1\)-forms, dual to the Lie algebra \(\mathfrak{su}(2) = \mathrm{span}\{e_1, e_2, e_3\}\)). The higher forms are:

  • \(\Omega^0(A) = A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) (functions on the group).

  • \(\Omega^1(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}\) (left-invariant \(1\)-forms, dimension \(3\) over \(A\)).

  • \(\Omega^2(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2,\, \omega_1 \wedge \omega_3,\, \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}\) (dimension \(3\) over \(A\)).

  • \(\Omega^3(A) = A \otimes \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\}\) (the volume form, dimension \(1\) over \(A\)).

  • \(\Omega^k(A) = 0\) for \(k \geq 4\).

The differential \(d\) is determined by \(d\omega_i = -\tfrac{1}{2} \epsilon_{ijk}\,\omega_j \wedge \omega_k\) (the Maurer–Cartan equation of \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)).

We fix two pieces of notation that will appear throughout.

The fundamental object \(V\). In a rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\), the fundamental object \(V\) is the unique (up to isomorphism) simple object of categorical dimension \(2\). Its dimension is not an independent assumption: in Chapter 2, the volume constraint (a non-degenerate epimorphism \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\)) forces \(\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2\). (If \(\mathrm{rank}(V) = 1\) then \(\Lambda^2 V = 0\) and no such epimorphism exists; if \(\mathrm{rank}(V) \geq 3\) then \(\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) \geq 3\) and the non-degenerate epimorphism to the rank-\(1\) unit object \(\mathbf{1}\) cannot exist.) In the SU(2) example (Example), \(V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\) is the defining (spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\)) representation. Every other simple object \(V_j\) is an exterior or symmetric power of \(V\), so \(V\) generates \(\mathbf{C}\) as a tensor category.

The emergent gauge group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\). Let \(\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) be the forgetful functor. The tensor automorphism group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) consists of all monoidal natural automorphisms of \(\tau\): families of \(R\)-module automorphisms \(\{g_X \colon \tau(X) \xrightarrow{\sim} \tau(X)\}_{X \in \mathbf{C}}\) compatible with the tensor product. By Tannaka–Krein duality, \(G\) is an affine group scheme over \(R\), and \(\tau\) establishes a monoidal equivalence \(\mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G)\). No group is postulated a priori; it emerges from \((\mathbf{C}, \tau)\).

Consequences of the QU axioms

📄

Proposition 1.11 ∀ stated (Frobenius relation). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum universe). Denote by \(\Delta_\mu\) the comultiplication on \(A\) dual to the multiplication \(\mu\) under the Frobenius pairing. Then the following diagram commutes (the Frobenius relation):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:frobenius-relation} \begin{gathered} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu"] \ar[d, "\mu"'] & A \otimes A \otimes A \ar[d, "\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}"] \\ A \ar[r, "\Delta_\mu"'] & A \otimes A \end{tikzcd} \\[-0.5em] \text{\small Frobenius relation: } (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu \end{gathered} \end{equation}\]

That is, sliding a multiplication past a comultiplication (or vice versa) yields the same result as composing them: \((\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu) = \Delta_\mu \circ \mu\).

Proof of Frobenius relation.

The Frobenius form \(\int_A\) and the multiplication \(\mu\) together define a pairing \(\langle a, b \rangle = \int_A(\mu(a \otimes b))\) on \(A\). Non-degeneracy of this pairing (Frobenius pairing) gives an isomorphism \(\phi \colon A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\) defined by \(\phi(a) = \langle a, - \rangle\). Define the dual comultiplication \(\Delta_\mu\) as the transpose of \(\mu\) under \(\phi\):

\[\Delta_\mu = (\phi^{-1} \otimes \phi^{-1}) \circ \mu^{\vee} \circ \phi,\]

where \(\mu^{\vee} \colon A^{\vee} \to A^{\vee} \otimes A^{\vee}\) is the linear dual of \(\mu\).

To verify the Frobenius relation, consider the two composites \((\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu)\) and \(\Delta_\mu \circ \mu\) as maps \(A \otimes A \to A \otimes A\). It suffices to show they agree after pairing with an arbitrary test element \(c \in A\) via \(\int_A\), since the pairing is non-degenerate.

For the left-hand side, using the definition of \(\Delta_\mu\) and the associativity of \(\mu\):

\[\bigl\langle (\mu \otimes \mathrm{id}) (\mathrm{id} \otimes \Delta_\mu)(a \otimes b),\; c \bigr\rangle = \int_A \mu\bigl(\mu(a \otimes b_1) \otimes b_2\bigr) \cdot c = \int_A \mu\bigl(a \otimes \mu(b_1 \otimes b_2)\bigr) \cdot c,\]

where \(\Delta_\mu(b) = b_1 \otimes b_2\) (Sweedler notation) and the second equality is associativity of \(\mu\).

For the right-hand side:

\[\bigl\langle \Delta_\mu(\mu(a \otimes b)),\; c \bigr\rangle = \int_A \mu\bigl(a \otimes \mu(b_1 \otimes b_2)\bigr) \cdot c.\]

Both sides equal the same expression, so the Frobenius relation holds. The key step is that \(\Delta_\mu\) is defined as the transpose of \(\mu\), and associativity of \(\mu\) — the only non-trivial axiom used — ensures the two ways of "sliding" multiplication past comultiplication agree. ◻

📄

Definition 1.12 ∀ stated (Involutive structure (\(\ast\)-structure)). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})\) be an \(R\)-linear rigid monoidal category. An involutive structure (also called a \(\ast\)-structure or dagger structure) on \(\mathbf{C}\) is a contravariant endofunctor \(\dagger \colon \mathbf{C}^{\mathrm{op}} \to \mathbf{C}\) satisfying:

  1. Identity on objects: \(X^{\dagger} = X\) for every object \(X\).

  2. Involutivity: \(f^{\dagger\dagger} = f\) for every morphism \(f\), depicted: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:involutivity-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] X \ar[r, "f"] \ar[rr, bend left=30, "f^{\dagger\dagger} = f"] & Y \ar[r, "f^{\dagger}"{description}] & X \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

  3. Monoidal compatibility: \((\mathrm{id}_X \otimes f)^{\dagger} = \mathrm{id}_X \otimes f^{\dagger}\), i.e. the following square commutes: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:monoidal-dagger-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] X \otimes Y \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f"] \ar[d, "(\mathrm{id} \otimes f)^{\dagger}"'] & X \otimes Z \ar[d, "\mathrm{id} \otimes f^{\dagger}"] \\ X \otimes Z \ar[r, equal] & X \otimes Z \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

  4. Contravariance: \((g \circ f)^{\dagger} = f^{\dagger} \circ g^{\dagger}\): \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:dagger-contravariance} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] X \ar[r, "f"] & Y \ar[r, "g"] & Z \end{tikzcd} \quad\xmapsto{\;\dagger\;}\quad \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] Z \ar[r, "g^{\dagger}"] & Y \ar[r, "f^{\dagger}"] & X \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(contravariance)} \end{equation}\]

For the Hopf algebra \(A\) in a quantum universe, the antipode \(S\) provides a natural involutive structure on the representation category via \(f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)\). In the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) example, this is the Hilbert-space adjoint (dagger on SU(2)).

📄

Proposition 1.13 ∀ stated (Frobenius dagger is positive-definite). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe with Frobenius pairing \(\langle a, b \rangle = \int_A(\mu(a \otimes b))\) and antipode \(S\). Define the Frobenius dagger on morphisms by

\[f^{\dagger} \;=\; \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -).\]

Then \(\dagger\) is a positive-definite involutive structure on \(\mathbf{C}\): for every non-zero morphism \(f \colon \mathbf{1} \to X\), the composite \(f^{\dagger} \circ f\) is a positive element of \(\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R\).

Proof that the Frobenius dagger is positive-definite.

Involutivity. The antipode of a Hopf algebra satisfies \(S^2 = \mathrm{id}\) (since the Frobenius pairing forces \(A\) to be commutative via faithfulness of \(\tau\)). Therefore \(f^{\dagger\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(S(f)) \otimes -) = \int_A \circ \mu(f \otimes -) = f\), confirming \(\dagger\) is an involution.

Contravariance. For composable morphisms \(f, g\): \((g \circ f)^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(g \circ f) \otimes -) = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \cdot S(g) \otimes -)\) since \(S\) is an anti-homomorphism. The Frobenius associativity then gives \(f^{\dagger} \circ g^{\dagger}\).

Positive-definiteness. Let \(f \colon \mathbf{1} \to X\) be non-zero. The composite \(f^{\dagger} \circ f \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong R\) evaluates as

\[f^{\dagger} \circ f \;=\; \int_A \mu(S(f) \otimes f) \;=\; \int_A |f|^2\]

where \(|f|^2 = S(f) \cdot f = \overline{f} \cdot f\) under the identification \(S = \overline{(\cdot)}\) on functions. Since \(\int_A\) is the categorical integral (non-degenerate by the Frobenius axiom) and \(|f|^2 \neq 0\) for \(f \neq 0\) (faithfulness of \(\tau\)), the result is a positive element of \(R\). ◻

Structures on a Quantum Universe

📄

Definition 1.14 ∀ stated (Categorical connection and curvature). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe over \(R\) with differential forms \(\Omega^k(A)\) (higher forms).

A connection on \(A\) is a morphism \(\nabla \colon A \to A \otimes \Omega^1(A)\) in \(\mathbf{C}\) satisfying the Leibniz rule: \(\nabla(\mu(a \otimes b)) = \nabla(a) \cdot b + a \cdot \nabla(b)\), expressed by the commutativity of the Leibniz triangle:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:leibniz-triangle} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mu"] \ar[dr, "{\nabla \otimes 1 \,+\, 1 \otimes \nabla}"'] & A \ar[d, "\nabla"] \\ & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

The curvature of \(\nabla\) is the composition

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:curvature-composition} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\nabla"] & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\nabla"] & A \otimes \Omega^2(A) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

denoted \(F_\nabla = \nabla^2\), which is \(A\)-linear (a standard consequence of the Leibniz rule).

📄

Definition 1.15 ∀ stated (Categorical jet object). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum universe) with connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection). The jet object is

\[J^1(A) := A \otimes_{\mathbf{C}} \Omega^1(A),\]

where \(\Omega^1(A) = \ker(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A)\) is the bimodule of K"ahler differentials. The jet object fits into the universal extension

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:jet-ses} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] 0 \ar[r] & A \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r] & J^1(A) \ar[r, "j^1"] & A \ar[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

where \(j^1 \colon J^1(A) \to A\) is the jet evaluation (the counit of the tensor–hom adjunction).

📄

Definition 1.16 ∀ stated (Categorical Hodge star). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe over \(R\) (quantum universe) with higher differential forms \(\Omega^k(A)\) (higher forms). The categorical Hodge star is the involution \(\star \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A)\) defined by

\[\alpha \wedge \star \beta = \int_A\!\bigl(\alpha^* \cdot \beta\bigr)\;\mathrm{vol},\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-hodge-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\star"] \ar[d, "\star"'] & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[d, "\star"] \\ \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[r, equal] & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad (\star^2 = \mathrm{id}) \end{equation}\]

where \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) is the Frobenius form, \(\alpha^* = S(\alpha)\) is the antipode-conjugate, and \(\mathrm{vol} \in \Omega^n(A)\) is the volume form (the unique \(G\)-invariant top form normalised by \(\int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1\)). That \(\star^2 = \mathrm{id}\) (i.e. \(\star\) is an involution) follows from the non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) and the involutivity of the antipode. More precisely: \(S^2 = \mathrm{id}\) holds on \(A\) because a commutative Hopf algebra has involutive antipode (and our Frobenius–Hopf axioms imply commutativity of \(A\) via the faithfulness of \(\tau\) into \(R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\)). The extension to \(\Omega^k(A)\) follows from the graded Leibniz rule for \(S\) on the differential graded algebra.

📄

Example 1.17 ∀ stated (Hodge star on \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing higher forms on SU(2), the Hodge star on \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) acts on the \(3D\)-calculus \(\Omega^{\bullet}(A)\) as follows. The volume form is \(\mathrm{vol} = \omega_1 \wedge \omega_2 \wedge \omega_3\) (normalised by \(\int_A(\mathrm{vol}) = 1\)). Then:

  • \(\star 1 = \mathrm{vol}\), \(\star\mathrm{vol} = 1\).

  • On \(1\)-forms: \(\star\omega_i = \tfrac{1}{2}\epsilon_{ijk}\, \omega_j \wedge \omega_k\) (each basis form maps to its complementary \(2\)-form).

  • On \(2\)-forms: \(\star(\omega_i \wedge \omega_j) = \epsilon_{ijk}\,\omega_k\) (each basis \(2\)-form maps to its complementary \(1\)-form).

The Hodge star is the categorical version of "rotating a form into its complement": it identifies \(\Omega^k(A)\) with \(\Omega^{n-k}(A)\) using the Frobenius form as the inner product. The self-dual \(2\)-forms \(\Omega^+(A)\) are the \(+1\)-eigenspace of \(\star\); in \(3\) dimensions, \(\star\) on \(\Omega^2(A)\) maps to \(\Omega^1(A)\), so the self-dual/anti-self-dual decomposition is trivial. The non-trivial decomposition arises when \(\dim H = 4\) (the archimedean case, self-dual curvature).

📄

Definition 1.18 ∀ stated (Internal Poisson object). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe with Frobenius pairing \(\int_A \circ \mu \colon A \otimes A \to \mathbf{1}\) and higher forms \(\Omega^k(A)\).

An internal Poisson object on \(A\) is a morphism

\[\pi \colon \mathbf{1} \longrightarrow \Lambda^2\bigl(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee}\bigr)\]

in \(\mathbf{C}\) (a bivector), subject to the conditions below.

Construction via pullback. The Frobenius self-duality \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\) induces an identification \(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee} \cong \Omega^1(A)\) (dualising the bimodule of Kähler differentials through the non-degenerate pairing). Composing with the exterior square gives the Poisson bivector object

\[\Pi \;:=\; \Lambda^2\bigl(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee}\bigr) \;\cong\; \Lambda^2\bigl(\Omega^1(A)\bigr) \;=\; \Omega^2(A).\]

A global section \(\pi \colon \mathbf{1} \to \Pi\) then defines a Poisson bracket on \(A\) by the composite

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:poisson-bracket-pullback} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=2.2em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "d \otimes d"] & \Omega^1(A) \otimes \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\wedge"] & \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "\langle \pi{,}\, {-} \rangle"] & A \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

where \(d\) is the universal derivation, \(\wedge\) the exterior product, and the contraction \(\langle \pi, {-} \rangle\) is the pullback of \(\pi\) through the Frobenius isomorphism. Explicitly, \(\{f, g\} := \langle \pi,\, df \wedge dg \rangle\) for \(f, g \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\).

Axioms. The morphism \(\pi\) must satisfy:

  1. Jacobi identity. The Jacobiator \(\{f, \{g, h\}\} + \{g, \{h, f\}\} + \{h, \{f, g\}\} = 0\) vanishes, equivalently the Schouten–Nijenhuis condition \([\pi, \pi]_{\mathrm{SN}} = 0\) on the bivector.

  2. Leibniz rule. \(\{f, gh\} = \{f, g\}\,h + g\,\{f, h\}\), ensuring the bracket is a biderivation with respect to the multiplication \(\mu\) on \(A\).

Anti-symmetry \(\{f, g\} = -\{g, f\}\) is automatic: since \(\pi\) factors through \(\Lambda^2(\Omega^1(A)^{\vee})\) (the exterior square, not the full tensor square), the bracket inherits the anti-symmetry of the wedge product.

The triple \((A, \mu, \pi)\) is then a Poisson algebra object in \(\mathbf{C}\).

Quantum Observable Universes

The Quantum Observable Universe

📄

Definition 2.1 ∀ stated (Quantum Observable Universe). \(\forall\)

A quantum universe \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) over \(R\) (quantum universe) is observable if the forgetful functor \(\tau\) (Example) is faithful and the following conditions hold:

  1. (non-degenerate integration) the Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) induces a non-degenerate pairing \((a, b) \mapsto \int_A ab\) (Frobenius pairing), giving an isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\);

  2. (observability) there are no hidden global symmetries: \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\), where \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is the adjoint object (\(A\) acted on by conjugation). Physically, this means every internal degree of freedom is accessible to measurement — no gauge transformation acts trivially on all observables. The formal statement is that every morphism \(\mathbf{1} \to \mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is zero: \[\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "0"] & \mathrm{Ad}(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(observability)}\]

  3. (measurability / anomaly-free) the primary Chern classes of the adjoint object vanish. Precisely, define the Chern classes of a categorical object \(X\) by pulling back through the fibre functor: \[c_i(X) \;:=\; c_i\!\bigl(\tau(X)\bigr) \;\in\; H^{2i}_{\mathrm{dR}}\!\bigl(\mathrm{Spec}\,R\bigr),\] where the right-hand side is the classical Chern class of the realised \(R\)-module (or, in the archimedean setting, of the associated vector bundle \(\tau(X) \times_G M\)). This definition is intrinsic to the pair \((\mathbf{C}, \tau)\) — the fibre functor \(\tau\) is part of the QOU datum — and reduces to the standard topological Chern classes in every geometric realisation. The measurability axiom requires: \[c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.\] The first condition ensures the adjoint bundle is orientable, precluding global anomalies; the second ensures the volume form acquires no topological phases (see Remark for the connection to categorical flatness via Yekutieli’s nonabelian Stokes theorem). For many applications, axioms (1), (2), and (3) suffice — axiom (3) is needed only when global topology of \(M\) matters.

  4. (categorical volume constraint) let \(V\) denote the fundamental object of \(\mathbf{C}\) (Remark); there exists a non-degenerate epimorphism \(\epsilon\) preserved by the rigid dualities, making the following diagram commute for every \(g \in \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\): \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-volume-constraint} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Lambda^2 V \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"] \ar[d, "\epsilon"', two heads] & \Lambda^2 V \ar[d, "\epsilon", two heads] \\ \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"'] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(volume constraint)} \end{equation}\]

The braiding \(c_{V,V}\) on \(\mathbf{C}\) (which is non-symmetric: \(c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\), since \(\mathbf{C}\) is braided monoidal but not symmetric monoidal) induces a canonical admissible well-ordering on the Hecke basis. See braiding-induced ordering.

📄

Proposition 2.2 ∀ stated (The braiding induces a canonical admissible well-ordering on the Hecke basis). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe (QOU) whose braiding \(c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V\) is non-symmetric (\(c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\)). Then \(c_{V,V}\) determines a canonical admissible well-ordering \(\prec_c\) on the monomial basis \(B\) of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\) of \(A\).

Construction. The monomial basis \(B\) of \(H_n(q)\) consists of reduced positive braid monomials \(w = \sigma_{i_1}\sigma_{i_2}\cdots\sigma_{i_k}\) — the images of the braiding \(c_{V,V}\) under \(\rho_n(\sigma_i) = \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(i-1)} \otimes c_{V,V} \otimes \mathrm{id}^{\otimes(n-i-1)}\) (braid action on tensor powers). The braiding \(c_{V,V}\) (as opposed to its inverse \(c_{V,V}^{-1}\)) defines "positive crossing" — forward time.

Definition. A well-ordering on a set \(S\) is a total order \(\prec\) such that every non-empty subset of \(S\) has a least element. Equivalently: there are no infinite strictly descending chains \(s_1 \succ s_2 \succ s_3 \succ \cdots\).

Definition. The degree-lexicographic ordering \(\prec_c\) on \(B\) is: \(w \prec_c w'\) if and only if

\[\ell(w) < \ell(w'), \quad\text{or}\quad \ell(w) = \ell(w') \;\text{and}\; (i_1, \ldots, i_k) <_{\mathrm{lex}} (i_1', \ldots, i_k')\]

where \(\ell(w) = k\) is the word length (number of crossings) and \(<_{\mathrm{lex}}\) is lexicographic order on the generator indices \(i_j \in \{1, \ldots, n-1\}\).

Proof that \(\prec_c\) is a well-ordering on \(B\). Let \(S \subseteq B\) be non-empty.

(a) Degree is bounded below. Every \(w \in B\) has \(\ell(w) \geq 0\). Let \(d = \min\{\ell(w) : w \in S\}\). The set \(S_d = \{w \in S : \ell(w) = d\}\) is non-empty.

(b) Finite alphabet at each degree. Each \(w \in S_d\) is a word of length \(d\) over the finite alphabet \(\{1, \ldots, n-1\}\). There are at most \((n-1)^d\) such words — a finite set. Every finite totally ordered set has a minimum. Let \(w_0\) be the lex-minimum of \(S_d\).

(c) \(w_0\) is the minimum of \(S\). For any \(w \in S\): if \(\ell(w) > d\) then \(w_0 \prec_c w\) (shorter words first); if \(\ell(w) = d\) then \(w_0 \leq_{\mathrm{lex}} w\) by construction. \(\square\)

Admissibility. The ordering \(\prec_c\) is admissible in the sense of (admissible system): left and right multiplication by basis elements preserves the ordering (\(w \prec_c w'\) implies \(u \cdot w \cdot v \prec_c u \cdot w' \cdot v\) whenever both products are non-zero), because degree-lex is compatible with any associative multiplication whose defining relations (Hecke, Yang–Baxter) have leading terms of bounded degree — the Hecke relation is quadratic.

Two faces of the arrow of time. The braiding \(c_{V,V}\) and the Reeb vector field \(\xi\) (categorical Reeb) express the same arrow of time from two complementary viewpoints:

  • Categorical arrow (\(c_{V,V}\)): which strand crosses over. A positive crossing \(\sigma_i\) applies \(c_{V,V}\); a negative crossing \(\sigma_i^{-1}\) applies \(\bar{c}_{V,V} := c_{V,V}^{-1}\). The ordering \(\prec_c\) is the algebraic encoding: forward time = Gröbner–Shirshov reduction under \(\prec_c\).

  • Geometric arrow (\(\xi\)): which direction the Reeb flow runs. The one-parameter subgroup \(\phi_t^q\) generated by \(\xi\) is the flow of forward time on the state bundle \(\mathcal{S}\). At each Planck step, one application of \(c_{V,V}\) advances \(\phi_t^q\) by one tick.

Crossing reversal = time reversal. The crossing reversal involution \(\sigma \colon K \mapsto K^{\sigma}\) (mirror all crossings) corresponds to switching the braiding: \(c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V}\). This flips the ordering \(\prec_c\) and reverses the Reeb flow \(\xi \mapsto -\xi\). In the Feynman–Stueckelberg interpretation, an antiparticle (\(K^{\sigma}\)) is its particle (\(K\)) with time reversed — precisely the opposite braiding. CPT symmetry is the statement that the QOU axioms are invariant under simultaneous \(c_{V,V} \leftrightarrow \bar{c}_{V,V}\) (T), \(K \mapsto K^{\sigma}\) (C), and \(\sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_{n-i}\) (P, strand reflection).

The Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) extends to a pairing on products:

\[\int_A ab \;:=\; \int_A \!\circ\; \mu(a \otimes b).\]

The non-degeneracy condition (i) of quantum observable universe then reads: the pairing \((a, b) \mapsto \int_A ab\) induces an isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\).

Readers familiar with TQFT will recognise \(\int_A\) as a categorical Haar measure: the unique (up to scalar) \(G\)-invariant functional on \(A\). The existence of the volume \(\epsilon\) (categorical volume constraint) may then be read as the normalisation condition \(\int_A \mathbf{1}\) is a well-defined topological constant.

📄

Remark 2.3 ✗ no Lean (Nonabelian Stokes and the measurability conditions).

The measurability condition \(c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\), \(c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) can be understood through the lens of Yekutieli’s nonabelian Stokes theorem . The core of that theorem is: for a nonabelian integral to be well-defined over a surface or volume, the curvature of the connection must vanish (or be highly constrained).

In the QOU setting, the vanishing of \(c_1(\mathrm{Ad}(A))\) imposes a categorical flatness on the adjoint representation — the condition required for the parallel transport around a boundary to be path-independent. The existence of the volume \(\epsilon\) (categorical volume constraint) can therefore be viewed as a categorical realisation of the nonabelian Stokes theorem: the flatness conditions guarantee the global coherence of the volume form.

The additional condition \(c_2(\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) ensures that \(\epsilon\) is canonically unique and does not acquire topological phases under transport around non-contractible cycles. Together, the two vanishing conditions make \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) anomaly-free: the adjoint bundle carries no hidden topological obstructions to integration.

📄

Example 2.4 ∀ stated (\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) is observable). \(\forall\)

Continuing Examples and quantum universe on SU(2), write \(V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\):

  1. Non-degeneracy. The Haar integral \(\int_A = \int_G\) on \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) is faithful: if \(\int_A(f^* f) = 0\) then \(f = 0\).

  2. Observability. The adjoint representation \(\mathrm{Ad} \cong V_1\) (spin-\(1\), dimension \(3\)) is irreducible, so it contains no copy of the trivial representation: \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, V_1) = 0\).

  3. Volume constraint. For \(v, w \in V = \mathbb{C}^2\), the determinant \(\epsilon(v \wedge w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1\) defines a non-degenerate map \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbb{C}\).

Emergence from observability

📄

Example 2.5 ∀ stated (Frobenius relation for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing QOU on SU(2), set \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with multiplication \(\mu(f \otimes g) = fg\) (pointwise product) and Frobenius form \(\int_A = \int_G\) (Haar integral). The dual comultiplication is \(\Delta_\mu(f)(g,h) = \int_G f(xg)\,\overline{h(x)}\,dx\), and the Frobenius relation expresses the associativity of convolution: \(\int_G f(xy)\,g(y)\,dy\) can be evaluated by convolving first with \(f\) or first with \(g\).

📄

Example 2.6 ∀ stated (Involutive structure on \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing Frobenius SU(2), the category \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) carries a canonical involutive structure built from the antipode:

  • What it does. For a morphism \(f \colon V_j \to V_k\) (an equivariant linear map between representations), \(f^{\dagger}\) is the Hilbert-space adjoint: the unique map \(f^{\dagger} \colon V_k \to V_j\) satisfying \(\langle f^{\dagger}(w),\, v \rangle_j = \langle w,\, f(v) \rangle_k\) for all \(v \in V_j\), \(w \in V_k\).

  • Why it exists. Each irreducible representation \(V_j\) carries a unique (up to scalar) \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-invariant inner product. The adjoint \(f^{\dagger}\) with respect to these inner products is automatically equivariant, so \(f^{\dagger}\) is again a morphism in \(\mathbf{C}\).

  • On the algebra. On \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), \(f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)\), where \(S(f)(g) = f(g^{-1})\) is the antipode. The involution \(f \mapsto f^{\dagger}\) is complex conjugation composed with pullback by inversion: \(f^{\dagger}(g) = \overline{f(g^{-1})}\).

  • Positive-definiteness. For a non-zero state \(f \colon \mathbb{C} \to V_j\), the composite \(f^{\dagger} \circ f = \lVert f(1) \rVert^2 > 0\). This is the statement that the inner product on each \(V_j\) is positive-definite — the categorical encoding of unitarity.

📄

Lemma 2.7 ∀ stated (Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, \otimes, \mathbf{1})\) be an \(R\)-linear rigid monoidal category, and let \(V\) be a simple object that is symplectically self-dual: there exists an isomorphism \(\phi \colon V \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} V^{\vee}\) satisfying \(\phi^{\vee} = -\phi\) (alternating). The alternating condition forces \(\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2\): the composite \(\mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi)\) factors through \(\Lambda^2 V\), and for the resulting morphism \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\) to be a non-degenerate epimorphism one needs \(\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = 1\), i.e., \(\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2\). The factorisation is (the volume form factorisation):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:volume-form-factorisation} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] V \otimes V \ar[r, "\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi"] \ar[d, "\pi"', two heads] & V \otimes V^{\vee} \ar[d, "\mathrm{ev}_V"] \\ \Lambda^2 V \ar[r, "\epsilon"', dashed] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

and \(\epsilon\) is non-degenerate; that is, condition (iii) of quantum observable universe holds.

Proof of Volume form from rigidity and symplectic self-duality.

Because \(\phi\) is alternating, the pairing \(B = \mathrm{ev}_V \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \phi)\) satisfies \(B \circ \tau_{V,V} = -B\), where \(\tau_{V,V}\) is the symmetry (or braiding) isomorphism. Hence \(B\) vanishes on symmetric tensors and factors as \(B = \epsilon \circ \pi\), where \(\pi \colon V \otimes V \twoheadrightarrow \Lambda^2 V\) is the canonical projection. Non-degeneracy of \(\epsilon\) follows from non-degeneracy of \(\mathrm{ev}_V\) (guaranteed by rigidity) and the isomorphism \(\phi\). The duality axioms \((\mathrm{ev}_V \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{coev}_V) = \mathrm{id}_V\) ensure that \(\epsilon\) is preserved by the rigid dualities of \(\mathbf{C}\). ◻

📄

Example 2.8 ✗ no Lean (\(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) volume form from the lemma).

Continuing QOU on SU(2), take \(V = V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\). The symplectic form is \(\phi = \begin{smallmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -1 & 0 \end{smallmatrix}\), identifying \(V \cong V^{\vee}\) with \(\phi^{\vee} = -\phi\) (alternating). volume from rigidity then gives:

  • The evaluation pairing becomes \(B(v, w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1\) (the determinant).

  • \(B\) is alternating, so it factors through \(\Lambda^2 V\): the map \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbb{C}\) is \(\epsilon(v \wedge w) = \det(v, w)\).

  • Non-degeneracy: \(\epsilon\) is an isomorphism \(\Lambda^2 \mathbb{C}^2 \cong \mathbb{C}\).

  • For \(g \in G\), \(\Lambda^2 g = \det(g) \cdot \mathrm{id}\), so \(\epsilon\)-preservation forces \(\det(g) = 1\): this is why the gauge group is \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) rather than \(\mathrm{GL}(2, \mathbb{C})\) or \(\mathrm{U}(2)\).

📄

Theorem 2.9 ∀ stated (Emergence of the gauge group). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe). Then \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\) (or \(\mathrm{SL}(2, R)\) depending on the signature of the Frobenius pairing).

Proof of Emergence of the gauge group.

The gauge group \(G\) is defined via Tannaka–Krein duality as the group scheme of tensor-preserving natural automorphisms of the fibre functor \(\tau\). An element \(g \in G\) assigns an invertible linear map \(g_X \colon \tau(X) \to \tau(X)\) to every object \(X \in \mathbf{C}\).

Because \(g\) is a natural transformation, it commutes with all morphisms in \(\mathbf{C}\), including the volume constraint \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\) volume constraint. Applying \(\tau\) yields the commutative diagram of \(R\)-modules

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:su2-emergence-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em] \Lambda^2 \tau(V) \ar[r, "\Lambda^2 g_V"] \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"'] & \Lambda^2 \tau(V) \ar[d, "\tau(\epsilon)"] \\ \tau(\mathbf{1}) \ar[r, "g_{\mathbf{1}} = \mathrm{id}"'] & \tau(\mathbf{1}) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

The volume constraint requires a non-degenerate epimorphism \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\), which forces \(\mathrm{rank}(V) = 2\): the epimorphism is non-degenerate only when \(\Lambda^2 V\) has rank \(1\), and \(\mathrm{rank}(\Lambda^2 V) = \binom{r}{2}\) equals \(1\) precisely for \(r = 2\) (see Remark). Thus \(\tau(V)\) is a rank-\(2\) free \(R\)-module and \(\Lambda^2 \tau(V)\) has rank \(1\). The induced operator \(\Lambda^2 g_V\) acts on this rank-\(1\) module as scalar multiplication by \(\det(g_V)\). Following diagram above from the top-left to the bottom-right:

\[\tau(\epsilon) \circ \Lambda^2 g_V = g_{\mathbf{1}} \circ \tau(\epsilon) = \tau(\epsilon).\]

Since \(\tau(\epsilon)\) is non-degenerate (hence non-zero), this forces

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:det-one} \det(g_V) \;=\; 1, \end{equation}\]

restricting the natural automorphisms from \(\mathrm{GL}(2)\) to the special subgroup \(\mathrm{SL}(2)\).

The QOU non-degeneracy axiom ensures the Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) is non-degenerate, inducing the Frobenius self-duality \(A \cong A^{\vee}\) (fibre adjoint involution). Define a dagger on morphisms by \(f^{\dagger} = \int_A \circ \mu(S(f) \otimes -)\), where \(S\) is the antipode. Non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) and faithfulness of \(\tau\) imply \(f^{\dagger} \circ f = 0 \Rightarrow f = 0\), so this is a positive-definite dagger structure (positive definite dagger). Every tensor automorphism \(g \in G\) preserves the dagger (it commutes with \(S\) and \(\int_A\)), forcing \(g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}\) and restricting \(G\) to the unitary subgroup \(\mathrm{U}(2)\).

Combining both constraints:

\[G \;=\; \mathrm{SL}(2) \;\cap\; \mathrm{U}(2) \;=\; \mathrm{SU}(2).\]

The volume constraint provides the special-linear condition (\(\det = 1\)), while the positive-definite dagger structure provides the compactness (unitarity), locking the gauge group exclusively to \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\). ◻

📄

Example 2.10 ∀ stated (Emergence of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\): the full chain). \(\forall\)

Continuing Examples–Example, let \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), \(\tau\) the forgetful functor.

  1. Volume constraint \(\Rightarrow\) \(\det(g_V) = 1\). The alternating form \(\epsilon(v \wedge w) = v_1 w_2 - v_2 w_1\) on \(V = \mathbb{C}^2\) is \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-invariant. Any tensor automorphism \(g\) preserves \(\epsilon\), forcing \(g_V \in \mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C})\).

  2. Dagger structure \(\Rightarrow\) unitarity. The dagger on \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) (dagger on SU(2)) forces \(g_V^{-1} = g_V^{\dagger}\), cutting from \(\mathrm{SL}(2, \mathbb{C})\) to its compact real form \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\).

  3. Conclusion. \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\), recovering the input gauge group from the categorical axioms alone.

📄

Remark 2.11 ✗ no Lean (The spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) representation \(V_{1/2}\)).

After SU(2) emergence identifies \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\), the abstract fundamental object \(V\) acquires its concrete incarnation as the spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) representation:

\[V_{1/2} \;=\; \tau(V) \;\cong\; \mathbb{C}^2,\]

the defining two-dimensional representation of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\).

The spin label indexing \(j \in \{0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \tfrac{3}{2}, \ldots\}\) identifies each simple object \(V_j\) with the unique irreducible representation of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) of dimension \(2j+1\). In particular:

  • \(V_0 = \mathbf{1}\) (the trivial representation),

  • \(V_{1/2} = V \cong \mathbb{C}^2\) (the fundamental representation),

  • \(V_1 = \mathrm{Ad}(A) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbb{R}^3\) (the adjoint representation).

The standard basis \(\{e_+, e_-\}\) of \(V_{1/2}\) consists of weight vectors for the maximal torus \(T \subset \mathrm{SU}(2)\):

\[T \cdot e_{\pm} \;=\; e^{\pm i\theta}\, e_{\pm}, \qquad T = \left\{\! \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{pmatrix} \right\}.\]

The Clebsch–Gordan decomposition

\[V_{1/2} \otimes V_{1/2} \;\cong\; V_0 \;\oplus\; V_1\]

decomposes the tensor square into the singlet (antisymmetric, \(\Lambda^2 V_{1/2}\)) and the triplet (symmetric, \(\mathrm{Sym}^2 V_{1/2}\)). This is the simplest instance of tensor generation: all \(V_j\) arise as summands of \(V_{1/2}^{\otimes 2j}\).

Maximal torus and weight decomposition

📄

Definition 2.12 ∀ stated (Maximal torus and weight subcategory). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with fundamental object \(V\) (the unique simple object of categorical dimension \(2\); see spin labels for the full labelling). The weight subcategory \(\langle V \rangle \subset \mathbf{C}\) is the full subcategory whose objects are direct sums of weight spaces of \(V\) (i.e. simultaneous eigenspaces of the Cartan subalgebra action). The maximal torus of the gauge group is

\[T = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau|_{\langle V \rangle}),\]

the sub-group scheme of \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) (SU(2) emergence) consisting of those natural automorphisms that act diagonally on each weight space of \(V\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:maximal-torus-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] T \ar[r, hook] \ar[d, "\mathrm{diag}"'] & G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \ar[d] \\ \mathrm{Aut}(\tau(V)) & \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \ar[l] \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(maximal torus)} \end{equation}\]

Equivalently, \(T\) is the largest subgroup of \(G\) for which every object in \(\langle V \rangle\) decomposes into one-dimensional \(T\)-eigenspaces.

📄

Example 2.13 ∀ stated (Maximal torus for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing spin labels on SU(2), the fundamental object is \(V = \mathbb{C}^2\) with the standard \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-action. The weight decomposition is \(V = \mathbb{C} e_+ \oplus \mathbb{C} e_-\) (the \(\pm\tfrac{1}{2}\)-eigenspaces of \(e_3 = \frac{1}{2}\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix}\)). The weight subcategory \(\langle V \rangle\) consists of representations that decompose into weight spaces: \(V\) itself, \(\mathbf{1}\), and their direct sums. The maximal torus is

\[T = \mathrm{U}(1) = \left\{ \begin{pmatrix} e^{i\theta} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-i\theta} \end{pmatrix} : \theta \in \mathbb{R} \right\},\]

the diagonal matrices in \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\). Each element of \(T\) acts on \(e_{\pm}\) by \(e^{\pm i\theta}\): one-dimensional eigenspaces, as required.

📄

Definition 2.14 ∀ stated (Weight decomposition). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with maximal torus \(T\) (maximal torus) and higher differential forms \(\Omega^k(A)\) (higher forms). The \(T\)-action on \(\Omega^k(A)\) induces a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-grading by weights. Denoting by \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) the projections onto the weight-\(0\) and non-zero-weight summands, every \(\alpha \in \Omega^k(A)\) decomposes uniquely:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:weight-decomposition-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2em, column sep=3em] & \Omega^k(A) \ar[dl, "\pi_H"'] \ar[dr, "\pi_V"] & \\ \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[rr, hook, "\oplus"'] & & \Omega^k_V(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad \alpha = \alpha_H + \alpha_V. \end{equation}\]

Here \(\alpha_H = \pi_H(\alpha)\) is the horizontal component (weight-\(0\) under \(T\)) and \(\alpha_V = \pi_V(\alpha)\) is the vertical component (non-zero weight). A form is purely horizontal if and only if \(\alpha_V = 0\).

📄

Theorem 2.15 ∀ stated (Existence of the weight decomposition). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with maximal torus \(T\) acting on higher forms \(\Omega^k(A)\). Then there exists a weight decomposition \((\pi_H, \pi_V)\) of \(\Omega^k(A)\) satisfying:

  1. Complementarity: \(\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}\).

  2. Idempotency: \(\pi_H^2 = \pi_H\) and \(\pi_V^2 = \pi_V\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:weight-decomposition-exists-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\pi_H"] \ar[d, "\pi_V"'] & \Omega^k_H(A) \\ \Omega^k_V(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad (\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id},\; \pi_H \pi_V = 0) \end{equation}\]

Proof of existence of the weight decomposition.

The projections are constructed from the torus averaging operator: for each weight \(\lambda\) of the \(T\)-action, the \(\lambda\)-isotypic projector \(e_\lambda\) is idempotent, and \(\pi_H = e_0\), \(\pi_V = \mathrm{id} - e_0\). ◻

Vectors, hadrons, and the PawLei basis

📄

Remark 2.16 ✗ no Lean (Adjoint trace and the categorical inner product).

The Frobenius pairing and the fibre-adjoint involution together equip every hom-space \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(X, Y)\) with a canonical sesquilinear form. Define the adjoint trace on endomorphisms of \(V\) by

\[\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f) \;=\; \int_A \!\circ\; \mu \circ (f \otimes \mathrm{id}_{V^{\vee}}) \circ \mathrm{coev}_V \;\in\; \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathbf{1}) \cong R,\]

where \(\mathrm{coev}_V \colon \mathbf{1} \to V \otimes V^{\vee}\) is the coevaluation (from rigidity) and \(\mu\) is the Frobenius multiplication on \(A\).

This trace has two key properties:

  1. Cyclicity: \(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f \circ g) = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(g \circ f)\), inherited from the Frobenius relation.

  2. Non-degeneracy: the induced pairing \(\langle f, g \rangle_{\mathrm{Ad}} = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f^{\dagger} \circ g)\) is non-degenerate, because \(\int_A\) is non-degenerate and the dagger is positive-definite.

In the archimedean realisation with \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\), the adjoint trace recovers the Killing form on \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\):

\[\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}(f) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{ad}(f)) \;=\; -2\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathbb{C}^2}(f).\]

📄

Proposition 2.17 ∀ stated (Pawlowski–Leitner basis for \(\mathrm{Hom}(V_j, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n})\)). \(\forall\)

Let \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\) be the emergent gauge group (SU(2) emergence) and let \(V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\) be the spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) representation. For each simple object \(V_j\) and tensor power \(V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\) with \(n \geq 2j\), the intertwiner space

\[\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j,\; V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr)\]

admits a canonical basis — the PawLei basis — indexed by standard Young tableaux of shape \(\lambda \vdash n\) with at most \(2\) rows and with \(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 = 2j\).

The construction rests on the PBW theorem over commutative rings: the unital Gröbner–Shirshov basis for \(U(\mathfrak{su}(2))\) provides a monomial basis for the enveloping algebra, from which the intertwiner basis is derived by contraction with the volume form.

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:pawlei-basis-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\epsilon^{\vee}"] & \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \ar[r, hook] & V_{1/2}^{\otimes n} \ar[r, "\pi_j"] & V_j \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(PawLei contraction)} \end{equation}\]

Concretely, the volume form \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V_{1/2} \to \mathbf{1}\) and its dual \(\epsilon^{\vee} \colon \mathbf{1} \to \Lambda^2 V_{1/2}\) generate contraction operators on tensor powers. The PawLei basis elements are obtained by applying a specific sequence of pairwise contractions (determined by the tableau) to the highest-weight vector \(e_+^{\otimes (j+m)} \otimes e_-^{\otimes (j-m)}\), then symmetrising according to the row structure of the tableau.

The dimension of the intertwiner space is given by the hook-length formula:

\[\dim\,\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}\!\bigl(V_j,\; V_{1/2}^{\otimes n}\bigr) \;=\; \frac{(2j+1)\, n!}{(\tfrac{n}{2}+j+1)!\;(\tfrac{n}{2}-j)!}\]

when \(n \equiv 2j \pmod{2}\), and zero otherwise.

The PBW basis underlying this construction is established via unital Gröbner–Shirshov bases in .

📄

Proposition 2.18 ∀ stated (Inner product on intertwiner spaces). \(\forall\)

The adjoint trace induces a canonical inner product on intertwiner spaces. For \(\phi, \psi \in \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathrm{SU}(2)}(V_j,\, V_{1/2}^{\otimes n})\), define

\[\langle \phi, \psi \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}} \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}}\!\bigl(\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi\bigr) \;=\; \int_A \!\circ\; \mu \circ (\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \mathrm{coev}_{V_j}.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:pawlei-inner-product-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev}_{V_j}"] & V_j \otimes V_j^{\vee} \ar[r, "\phi^{\dagger} \circ \psi \,\otimes\, \mathrm{id}"] & A \otimes V_j^{\vee} \ar[r, "\int_A \circ \mu"] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(PawLei inner product)} \end{equation}\]

The PawLei basis \(\{T_{\lambda}\}\) is orthogonal with respect to this pairing:

\[\langle T_{\lambda}, T_{\mu} \rangle_{\mathrm{PL}} \;=\; \delta_{\lambda\mu}\; \|T_{\lambda}\|^2,\]

where the norm-squared \(\|T_{\lambda}\|^2\) is a positive rational number computable from the hook lengths of the tableau \(\lambda\).

This orthogonality has two consequences for the QOU framework:

  1. Decomposition of hadron states. A categorical hadron of valence \(n\) can be uniquely expanded in the PawLei basis, with coefficients that are physically interpretable as partial-wave amplitudes.

  2. Compatibility with the Frobenius form. The inner product \(\langle{-},{-}\rangle_{\mathrm{PL}}\) agrees with the restriction of the Frobenius pairing to \(\mathrm{End}(V_j) \subset A\), ensuring that integration over the fibre and decomposition into basis elements commute.

The algebraic foundations (PBW bases over commutative rings) are established in ; norm formulas follow from the Temperley–Lieb calculus and \(6j\)-symbols.

Differential structures and gauge actions

📄

Proposition 2.19 ∀ stated (Spin labels and the fundamental object). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe). Because \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\) (SU(2) emergence), the simple objects of \(\mathbf{C}\) are indexed by a spin label \(j \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \ldots\}\), with \(V_j\) denoting the simple object of categorical dimension \(2j + 1\). The fundamental object is \(V = V_{1/2}\), the unique simple object of categorical dimension \(2\). The adjoint object is \(V_1 \cong \mathrm{Ad}(A)\), of dimension \(3\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:spin-labels-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2em] V_0 = \mathbf{1} & V_{1/2} = V & V_1 = \mathrm{Ad}(A) & V_{3/2} & \cdots \end{tikzcd} \qquad (\dim V_j = 2j+1) \end{equation}\]

Proof of spin labels.

Because \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\) (SU(2) emergence), the simple objects of \(\mathbf{C}\) are indexed by a spin label \(j \in \{0, \tfrac12, 1, \tfrac32, \ldots\}\), with \(V_j\) denoting the simple object of categorical dimension \(2j + 1\).

The symplectic form \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\) (quantum observable universe, axiom (iii)) is the unique (up to scalar) \(G\)-invariant alternating pairing on \(V\). ◻

📄

Example 2.20 ∀ stated (Spin decomposition of \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing QOU on SU(2), the simple objects of \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) are the irreducible representations \(V_j \cong \mathbb{C}^{2j+1}\):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:spin-decomposition} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=1.5em, column sep=1.5em] V_0 \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & V_{1/2} \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & V_1 \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & V_{3/2} \ar[d, phantom, "\cong"] & \cdots \\ \mathbb{C} & \mathbb{C}^2 & \mathbb{C}^3 & \mathbb{C}^4 & \cdots \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

In concrete terms:

  • \(V_0 = \mathbb{C}\) (the trivial representation: \(g \cdot z = z\)).

  • \(V_{1/2} = \mathbb{C}^2\) (the defining representation: \(g \cdot v = gv\) by matrix multiplication). This is the fundamental object \(V\).

  • \(V_1 = \mathfrak{su}(2)_{\mathbb{C}} \cong \mathbb{C}^3\) (the adjoint representation: \(g \cdot X = gXg^{-1}\)). This is \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\).

  • \(V_{3/2} = \mathrm{Sym}^3(\mathbb{C}^2) \cong \mathbb{C}^4\) (homogeneous cubics in two variables).

Every finite-dimensional representation decomposes as \(W \cong \bigoplus_j V_j^{\oplus m_j}\), with multiplicities \(m_j \in \mathbb{N}\). The polynomial ring \(\mathbb{C}[z] = \bigoplus_{n \geq 0} \mathrm{Sym}^n V\) is the coordinate ring of \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) = \mathbb{P}(V)\) (projective line object), and each homogeneous component \(\mathrm{Sym}^n V \cong V_{n/2}\) is an irreducible representation of dimension \(n + 1\).

📄

Definition 2.21 ∀ stated (Categorical Reeb derivation). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with maximal torus \(T\) (maximal torus) and weight decomposition \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) (weight decomposition). The categorical Reeb derivation is the endomorphism \(\xi \colon A \to A\) that generates the \(T\)-action: \(\xi\) is the infinitesimal generator of the one-parameter subgroup \(T \cong \mathrm{U}(1) \subset G\), acting on the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\) via the adjoint coaction. It satisfies:

  1. Vertical generator: \(\pi_V \circ d = \iota_\xi\, d\theta_A\), where \(\iota_\xi\) denotes the interior product (contraction with \(\xi\)) and \(\theta_A \in \Omega^1(A)\) is the canonical \(1\)-form dual to \(\xi\).

  2. Normalisation: \(\theta_A(\xi) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}\).

  3. Kernel: \(\Omega^k_H(A) = \ker(\iota_\xi)\) (horizontal forms are precisely those annihilated by contraction with \(\xi\)).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:reeb-decomposition-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\pi_H"] \ar[d, "\pi_V"'] & \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[d, hook] \\ \theta_A \wedge \Omega^{k-1}_H(A) \ar[r, hook] & \Omega^k(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad (\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}) \end{equation}\]

📄

Theorem 2.22 ∀ stated (Existence of the categorical Reeb derivation). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with maximal torus \(T\) and weight decomposition \((\pi_H, \pi_V)\). Then there exists a categorical Reeb derivation \((\xi, \theta_A)\) on \(A\) satisfying:

  1. Vertical generator: \(\pi_V \circ d = \iota_\xi\, d\theta_A\).

  2. Normalisation: \(\xi \mathbin{;} \theta_A = \theta_A\) (categorically: \(\theta_A(\xi) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}\)).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:reeb-exists-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\xi"] \ar[d, "d"'] & A \ar[d, "\theta_A"] \\ \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\iota_\xi"'] & A \end{tikzcd} \qquad (\theta_A(\xi) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}) \end{equation}\]

Proof of existence of the categorical Reeb derivation.

The derivation \(\xi\) is the infinitesimal generator of the one-parameter subgroup \(T \cong \mathrm{U}(1) \subset G\), and \(\theta_A\) is its Maurer–Cartan dual, uniquely determined by the normalisation condition. ◻

📄

Example 2.23 ∀ stated (Reeb derivation for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing maximal torus of SU(2), the maximal torus is \(T = \mathrm{U}(1)\) with generator \(\xi = e_3 = \frac{1}{2}\begin{smallmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & -1 \end{smallmatrix} \in \mathfrak{su}(2)\). On \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), \(\xi\) acts by \((\xi \cdot f)(g) = \frac{d}{dt}\big|_{t=0} f(e^{-t\xi} g)\) (left-invariant vector field). The canonical \(1\)-form is \(\theta_A = \omega_3\) (the left-invariant \(1\)-form dual to \(e_3\)), and:

  • \(\omega_3(\xi) = 1\) (normalisation).

  • \(\Omega^k_H(A) = \{\alpha : \iota_\xi\,\alpha = 0\}\) (forms with no \(\omega_3\) component).

  • In the archimedean realisation on a CR manifold \((M, \theta)\), \(\xi\) becomes the Reeb vector field with \(\iota_\xi\,d\theta = 0\) and \(\theta(\xi) = 1\) (Reeb decomposition).

📄

Definition 2.24 ∀ stated (Projective line object). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with maximal torus \(T \subset G\) (maximal torus). The projective line object is the quotient

\[\mathbb{P}(V) = G / T,\]

regarded as an object of \(\mathrm{Ind}(\mathbf{C})\) via its function algebra \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}(V)) = A^{\mathrm{co}\,T}\) (the \(T\)-coinvariant subalgebra of \(A\)).

Under the fibre functor \(\tau\), the categorical projective line realises as the scheme-theoretic projective line over \(R\):

\[\tau\bigl(\mathbb{P}(V)\bigr) \;=\; \mathbb{P}^1(R)\]

(scheme notation). The notation \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) is used when the categorical construction matters (built from the fundamental object \(V\)); the notation \(\mathbb{P}^1(R)\) is used in scheme-theoretic or coordinate contexts (contact affine chart).

📄

Example 2.25 ∀ stated (Projective line for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing maximal torus of SU(2), \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\) and \(T = \mathrm{U}(1)\). The quotient is \(\mathbb{P}(V) = \mathrm{SU}(2)/\mathrm{U}(1) \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). A point \([\ell] \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) is a line \(\ell \subset V = \mathbb{C}^2\); equivalently, it is the kernel of a linear form on \(V\), well-defined up to scalar. The function algebra is the polynomial ring \(\mathcal{O}(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})) = \mathbb{C}[z]\) in the affine coordinate \(z = v_1 / v_2\).

📄

Definition 2.26 ∀ stated (Contact affine chart on \(\mathbb{P}(V)\)). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be the state bundle over \(M\) whose fibres are the spaces of \(1\)-forms, and let \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) be the projective line object (projective line object). Using the Reeb decomposition (Reeb decomposition), every form splits as \(\alpha = \alpha_H + \theta \wedge \iota_\xi \alpha\).

The contact affine chart \(U_\xi \subset \mathbb{P}(V)\) is the open dense subset of states with non-vanishing Reeb component:

\[U_\xi \;=\; \bigl\{\, [\alpha] \in \mathbb{P}(V) \;\big|\; \iota_\xi\,\alpha \neq 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

On \(U_\xi\), the explicit affine coordinate is defined by the ratio of horizontal spatial diffusion to vertical quantum spin:

\[Z([\alpha]) \;=\; \frac{\alpha_H}{\iota_\xi\,\alpha}.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:contact-affine-chart-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] U_\xi \ar[r, hook] \ar[d, "Z"'] & \mathbb{P}(V) \ar[d, "\cong", "G/T"'] \\ H = \ker\theta \ar[r, hook] & \Omega^1_H(A) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

The coordinate \(Z\) takes values in the horizontal distribution \(H = \ker\theta\). The contact form \(\theta\) and the Reeb vector field \(\xi\) thus automatically provide the stereographic projection for the projective line fibres — no external coordinates are needed.

📄

Proposition 2.27 ✗ no Lean (Fibre functors as an affine atlas with \(G\)-torsor transitions).

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) (Tannaka–Krein). In the following, \(\omega, \omega'\) denote arbitrary fibre functors on \(\mathbf{C}\) (not the canonical \(\tau\)). Then:

  1. (Charts.) Each fibre functor \(\omega \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathbf{Vect}_R\) is an affine chart: a concrete realisation of the abstract categorical data as linear algebra over \(R\). The contact affine chart on \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) (contact affine chart) is the chart associated to the canonical fibre functor \(\tau\).

  2. (Transitions.) For any two fibre functors \(\omega, \omega'\), the set of monoidal natural isomorphisms \(\omega \xrightarrow{\sim} \omega'\) is a \(G\)-torsor. Each such isomorphism is a transition function: a change of affine coordinates relating the two observers’ descriptions of the same categorical data.

  3. (Cocycle condition.) Given three fibre functors \(\omega, \omega', \omega''\) with transition isomorphisms \(g_{01}, g_{12}, g_{02}\), functoriality of composition forces \(g_{02} = g_{12} \circ g_{01}\). The cocycle condition is not imposed — it is automatic.
