  4. (Atlas.) The category of all fibre functors on \(\mathbf{C}\), with monoidal natural isomorphisms as morphisms, is a \(G\)-gerbe: a connected groupoid on which \(G\) acts simply transitively. This is the affine atlas of the quantum observable universe.

Proof. (1) A fibre functor \(\omega\) assigns to each object \(X\) in \(\mathbf{C}\) a vector space \(\omega(X)\) and to each morphism \(f\) a linear map \(\omega(f)\), preserving the tensor product. This is a concrete coordinate system for the abstract category — an affine chart.

(2) By the Tannaka–Krein theorem (SU(2) emergence), any monoidal natural isomorphism \(\eta \colon \omega \xrightarrow{\sim} \omega'\) is determined by an element \(g \in G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) acting on the fibre. The set of all such isomorphisms is a principal homogeneous space for \(G\) — a \(G\)-torsor.

(3) If \(\eta_{01} \colon \omega \to \omega'\) and \(\eta_{12} \colon \omega' \to \omega''\) are monoidal natural isomorphisms, their composition \(\eta_{12} \circ \eta_{01}\) is the unique monoidal natural isomorphism \(\omega \to \omega''\) corresponding to the group product \(g_{12} \cdot g_{01}\). The cocycle identity \(g_{02} = g_{12} \cdot g_{01}\) is the associativity of composition in the functor category.

(4) Connectedness: any two fibre functors are isomorphic (Tannaka–Krein). Simple transitivity: the isomorphism is unique up to \(G\). \(\square\)

📄

Proposition 2.28 ∀ stated (Substrate parameter as the radial coordinate). \(\forall\)

Within the contact affine chart \(U_\xi\) (contact affine chart), the substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter) governs the radial and phase coordinates of the state. Let \(Z\) be the affine coordinate of a state. Then \(Z \to 0\) as \(q \to \infty\) (deep-quantum origin) and \(Z \to \infty\) as \(q \to 1\) (classical boundary). The \(q\)-deformed Reeb flow rotates the phase of \(Z\):

\[\mathcal{L}_\xi\,Z \;=\; J\,\hbar_q\,Z,\]

where \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) (quantum Planck constant) and \(J\) is the complex structure on \(H\).

Proof of substrate radial coordinate.

Within the contact affine chart \(U_\xi\) (contact affine chart), let \(Z\) be the affine coordinate of a state.

  1. Deep-quantum origin (\(Z \to 0\)): as \(q \to \infty\) (collapsing instanton), the state becomes purely vertical (\(\alpha_H \to 0\)). The affine coordinate vanishes, locating the primordial fermion at the origin of the chart.

  2. Classical boundary (\(Z \to \infty\)): as \(q \to 1\) (classical vacuum), the state becomes purely horizontal (\(\iota_\xi\,\alpha \to 0\), a boson). The affine coordinate diverges, pushing the state to the point at infinity of the \(\mathbb{CP}^1\) fibre.

Furthermore, the \(q\)-deformed Reeb flow (q-Reeb flow) rotates the phase of \(Z\) at a rate proportional to the quantum Planck constant:

\[\mathcal{L}_\xi\,Z \;=\; J\,\hbar_q\,Z,\]

where \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) (quantum Planck constant) and \(J\) is the complex structure on \(H\).

This unifies bosons and fermions geometrically: \(q\) controls the radial position in \(\mathbb{P}(V)\), with the bosonic sector at the boundary and the fermionic sector at the origin. ◻

📄

Proposition 2.29 ∀ stated (Fiber–adjoint-fiber involution). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe). The Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) induces an isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} A^{\vee}\) (the Frobenius self-duality), under which:

  1. the projective line object \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) (projective line object) embeds in the adjoint object \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) as the coadjoint orbit of a highest-weight vector;

  2. the assignment \(\sigma \colon \mathbb{P}(V) \hookrightarrow \mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is an involution in the sense that \(\sigma\) determines \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) from \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) and vice versa;

  3. the non-degeneracy of the Frobenius pairing forces the observability condition: \[\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:fiber-adjoint-involution-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathbb{P}(V) \ar[r, hook, "\sigma"] \ar[d, "\cong"'] & \mathrm{Ad}(A) \ar[d, "\cong", "\int_A"'] \\ G/T \ar[r, hook, "\text{coadjoint orbit}"] & A^{\vee} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(fibre--adjoint involution)} \end{equation}\]

Proof of Fiber–adjoint-fiber involution.

The Frobenius isomorphism \(A \cong A^{\vee}\) sends \(a \mapsto \int_A \circ \mu(a \otimes -)\), which is non-degenerate by the Frobenius–Hopf axiom.

(1) Embedding via rank-\(1\) projectors. Let \(\rho \colon V \to V\) be a rank-\(1\) projector in \(\mathbf{C}\): an endomorphism satisfying \(\rho^2 = \rho\) and \(\mathrm{tr}(\rho) = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}\) (categorical trace via evaluation and coevaluation). Since \(V\) has categorical dimension \(2\), define the traceless component

\[\sigma(\rho) = \rho - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{id}_V \;\in\; \mathrm{Ad}(A).\]

This is well-defined because \(\mathrm{tr}(\sigma(\rho)) = 1 - \tfrac{1}{2} \cdot 2 = 0\). The set of such projectors is precisely \(\mathbb{P}(V) = G/T\), the quotient by the maximal torus.

(2) The involution. Under the positive-definite involutive structure \(\dagger\) (involutive structure), every rank-\(1\) projector satisfies \(\rho^{\dagger} = \rho\) (self-adjointness). Computing the square of the traceless component:

\[\sigma(\rho)^2 = \bigl(\rho - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{id}_V\bigr)^2 = \rho^2 - \rho + \tfrac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{id}_V = \tfrac{1}{4}\,\mathrm{id}_V.\]

Thus \(2\sigma(\rho)\) is an involution in \(\mathrm{End}(V)\): it squares to the identity. Geometrically, \(\sigma\) identifies \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) with a coadjoint orbit in \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\). The orbit is closed by rigidity of \(\mathbf{C}\) and determines a sub-object of \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) isomorphic to \(\mathbb{P}(V)\). Conversely, given this sub-object, the stabiliser of any point is \(T\), so \(\mathbb{P}(V) \cong G/T\) as \(G\)-spaces.

(3) Observability. Suppose there exists a non-zero morphism \(f \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathrm{Ad}(A)\). Such a morphism would represent a \(G\)-invariant element in the adjoint representation. By the SU(2) emergence theorem (SU(2) emergence), the reconstructed gauge group is \(G \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\), and \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) carries the irreducible adjoint representation \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) (dimension \(3\)). By Schur’s lemma, the only intertwining morphism from the trivial representation \(\mathbf{1}\) to an irreducible non-trivial representation is the zero morphism. Therefore \(f = 0\), contradicting our assumption.

Hence \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\). The non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) excludes any hidden global symmetry: there is no non-trivial invariant section of the adjoint bundle. ◻

📄

Example 2.30 ∀ stated (Fiber–adjoint-fiber involution for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing projective line on SU(2), take \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\), \(T = \mathrm{U}(1)\), and \(V = \mathbb{C}^2\). The projective line object is \(\mathbb{P}(V) = \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), and the adjoint object is \(\mathrm{Ad}(A) \cong \mathfrak{su}(2) \cong \mathbb{R}^3\) (trace-free skew-Hermitian \(2 \times 2\) matrices under the Killing form). The embedding \(\sigma\) sends a line \(\ell = \mathrm{span}(v) \subset \mathbb{C}^2\) to the rank-\(1\) projector

\[\sigma([\ell]) = \frac{v v^{\dagger}}{\lVert v \rVert^2} - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{id}_V \in \mathfrak{su}(2).\]

This identifies \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) with the unit \(2\)-sphere \(S^2 \subset \mathfrak{su}(2)\) (the coadjoint orbit of \(\tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{diag}(i, -i)\)). Observability follows: a \(G\)-fixed point in \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) would be a matrix commuting with all of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\), hence a scalar — but trace-free matrices have no non-zero scalars, so \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\).

📄

Example 2.31 ∀ stated (Connection and curvature on \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\)). \(\forall\)

Continuing fibre adjoint on SU(2), take \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with its left-invariant calculus \(\Omega^1(A) = \mathrm{span}\{\omega_1, \omega_2, \omega_3\}\) (higher forms on SU(2)). A connection is a covariant derivative \(\nabla f = df + \mathcal{A} \cdot f\) for \(f \in A\), where \(\mathcal{A} = A_1\,\omega_1 + A_2\,\omega_2 + A_3\,\omega_3\) is the connection \(1\)-form. The Leibniz triangle says \(\nabla(fg) = (\nabla f)\,g + f\,(dg)\). The curvature is the \(2\)-form \(F_\nabla = d\mathcal{A} + \mathcal{A} \wedge \mathcal{A} \in \Omega^2(A)\), which is \(A\)-linear (\(F_\nabla(f \cdot s) = f \cdot F_\nabla(s)\)). (When the substrate parameter \(q\) is introduced in substrate parameter, this calculus deforms to the Woronowicz \(3D\)-calculus on \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\).)

Substrate parameter and deformation

The substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) is not part of the categorical definition of a quantum universe or observable universe; it parametrises the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family of interpolations between the full differential \(d\) and the vertical projection \(\pi_V \circ d\) (substrate parameter). The triple \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) carries both endomorphisms canonically; \(q\) records where one sits in the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family they span. Once a substrate parameter is fixed, the categorical dimension of the fundamental object \(V\) deforms from \(2\) to \([2]_q = q + q^{-1}\), and the gauge group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) (SU(2) emergence) deforms from \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) to \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\).

📄

Proposition 2.32 ∀ stated (Extraction of \(q\) from the braiding eigenvalues). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with fundamental object \(V\) of rank \(2\) and braiding \(c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V\). Then:

  1. Spectral decomposition. The tensor square decomposes as \(V \otimes V = S^2 V \oplus \Lambda^2 V\), where \(S^2 V\) (symmetric) and \(\Lambda^2 V\) (antisymmetric) are the eigenspaces of \(c_{V,V}\). This decomposition is intrinsic to \(\mathbf{C}\) — it depends only on the braiding, not on any external parameter.

  2. Eigenvalue definition of \(q\). Since \(\Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbf{1}\) (volume constraint) is simple, \(c_{V,V}\) acts on it by a scalar \(\lambda_- \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k\). Similarly, \(c_{V,V}\) acts on the \(3\)-dimensional \(S^2 V\) by a scalar \(\lambda_+\). Define \[q \;:=\; \lambda_+, \qquad \lambda_- \;=\; -q^{-1}.\] This is a categorical invariant: it is determined by the braiding endomorphism of \(\mathbf{C}\) alone.

  3. Hecke relation. The eigenvalue pair \((\lambda_+, \lambda_-) = (q, -q^{-1})\) is equivalent to the Hecke relation on \(T = \tau(c_{V,V})\): \[(T - q)(T + q^{-1}) \;=\; 0,\] and the product \(\lambda_+ \cdot \lambda_- = -1\) (which follows from \(\det(c_{V,V}) = -1\) on a rank-\(2\) object with trivial determinant). The Hecke relation is intrinsic: it is a polynomial identity on the braiding morphism in \(\mathbf{C}\).

  4. Classical vs.\{} quantum. When \(c_{V,V}^2 = \mathrm{id}\), the eigenvalues are \(+1\) and \(-1\), giving \(q = 1\) (symmetric monoidal, classical). When \(c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\), \(q \neq 1\) and the category is genuinely braided — this is the quantum regime.

  5. Connection to the substrate parameter. The categorical \(q\) extracted here coincides with the (substrate parameter): the one-parameter family \(d_q = q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1}) \pi_V \circ d\) is parametrised by the same \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) that appears as the braiding eigenvalue. The braiding determines the differential geometry.

Summary. The deformation parameter \(q\) is not imposed externally. It is the eigenvalue of the braiding \(c_{V,V}\) on the symmetric summand of \(V \otimes V\) — a purely categorical datum, extracted from the monoidal structure of \(\mathbf{C}\) via the Hecke relation. The Tannaka–Krein reconstruction (reconstruction) then recovers the quantum group \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) as \(\mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau)\), with \(q\) already determined by the category.

📄

Proposition 2.33 ∀ stated (Tannaka–Krein reconstruction of the quantum gauge group). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with fibre functor \(\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\). Then the coend

\[H \;=\; \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau) \;=\; \int^{X \in \mathbf{C}} \tau(X)^{\vee} \otimes_R \tau(X)\]

carries a canonical Hopf algebra structure \((\mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S)\) such that:

  1. Reconstruction. There is a monoidal equivalence \(\mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(H)\) under which \(\tau\) corresponds to the forgetful functor \(U \colon \mathrm{Rep}(H) \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\).

  2. Universal property. \(H\) is the universal Hopf algebra through which \(\tau\) factors: for every Hopf algebra \(H'\) and monoidal natural transformation \(\alpha \colon \tau \Rightarrow U \circ F\) (where \(F \colon \mathbf{C} \to \mathrm{Rep}(H')\)), there exists a unique Hopf map \(\phi \colon H \to H'\) with \(\alpha = U(\phi) \circ \mathrm{can}\).

  3. Naturality in \(\tau\). The group of monoidal natural automorphisms of \(\tau\) is \(\mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong G(H)\), the group-like elements (characters) of \(H\).

In the classical case (\(\mathbf{C}\) symmetric), this is Tannaka’s theorem as algebraised by Deligne : The sheaf \(H = \mathcal{O}(G)\) is the coordinate ring of a compact group \(G\), and \(\mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong G\).

In the quantum case (\(\mathbf{C}\) braided but not symmetric), the reconstruction is due to Woronowicz : \(H\) is a compact quantum group algebra \(\mathcal{O}_q(G)\), and the braiding \(c_{V,W}\) on \(\mathbf{C}\) encodes the universal \(R\)-matrix of \(H\). The deformation parameter \(q\) is not an external input — it is determined by the braiding, as shown in (braiding eigenvalue extraction).

📄

Definition 2.34 ∀ stated (Substrate parameter). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe (quantum observable universe) with weight decomposition \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) (weight decomposition) and Reeb derivation \(\xi\) (categorical Reeb). The non-commutative de Rham complex \((\Omega^\bullet(A), d)\) carries two canonical endomorphisms:

  1. the full differential \(d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)\);

  2. the vertical differential \(\pi_V \circ d\), which retains only the component along the Reeb direction.

These span a one-parameter family of first-order operators parametrised by \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k^{\times}\):

\[d_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,d \;+\; (1 - q^{-1})\,\pi_V \circ d.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:substrate-family-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "d"] \ar[d, "\pi_V \circ d"'] \ar[dr, "d_q"] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \\ \Omega^{k+1}(A) & {} \ar[u, phantom, "q{=}1"' near start] \ar[l, phantom, "q{\to}\infty" near start] \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(substrate family)} \end{equation}\]

The substrate parameter is the unique element \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k\) such that \(d_q\) acts as \(q^{-1}\,d\) on horizontal forms and as \(d\) on vertical forms. Geometrically, \(q\) is the fibre coordinate on the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family of interpolations.

At \(q = 1\) the operator \(d_q\) recovers \(d\) (classicality: horizontal and vertical differentiation are treated equally). As \(q \to \infty\), \(d_q\) projects onto \(\pi_V \circ d\) (deep-quantum regime: only the Reeb direction contributes). The substrate parameter is not intrinsic to the triple \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\); it records where one sits in the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family that \(q\) parametrises.

When the quantum universe is fibred over a space \(M\) (as in the archimedean realisation, \(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum universe), the categorical substrate parameter specialises to a substrate field \(q \colon M \to k^{\times}\), encoding the local value of the \(\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\)-element at each point.

Algebraic perspective. The Lusztig integral form \(\mathcal{U}^{\mathbb{Z}}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\) is the universal \(\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]\)-algebra generated by \(K^{\pm 1}\) and the divided powers \(E^{(n)}, F^{(n)}\). A ring homomorphism \(\iota \colon \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}] \to k\), \(q \mapsto q_0\), base-changes this to the quantised enveloping algebra at \(q_0\). The categorical and algebraic viewpoints agree: the interpolation parameter \(q\) in \(d_q\) and the specialisation target \(q_0 = \iota(q)\) determine the same deformation.

📄

Theorem 2.35 ∀ stated (Existence of the substrate parameter). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with weight decomposition \((\pi_H, \pi_V)\) and categorical Reeb derivation \((\xi, \theta_A)\). Then there exists a substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k\), with \(q \notin \mu_\infty(k)\) (not a root of unity). In the archimedean realisation this specialises to a substrate field \(q \colon M \to \mathbb{R}_{>0}\) with \(q(p) \ge 1\), such that the \(q\)-deformed differential

\(d_q = q^{-1}\, d + (1 - q^{-1})\, \pi_V \circ d\)

interpolates between the full differential \(d\) (at \(q = 1\)) and the vertical projection \(\pi_V \circ d\) (as \(q \to \infty\)).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:substrate-parameter-exists-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] d \ar[r, phantom, "\xleftarrow{q=1}"] & d_q \ar[r, phantom, "\xrightarrow{q \to \infty}"] & \pi_V \circ d \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(substrate interpolation)} \end{equation}\]

Proof of existence of the substrate parameter.

The braiding \(c_{V,V} \colon V \otimes V \to V \otimes V\) of the QOU provides the substrate parameter categorically — no external choice is needed.

Step 1 (spectral decomposition). The volume constraint \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \twoheadrightarrow \mathbf{1}\) splits \(V \otimes V = S^2 V \oplus \Lambda^2 V\) into eigenspaces of \(c_{V,V}\). Since \(\Lambda^2 V \cong \mathbf{1}\) is simple and \(\dim S^2 V = 3\), the braiding acts by scalars \(\lambda_+ \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) on \(S^2 V\) and \(\lambda_- \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) on \(\Lambda^2 V\).

Step 2 (define \(q\)). Set \(q := \lambda_+\). The determinant constraint \(\lambda_+ \cdot \lambda_- = -1\) (from \(\det(c_{V,V}) = -1\) on a rank-\(2\) object with trivial determinant) forces \(\lambda_- = -q^{-1}\). Therefore \(c_{V,V}\) satisfies the Hecke relation \((T - q)(T + q^{-1}) = 0\) (braiding eigenvalue extraction).

Step 3 (non-degeneracy). The QOU assumption \(c_{V,V}^2 \neq \mathrm{id}\) ensures \(q \neq \pm 1\). The positive-definite dagger structure forces \(q \in \mathbb{R}_{>0}\), and the non-root-of-unity condition \(q \notin \mu_\infty(k)\) follows from transcendence over \(\mathbb{Q}\) in the archimedean realisation.

Step 4 (agreement with \(d_q\)). The categorical \(q\) extracted from the braiding coincides with the interpolation parameter in \(d_q = q^{-1}\,d + (1 - q^{-1})\,\pi_V \circ d\): both are characterised as the unique \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) for which the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\) acts faithfully on \(V^{\otimes n}\).

In the archimedean realisation, the constant substrate field \(q(p) = q_0 > 1\) for all \(p\) satisfies the classicality bound \(q \ge 1\) and positivity. Non-constant substrate fields arise from the Reeb flow parameterisation of the categorical \(\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\)-valued coordinate. ◻

📄

Example 2.36 ✗ no Lean (Substrate parameter for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)).

Continuing the quantum universe for SU(2), we specify the substrate parameter that controls the deformation from classical \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) to quantum \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\).

The specialisation map. The categorical substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) is realised via a ring homomorphism \(\iota \colon \mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}] \to \mathbb{C}\) determined by its value on the generator: \(\iota(q) = q_0 \in \mathbb{C}^\times\). All algebraic structures (multiplication, comultiplication, antipode, \(R\)-matrix) are defined over \(\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]\) and specialise to concrete \(\mathbb{C}\)-algebras via \(\iota\).

Classical case. Setting \(q_0 = 1\) recovers the undeformed coordinate ring \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with its commutative multiplication:

\[\iota_{q_0 = 1} \colon \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2)) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2)), \qquad \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix} \mapsto \begin{pmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{pmatrix},\]

where \(ab = ba\), \(ac = ca\), etc. This is the setting of the classical brane tower.

Quantum case. For \(q_0 = e^{\pi i / \kappa}\) with \(\kappa \in \mathbb{Z}_{\geq 2}\) the Chern–Simons level, the specialisation produces \(\mathcal{O}_{q_0}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with non-commutative relations:

\[ab = q_0\, ba, \quad ac = q_0\, ca, \quad bc = cb, \quad ad - da = (q_0 - q_0^{-1})\, bc.\]

The representation category \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_{q_0}(2))\) is a modular tensor category with finitely many simple objects \(V_0, V_{1/2}, \ldots, V_{(\kappa - 2)/2}\) when \(q_0\) is a root of unity.

Root-of-unity truncation. At \(q_0 = e^{\pi i / \kappa}\), the spin-\(j\) representations with \(2j \geq \kappa - 1\) become reducible or zero, leaving a finite semisimple category. The quantum dimension of \(V_j\) is

\[\dim_q(V_j) = \frac{q_0^{2j+1} - q_0^{-(2j+1)}}{q_0 - q_0^{-1}} = [2j + 1]_{q_0},\]

the quantum integer. For \(q_0 = 1\) this reduces to the classical dimension \(2j + 1\).

Physical interpretation. The substrate parameter \(q_0\) interpolates between the classical gauge theory (\(q_0 = 1\), infinite-dimensional representation category) and the topological quantum field theory (\(q_0\) a root of unity, finite modular category). The Chern–Simons level \(\kappa\) controls the "granularity" of the quantum geometry.

📄

Definition 2.37 ∀ stated (Quantum Gauge Group). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) (substrate parameter), where \(q\) is the braiding eigenvalue on the symmetric summand of \(V \otimes V\) (braiding eigenvalue extraction). The quantum gauge group is the Hopf algebra \(H = \mathrm{End}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) reconstructed via Tannaka–Krein duality (reconstruction). By the universal property, \(H \cong \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) — the coordinate ring of \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) at the categorically determined \(q\):

\[G_q \;=\; \mathrm{SU}_q(2), \qquad q = \text{eigenvalue of } c_{V,V} \text{ on } S^2 V.\]

The classical gauge group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}(2)\) (SU(2) emergence) is the \(q = 1\) case (symmetric braiding). In the archimedean realisation, where the substrate parameter specialises to a substrate field over \(M\), this yields a field of quantum groups \(\{G_{q(p)}\}_{p \in M}\).

📄

Definition 2.38 ∀ stated (Quantum Planck Constant). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k\) (substrate parameter). The quantum Planck constant is the element \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} \in k\). When the categorical substrate parameter specialises to a substrate field over a space \(M\), this defines a field \(\hbar_q \colon M \to k\) by \(\hbar_q(p) = 1 - q(p)^{-1}\).

📄

Definition 2.39 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Hodge star). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with categorical Hodge star \(\star\) (categorical hodge star) and substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter). The \(q\)-Hodge star is the \(q\)-deformed involution \(\star_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{n-k}(A)\) defined by

\[\alpha \wedge_q \star_q \beta \;=\; q \cdot \int_A\!\bigl(\alpha^* \cdot \beta\bigr)\;\mathrm{vol}.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:q-hodge-star-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\star_q"] \ar[d, "\star"'] & \Omega^{n-k}(A) \\ \Omega^{n-k}(A) \ar[ur, "q \cdot \mathrm{id}"'] \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{($q$-Hodge star)} \end{equation}\]

At \(q = 1\) this recovers the categorical Hodge star: \(\star_1 = \star\). The factor of \(q\) rescales the inner product on forms, coupling the Hodge duality to the local deformation strength.

Examples of quantum observable universes

We now specialise the categorical framework to the archimedean setting, where the base ring is an archimedean field \(K\) (e.g. \(\mathbb{Q}\), \(\mathbb{R}\), or \(\mathbb{C}\)) and the quantum universe is realised by CR geometry on a contact manifold. The abstract categorical structures — Frobenius form, weight decomposition, \(q\)-deformed operators — acquire concrete geometric meaning as differential-geometric objects on a CR manifold equipped with a pseudo-Hermitian structure. The main result (§\{}ref{sec:physical-interpretation}) places gravity, gauge theory, and quantum mechanics in a unified commutative diagram within this setting.

📄

Example 2.40 ∀ stated (Archimedean realisation: quantum universe). \(\forall\)

Let \(K\) be an archimedean field. A quantum universe over \(K\) (quantum universe) is realised by the \(4\)-tuple \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\): here \(\theta\) is a contact form on a CR manifold \(M\) (encoding the contact geometry and Reeb structure), \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\) is the gauge group, and \(\mathcal{S}\) is the state bundle carrying the quantum degrees of freedom. The base manifold \(M\) is implicit as the domain of \(\theta\); the principal bundle \(P\) is implicit as the frame bundle of \(\mathcal{S}\) under \(G\). The precise requirements are:

  1. \(M\) (the domain of \(\theta\)) is a CR manifold of hypersurface type (real dimension \(2n+1\), \(n \geq 1\)) with non-degenerate Levi form of signature \((r,s)\), \(r + s = n\);

  2. \(\theta\) is a pseudo-Hermitian structure (contact form) on \(M\), determining the Levi distribution \(H = \ker\theta\), the Reeb vector field \(\xi\), the Webster metric \(g_\theta\) (of signature \((2r,2s)\) on \(H\)), and the Levi form \(L_\theta\);

  3. \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\);

  4. \(\mathcal{S} = P \times_G \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \to M\) is the associated state bundle, where \(P \to M\) is the principal \(G\)-bundle (with holonomy reducing to \(\mathrm{SO}(3) \subset \mathrm{SU}(2)/\{\pm I\}\)) and \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) acts on \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) by Möbius transformations.

The monoidal category is \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_{q(p)}(2))\) (the representation category of the quantum group at the substrate parameter \(q(p)\), substrate parameter), the Frobenius–Hopf object is \(A = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with Frobenius form given by the Haar state, and the fibre functor \(\tau\) is the forgetful functor to \(K\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\).

When the category \(\mathbf{C}\) is understood from context, we abbreviate to \((\theta, G, \mathcal{S})\). The strictly pseudoconvex case corresponds to signature \((n,0)\), where \(L_\theta\) is positive definite — this is the primary case of physical interest, giving a positive-definite Webster metric \(g_\theta\) and a well-defined Hodge star. The indefinite case (signature \((r,s)\) with \(s > 0\)) admits analogous constructions with the Webster metric of mixed signature; see (Levi generalisation) for the extension.

📄

Example 2.41 ∀ stated (Archimedean realisation: quantum observable universe). \(\forall\)

An archimedean quantum observable universe is an archimedean quantum universe \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum universe) that satisfies the vanishing conditions

\[H^0(M, \mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0 \qquad\text{and}\qquad \Gamma_c(M, \mathcal{S}) = 0.\]

These analytic conditions are the archimedean realisation of the categorical observability conditions of quantum observable universe: the Frobenius non-degeneracy of the Haar state on \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), combined with irreducibility of the instanton connection (irreducible connection), forces \(H^0(M, \mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0\); the section-vanishing \(\Gamma_c(M, \mathcal{S}) = 0\) follows from the non-existence of \(A\)-equivariant sections of the associated \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\)-bundle.

Categorical action and variational equations

📄

Definition 2.42 ∀ stated (Categorical Dirac operator). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) equipped with connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection), substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter), and Reeb derivation \(\xi\) (categorical Reeb derivation). The categorical Dirac operator is the morphism

\[\mathcal{D}_\nabla \;=\; q^{-1}\,\nabla \;+\; (1 - q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi\,\nabla \;\colon\; A \to \Omega^1(A).\]

When \(q = 1\) this reduces to \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla = \nabla\), the undeformed covariant derivative. The \(q\)-deformation interpolates between the full connection and its projection onto the Reeb direction: as \(q \to \infty\) we obtain \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla \to \iota_\xi\nabla\), the purely contact component.

📄

Definition 2.43 ∀ stated (Categorical Lagrangian). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with categorical Dirac operator \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\) (categorical Dirac operator) and a state \(\psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\). The categorical Lagrangian is the endomorphism

\[\mathcal{L}_q(\nabla, \psi) \;=\; \mathcal{D}_\nabla^{\,2} \;+\; \psi^* \otimes \mathcal{D}_\nabla\,\psi \;\;\in\; \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A),\]

where \(\psi^* = \int_A \!\circ\, S(\psi) \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) is the adjoint section (antipode composed with the Frobenius form).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-lagrangian-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\mathcal{D}_\nabla"] \ar[dr, "\mathcal{L}_q(\nabla{,}\,\psi)"'] & \Omega^1(A) \otimes A \ar[d, "\mathcal{D}_\nabla \,+\, \psi^* \otimes (-)"] \\ & \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(Lagrangian)} \end{equation}\]

The Lagrangian is an endomorphism of \(A\) — the categorical analog of a Lagrangian density \(\mathscr{L}(x)\) before integration over spacetime. Its first summand \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla^2\) encodes the bosonic sector (gravity + gauge curvature); the second summand encodes the fermionic coupling of the state to the connection.

📄

Definition 2.44 ∀ stated (Categorical action). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe). A categorical action on \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) is a morphism \(\mathcal{S} \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{1}\) of the form

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-action} \mathcal{S} \;=\; \mathrm{ev}_A \;\circ\; \bigl(\mathrm{id}_{A^\vee} \otimes \Phi\bigr) \;\circ\; \mathrm{coev}_A, \end{equation}\]

where \(\Phi \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A)\) is called the physics endomorphism.

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-action-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\mathrm{coev}_A"] \ar[rr, bend right=25, "\mathcal{S}"'] & A \otimes A^{\vee} \ar[r, "\Phi \otimes \mathrm{id}"] & A \otimes A^{\vee} \ar[r, "\mathrm{ev}_A"] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(categorical action)} \end{equation}\]

The evaluation \(\mathrm{ev}_A \colon A^\vee \otimes A \to \mathbf{1}\) and coevaluation \(\mathrm{coev}_A \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A^\vee\) are the structure maps of the rigid duality on \(A\) (rigid monoidal category). Composing them with an inserted endomorphism produces the categorical trace:

\[\mathcal{S} = \mathrm{tr}(\Phi).\]

As a string diagram, the action is a single closed loop with \(\Phi\) inserted — the morphism \(\mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{1}\) obtained by "tracing out" the internal degrees of freedom of \(A\). The rigid structure provides the integration; the physics endomorphism encodes the dynamics.

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) equipped with substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter), \(q\)-Hodge star \(\star_q\) (\(q\)-Hodge star), a connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection), and a section \(\psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) (a "state"). The following notation is used in categorical action:

  • \(\mathrm{tr} \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A) \to R\) is the categorical trace (the composition \(\mathrm{coev} \to \mathrm{id} \to \mathrm{ev}\) via the rigid structure).

  • \(R_{\int} \in \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A)\) is the Frobenius–Ricci endomorphism: the curvature of the Frobenius form \(\int_A\) itself, defined by \(R_{\int} = (\mathrm{id}_A \otimes \int_A) \circ F_{\nabla_{\int}}\), where \(\nabla_{\int}\) is the canonical connection on \(A\) induced by \(\int_A\) via \(\nabla_{\int}(a) = \int_A(a_{(1)}) \otimes a_{(2)} - a \otimes 1\) (Sweedler notation: \(\Delta(a) = a_{(1)} \otimes a_{(2)}\), summation suppressed).

  • \(\mathrm{tr}_A \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A \otimes \Omega^{\bullet}(A)) \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(\Omega^{\bullet}(A))\) is the partial trace over the \(A\) factor.

  • \(\psi^* = \int_A \circ S(\psi) \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) is the adjoint section (antipode composed with the Frobenius form).

  • \(D_\nabla = q^{-1}\,\nabla + (1 - q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi\,\nabla\) is the \(q\)-deformed covariant derivative, where \(\xi\) is the Reeb derivation of \(A\) (Reeb decomposition).

Example 2.45 ✗ no Lean (Categorical-action notation for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)).

Continuing connection on SU(2), take \(A = \mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with Haar integral \(\int_A = \int_G\), connection \(\nabla f = df + \mathcal{A} \cdot f\), and a state \(\psi \in A\) (a function on the group).

  • Categorical trace. For \(T \in \mathrm{End}(V_j)\), \(\mathrm{tr}(T) = \sum_m \langle j,m \mid T \mid j,m \rangle\) is the usual matrix trace.

  • Frobenius–Ricci. \(R_{\int}\) measures curvature of the Haar integral itself: on \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) (flat Haar measure), \(R_{\int} = 0\) in the classical limit \(q = 1\).

  • Adjoint section. For \(\psi \colon \mathbb{C} \to A\), the adjoint is \(\psi^*(f) = \int_G \overline{\psi(g)}\,f(g)\,dg\), i.e. the inner product with \(\psi\) under the Haar integral.

  • \(q\)-deformed derivative. At \(q = 1\), \(D_\nabla = \nabla\) (ordinary covariant derivative). For \(q \neq 1\), the Reeb component is re-weighted, coupling the connection to the contact geometry.

📄

Proposition 2.46 ∀ stated (Canonical action of a quantum observable universe). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) equipped with connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection), substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter), \(q\)-Hodge star \(\star_q\) (\(q\)-Hodge star), and state \(\psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\). Then \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) determines a (categorical action), unique up to a scalar \(\lambda \in R^{\times}\),

\[\mathcal{S}_q \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}_q),\]

where \(\mathcal{L}_q = \mathcal{L}_q(\nabla, \psi)\) is the categorical Lagrangian (categorical Lagrangian). The physics endomorphism is \(\Phi_q = \mathcal{L}_q\).

The square of the Dirac operator (categorical Dirac operator) decomposes via the Frobenius–Hopf structure as

\[\mathcal{D}_\nabla^{\,2} \;=\; q \cdot R_{\int} \;+\; \mathrm{tr}_A\!\bigl( F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla \bigr),\]

so the categorical action expands to three terms:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:canonical-action-decomposition} \mathcal{S}_q[\nabla,\, \textstyle\int_A,\, \psi] \;=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{tr}\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr) }_{\text{gravity}} \;+\; \underbrace{\int_A \!\circ\, \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl( F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla \bigr) }_{\text{gauge}} \;+\; \underbrace{\int_A\!\bigl(\psi^* \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\,\psi\bigr) }_{\text{matter}}, \end{equation}\]

with notation as in categorical action notation. Here \(\mathrm{tr} = \mathrm{ev}_A \circ (\mathrm{id}_{A^\vee} \otimes {-}) \circ \mathrm{coev}_A\) is the categorical trace, which plays the role of spacetime integration; \(R_{\int}\) is the Frobenius–Ricci endomorphism; and \(F_\nabla = \nabla^2\) is the curvature.

Uniqueness up to scalar. The evaluation and coevaluation maps are determined up to unique isomorphism by the duality data, and the Frobenius–Hopf axioms fix the decomposition of \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla^2\) into curvature terms. The residual ambiguity is a single scalar \(\lambda \in R^{\times}\): the normalization of the Frobenius form \(\int_A\). Replacing \(\int_A\) by \(\lambda\!\int_A\) sends \(\mathcal{S}_q \mapsto \lambda\,\mathcal{S}_q\). This is the categorical analog of the choice of physical units — it corresponds to the freedom in choosing \(G\), \(g^2\), and \(\hbar\) in the archimedean realization (Remark).

The scalar ambiguity is controlled by the same obstruction that governs the forgetful functor \(\tau\): the observability axiom \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) (QOU axiom 2) ensures that the trace \(\mathrm{tr} \colon \mathrm{End}(A) \to R\) is faithful — no endomorphism is "invisible" to integration. Relaxing this condition (allowing hidden symmetries, \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) \neq 0\)) introduces a nontrivial kernel in the trace, and the obstruction to recovering a well-defined action is classified by the same cohomology class \(\kappa \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B})\) that obstructs lifting in the Yekutieli sense (Yekutieli lifting condition; Yekutieli–Stokes remark).

📄

Remark 2.47 ✗ no Lean (Archimedean realization of the categorical action).

In the archimedean realization (archimedean QOU) where \(\mathbf{C} = \mathbf{Vect}_{\mathbb{R}}\), \(A = C^{\infty}(M)\) for a Riemannian manifold \(M\), and \(\nabla\) is an Ehresmann connection on a principal \(G\)-bundle \(P \to M\), the three constituents of the (categorical action) acquire their classical meanings:

  1. The categorical trace \(\mathrm{tr} = \mathrm{ev}_A \circ (\mathrm{id}_{A^\vee} \otimes {-}) \circ \mathrm{coev}_A\) becomes integration against the volume form: \(\mathrm{tr}(\cdot) \to \int_M (\cdot)\,\mathrm{dvol}\).

  2. The physics endomorphism \(\Phi_q = \mathcal{L}_q\) becomes the Lagrangian density \(\mathscr{L}(x)\), a section of the density bundle.

  3. The categorical Dirac operator \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\) reduces to the gauge-covariant Dirac operator \(D\!\!\!\!/\, = \gamma^\mu D_\mu\).

The three-term decomposition (Proposition) then reads

\[\mathcal{S}_q \;\longrightarrow\; \frac{1}{16\pi G}\!\int_M R\,\mathrm{dvol} \;-\; \frac{1}{4g^2}\!\int_M \mathrm{Tr}(F \wedge \star F) \;+\; \int_M \bar\psi\, D\!\!\!\!/\;\psi\,\mathrm{dvol},\]

the Einstein–Hilbert + Yang–Mills + Dirac action, with \(q \to 1\). The coupling constants \(G\), \(g\) emerge from the normalization of the Frobenius form \(\int_A\) and the substrate parameter \(q\) respectively; they are not free parameters of the categorical theory but are determined by the choice of archimedean realization.

📄

Proposition 2.48 ∀ stated (Variational equations of the categorical action). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{S}_q\) be the (categorical action). The three variational equations are:

  1. Gravity (vary \(\int_A\)): \(\delta\mathcal{S}_q / \delta\!\int_A = 0\) yields the categorical Einstein equation: \[R_{\int} - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\,\mathrm{id}_A \;=\; T_q[\nabla, \psi],\] where \(T_q\) is the stress-energy endomorphism constructed from the gauge and matter terms.

  2. Gauge (vary \(\nabla\)): \(\delta\mathcal{S}_q / \delta\nabla = 0\) yields the categorical Yang–Mills equation: \[\nabla \star_q F_\nabla + q \cdot [F_\nabla,\, \star_q F_\nabla] \;=\; J_\psi,\] where \(J_\psi = \psi^* \otimes D_\nabla\psi - D_\nabla\psi^* \otimes \psi\) is the matter current.

  3. Matter (vary \(\psi\)): \(\delta\mathcal{S}_q / \delta\psi = 0\) yields the categorical transport equation: \[D_\nabla\,\psi \;=\; 0.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:variational-equations-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathcal{S}_q \ar[r, "\delta/\delta\!\int_A"] \ar[d, "\delta/\delta\nabla"'] \ar[dr, "\delta/\delta\psi"] & R_{\int} - \tfrac{1}{2}\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\,\mathrm{id} = T_q \\ \nabla \star_q F + q[F, \star_q F] = J_\psi & D_\nabla \psi = 0 \ar[from=ul, crossing over] \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(variational equations)} \end{equation}\]

Proof of Variational equations of the categorical action.

Each equation is obtained by computing \(\delta\mathcal{S}_q = 0\) with respect to the indicated variable, using the non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\).

Item (1): Vary \(\int_A\). The gravity term \(\mathrm{tr}(q \cdot R_{\int})\) depends on \(\int_A\) through the Frobenius–Ricci endomorphism \(R_{\int}\). Varying \(\int_A \mapsto \int_A + \delta\!\int_A\) and requiring \(\delta\mathcal{S}_q = 0\) for all \(\delta\!\int_A\) gives, by non-degeneracy of the categorical trace, \(R_{\int} - \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\,\mathrm{id}_A = T_q[\nabla, \psi]\), where the stress-energy \(T_q\) collects the \(\int_A\)-dependence of the gauge and matter terms. The trace subtraction ensures \(\mathrm{tr}(T_q) = \tfrac{1}{2}\,\mathrm{tr}(R_{\int})\) (the contracted Bianchi identity).

Item (2): Vary \(\nabla\). The gauge term \(\int_A \circ \mathrm{tr}_A(F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla)\) depends on \(\nabla\) through \(F_\nabla = \nabla^2\). A standard computation using \(\delta F_\nabla = \nabla(\delta\nabla)\) and integration by parts (via non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\)) yields \(\nabla \star_q F_\nabla + q \cdot [F_\nabla,\, \star_q F_\nabla] = J_\psi\). The commutator term \(q \cdot [F_\nabla, \star_q F_\nabla]\) arises from the non-commutativity of the \(q\)-deformed wedge product; it vanishes when \(q = 1\) (the abelian/classical limit).

Item (3): Vary \(\psi\). The matter term \(\int_A(\psi^* \cdot D_\nabla\,\psi)\) is linear in \(\psi\). Varying \(\psi \mapsto \psi + \delta\psi\) and using \((\delta\psi)^* \cdot D_\nabla\,\psi = 0\) for all \(\delta\psi\) gives \(D_\nabla\,\psi = 0\) by non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) and the dagger structure (positive definite dagger). ◻

📄

Example 2.49 ✗ no Lean (Continuing example: photon wavefront through a double slit).

We trace the wavefront propagation equation \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi = 0\) (wavefront propagation) through the concrete geometry of a double-slit experiment, with the photon as the test particle. In the QOU, a photon is not the bare identity \(\mathbf{1}\) but a photon with color content \(\gamma = \mathbf{1} + \varphi_0\,\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\,\sigma_1\) (color content), where the Hecke generators encode polarisation on the exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_p \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). The identity component (\(K = \varnothing\), the empty knot) is purely horizontal (boson: vertical component \(\alpha_V = 0\)); the color dressing \(\varphi_i\,\sigma_i\) adds polarisation-dependent Reeb phase.

Setup. A photon source emits a state \(\psi \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) with \(\psi \in \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k\) (purely horizontal, boson: \(\alpha_V = 0\)). The photon travels through three regions:

  1. Free propagation (source \(\to\) barrier). The connection is the flat instanton: \(F_\nabla = 0\), so \(c_2 = 0\). The Dirac operator reduces to \[\mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi \;=\; q^{-1}\,\nabla\psi + (1-q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi\,\nabla\psi \;=\; 0.\] Since \(\psi\) is horizontal (\(\pi_V\psi = 0\)), the Reeb contraction \(\iota_\xi\nabla\psi\) extracts only the vertical part of the connection’s action on \(\psi\). On a flat background this produces a Gaussian spreading: the beam waist \(w_0\) is set by \(q\) and the source geometry. As \(q \to 1\), \(\hbar_q \to 0\) and \(w_0 \to 0\) (ray limit); as \(q\) increases, the beam spreads.

  2. Slit interaction (barrier). The barrier material consists of localized knots (localized knot) with knot type \(K_{\mathrm{mat}}\) (e.g. Borromean rings \(6_2^3\) for nucleons). At the slit walls the connection \(\nabla\) is no longer flat: \(F_\nabla \neq 0\), and the instanton condition \(\star_q F_\nabla = F_\nabla\) constrains the curvature to be self-dual with topological charge determined by \(K_{\mathrm{mat}}\). The photon wavefront encounters two openings (slits of width \(d\), separation \(D\)). At each slit wall, the Reeb term \((1-q^{-1})\iota_\xi\nabla\) imparts a torsion phase: \[\tau(y) \;=\; \hbar_q \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(K_{\mathrm{mat}}) \cdot \eta(y)^2 \cdot k w,\] where \(\eta = |y|/(d/2)\) is the normalized slit coordinate, \(k = 2\pi/\lambda\) is the wavenumber, and \(w\) is the slit thickness. This is the \(q\)-deformed Huygens–Fresnel correction: the torsion is strongest at the slit walls (\(\eta = 1\)) and vanishes at center (\(\eta = 0\)).

  3. Post-slit propagation (barrier \(\to\) screen). After passing through the slits, \(\psi\) again satisfies \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi = 0\) on a flat background, but now with boundary conditions set by the two slit openings. The wavefront from each slit interferes, producing the intensity pattern \[I(x) \;=\; \left| \sum_{s=1}^{2}\; \int_{-d/2}^{d/2} e^{ik(r_1+r_2)}\; e^{i\,\tau(y)}\; e^{-y_s^2/w_0^2}\; dy \right|^2,\] where \(r_1, r_2\) are the source-to-slit and slit-to-screen distances, \(y_s\) is the slit coordinate measured from slit center \(s\), and the Gaussian factor \(e^{-y_s^2/w_0^2}\) is the beam envelope determined by the free-propagation solution.

QOU prediction. The torsion correction \(\tau(y)\) is absent in the classical (\(q = 1\)) double-slit formula. Its magnitude depends on \(\mathrm{Vol}(K_{\mathrm{mat}})\), the hyperbolic volume of the barrier material’s knot type. Different slit materials (silicon vs. gold vs. carbon) have different dominant knot types and hence different \(\mathrm{Vol}(K_{\mathrm{mat}})\), producing material-dependent fringe shifts — a signature absent in standard quantum mechanics, testable with current technology.

Color-content correction. When the photon carries non-trivial color content \((\varphi_0, \varphi_1)\), each polarisation mode \(\sigma_i\) acquires its own Hecke eigenvalue (\(+q\) or \(-q^{-1}\)) weighting the torsion phase \(\tau(y)\). The corrected torsion becomes

\[\tau^{(\mathrm{color})}(y) \;=\; \tau(y) \;+\; (\varphi_0\,q - \varphi_1\,q^{-1})\, \hbar_q \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(K_{\mathrm{mat}}) \cdot \eta(y)^2 \cdot k w,\]

which reduces to \(\tau(y)\) for bare photons (\(\varphi_0 = \varphi_1 = 0\)). For linearly polarised light the correction is first order in \(\hbar_q\) and depends on the polarisation angle, providing a measurable signature distinct from classical birefringence.

Particles, fermions, bosons, and observation

📄

Definition 2.50 ∀ stated (Categorical \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection), substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter), and weight decomposition \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) (weight decomposition). The \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative \(d_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)\) is

\[d_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,d + (1 - q^{-1})\,\pi_V \circ d,\]

where \(d \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)\) is the differential of the non-commutative de Rham complex. Equivalently, \(d_q\) acts as \(q^{-1}\,d\) on horizontal forms and as \(d\) on vertical forms:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-dq-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=2.5em] \Omega^k_H(A) \ar[r, "d"] \ar[d, hook] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \ar[r, "q^{-1}"] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \\ \Omega^k(A) \ar[rru, "d_q"'] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

The \(q\)-adjoint \(\delta_q \colon \Omega^{k+1}(A) \to \Omega^k(A)\) is the adjoint of \(d_q\) with respect to the dagger structure (positive definite dagger).

📄

Definition 2.51 ∀ stated (Particle (\(q\)-harmonic form)). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative \(d_q\) (categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative). The \(q\)-Laplacian on \(\Omega^k(A)\) is \(\Delta_q = d_q\,\delta_q + \delta_q\,d_q\). A particle is an element \(\alpha \in \Omega^k(A)\) that is \(q\)-harmonic:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:q-harmonic-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^{k-1}(A) \ar[r, "d_q"] & \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "d_q"] \ar[d, "\delta_q"'{near start}, "{\scriptstyle \Delta_q \alpha = 0}"{description, near end}] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \\ & \Omega^{k-1}(A) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

📄

Definition 2.52 ∀ stated (Fermion–Boson decomposition). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{H}_q^k = \ker\Delta_q \subset \Omega^k(A)\) denote the space of particles (\(q\)-harmonic form). The weight decomposition (weight decomposition) restricts to a short exact sequence

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:fermion-boson-ses} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] 0 \ar[r] & \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k \ar[r, hook] & \mathcal{H}_q^k \ar[r, "\pi_V"] & \mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k \ar[r] & 0 \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

where \(\mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k = \mathcal{H}_q^k \cap \Omega^k_H(A)\) and \(\mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k = \pi_V(\mathcal{H}_q^k)\). A boson is a particle in the kernel \(\mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k\) (purely horizontal: \(\alpha_V = 0\)). A fermion is a particle with \(\alpha_V \neq 0\), i.e. one whose image under \(\pi_V\) is non-zero.

The sequence splits via \(\pi_H\):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:fermion-boson-split} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \mathcal{H}_q^k \ar[r, "\pi_H \oplus \pi_V", "\sim"'] & \mathcal{H}_{q,H}^k \;\oplus\; \mathcal{H}_{q,V}^k \end{tikzcd} \qquad \text{(bosons $\oplus$ fermion vertical parts).} \end{equation}\]

📄

Definition 2.53 ∀ stated (Categorical point). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum universe). A categorical point of \(A\) is a morphism

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-point} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=3em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "p"] & A \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(categorical point)} \end{equation}\]

In the archimedean realisation \(A = \mathcal{O}(G)\), a categorical point \(p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) is a character \(\mathrm{ev}_g \colon f \mapsto f(g)\) for some \(g \in G\); equivalently, a point of the group \(G\). For a manifold \(M\) with \(A = C^{\infty}(M)\), a point \(p\) corresponds to evaluation at \(p \in M\):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:point-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \{*\} \ar[r, "p"] & M \end{tikzcd} \qquad\longleftrightarrow\qquad \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "p"] & A \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

The augmentation ideal at \(p\) is \(\mathfrak{m}_p = \ker(p^* \colon A \to \mathbf{1})\), where \(p^* = \int_A \circ \mu(p \otimes -)\). The germ of \(A\) at \(p\) is the quotient \(A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2\), which captures the first-order behaviour of \(A\) near \(p\).

📄

Definition 2.54 ∀ stated (Observation). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with state bundle \(\mathcal{S} \to M\), let \(q\) denote the (substrate parameter), let \(p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) be a (categorical point), and let \(U \subset M\) be an open causal neighbourhood of \(p\).

An intent on \(U\) is a pair \((\mathfrak{I}, \epsilon)\) where \(\epsilon \in \{+1, -1\}\) is the direction and

\[\mathfrak{I} \;\in\; \Gamma\bigl(U,\; \mathrm{Ad}(J^1 \mathcal{S})\bigr)\]

is a section of the adjoint bundle of the \(1\)-jet prolongation of \(\mathcal{S}\). The sign \(\epsilon\) determines the arrow of time: \(\epsilon = +1\) (braiding, \(\sigma_i\), forward under \(\prec_c\)) or \(\epsilon = -1\) (unbraiding, \(\sigma_i^{-1}\), backward).

The section \(\mathfrak{I}\) satisfies:

  1. Frobenius compatibility. The observation preserves the Frobenius form on \(U\): \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:observation-frobenius} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2 \ar[r, "\mathfrak{I}_p"] \ar[dr, "\int_{A,p}"'] & A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2 \ar[d, "\int_{A,p}"] \\ & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\] at every \(p \in U\), where \(\int_{A,p}\) is the germ of the Frobenius form. Measurement is consistent: the trace is preserved.

  2. Adjoint backreaction. The observation acts on the colour fibre via the adjoint representation of \(G\). At each point \(p\), the section \(\mathfrak{I}_p\) conjugates by \(G\): it rotates the colour degrees of freedom, shifting the substrate parameter \(q \mapsto q' = q + \delta q\) via the Hopf coaction: \[\begin{equation} \label{eq:observation-substrate} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\Delta"] \ar[d, "\mathfrak{I}_p"'] & A \otimes A \ar[r, "\mathfrak{I}_p \otimes S"] & A \otimes A \ar[d, "\mu"] \\ A \ar[rr, "\int_A"'] & & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\] with \(\delta q(p) = \int_A(\mathfrak{I}_p(a_{(1)})\,S(a_{(2)}))\). Observing the universe changes it: the act of reading the field feeds back through the colour fibre into the Reeb flow.

An intent at a point is the restriction \(\mathfrak{I}_p = \mathfrak{I}|_p\), recovering the germ-level endomorphism \(\mathfrak{I}_p \colon A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2 \to A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2\). The sign \(\epsilon\) determines whether the crossing injected at \(p\) is \(\sigma_i\) (forward, \(\epsilon = +1\)) or \(\sigma_i^{-1}\) (backward, \(\epsilon = -1\)) in the braiding-induced ordering \(\prec_c\).

📄

Proposition 2.55 ✗ no Lean (Observation increases quantum energy and deforms the action).

Proposition. Let \(\mathfrak{I}\in \Gamma(U, \mathrm{Ad}(J^1 \mathcal{S}))\) be an observation (observation) with substrate perturbation \(\delta q\). Then:

  1. (Quantum energy increases.) The quantum Planck constant \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) (quantum Planck constant) satisfies \[\hbar_{q + \delta q} - \hbar_q \;=\; \frac{\delta q}{q(q + \delta q)} \;>\; 0\] for \(\delta q > 0\). Every observation with positive substrate perturbation strictly increases the quantum energy of the system.

  2. (Action deformation.) The categorical action \(S_q[\nabla, \lambda, \psi]\) (categorical action) evaluated at the perturbed parameter \(q' = q + \delta q\) satisfies \[S_{q'} \;=\; S_q \;+\; \delta q \cdot \frac{\partial S_q}{\partial q} \;+\; O((\delta q)^2)\] The first-order shift \(\partial S_q / \partial q\) is the observation cost: the rate at which the action changes per unit of substrate perturbation.

  3. (Classical energy is unconstrained in sign.) The classical energy (the \(q \to 1\) shadow of the action) can increase or decrease under observation, provided the change is continuous. Only the quantum energy (the \(\hbar_q\)-dependent terms) is monotonically increased.

Proof of Observation increases quantum energy and deforms the action. (1) \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) is strictly increasing in \(q\) for \(q > 0\). Its derivative \(d\hbar_q/dq = q^{-2} > 0\). Hence \(\delta q > 0\) implies \(\delta\hbar_q > 0\).

(2) Direct Taylor expansion of \(S_{q'}\) about \(q\).

(3) The classical action \(S_1 = \lim_{q \to 1} S_q\) depends on \(\nabla, \lambda, \psi\) but not on \(q\). An observation that changes \(\nabla\) or \(\psi\) while holding \(q\) fixed modifies the classical energy by the variational equations (Einstein, Yang–Mills, transport). The sign of this modification is unconstrained — it depends on the observer’s choice of how to act on the state bundle. The continuity requirement is the Frobenius compatibility axiom: the observation must preserve the trace. \(\square\) ◻

Geometric interpretations

📄

Proposition 2.56 ∀ stated (Closed formula for the \(q\)-codifferential \(\delta_q\)). \(\forall\)

Let \(d_q = q^{-1}\,d + (1 - q^{-1})\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\) be the \(q\)-exterior derivative (categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative). The formal adjoint of \(d_q\) with respect to the Webster inner product \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_\theta\) is

\[\delta_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,\delta \;+\; (1 - q^{-1})\,\mathcal{L}_\xi^* \circ \iota_\xi,\]

characterised uniquely by the adjoint relation

\[\langle d_q\,\alpha,\, \beta \rangle_\theta \;=\; \langle \alpha,\, \delta_q\,\beta \rangle_\theta\]

for all compactly supported forms \(\alpha, \beta\).

Categorical instanton and self-duality

📄

Definition 2.57 ∀ stated (Categorical instanton). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) with connection \(\nabla\) (categorical connection) and \(q\)-Hodge star \(\star_q\) (\(q\)-Hodge star). The connection \(\nabla\) is an instanton if its curvature \(F_\nabla \in \Omega^2(A)\) is \(\star_q\)-self-dual:

\[\star_q\, F_\nabla \;=\; F_\nabla.\]

Equivalently, the curvature factors through the self-dual projection:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:instanton-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \otimes A \ar[r, "\nabla \circ \nabla"] \ar[dr, "0"'] & \Omega^2(A) \ar[d, "\pi^-"] \\ & \Omega^-(A) \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

where \(\pi^- = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mathrm{id} - \star_q)\) is the anti-self-dual projector and \(\Omega^-(A) = \ker(\mathrm{id} + \star_q)\).

📄

Lemma 2.58 ∀ stated (Irreducibility from observability). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe. Any categorical instanton \(\nabla\) (categorical instanton) is irreducible: \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1},\,\mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-irreducible-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[column sep=2.5em] \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "0"] & \mathrm{Ad}(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(the only morphism is zero)} \end{equation}\]

Proof of Irreducibility from observability. \(\forall\)

Suppose \(s \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is a non-zero invariant morphism. The following diagram commutes:

Since \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is the trace-free part of \(A \otimes A^*\), the Frobenius form \(\int_A\) vanishes on it: \(\int_A \circ s = 0\). But \(\int_A\) is non-degenerate by the observability axiom, so \(s = 0\). ◻

📄

Proposition 2.59 ∀ stated (Categorical self-duality). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with volume form \(\mathrm{vol} \in \Omega^n(A)\) (\(q\)-Hodge star). Every connection \(\nabla\) that is a critical point of the categorical Yang–Mills functional

\[S[\nabla] \;=\; \int_A\!\bigl(\star_q(F_\nabla) \cdot F_\nabla\bigr)\]

is an instanton (categorical instanton). That is, the following diagram commutes:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:self-duality-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3.5em] \Omega^2(A) \ar[r, "\star_q"] \ar[d, "\int_A(\,\cdot\, {*}\, \cdot\,)"'] & \Omega^2(A) \ar[d, "\int_A(\,\cdot\, {*}\, \cdot\,)"] \\ \mathbf{1} \ar[r, "\mathrm{id}"'] & \mathbf{1} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad F_\nabla \in \Omega^+(A). \end{equation}\]

Proof of Categorical self-duality. \(\forall\)

By the Bogomolny decomposition in the dagger category,

\[\int_A(F_\nabla^* \cdot F_\nabla) \;=\; 2\,\int_A({F_\nabla^-}^* \cdot F_\nabla^-) + \int_A(F_\nabla \wedge_q F_\nabla),\]

where the second term is topological (determined by the class \([F_\nabla] \in \Omega^2(A)/\mathrm{exact}\)). Minimising \(S[\nabla]\) forces \(F_\nabla^- = 0\), which is exactly the self-duality condition. ◻

Non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\) and jet prolongation

📄

Proposition 2.60 ∀ stated (Non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)). \(\forall\)

Let \(d_q\) be the categorical \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative (categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative). The composition \(d_q^2 = d_q \circ d_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+2}(A)\) is given by

\[d_q^2\,\alpha \;=\; q^{-1}(1 - q^{-1})\;\omega_V \wedge_q [\xi,\, \alpha],\]

where \(\omega_V \in \Omega^2(A)\) is the curvature of the weight decomposition (the image of the unit \(1_A\) under \(\pi_V \circ d \circ d\)) and \([\xi, \alpha]\) is the Lie derivative along the generator \(\xi\) of the \(T\)-action (weight decomposition). The following diagram displays the obstruction to nilpotence:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:dq-squared-cd} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=2.5em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "d_q"] \ar[dr, "d_q^2"'] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \ar[d, "d_q"] \\ & \Omega^{k+2}(A) \end{tikzcd} \qquad d_q^2 = 0 \;\Longleftrightarrow\; q = 1 \;\text{ or }\; [\xi, \alpha] = 0. \end{equation}\]

In particular, \(d_q^2 \neq 0\) for generic \(\alpha\) whenever \(q \neq 1\): the \(q\)-deformed de Rham complex is not a cochain complex. On \(\xi\)-invariant forms (the horizontal subcomplex \(\Omega^k_H(A)\)), \(d_q\) does reduce to \(q^{-1} d\) and \(d_q^2 = 0\).

Proof of Non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\). \(\forall\)

Write \(a = q^{-1}\) and \(b = 1 - q^{-1}\), so \(d_q = a\,d + b\,\pi_V d\). Then

\[\begin{align*} d_q^2 &= (a\,d + b\,\pi_V d)(a\,d + b\,\pi_V d) \\ &= a^2\,\underbrace{d^2}_{= 0} + ab\,(d \circ \pi_V d + \pi_V d \circ d) + b^2\,\underbrace{\pi_V d \circ \pi_V d}_{= 0}. \end{align*}\]

The first term vanishes because \(d^2 = 0\) in the non-commutative de Rham complex. The last term vanishes because \(\pi_V\) is the projection onto the vertical (weight-\(1\)) summand of the Reeb decomposition \(\Omega^k(A) = \Omega^k_H(A) \oplus \theta_A \wedge \Omega^{k-1}_H(A)\): the exterior derivative \(d\) applied to a vertical form produces a form whose vertical component has weight \(\geq 2\) in \(\theta_A\), but the contact distribution forces \(\theta_A \wedge \theta_A = 0\) (since \(\theta_A\) is a \(1\)-form), so \(\pi_V(d(\pi_V\alpha)) = 0\). For the middle term, we first establish the key commutation relation. Since \(\pi_V\) is the projection onto the non-zero-weight summand of the \(T\)-action on \(\Omega^k(A)\), and \(d\) is the universal derivation, the commutator \([d, \pi_V] = d \circ \pi_V - \pi_V \circ d\) measures how much \(d\) fails to preserve the weight grading. On a weight-\(n\) form \(\alpha_n\), we have \(d\alpha_n = (d\alpha_n)_H + (d\alpha_n)_V\); the weight-shift arises from the Lie derivative along \(\xi\) (the generator of \(T\)), giving

\[[d, \pi_V]\,\alpha = \mathcal{L}_\xi(\alpha) - \pi_V(\mathcal{L}_\xi(\alpha)) = \pi_H(\mathcal{L}_\xi\,\alpha).\]

Since \(\pi_H + \pi_V = \mathrm{id}\) and \(\mathcal{L}_\xi = \iota_\xi \circ d + d \circ \iota_\xi\) (Cartan’s formula), the middle term simplifies: \(d(\pi_V d\,\alpha) + \pi_V d(d\,\alpha) = \omega_V \wedge_q [\xi, \alpha]\) where \(\omega_V = d(\pi_V(d\,1_A)) \in \Omega^2(A)\) is the curvature of the weight projection — a canonical \(2\)-form measuring the failure of the horizontal distribution to be integrable. ◻

📄

Definition 2.61 ∀ stated (Categorical \(q\)-Lie bracket). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with Reeb derivation \(\xi\) (categorical Reeb derivation) and substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter). The \(q\)-deformed Lie bracket on derivations of \(A\) is

\[[X, Y]_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,[X, Y] + (1 - q^{-1})\,\bigl(\theta_A(X)\,[\xi, Y] - \theta_A(Y)\,[\xi, X]\bigr),\]

where \(\theta_A\) is the canonical \(1\)-form dual to \(\xi\) and \([X, Y]\) is the commutator of derivations in \(\mathbf{C}\).

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:q-lie-bracket-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathrm{Der}(A) \otimes \mathrm{Der}(A) \ar[r, "{[\,\cdot\,,\cdot\,]}"] \ar[d, "{[\,\cdot\,,\cdot\,]_q}"'] & \mathrm{Der}(A) \\ \mathrm{Der}(A) \ar[ur, equal, "q{=}1"'] \end{tikzcd} \end{equation}\]

📄

Definition 2.62 ∀ stated (Categorical \(q\)-deformed connection). \(\forall\)

Let \(\nabla\) be a connection on \(A\) (categorical connection) and \(\xi\) the Reeb derivation (categorical Reeb derivation). The \(q\)-deformed connection is

\[\nabla_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,\nabla + (1 - q^{-1})\,(\iota_\xi\, \nabla)\,\theta_A.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:q-connection-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\nabla"] \ar[dr, "\nabla_q"'] & \Omega^1(A) \otimes A \ar[d, "q^{-1}\,\mathrm{id} \,+\, (1 - q^{-1})\,\theta_A \circ \iota_\xi"] \\ & \Omega^1(A) \otimes A \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{($q$-connection)} \end{equation}\]

At \(q = 1\), \(\nabla_q = \nabla\).

\(q\)-Deformed operators

📄

Example 2.63 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Deformed exterior derivative). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean realisation, the categorical \(d_q\) (categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative) specialises to \(d_q \colon \Omega^k(M) \to \Omega^{k+1}(M)\):

\[d_q\,\alpha = q^{-1}\,d\alpha + (1 - q^{-1})\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\,\alpha.\]

The vertical projection \(\pi_V \circ d\) becomes \(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\) via the (Reeb decomposition), and \(d_q^2 = q^{-1}(1-q^{-1})\,d\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\) (categorical \(d_q^2 = 0\)) specialises via \(\omega_V = d\theta\).

📄

Example 2.64 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Deformed Lie bracket). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean realisation, the categorical Reeb derivation (categorical Reeb derivation) induces the \(q\)-deformed Lie bracket on smooth vector fields \(V, W \in \mathfrak{X}(M)\):

\[[V, W]_q = q^{-1}\,[V, W] + (1 - q^{-1})\,\bigl(\theta(V)\,\mathcal{L}_\xi W - \theta(W)\,\mathcal{L}_\xi V\bigr).\]

📄

Example 2.65 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Deformed connection). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean realisation, the categorical \(q\)-connection (categorical \(q\)-connection) specialises to \(A_q = q^{-1}\,A + (1 - q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi\,A\;\theta\), where \(q\) is the substrate parameter (substrate parameter). At \(q = 1\) this recovers the full instanton connection \(A\); as \(q \to \infty\), the connection reduces to its Reeb component \(\iota_\xi A\;\theta\), retaining only the vertical (internal spin) part of the gauge potential.

📄

Example 2.66 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Deformed Reeb vector field). \(\forall\)

The categorical Reeb derivation \(\xi\) (categorical Reeb derivation) deforms in the archimedean setting to \(\xi_q\), acting on smooth functions \(f \in C^\infty(M)\) by

\[\xi_q(f) \;=\; q^{-1}\,\xi(f) + (1 - q^{-1})\,[\xi, X_f]_q,\]

where \(X_f\) is the horizontal lift of \(\mathrm{grad}_{g_\theta}\,f\) to \(H = \ker\theta\) and \([\,\cdot\,,\cdot\,]_q\) is the \(q\)-deformed Lie bracket (\(q\)-Lie bracket).

📄

Example 2.67 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Deformed Reeb flow). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean realisation, the categorical \(q\)-Reeb derivation (categorical \(q\)-Reeb flow) specialises to the \(q\)-deformed Reeb vector field \(\xi_q\) (\(q\)-Reeb vector field), which generates a one-parameter family of diffeomorphisms \(\phi_t^q \colon M \to M\), \(t \in \mathbb{R}\):

\[\frac{d}{dt}\,\phi_t^q \;=\; \xi_q \circ \phi_t^q, \qquad \phi_0^q = \mathrm{id}_M.\]

📄

Example 2.68 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Torsion leaf). \(\forall\)

Let \(H = \ker\theta \subset TM\) be the horizontal distribution on the CR manifold \(M\). A \(q\)-torsion leaf is a maximal integral submanifold \(L \hookrightarrow M\) of \(H\) that is invariant under the \(q\)-deformed Reeb flow (\(q\)-Reeb flow):

\[T_p L \;\subset\; H_p \quad\text{for all } p \in L, \qquad\text{and}\qquad \phi_t^q(L) = L \quad\text{for all } t \in \mathbb{R}.\]

Elaboration: categorical context

We see colours — three of them mix to white. We rotate, translate, and boost, yet measurements remain invariant. Time flows forward. Multiple observers share one world, not private copies. We integrate, differentiate, and compute; the universe has volume. Free will — the ability to choose what to measure — produces outcomes not determined by initial conditions.

These observations, once stated precisely, determine a specific algebraic structure: a rigid monoidal category equipped with a fibre functor and a Frobenius trace \(\int_A\). We call this structure a quantum observable universe (QOU). Its axioms encode the features listed above and nothing more.

An assumption this paper does not make is that the constants of our universe are constant. We allow them to vary — in a controlled, algebraic way — and ask: what does that change?

We do not ask what the universe is; we ask what its mechanics do. Category theory is the natural language, because it describes transformation without committing to ontology. Noether’s principle converts observed symmetries into conserved quantities; the Frobenius trace \(\int_A\) is the categorical Noether current. The \(q\)-deformation of the substrate shifts conservation laws from exact identities to approximate ones, with anomalies that are themselves measurable.

What follows from these axioms is broad in scope and specific in detail. The symmetry group \(\mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) is not assumed; it emerges via Tannaka–Krein reconstruction. Particles are knots; interactions are braid relations. The capacity for computation is a consequence, not an input.

The paper is organised as follows.

Part I: Foundations. Chapter 1 introduces the quantum universe (QU): a rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\), a Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\), and a fibre functor \(\tau\). The Frobenius trace \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) provides categorical integration; combined with Kähler differentials on \(A\), it provides differentiation. Self-duality \(A \cong A^{\vee}\) ensures these operations are compatible. From these ingredients the chapter derives the Frobenius relation, the dagger involution, and the Tannaka–Krein reconstruction of the symmetry group.

Chapter 2 imposes three cohomological constraints — observability, measurability, and volume — that promote the QU to a quantum observable universe (QOU). These constraints remove unobservable hidden structures and bad behaviour. Self-duality within this constrained space forces the gauge group \(G = \mathrm{SU}_2(R)\) to emerge naturally, together with a natural coordinate \(q\), an ordering direction, and a strict genus limitation of four on the state space. The QOU is characterised by the archimedean tuple

\[(\mathbf{C},\; \theta,\; G,\; \mathcal{S}).\]

A categorical Dirac operator \(\mathcal{D}_\nabla\), forced by the Frobenius–Hopf structure, decomposes into gravity (Ricci), gauge (Yang–Mills), and matter terms — yielding the categorical action

\[\mathcal{S}_q[\nabla, \textstyle\int_A, \psi] \;=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{tr}\bigl(q \cdot R_{\int}\bigr)}_{\text{gravity}} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A \!\circ\, \mathrm{tr}_A\bigl( F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla \bigr)}_{\text{gauge}} \;+\; \underbrace{\textstyle\int_A\!\bigl(\psi^{\ast} \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\,\psi\bigr)}_{\text{matter}},\]

from which quantum versions of the Einstein, Yang–Mills, and Dirac equations follow.

Chapter 3 addresses the obstructions that arise when local categorical data is extended globally. The Yekutieli lifting condition makes this precise: an object admits a lift if and only if its obstruction class \(\kappa(x) \in H^2(S, B)\) vanishes. A key result is the Descartes condition \(\chi(A) = -6\), forced by the lifting obstructions and the Archimedean constraint.

Part II: Structure. Chapter 4 replaces continuum path integrals with discrete braid-group computations. Fundamental particles — photons, electrons, protons — are defined purely mathematically as specific knots and words on the genus-\(4\) state space. Particle interactions are modelled through braid relations by computing the Gröbner–Shirshov basis normal form of knot words using Hecke relations, where the parameter \(q\) tracks the energy cost of each crossing. The topological mass formula

\[\mathfrak{m}(K) \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K)}{\hbar_q^{\,2}}\]

acts as a Feynman path integral via the non-abelian Stokes formula, but because the space is finite-dimensional it naturally avoids standard infinities. The embeddability bound on \(\Sigma_4\) yields exactly \(7\) transfer matrices — six non-trivial force operators and the identity (interaction completeness).

Chapter 5 examines concrete realisations of the QOU axioms: archimedean, \(p\)-adic, and finite-field models.

Chapter 6 develops the spectral theory of the Frobenius–Hopf algebra. The local \(q\)-zeta function of Bring’s curve encodes the Frobenius eigenvalues, and the Hasse–Weil bound confines them to the critical line \(|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}\). The categorical machinery provides a natural framing for classical questions in analytic number theory — including the Riemann hypothesis, the Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture , and the Collatz problem — through the Kummer tower associated to the Frobenius–Hopf algebra.

Chapter 7 explores the correlation between the knot structures developed in earlier chapters and topological fluid dynamics, offering an obstruction-based perspective on Navier–Stokes regularity.

Chapter 8 examines the categorical framework through the lens of information theory and computational complexity. The Gröbner–Shirshov basis makes computation confluent; the Reeb flow generates a dynamical system whose boundary is a Julia-set fractal. The framework provides an interesting perspective on questions such as P versus NP in terms of categorical obstructions and event horizons for information flow. Crossing energy relates to categorical mass by \(E_{\mathfrak{H}} = \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot c_q^{\,2}\) where \(c_q = 1/(q - 1)\).

Part III: The Descartes Universe and Observations. Chapter 9 maps the genus-\(4\) constraint to Bring’s surface \(\Sigma_4\), a complex curve with Euler characteristic \(-6\) and maximal automorphisms (\(S_5\)). This surface serves as the foundational state space: its coral tubes — the exceptional divisors — provide coordinate systems for spacetime and the electromagnetic field, mapping exactly where vertex operators interact. Within this space, embeddable knots form a basis for homology and cohomology; specific knots and torus-knot words define the full particle spectrum. The geometric structure also provides a natural setting in which to examine Yang–Mills theory and the question of a mass gap.

Chapter 10 confronts theory with experiment. We use observed CODATA values for the muon and electron mass to determine \(q_0\) for our local patch of the universe:

\[(1 - q^{-1})^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)}{m_\mu / m_e} \qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad q \;=\; q_0 \;+\; O\!\bigl(2.2 \times 10^{-8}\bigr).\]

From this single parameter we derive formulas for the masses of all atoms parametrised by \(q_0\), which align with observed values to good precision. The transfer matrices describe hadron half-lives that match observation.

Chapter 11 develops the \(q\)-geometric Langlands correspondence that connects the categorical framework to the geometric Langlands programme.

The Glossary maps paper terminology to Mathlib declarations, the Knot-Periodic Table collects the elements with their knot assignments, and the Index of Definitions provides a searchable reference.

In \(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum observable universe, the condition \(H^0(M, \mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0\) eliminates all infinitesimal gauge symmetries, while \(\Gamma_c(M,\mathcal{S}) = 0\) ensures the jet-bundle map \(\Gamma(J^1 \mathcal{S}) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{A}(P)\) is injective.

📄

Proposition 2.69 ∀ stated (From Tannakian emergence to 2-group quantum flatness). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe satisfying the (categorical volume constraint), so that \(G_q = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau) \cong \mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) (SU(2) emergence). Then the inner-automorphism \(2\)-group \(\mathrm{INN}(G_q)\) is the unique strict \(2\)-group whose quantum flatness condition \(F_A = B\) reproduces the instanton equation \(F_A^{-} = 0\) under the simplicity constraint.

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:emergence-to-quantum-flat-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] F_A \ar[r, equal, "\text{instanton}"] \ar[d, "F_A = B"'] & F_A^+ \ar[d, equal, "\text{simplicity}"] \\ B \ar[r, equal] & F_A^+ \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(derived quantum flatness)} \end{equation}\]

Quantum flatness is not an independent assumption: it is a derived consequence of the instanton axiom. The instanton condition \(F_A = F_A^+\) (self-dual curvature) combined with the simplicity constraint \(B = F_A^+\) gives \(F_A = B\) automatically. The \(2\)-group language is a descriptive overlay that makes the higher-categorical structure manifest, not an additional physical constraint.

Proof of From Tannakian emergence to 2-group quantum flatness.

The argument proceeds in three steps.

Step 1: The volume constraint determines the Lie algebra. The categorical volume constraint provides a non-degenerate epimorphism \(\epsilon \colon \Lambda^2 V \to \mathbf{1}\). Under the forgetful functor \(\tau\), this endows the rank-\(2\) module \(\tau(V)\) with a \(q\)-antisymmetric pairing whose invariance algebra is \(\mathfrak{su}_q(2)\). This is the Lie algebra of the reconstructed group \(G_q\), and hence of the crossed module \(\partial \colon G_q \xrightarrow{\mathrm{id}} G_q\) defining \(\mathrm{INN}(G_q)\).

Step 2: The determinant-one condition descends to the 2-form datum. A \(2\)-connection \((A, B)\) for the principal \(2\)-bundle of \(\mathrm{INN}(G_q)\) takes values in \(\mathfrak{g}_q = \mathfrak{su}_q(2)\). Quantum flatness sets \(B = F_A\), so \(B\) inherits the tracelessness forced by the determinant constraint \(\det(g_V) = 1\) of SU(2) emergence: \(B\) is \(\mathrm{Ad}(P)\)-valued with \(\mathrm{tr}\,B = 0\), i.e. \(\mathfrak{su}_q(2)\)-valued rather than \(\mathfrak{gl}_q(2)\)-valued.

Step 3: Simplicity plus quantum flatness gives the instanton equation. Imposing the simplicity constraint \(B \in \Gamma(\Lambda^+\!H^* \otimes \mathrm{Ad}(P))\) (self-dual 2-group) and combining with \(F_A = B\) yields \(F_A = F_A^+\), hence \(F_A^- = 0\). Step 1 guarantees the structure group is \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\)—not a quotient of \(\mathrm{GL}_q(2)\)—so the instanton moduli space carries the gauge symmetry dictated by the categorical axioms. ◻

Non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\) and the \(q\)-jacobiator

📄

Proposition 2.70 ∀ stated (\(d_q^2\) does not vanish). \(\forall\)

The archimedean specialisation of the categorical \(d_q^2\) formula (non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)) yields, for the \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative (\(q\)-exterior derivative) acting on \(\Omega^k(M)\):

\[d_q^2\,\alpha \;=\; q^{-1}(1 - q^{-1})\,d\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\,\alpha.\]

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:dq-squared-archimedean-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(M) \ar[r, "d_q"] \ar[rr, bend left=25, "d_q^2"] & \Omega^{k+1}(M) \ar[r, "d_q"] & \Omega^{k+2}(M) \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{($d_q^2 \neq 0$ for $q \neq 1$)} \end{equation}\]

Here the categorical curvature \(\omega_V\) of the weight projection specialises to \(d\theta\) (the symplectic form on \(H\)) via the (categorical–geometric correspondence), and \([\xi, \alpha]\) becomes \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\,\alpha\).

In particular, \(d_q^2 = 0\) if and only if \(q = 1\) (classical case) or \(\alpha\) lies in the kernel of \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\) (Reeb-invariant forms). On horizontal \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\)-invariant forms, \(d_q\) does define a cochain complex.

Proof of \(d_q^2\) does not vanish.

Write \(a = q^{-1}\) and \(b = 1 - q^{-1}\), so \(a + b = 1\). Then

\[\begin{align*} d_q^2\,\alpha &= d_q\bigl(a\,d\alpha + b\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\bigr) \\ &= a^2\,d^2\alpha + ab\,d(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha) + ab\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\,d\alpha + b^2\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha). \end{align*}\]

The first term vanishes since \(d^2 = 0\). The second expands as \(ab\,d\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha - ab\,\theta \wedge d\mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\). The third term cancels the second’s negative part because \([d,\, \mathcal{L}_\xi] = 0\) implies \(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\,d\alpha = \theta \wedge d\,\mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\). For the fourth term, the Reeb field satisfies \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\theta = 0\) (since \(\iota_\xi d\theta = 0\) and \(\theta(\xi)=1\)), so \(\mathcal{L}_\xi(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha) = \theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi^2\alpha\); the factor \(\theta \wedge \theta = 0\) in \(b^2\,\theta \wedge \theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi^2\alpha\) kills this term. Hence \(d_q^2\alpha = ab\,d\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\). ◻

📄

Proposition 2.71 ∀ stated (Jacobiator of the q-Lie bracket). \(\forall\)
