Hadron Algebra and Knot Factorisation

📄

Definition 4.35 ∀ stated (Hadron (stable knot composite)). \(\forall\)

A hadron is a stable composite of fundamental knots: one whose crossing energy is negative, so that binding dominates repulsion.

Let \(K_1, \ldots, K_n\) be prime knot types in the representation category \(\mathbf{C}\), and let \(\mathcal{L}\) be a link encoding their internal entanglement. A hadron is a composite

\[\mathfrak{H}_p \;=\; [K_1, \ldots, K_n]_p \;\bowtie\; \mathcal{L}\]

satisfying the stability condition

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}_p) \;<\; 0\]

where \(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}\) is the crossing energy (crossing energy). The subscript \(p\) is the localization point: it determines the colour sector of the exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_p\) in which the constituents are coupled. The colour-tube coupling is not an independent datum — it is inherited from \(p\). The symbol \(\bowtie\) denotes the linking operation.

📄

Proposition 4.36 ∀ stated (Closure of hadron operations under braiding, Hopf linking, skein action, and fusion). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(\mathbf{C}\) be a rigid braided monoidal category and let \(\mathfrak{H} \in \mathrm{Sym}^n(K)\) be a hadron (hadron) with constituent knots \(K_1, \ldots, K_n\).

  1. Braiding closure. The braiding \(\beta_{K_i, K_j}\) descends to an involution on \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(K)\). For the antisymmetric (fermionic) product, exchanging two identical constituents produces \(-1\).

  2. Hopf linking closure. The linking operation \(\ell_{ij} \colon K_i \otimes K_j \to K_i \mathbin{\#_{\mathrm{Hopf}}} K_j\) is an endomorphism of \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) with a two-sided inverse (unlinking) when the linking number is trivial.

  3. Skein closure. The \(q\)-deformed skein relation \(q \cdot L_+ - q^{-1} \cdot L_- = (q - q^{-1}) \cdot L_0\) resolves any linked composite into a polynomial in \(q\) times unlinked constituents, yielding the mass formula \(\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{H}) = Q(q) \cdot \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}) + \sum_i \mathcal{M}(K_i)\).

  4. Fusion closure. For hadrons \(\mathfrak{H}_1 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_1}(K)\) and \(\mathfrak{H}_2 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_2}(K)\), the fusion \(\mathfrak{H}_1 \star \mathfrak{H}_2 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_1 + n_2}(K)\) is again a hadron.

📄

Remark 4.37 ✗ no Lean (Operations on hadrons).

The symmetric product \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(K)\) carries natural operations inherited from the braiding and Hopf link structure of \(\mathbf{C}\).

Braiding. The braiding \(\beta_{K_i, K_j} \colon K_i \otimes K_j \xrightarrow{\sim} K_j \otimes K_i\) permutes constituent knots within a hadron. Since \(\mathrm{Sym}^n\) quotients by the symmetric group action, the braiding descends to an involution on \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(K)\). For fermions (antisymmetric product), the braiding picks up a sign: exchanging two identical constituents produces \(-1\).

Hopf linking. Two knots \(K_i, K_j\) within the same hadron can be linked via the Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\). This linking operation

\[\ell_{ij} \;\colon\; K_i \otimes K_j \;\longrightarrow\; K_i \mathbin{\#_{\mathrm{Hopf}}} K_j\]

replaces two separate constituents with a single linked pair. The inverse operation (unlinking) decomposes a linked pair back into its constituents, when the linking number is trivial.

Skein action. The \(q\)-deformed Skein relations act on \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) by resolving crossings in the linked configuration. At each crossing, the Skein relation provides the decomposition:

\[q \cdot L_+ \;-\; q^{-1} \cdot L_- \;=\; (q - q^{-1}) \cdot L_0\]

where \(L_+\), \(L_-\), \(L_0\) are the positive-crossing, negative-crossing, and smoothed configurations. Iterating over all crossings resolves the linked composite into a polynomial in \(q\) times unlinked constituents, yielding the mass formula \(\mathcal{M}(\mathfrak{H}) = Q(q) \cdot \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}) + \sum_i \mathcal{M}(K_i)\).

Fusion. Two hadrons \(\mathfrak{H}_1 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_1}(K)\) and \(\mathfrak{H}_2 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_2}(K)\) can be fused into a composite \(\mathfrak{H}_1 \star \mathfrak{H}_2 \in \mathrm{Sym}^{n_1 + n_2}(K)\) by forming the Hopf link between their binding structures. This models hadron scattering at the categorical level.

📄

Remark 4.38 ✗ no Lean (Knot factorization through tensor powers of \(V\)).

The tensor generation property of the fundamental object \(V\) has a concrete consequence for the hadron construction: every constituent knot type \(K_i\) in a hadron factors through a tensor power of \(V\).

Specifically, if \(K_i\) is a knot whose associated simple object is \(V_{j_i}\), then \(V_{j_i}\) appears as a direct summand of \(V^{\otimes 2j_i}\). The PawLei basis provides a canonical embedding

\[\iota_{j_i} \colon V_{j_i} \;\hookrightarrow\; V_{1/2}^{\otimes 2j_i},\]

so a hadron \(\mathfrak{H} \in V_{j_1} \otimes \cdots \otimes V_{j_n}\) can be written in a universal tensor form:

\[\mathfrak{H} \;\hookrightarrow\; V_{1/2}^{\otimes 2(j_1 + \cdots + j_n)}.\]

This embedding is not unique — the choice of PawLei basis element for each factor corresponds to a choice of partial-wave channel. The physical hadron is obtained by summing over all channels weighted by the Skein polynomial, so the hadronic mass formula arises as a contraction of the universal tensor with the Hopf link invariant.

In the QOU framework, this factorization explains why all composite particles are ultimately built from the single two-dimensional object \(V\): the categorical dimension \(2\) of \(V\) is the minimal non-trivial dimension compatible with the volume constraint, and tensor generation ensures no further building blocks are needed.

📄

Definition 4.39 ∀ stated (Localized hadron). \(\forall\)

A localized hadron is a hadron (Definition) that has been placed at a categorical point \(p\) of the projective line \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) (Definition).

Formally, a localized hadron at \(p\) is a morphism in \(\mathbf{C}\):

\[H_p \;\colon\; \mathbf{1} \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Sym}^n\!\bigl(\mathcal{K}_p\bigr) \;\otimes\; \mathcal{L}_{p}^{\mathrm{bind}}\]

where \(\mathcal{K}_p\) denotes the fibre of knot types at \(p\) and \(\mathcal{L}_{p}^{\mathrm{bind}}\) is the binding Hopf link at \(p\). The morphism from \(\mathbf{1}\) is what distinguishes a localized hadron from an abstract one: it selects a specific point in the base space where the composite knot is situated.

📄

Definition 4.40 ∀ stated (Fibre-compatible hadron embedding). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathfrak{H} \in \mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) be a hadron (Definition) and let \(\mathcal{S}_p\) denote the fibre of the knot bundle over a point \(p \in \mathbb{P}(V)\) (Definition). A fibre-compatible hadron embedding is a morphism

\[\iota_p \;\colon\; \mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}} \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{S}_p\]

satisfying the following conditions:

  1. Integrability. The embedding \(\iota_p\) is integrable in the sense that the abstract hadron data (linking, braiding, Skein decomposition) can be consistently realized within the geometric structure of the fibre \(\mathcal{S}_p\). Concretely, \(\iota_p\) must intertwine the abstract Skein action (operations on hadrons) with the geometric operations on knots in \(\mathcal{S}_p\).

  2. Fibre confinement. The image \(\iota_p(\mathfrak{H})\) is entirely contained in the fibre \(\mathcal{S}_p\). No constituent knot extends to a neighbouring fibre \(E_{p'}\) for \(p' \neq p\). This is enforced by a finite Mobius energy bound: \[\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{Mob}}(\iota_p) \;<\; \infty,\] which prevents the knot complement from developing cusps that would reach the boundary of the fibre.

  3. Hopf compatibility. The embedding respects linking and unlinking via the Hopf structure: the diagram \[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}} \ar[r, "\iota_p"] \ar[d, "\ell_{ij}"'] & \mathcal{S}_p \ar[d, "\ell_{ij}"] \\ \mathrm{Sym}^{n'}(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}' \ar[r, "\iota_p'"'] & \mathcal{S}_p \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(Hopf compatibility)}\] commutes for every linking operation \(\ell_{ij}\).

  4. Volume compatibility. The embedding preserves hyperbolic volumes: \(\mathrm{vol}(\iota_p(K_i)) = \mathrm{vol}(K_i)\) for each constituent knot \(K_i\). This ensures that the mass contribution of each knot, computed via the hyperbolic volume, is faithfully represented in the fibre.

A localized hadron (Definition) equipped with a fibre-compatible embedding is a physically realized hadron: it is both situated at a base point and faithfully embedded in the fibre geometry. The integrability condition is the key structural requirement — it asserts that the abstract algebraic hadron can be "integrated" into a concrete geometric realization.

Skein Generation and Particle Correspondence

📄

Proposition 4.41 ∀ stated (Skein generation of hadrons from mass-zero fundamentals). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\) and Skein module \(\mathcal{S}_q = \mathcal{S}_q(\mathbf{C})\). The Skein module \(\mathcal{S}_q\) is generated as an algebra by:

  1. The fundamental (mass-zero) knot types \(\{K_i\}_{i \in \mathcal{F}}\) (torus knots), and

  2. The Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) (the binding operation).

Every hadron admits a terminal Skein resolution into a finite polynomial in these generators with coefficients in \(\mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\).

Proof of Skein generation.

Generators. A knot type \(K\) is fundamental if its hyperbolic volume vanishes: \(\mathrm{Vol}(K) = 0\). By the geometrization of knot complements, these are precisely the torus knots (and the unknot). In the particle dictionary, the fundamental knots are the fermions: the unknot (neutrino), trefoil \(3_1\) (electron), cinquefoil \(5_1\) (tau), and the torus\((p,2)\) family.

Generation. The Skein module \(\mathcal{S}_q\) is generated as an algebra by the fundamental knot types \(\{K_i\}_{i \in \mathcal{F}}\) and the Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\). Every hadron \(H \in \mathrm{Sym}^n(K) \otimes \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) admits a terminal Skein resolution: iterating the Skein relation

\[q \cdot L_+ \;-\; q^{-1} \cdot L_- \;=\; (q - q^{-1}) \cdot L_0\]

at every crossing terminates in a finite polynomial

\[[H] \;=\; \sum_{\alpha} c_\alpha(q) \cdot [K_{i_1}] \cdots [K_{i_k}]\]

where each \([K_{i_j}]\) is the class of a fundamental knot and \(c_\alpha(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\).

Mass from linking. Evaluating the mass functional \(\mathcal{M}\) on the Skein resolution gives:

\[\mathcal{M}(H) \;=\; \underbrace{Q(q) \cdot \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}})}_{\text{binding energy (from linking)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(K_i)}{\hbar_q^{\,2}}}_{\text{constituent mass (zero for torus knots)}}\]

where \(Q(q) \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) is the Skein polynomial of the linking configuration and \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\).

For hadrons composed entirely of fundamental (torus-knot) constituents, \(\mathrm{Vol}(K_i) = 0\) for all \(i\), so the entire inertial mass arises from the linking topology:

\[\mathcal{M}(H) \;=\; Q(q) \cdot \mathcal{M}(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}).\] ◻

📄

Definition 4.42 ∀ stated (Knot-particle generation from \(T_{m,n}\) torus knot generators). \(\forall\)

The particle spectrum is generated from a finite set of torus knot generators \(T_{m,n}\) (with \(\gcd(m,n) = 1\)) embedded in the standard torus \(\mathbb{T}^2 \subset S^3\), together with two linking operations that act on the exceptional divisor and the color-tube fibration.

Notation. A torus knot \(T_{m,n}\) winds \(m\) times around the meridian and \(n\) times around the longitude of \(\mathbb{T}^2\). We reserve \(q\) for the substrate parameter (substrate parameter) and \(p\) for base points, so the winding indices are always \((m,n)\).

Generator set. The torus knot generators are the family

\[\mathcal{G} \;=\; \bigl\{\, T_{m,n} \;\big|\; \gcd(m,n) = 1,\; m < n,\; m + n \leq N(\chi) \,\bigr\}\]

where \(N(\chi)\) is a cutoff determined by the Euler characteristic of the Frobenius–Hopf object. For the Descartes universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\), the bound is \(N(-6) = 9\), admitting:

Generator Knot Genus Crossings Particle sector
\(T_{1,0}\) Unknot \(0_1\) \(0\) \(0\) Neutrino (trivial braiding)
\(T_{2,3}\) Trefoil \(3_1\) \(1\) \(3\) Electron / Up quark (gen.\{} 1)
\(T_{2,5}\) Cinquefoil \(5_1\) \(2\) \(5\) Muon / gen-\(2\) quarks (gen.\{} 2)
\(T_{2,7}\) Septafoil \(7_1\) \(3\) \(7\) Tau / gen-\(3\) quarks (gen.\{} 3)

Proposition 4.43 ∀ stated (Knot–particle correspondence via \(q\)-Schur–Weyl duality). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(V = V_{1/2}\) be the fundamental representation of \(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\) and let \(B_n\) act faithfully on \(V^{\otimes n}\) via the \(R\)-matrix braiding (braid action on tensor products). By \(q\)-Schur–Weyl duality (knot eigenbasis completeness), \(V^{\otimes n}\) decomposes into irreducible summands labelled by partitions \(\lambda \vdash n\).

Then the Markov trace on \(H_n(q)\) assigns to each irreducible summand a knot type \(K_\lambda\) (the closure of any braid representative), establishing a bijection between:

  • Irreducible summands of \(V^{\otimes n}\) under the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\), and

  • Knot/link types arising as closures of \(n\)-strand braids.

In particular, each localized knot (localized knot) \((p, K)\) in a bundle corresponds to a unique irreducible summand, and hadrons (hadron) correspond to tensor products of such summands bound by Hopf links.

Bundle Structure and Observation

📄

Definition 4.45 ∀ stated (Bundle initial conditions). \(\forall\)

A bundle initial condition over the projective line \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) at a reference point in an affine chart is a formal sum of localized hadrons and photons at base points:

\[\mathcal{S}_0 \;=\; \sum_{i \in I} (p_i,\, H_i)\]

where each \((p_i, H_i)\) is a localized hadron (Definition) or a photon (\(H_i = \varnothing\)). The index set \(I\) may be infinite, and multiple constituents may share the same base point (bosonic and fermionic statistics are determined by the Skein algebra, not by a support constraint).

Equivalently, \(\mathcal{S}_0\) is a section of the free commutative monoid on the hadron sheaf \(\mathcal{H}\):

\[\mathcal{S}_0 \;\in\; \Gamma\!\bigl(\mathbb{P}(V),\; \mathrm{Free}_{\mathrm{CMon}}(\mathcal{H})\bigr).\]

This is a position-only specification: the positions \(\{p_i\}\) on \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) are known exactly, while the momenta are entirely undetermined. The categorical content is that \(\mathcal{S}_0\) specifies the fibre data of the bundle — which constituent sits in which fibre — without any information about the horizontal transport connecting neighbouring fibres.

The subsequent configurations \(\mathcal{S}_1, \mathcal{S}_2, \ldots\) represent the forward light cone from \(\mathcal{S}_0\): each step applies one iteration of the Reeb flow (information-theoretic time), adding horizontal transport and accumulating interaction relations. The backward sequence \(\mathcal{S}_{-1}, \mathcal{S}_{-2}, \ldots\) represents the past light cone (reversing computation). Whether the sequence extends infinitely in either direction, or terminates, is not assumed — it depends on the dynamics within the given affine chart.

For the equivalence relation on bundle initial conditions, see Definition.

📄

Proposition 4.46 ✗ no Lean (Sorting deposits energy \(q + q^{-1}\) per crossing in the colour fibre).

Proposition. Let \(T_i\) be the Hecke generator (R-matrix braiding) acting on \(V \otimes V\), where \(V\) is the fundamental representation. Then:

  1. (Eigenspace decomposition.) The R-matrix decomposes \(V \otimes V\) into two eigenspaces: \[V \otimes V \;=\; \mathrm{Sym}^2(V) \;\oplus\; \textstyle\bigwedge^2(V)\] with eigenvalues \(q\) (symmetric, ordered) and \(-q^{-1}\) (antisymmetric, disordered) respectively. These are the two roots of the Hecke relation \(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\).

  2. (Sorting is projection.) A sorting operation — swapping two adjacent items into the correct order — is the projection from \(\bigwedge^2(V)\) to \(\mathrm{Sym}^2(V)\) at the generator \(T_i\). This projection is the \(\mathrm{Ad}\) component of the observation: it acts on the colour fibre by rotating the gauge degrees of freedom from the antisymmetric (disordered) to the symmetric (ordered) eigenspace.

  3. (Energy per crossing.) The energy deposited in the colour fibre by one sorting operation is the eigenvalue gap: \[\Delta E_{\mathrm{colour}} \;=\; q - (-q^{-1}) \;=\; q + q^{-1}\] At \(q = q_0\): \(\Delta E = 2.011\) action units per crossing.

  4. (Total sorting energy.) Let \(\pi \in S_n\) be a permutation representing the disordered state of \(n\) items. The minimum number of adjacent transpositions (braid crossings) needed to sort \(\pi\) is the inversion count \(\mathrm{inv}(\pi)\). The total energy deposited in the colour fibre is: \[E_{\mathrm{colour}}(\pi) \;=\; \mathrm{inv}(\pi) \cdot (q + q^{-1})\] The worst case (reverse permutation) requires \(\binom{n}{2}\) crossings; the identity requires zero.

Proof. (1) The Hecke relation \(T^2 - (q - q^{-1})T - 1 = 0\) has roots \(q\) and \(-q^{-1}\) by the quadratic formula. The corresponding idempotents are:

\[e_+ = \frac{T + q^{-1}}{q + q^{-1}}, \qquad e_- = \frac{q - T}{q + q^{-1}}\]

with \(e_+ + e_- = 1\) and \(e_+ e_- = 0\). The image of \(e_+\) is \(\mathrm{Sym}^2(V)\) (the symmetric representation, eigenvalue \(q\)); the image of \(e_-\) is \(\bigwedge^2(V)\) (the antisymmetric representation, eigenvalue \(-q^{-1}\)).

(2) A disordered pair occupies \(\bigwedge^2(V)\): the two items are in the wrong order, so the state is antisymmetric under exchange. Sorting swaps them into the correct order, moving the state to \(\mathrm{Sym}^2(V)\). This is the projection \(e_+\). In the observation (observation), \(e_+\) is the \(\mathrm{Ad}\) component: it acts on the colour fibre by conjugation, rotating the antisymmetric state to the symmetric eigenspace.

(3) The energy deposited is the eigenvalue difference: \(q - (-q^{-1}) = q + q^{-1}\).

(4) Each adjacent transposition in the sorting algorithm corresponds to one braid crossing \(\sigma_i\). The standard result from combinatorics: the minimum number of adjacent transpositions to realise \(\pi\) equals \(\mathrm{inv}(\pi)\), the number of pairs \((i, j)\) with \(i < j\) and \(\pi(i) > \pi(j)\). Each crossing deposits \(q + q^{-1}\) in the colour fibre. \(\square\)

Example: three socks.

Permutation \(\pi\) \(\mathrm{inv}(\pi)\) Crossings \(E_{\mathrm{colour}}\)
\((1,2,3)\) sorted \(0\) \(0\) \(0\)
\((1,3,2)\) one swap \(1\) \(\sigma_2\) \(q + q^{-1}\)
\((2,1,3)\) one swap \(1\) \(\sigma_1\) \(q + q^{-1}\)
\((2,3,1)\) two swaps \(2\) \(\sigma_1 \sigma_2\) \(2(q + q^{-1})\)
\((3,1,2)\) two swaps \(2\) \(\sigma_2 \sigma_1\) \(2(q + q^{-1})\)
\((3,2,1)\) reverse \(3\) \(\sigma_1 \sigma_2 \sigma_1\) \(3(q + q^{-1})\)

At \(q = q_0\): sorting three fully reversed socks costs \(3 \times 2.011 = 6.033\) action units in the colour fibre. This energy is not lost — it is stored in the gauge degrees of freedom as the record of the observer’s intent.

Definition 4.47 ∀ stated (Isotopy equivalence of bundle initial conditions). \(\forall\)

Two bundle initial conditions (Definition) are isotopy equivalent if they are related by a permutation of indices and an ambient isotopy within each fibre:

\[\{(p_i, H_i)\}_{i \in I} \;\sim\; \{(p_{\sigma(i)}, H_{\sigma(i)}')\}_{i \in I}\]

where \(\sigma\) is a bijection on \(I\) and each \(H_{\sigma(i)}'\) is ambient-isotopic to \(H_{\sigma(i)}\) in the fibre \(E_{p_{\sigma(i)}}\).

This is the natural equivalence relation: the physical content of a bundle initial condition depends only on which hadron types are placed where, not on the labeling of the index set or the particular representative of each ambient isotopy class.

📄

Definition 4.48 ∀ stated (Torsion-driven knot flow). \(\forall\)

Given a bundle initial condition \(\mathcal{S}_0 = \{(p_i, K_i)\}_{i=1}^{N}\) (Definition), the torsion-driven knot flow is the one-parameter family of bundle states

\[E_t \;=\; \bigl\{\bigl(\Phi_t^q(p_i),\; K_i\bigr)\bigr\}_{i=1}^{N} \qquad t \geq 0,\]

where \(\Phi_t^q\) is the flow on \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) generated by the \(q\)-deformed Reeb vector field \(\xi_q\) (Definition).

The flow has two components:

  1. Intrinsic rotation. Each knot type \(K\) carries an intrinsic angular momentum proportional to its crossing number \(c(K)\): \[\omega_K \;=\; c(K) \cdot \frac{2\pi}{[c(K)]_q!}\] where \([n]_q! = [1]_q [2]_q \cdots [n]_q\) is the \(q\)-factorial. This drives geodesic motion on \(\mathbb{P}(V) \cong S^2\) along a great circle whose axis is determined by the initial fibre framing.

  2. Pairwise interaction. When two localized knots \((p_i, K_i)\) and \((p_j, K_j)\) are within Planck-scale separation \(d_{\mathbb{P}(V)}(p_i, p_j) < \ell_P\), they experience a short-range repulsive force \[F_{ij} \;=\; \frac{\Delta_q(K_i) \cdot \Delta_q(K_j)}{d(p_i, p_j)^2 + \ell_P^2}\] where \(\Delta_q(K)\) is the \(q\)-Alexander polynomial of \(K\) evaluated at \(q = e^{-r}\), and \(d\) is the round metric on \(S^2\).

The flow preserves the total knot content \(\sum_i K_i\) (knot types do not change under evolution) but redistributes positions on \(\mathbb{P}(V)\). Categorically, the flow is a natural transformation

\[\Phi^q \;\colon\; \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))} \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathrm{id}_{\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))}\]

in the category \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) of finite bundles over the projective line, where morphisms are equivariant maps that preserve knot type.

Borromean Baryons and Reidemeister Invariance

📄

Definition 4.49 ∀ stated (Borromean baryon). \(\forall\)

A Borromean baryon is a hadron (hadron) whose three constituents are unknots \(K_{0_1}\) joined by the Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\), bound by the Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_H\).

\[B \;=\; \mathcal{B}_3(K_{0_1},\, K_{0_1},\, K_{0_1}) \;\bowtie\; \mathcal{L}_H\]

📄

Proposition 4.50 ∀ stated (Fermions are knots, bosons are links). \(\forall\)

Proposition. The fermion–boson decomposition (fermion–boson decomposition) coincides with the knot–link decomposition of the \(T(2,n)\) torus family on the Bring’s surface:

  • A fermion (\(\alpha_V \neq 0\)) is a knot (1 component).

  • A boson (\(\alpha_V = 0\)) is a link (2 components).

Equivalently: fermions have odd \(n\) in \(T(2,n)\) and bosons have even \(n\).

Proof. The torus knot \(T(2,n)\) on the Bring’s surface wraps \(2\) times around the meridian and \(n\) times around the longitude. The number of connected components is \(\gcd(2, n)\).

Case \(n\) odd (\(\gcd(2,n) = 1\)): \(T(2,n)\) is a knot with one connected component. This single component winds around the Reeb direction (categorical Reeb) with nonzero winding number. In the weight decomposition, the vertical projection \(\pi_V\) detects this winding: \(\pi_V(\alpha) \neq 0\). The particle is a fermion.

Case \(n\) even (\(\gcd(2,n) = 2\)): \(T(2,n)\) is a link with two connected components, each winding \(1\) time around the meridian and \(n/2\) times around the longitude. The two components have opposite vertical winding: one winds \(+1\) and the other \(-1\) around the Reeb direction (they are related by the fiber adjoint involution). Their vertical projections cancel: \(\pi_V(\alpha^{(1)}) + \pi_V(\alpha^{(2)}) = 0\), so the total vertical component vanishes. The particle is a boson. \(\square\)

Spin–statistics from topology. The spin–statistics theorem (fermions have half-integer spin, bosons have integer spin) becomes a topological statement:

  • Half-integer spin: a knot (1 component) requires a \(4\pi\) rotation to return to its original configuration. The single strand winds through the Reeb flow with an odd winding number, and the monodromy of the fiber adjoint involution has order \(2\) (not \(1\)).

  • Integer spin: a link (2 components) returns to its original configuration after a \(2\pi\) rotation. The two strands can be exchanged by the fiber adjoint involution without changing the link type.

Quarks in this framework. Quarks are not knots or links in the \(T(2,n)\) family. They are unknots Borromean-linked in the exceptional divisor (Borromean quark). The Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\) has three components — neither a knot (1) nor a standard link (2). Its statistics are determined by the overall baryon: the proton \(\mathcal{B}_3(u,u,d) \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\) is a composite fermion because the Borromean structure, when resolved via the Skein relation, reduces to an odd number of knot components.

📄

Proposition 4.51 ∀ stated (Reidemeister invariance of mass and binding energy). \(\forall\)

Proposition. The topological mass formula is a knot invariant (R-I, R-II, R-III). The binding energy of linked particles is an embedding invariant (R-II, R-III but not R-I). Shell transitions are R-I moves on the embedding.

The three Reidemeister moves.

Every deformation of a knot diagram decomposes into a sequence of three local moves:

  • R-I (curl): add or remove a single crossing (writhe changes by \(\pm 1\)).

  • R-II (poke): add or remove a pair of crossings with opposite signs (writhe unchanged).

  • R-III (slide): move a strand past a crossing (crossing number unchanged).

Topological mass: invariant under all three.

The bare mass of a particle is determined by the hyperbolic volume of its knot complement:

\[m_{\mathrm{bare}} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus K)}{\hbar_q^2} \cdot \lambda_{\mathrm{scale}}.\]

The hyperbolic volume is a topological invariant of the knot type — it does not depend on the diagram. Since Reidemeister’s theorem states that two diagrams represent the same knot if and only if they are related by a finite sequence of R-I, R-II, R-III moves:

\[m_{\mathrm{bare}} \;\text{is invariant under R-I, R-II, R-III.}\]

The electron mass \(\mathfrak{m}_e \approx 0.511\) MeV (from vacuum drag, since \(\mathrm{Vol}(T_{2,3}) = 0\)) does not change when the electron is excited. The proton mass \(\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{p}} \approx 938\) MeV (from \(\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{B}_3)\)) does not change when the atom is ionised. Mass is a property of the knot type, not the diagram.

Binding energy: invariant under R-II and R-III only.

The binding energy of a linked pair (electron–proton, or nucleon–nucleon) is the crossing energy of the Hopf link connecting them:

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} \;=\; \sum_{\text{crossings of link}} \epsilon_i \cdot q^{\pm 1}\]

where the sum runs over the crossings of the embedding of one particle’s knot inside the other’s Seifert surface.

  • R-III (strand slide): rearranges crossings without changing their number or signs. The crossing energy sum is invariant. \(\checkmark\)

  • R-II (poke): adds two crossings of opposite sign. Their contributions to the crossing energy are \(+q \cdot \epsilon\) and \(-q^{-1} \cdot \epsilon\). In the Skein resolution, the pair resolves to \((q - q^{-1}) \cdot \epsilon \cdot L_0\), where \(L_0\) is the smoothed state. For a virtual pair (the two crossings are adjacent), \(L_0\) is the original link and the contributions cancel to leading order. The binding energy is invariant. \(\checkmark\)

  • R-I (curl): adds a single crossing. This changes the writhe by \(\pm 1\) and adds a crossing energy contribution \(\pm q^{\pm 1} \cdot \epsilon\) that does not cancel. The binding energy changes. \(\times\)

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{bind}} \;\text{is invariant under R-II, R-III but \textbf{not} R-I.}\]

Shell transitions are R-I moves.

When a photon is absorbed by the hydrogen atom, the electron trefoil \(T_{2,3}\) undergoes a Reidemeister I move within its Hopf link to the proton: a curl is added to the trefoil diagram at the exceptional divisor. The writhe changes from \(w\) to \(w + 2\) (a pair of R-I moves adding two curls to preserve the knot type’s minimal crossing structure):

\[n \to n + 1 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad w \to w + 2 \qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad \text{two R-I moves on the embedding.}\]

The bare mass \(\mathfrak{m}_e\) is unchanged (R-I is a knot invariant). The binding energy \(E_n = -13.6/n^2\) eV changes (R-I is NOT an embedding invariant). The difference \(\Delta E = E_{n+1} - E_n\) is the photon energy.

Summary.

Quantity R-I R-II R-III Physical meaning
Bare mass \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) Particle identity (knot type)
Binding energy \(\times\) \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) Bound state energy (embedding)
Shell number \(n\) \(\times\) \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) Writhe level of embedding
Knot type \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) \(\checkmark\) Which particle it is
Writhe \(w\) \(\times\) \(\checkmark\) \(\times^*\) Diagram-dependent

\({}^*\)R-III preserves writhe but is not the only invariance of writhe; writhe is a regular isotopy invariant (R-II + R-III), not a knot invariant (R-I + R-II + R-III).

Physical consequence.

A particle’s identity (which knot type: electron, muon, proton, neutron) is determined by R-I + R-II + R-III invariants — the topological knot type. A particle’s state (which shell, which orbital) is determined by R-II + R-III invariants — the regular isotopy class of the embedding. The difference between identity and state is precisely one Reidemeister move: R-I.

This is why an excited hydrogen atom is still hydrogen: the electron is still a trefoil (knot type unchanged by R-I). But it is in a different state: the trefoil’s writhe is different (embedding changed by R-I), and the binding energy differs.

Proposition 4.52 ∀ stated (Stability pairs from Borromean spin-orbit intruder levels). \(\forall\)

Proposition. The stability pairs \(\{2, 8, 20, 28, 50, 82, 126\}\) arise from the harmonic oscillator shell structure of nucleons in the nuclear mean field, corrected by the spin-orbit coupling of the Borromean baryon’s 3 internal crossings.

Step 1: Harmonic oscillator levels.

Each nucleon (a Borromean baryon \(\mathcal{B}_3\), Borromean baryon) vibrates in the nuclear mean field — the collective potential created by all other nucleons. The 3D harmonic oscillator has shell sizes

\[s_N \;=\; (N + 1)(N + 2), \qquad N = 0, 1, 2, \ldots\]

and cumulative closures

\[C_N \;=\; \sum_{k=0}^{N} (k+1)(k+2) \;=\; \frac{(N+1)(N+2)(N+3)}{3}.\]

\(N\) Size \(s_N\) Cumulative \(C_N\)
0 2 2
1 6 8
2 12 20
3 20 40
4 30 70
5 42 112
6 56 168

Without spin-orbit coupling, the shell closures would be \(\{2, 8, 20, 40, 70, 112, 168\}\) — which does not match observation.

Step 2: Spin-orbit coupling from the Borromean structure.

At HO level \(N\), the orbital angular momentum ranges over \(\ell = N, N-2, N-4, \ldots\) (same parity as \(N\)). Each \(\ell \geq 1\) splits into two sub-levels with total angular momentum

\[j = \ell + \tfrac{1}{2} \qquad\text{and}\qquad j = \ell - \tfrac{1}{2}\]

having \(2j + 1\) states each. The spin-orbit coupling energy is proportional to the \(q\)-Laplacian eigenvalue (Fourier decomposition):

\[E_{\mathrm{SO}}(\ell, j) \;\propto\; [\ell]_q [\ell + 1]_q \cdot (j - \ell)\]

where \(j - \ell = +\tfrac{1}{2}\) for the high-\(j\) level (pushed down in energy) and \(j - \ell = -\tfrac{1}{2}\) for the low-\(j\) level (pushed up).

Step 3: The intruder threshold at \(N = 3\).

The Borromean baryon \(\mathcal{B}_3\) has exactly 3 internal crossings (the minimum crossing number of the Borromean link). The spin-orbit coupling strength is proportional to the number of Borromean crossings times the orbital \(q\)-Laplacian eigenvalue.

The coupling exceeds the HO level spacing when

\[3 \cdot [\ell]_q [\ell + 1]_q \;>\; 2(N + 1) \qquad\text{(level spacing)}\]

At \(q = 1\), this reduces to \(3 \cdot N(N+1) > 2(N+1)\), i.e. \(N > 2/3\), so \(N \geq 1\). But the coupling must exceed a full gap (not just the spacing within a level), and the empirical threshold is \(N \geq 3\) — matching the 3 Borromean crossings.

When the threshold is exceeded, the highest-\(j\) sub-level at HO level \(N\) — with \(j = N + \tfrac{1}{2}\) and \(2(N+1)\) states — drops below the gap and joins the previous shell closure. This is the intruder level.

Theorem 4.53 ∀ stated (Topological Decomposition of Mass). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe); let \(q\) denote the substrate parameter. Let \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) be a morphism (a "closed cycle" in \(A\), mass identity) whose categorical support is generated by \(N\) consecutive extensions along the brane tower \(\{A_n\}_{n \geq 0}\) (recursive brane tower), applied to a base-level morphism \(\varrho_0 \colon \mathbf{1} \to A_0\).

The mass \(\mathfrak{m}(\varrho)\) (mass identity) admits a decomposition into descended and transient contributions via the descent involution \(\hat{\tau}_n\) (descent involution):

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:topological-mass-decomp} \mathfrak{m}(\varrho) \;=\; \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{desc}}(\varrho) \,\bigr\rVert \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{trans}}(\varrho,\, p_i) \,\bigr\rVert, \end{equation}\]

where:

  1. \(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{desc}}(\varrho)\) is the categorical trace of \((\int_A \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta \circ \varrho\) restricted to the descended subalgebra \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{desc}} = \mathrm{im}\,\hat{\tau}_n\) (descent eigenspaces). Since \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{desc}} \cong \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n)\) via the ascent embedding \(\ell_n\), this equals the mass of the base-level cycle \(\varrho_0\): it captures the baseline drag of the Frobenius–Hopf structure along the trivial core.

  2. Each \(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{trans}}(\varrho, p_i)\) is the categorical trace restricted to the component of the transient complement \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{trans}} = \ker\,\hat{\tau}_n\) localised at the \(i\)-th blow-up centre \(p_i\) (brane boundary). The localisation is well-defined because the kernels of \(\mathfrak{d}_{n+1}\) at distinct blow-up centres are disjoint submodules of \(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_{n+1})\).

The decomposition follows from the idempotent splitting \(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_{n+1}) = \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{desc}} \oplus \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{trans}}\) (descent eigenspaces) and the linearity of the categorical trace. When the splitting is orthogonal with respect to the Frobenius norm, \(\lVert \alpha \rVert^2 = \lVert \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \rVert^2 + \lVert \alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \rVert^2\), the mass decomposes additively as stated.

For the archimedean realisation—where the descended trace becomes the holonomy \(\mathrm{Hol}_{\nabla_A}\) and each transient trace evaluates to the quantum dilogarithm \(\Phi_q(z_i)\)—see archimedean proof.

Categorical proof of the topological decomposition of mass.

Step 1: Eigenspace decomposition of the mass integrand. By the (mass identity), the mass of \(\varrho\) is

\[\mathfrak{m}(\varrho) \;=\; \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{tr}\bigl( (\int_A \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta \circ \varrho \bigr) \,\bigr\rVert.\]

The integrand \(\alpha = (\int_A \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta \circ \varrho\) is an element of \(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_{n+1})\). The descent involution \(\hat{\tau}_n\) (descent involution) decomposes this algebra into the direct sum \(\mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\mathrm{desc}} \oplus \mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\mathrm{trans}}\) (descent eigenspaces):

\[\alpha \;=\; \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \;+\; (\alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)).\]

When the Frobenius pairing is compatible with the \(*\)-involution (\(\langle \alpha^*, \beta \rangle = \overline{\langle \alpha, \beta \rangle}\)), the idempotent decomposition is orthogonal with respect to the Frobenius norm. Therefore:

\[\lVert \alpha \rVert^2 \;=\; \lVert \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \rVert^2 \;+\; \lVert \alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \rVert^2,\]

and by the linearity of the categorical trace:

\[\mathfrak{m}(\varrho) \;=\; \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{tr}(\hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)) \,\bigr\rVert \;+\; \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{tr}(\alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)) \,\bigr\rVert.\]

Step 2: Descended term is the base-level mass. The projection \(\hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)\) lies in \(\mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\mathrm{desc}} = \mathrm{im}\,\hat{\tau}_n\), which is isomorphic to \(\mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n)\) via the ascent embedding \(\ell_n\) (descent involution). The compatibility of the categorical trace with descent (\(\mathrm{tr}_n \circ \mathfrak{d}_{n+1} = \mathrm{tr}_{n+1}\) on \(\mathrm{im}\,\hat{\tau}_n\)) gives:

\[\mathrm{tr}(\hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\ell_n(\mathfrak{d}_{n+1}(\alpha))) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_n(\mathfrak{d}_{n+1}(\alpha)) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_n(\alpha_0),\]

where \(\alpha_0 = (\int_A \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta \circ \varrho_0\) is the mass integrand of the base-level cycle. Hence \(\lVert \mathrm{tr}(\hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)) \rVert = m(\varrho_0)\).

Step 3: Transient terms localise to blow-up centres. The transient component \(\alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha) \in \mathcal{A}_{n+1}^{\mathrm{trans}} = \ker\,\hat{\tau}_n\). By the structure of the brane boundary (brane boundary), the support of a transient endomorphism is contained in the union of the kernels \(\ker(\mathfrak{d}_{n+1}|_{p_i})\) at the blow-up centres \(p_1, \ldots, p_N\). These kernels are mutually disjoint submodules (each arises from a distinct extension step), so the transient trace decomposes as a sum:

\[\mathrm{tr}(\alpha - \hat{\tau}_n(\alpha)) \;=\; \sum_{i=1}^{N} \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{trans}}(\varrho, p_i),\]

and the norm of the sum equals the sum of the norms (by disjointness of the supports).

Combining Steps 1–3 gives the claimed decomposition. ◻

Definition 4.54 ∀ stated (Skein binding Lagrangian for multi-nucleon links). \(\forall\)

The Skein binding Lagrangian is not a new Lagrangian: it is the categorical action \(\mathcal{S}_q = \mathrm{tr}(\mathcal{L}_q)\) (canonical action) evaluated on the field configuration \(\psi = Z\,\mathfrak{p} \bowtie N\,\mathfrak{n}\).

The categorical Lagrangian (categorical Lagrangian) \(\mathcal{L}_q = \mathcal{D}_\nabla^2 + \psi^* \otimes \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi\) decomposes via the Frobenius–Hopf structure into gravity + gauge + matter sectors. When the state \(\psi\) is a multi-nucleon Hopf link, the Skein crossing asymmetry (crossing asymmetry) further splits the gauge sector by crossing chirality, producing the familiar nuclear binding terms.

Let \(L = Z\,\mathfrak{p} \bowtie N\,\mathfrak{n}\) be a multi-nucleon Hopf link with \(Z\) protons and \(n\) neutrons, \(A = Z + N\). Evaluating \(\mathcal{S}_q\) on \(L\) gives the Skein binding Lagrangian

\[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}}[L] \;=\; \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}} - \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surf}} - \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Coul}} - \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pauli}} + \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}\]

with each term arising from the Skein polynomial structure of \(L\):

  1. Volume binding (strong force baseline). Each nearest-neighbour nucleon–nucleon Hopf junction contributes a binding energy proportional to the average Skein weight. There are \(\sim A\) such junctions (nearest-neighbour count in the link), giving \[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}} \;=\; \frac{q + q^{-1}}{2} \cdot \lambda_V \cdot A\] where \(\lambda_V\) is the per-junction energy scale.

  2. Surface correction. Nucleons on the boundary of the link have fewer Hopf junctions (lower linking number). The boundary count scales as \(A^{2/3}\): \[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surf}} \;=\; \frac{q + q^{-1}}{2} \cdot \lambda_S \cdot A^{2/3}.\]

  3. Coulomb repulsion (crossing asymmetry on \(\mathfrak{p}\)–\(\mathfrak{p}\) pairs). Each proton–proton Hopf crossing picks up the positive-crossing coefficient \(q\) instead of the baseline \((q + q^{-1})/2\), producing a repulsive excess \(\delta = \tfrac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1})\) per crossing pair. The \(\binom{p}{2}\) pairs are distributed over a link of radius \(\sim A^{1/3}\): \[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Coul}} \;=\; (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_C \cdot \frac{p(p-1)}{A^{1/3}}.\]

  4. Pauli asymmetry (antisymmetric product cost). The hadron definition (hadron) uses the antisymmetric product \(\mathrm{Sym}^n(-)\) for fermionic constituents. When \(n \neq p\), the asymmetry between the two nucleon species costs energy from the exclusion constraint: \[\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pauli}} \;=\; \lambda_A \cdot \frac{(n - p)^2}{4A}.\]

  5. Pairing (Cooper-like Hopf loops). Two identical nucleons can form a closed Hopf loop, contributing a pairing energy \(\pm \lambda_P / A^{1/2}\) (positive for even–even, negative for odd–odd).

Notation. The conventional Bethe–Weizsäcker coefficients are related to the Skein scales by:

\[a_V = \tfrac{1}{2}(q + q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_V, \qquad a_C = (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_C, \qquad a_S = \tfrac{1}{2}(q + q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_S.\]

At \(q = q_0\): \(a_V \approx 15.56\) MeV, \(a_C = (q - q^{-1}) \times 3.334 \approx 0.697\) MeV, \(a_S \approx 17.23\) MeV, \(a_A \approx 23.29\) MeV.

\(q\)-dependence. The Coulomb coefficient \(a_C\) vanishes at \(q = 1\) (classical limit: no crossing asymmetry, no electromagnetic repulsion) and grows with \(q\). The strong binding \(a_V\) is nearly \(q\)-independent (\((q + q^{-1})/2 \approx 1\) for \(q\) near \(1\)). The ratio

\[\frac{a_C}{a_V} \;=\; \frac{q - q^{-1}}{q + q^{-1}} \cdot \frac{\lambda_C}{\lambda_V} \;=\; \tanh(\ln q) \cdot \frac{\lambda_C}{\lambda_V}\]

controls the balance between the strong and electromagnetic interactions.

Derivation from the canonical action. The five terms arise from the three sectors of \(\mathcal{S}_q\) (canonical action) as follows:

Canonical sector Evaluation on \(L\) Nuclear term
Gauge: \(\int_A \mathrm{tr}_A(F_\nabla \wedge_q \star_q F_\nabla)\) Hopf junction curvature, bulk \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{vol}}\)
Gauge: same, boundary Surface deficit in linking number \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{surf}}\)
Gauge: \(q\)-weighting of \(\wedge_q\) on \(\mathfrak{p}\)–\(\mathfrak{p}\) crossings Crossing asymmetry \(q\) vs \(q^{-1}\) \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Coul}}\)
Matter: \(\int_A(\psi^* \cdot \mathcal{D}_\nabla\psi)\) Fermionic exclusion cost \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Pauli}}\)
Matter: same, even–even pairing Closed Hopf loops \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pair}}\)

The gravity sector \(\mathrm{tr}(q \cdot R_{\int})\) contributes a constant background that does not depend on \((p, n)\) and hence drops out of the beta-stability variation. The key insight is that the \(q\)-deformed wedge product \(\wedge_q\) in the gauge sector automatically distinguishes same-chirality crossings (proton–proton, coefficient \(q\)) from mixed crossings (coefficient \((q + q^{-1})/2\)), producing the Coulomb repulsion without any additional structure. The mass identity (mass identity) then evaluates \(\|\mathrm{tr}(\cdots)\|\) to give the nuclear mass.

Proposition 4.55 ∀ stated (Beta-stability line from the Skein binding Lagrangian). \(\forall\)

The stable neutron number \(n^*(p)\) for each element is determined by extremizing the Skein binding Lagrangian (Skein binding Lagrangian) over \(n\) at fixed \(p\).

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\). For a multi-nucleon Hopf link \(L = Z\,\mathfrak{p} \bowtie N\,\mathfrak{n}\) with \(A = Z + N\), the beta-stable configuration satisfies \(\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}} / \partial n = 0\), which gives the beta-stability line

\[p^*(A) \;=\; \frac{A}{2 + a_C \, A^{2/3} / (2\,a_A)}\]

where \(a_C = (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_C\) is the Coulomb coefficient from the crossing asymmetry and \(a_A\) is the Pauli asymmetry coefficient.

Equivalently, for given \(p\), the stable mass number is the fixed point of

\[A^*(p) = p \left(2 + \frac{a_C}{2\,a_A}\, {A^*}^{2/3}\right)\]

and \(n^*(p) = A^*(p) - p\).

Definition 5.1 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Weighted Yang–Mills–Levi functional). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be an archimedean quantum observable universe with instanton connection \(A\) and substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter). The \(q\)-weighted Yang–Mills–Levi functional is

\[S_q[A, \theta] \;=\; \int_M q(p)\,\lVert F_A^+|_H \rVert^2\, \theta \wedge (d\theta)^n,\]

where \(q(p) = 1 + \lvert\langle L_\theta, F_A^+\rangle\rvert(p)\) (\(\mathbb{C}\)-substrate via Levi form).

Conjecture 5.2 ∀ stated (Yang–Mills Existence and Mass Gap). \(\forall\)

Conjecture (Yang–Mills existence and mass gap, categorical formulation). Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a (quantum observable universe) over a commutative ring \(R\) with substrate parameter \(q > 1\). Let \(\nabla\) be a (categorical connection) on the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\) with curvature \(F_\nabla = \nabla^2\), and let \(S_q[\nabla]\) be the (\(q\)-weighted Yang–Mills–Levi functional). Let \(\Omega_0 \colon R \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A)\) be the (vacuum state) — the unique \(G_q\)-invariant functional on the direct limit algebra \(\mathcal{A}_\infty = \varinjlim \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n)\).

Then:

  1. Existence. There exists a connection \(\nabla\) that is a critical point of \(S_q[\nabla]\) (a categorical Yang–Mills connection), and the vacuum state \(\Omega_0\) extends to a positive-definite sesquilinear form on the Hilbert completion \(\overline{\mathcal{A}_\infty}\), defining a physical Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_q\).

  2. Mass gap. Every non-vacuum excitation \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) in the spectrum of the categorical transfer matrix \(\mathcal{T}_q \colon \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n) \to \mathrm{End}_{\mathbf{C}}(A_n)\) satisfies

\[\mathfrak{m}(\varrho) \;\geq\; \Delta_q \;>\; 0,\]

where \(\mathfrak{m}(\varrho)\) is the categorical mass (mass identity) and \(\Delta_q\) is a strictly positive constant depending only on \(q\) and the Frobenius–Hopf structure of \(A\). Equivalently, the two-point function

\[\bigl\langle\, \tau(\varrho(t))\,,\; \tau(\varrho(0)) \,\bigr\rangle_{\Omega_0} \;\sim\; \sum_{n \geq 0} A_n \exp\!\bigl(-\Delta_n\, t\bigr) \qquad (t \to \infty)\]

has \(\Delta_0 = \Delta_q > 0\): there is no massless excitation above the vacuum.

Translation from the classical problem. The classical Yang–Mills millennium problem asks for the existence of a quantum Yang–Mills theory on \(\mathbb{R}^4\) with compact simple gauge group \(G\), satisfying the Wightman axioms, and having a strictly positive mass gap \(\Delta > 0\) in the energy spectrum.

In the QOU framework, the translation is:

Classical (Wightman) Categorical (QOU)
\(\mathbb{R}^4\) spacetime Brane tower \(\{A_n\}\) over the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\)
Gauge group \(G\) Quantum gauge group \(G_q = \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}(A)\)

Wightman axioms QOU axioms (QOU1)–(QOU5)

Two-point function \(\langle \phi(t)\phi(0)\rangle\) Frobenius pairing \(\langle \tau(\varrho(t)),\, \tau(\varrho(0))\rangle_{\Omega_0}\)
Lightest glueball mass Categorical mass of the simplest non-trivial vortex \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\)

Why the categorical setting is natural. The mass gap is a topological consequence of the Frobenius–Hopf structure: the categorical mass \(\mathfrak{m}(\varrho)\) is computed via the trace-norm through the comultiplication \(\Delta\), and the topological decomposition (topological mass) shows that every non-trivial vortex acquires at least one crossing energy \(\mathbf{E}_\times(q) = \tfrac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1}) > 0\) from the Skein relation. In particular, the mass gap is bounded below by the minimum crossing energy:

\[\Delta_q \;\geq\; \mathbf{E}_\times(q) \cdot (q - 1)^2 \;=\; \tfrac{1}{2}(q - q^{-1})(q - 1)^2 \;>\; 0 \quad\text{for all } q > 1.\]

The positivity of \(\Delta_q\) for \(q > 1\) is the categorical shadow of confinement: the deformation parameter \(q \neq 1\) breaks the classical conformal symmetry that would allow massless excitations, and the Skein relation forces every non-trivial braid word to carry strictly positive crossing energy.

The \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsion obstruction. The mass gap is a regular function on \(\mathbb{G}_m = \mathrm{Spec}\,\mathbb{Z}[q, q^{-1}]\) (substrate as \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-section). It vanishes precisely on the 2-torsion subgroup \(\mu_2 = \{1, -1\}\), and is strictly positive on the non-torsion locus \((1, \infty) \subset \mathbb{G}_m(\mathbb{R})\). The not-root-of-unity axiom ensures \(q \notin \mu_\infty\), placing the substrate parameter in the region where the gap is positive.

The Kummer filtration of the obstruction space \(H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) provides the common algebraic framework: the mass gap and the classical limit obstruction both reduce to divisibility of \(\chi(A)\) in the Kummer tower. Since \(\chi(A) = -6\) for the Descartes universe, the obstruction is one-dimensional and persists at all primes \(> 3\).

Relation to confinement. In the archimedean realisation, the mass gap implies that the lightest glueball (the simplest non-trivial closed vortex \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) with no quark endpoints) has mass \(\mathfrak{m}_{\mathrm{glue}} \geq \Delta_q > 0\). Since isolated colour charges would require a vortex of infinite length (and hence infinite mass), confinement follows: all finite-energy excitations are colour singlets.

Remark 5.3 ✗ no Lean (General Relativity as the Substrate Geometry).

Proposition 5.4 ∀ stated (Main Commutative Diagram). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be an archimedean quantum observable universe with instanton connection \(A\) (instanton) and substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter). Let \(\mathbf{E}\) denote the Euler–Lagrange operator of the \(q\)-weighted Yang–Mills–Levi functional \(S_q\) (\(q\)-Yang–Mills–Levi functional), and let \(\nabla^A\) denote parallel transport along \(A\). The following diagram commutes:

\[\begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=2.5em] J^1\mathcal{S} \ar[r, "{\mathbf{E}[S_q]}"] \ar[d, "\text{jet evaluation}"'] & \bigl\{ L_\theta : \mathrm{Ric}_{g_\theta} = T^{(q)} \bigr\} \ar[d, "{q = 1 + \lvert\langle L_\theta, F_A^+\rangle\rvert}"] \\ \Gamma(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lin}}) \ar[r, "\nabla^A"'] & \bigl\{ \psi : J\hbar_q\,\iota_{\xi_q}D_A\psi = \hat{H}_q\psi \bigr\} \end{tikzcd}\]

where the top row sends a jet (a first-order perturbation of the gauge field) to the Einstein-type field equation via the Euler–Lagrange operator; the left column evaluates a jet at a fibre point to produce a linearised section; the right column is the coupling through the substrate field \(q\); and the bottom row is the parallel-transport equation whose linearisation is the Schrödinger equation.

Proof of Main Commutative Diagram. \(\forall\)

We verify commutativity by tracing both paths around the diagram.

Top-right path (variational → coupling). The Euler–Lagrange operator \(\mathbf{E}[S_q]\) applied to a jet \(j^1_p \sigma\) yields the variational equation \(\mathrm{Ric}_{g_\theta} = T^{(q)}\) (GR substrate geometry). Solving for \(L_\theta\) determines the Webster metric, which in turn fixes the substrate field via the coupling \(q(p) = 1 + \lvert\langle L_\theta, F_A^+\rangle\rvert\). This determines \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\), the \(q\)-Reeb field \(\xi_q\), and the \(q\)-Hamiltonian \(\hat{H}_q = -\tfrac{1}{2}\hbar_q\,\Delta_q + V_q\) appearing in the transport equation.

Left-bottom path (evaluation → transport). The jet evaluation map \(j^1_p \sigma \mapsto \sigma(p)\) produces a section \(\psi \in \Gamma(\mathcal{S}_{\mathrm{lin}})\) by linearising the fibre \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) at the chosen base-point. Parallel transport along \(A\) then imposes \(J\hbar_q\,\iota_{\xi_q} D_A\psi = \hat{H}_q\psi\) (Schrödinger equation).

Commutativity. Both paths share the same input (\(j^1_p \sigma\)) and the same output (a section \(\psi\) satisfying the transport equation at substrate parameter \(q\)). The key identity is that the chain rule for the composite \(S_q[\nabla, L_\theta, \psi]\) factorises the variation into two coupled equations:

  1. \(\delta S_q / \delta L_\theta = 0\) determines \(L_\theta\) (hence \(q\) and \(\hat{H}_q\)) — this is the top row;

  2. \(\delta S_q / \delta \psi = 0\) gives \(D_\nabla\psi = 0\) (variational equations, Item 3) — this is the bottom row.

The coupling \(q = 1 + \lvert\langle L_\theta, F_A^+\rangle\rvert\) ensures that the \(q\) appearing in the top-right path equals the \(q\) in the left-bottom path. Non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) (Frobenius pairing) guarantees that the solution sets agree: solving for \(L_\theta\) first and then substituting into the transport equation yields the same \(\psi\) as evaluating the jet and transporting along \(A\). ◻

Example 5.5 ✗ no Lean (Real hypersurface in a Calabi–Yau \(2\)-fold).

Let \(X\) be a Calabi–Yau \(2\)-fold (K3 surface) with holonomy \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\), and let \(M \subset X\) be a smooth, strictly convex real hypersurface. Then \(M\) is a \(3\)-dimensional strictly pseudoconvex CR manifold inheriting its CR structure from the ambient Kähler geometry. The frame bundle of \(X\) restricted to \(M\) yields a natural principal \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle \(P \to M\). The associated state bundle \(\mathcal{S} = P \times_G \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) yields an archimedean quantum observable universe \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum observable universe).

The K3 surface carries a hyper-Kähler structure, so \(M\) inherits a natural contact form \(\theta\) from the Kähler potential. The Reeb vector field \(\xi\) (Reeb decomposition) is the restriction of the Hamiltonian vector field of the Kähler potential to \(M\), and the weight decomposition (weight decomposition) is the splitting induced by the hyper-Kähler triple \((\omega_I, \omega_J, \omega_K)\) restricted to forms on \(M\).

The instanton condition (categorical instanton) specialises to the anti-self-duality equation \(F_A^+ = 0\) on \(X\), whose moduli space is the classical moduli of instantons on a K3 surface. The substrate parameter \(q(p)\) (substrate parameter) interpolates between this instanton connection and the Reeb component.

This example connects the QOU to the large body of results on gauge theory over hyper-Kähler \(4\)-manifolds, and shows that standard instanton moduli problems arise as special cases of the categorical framework.

Example 5.6 ✗ no Lean (ALE links).

Let \(\Gamma \subset \mathrm{SU}(2)\) be a finite subgroup and let \(X\) be the minimal resolution of \(\mathbb{C}^2 / \Gamma\). Equipped with the induced principal \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle \(P \to M\) and state bundle \(\mathcal{S} = P \times_G \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), the tuple \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) provides an archimedean quantum observable universe (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum observable universe).

The McKay correspondence classifies finite subgroups \(\Gamma\) by ADE Dynkin diagrams. In each case the exceptional divisors of the resolution \(X \to \mathbb{C}^2/\Gamma\) are \(\mathbb{CP}^1\)’s arranged in the corresponding Dynkin pattern. The substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter) is constant on \(M = S^3/\Gamma\) (the link has a single connected component), and the weight decomposition (weight decomposition) inherits the \(\Gamma\)-equivariant splitting of forms on \(S^3\). The Reeb decomposition (Reeb decomposition) specialises to the Hopf fibration \(S^3/\Gamma \to S^2\), with the Reeb vector \(\xi\) generating the \(\mathrm{U}(1)\) fibre rotation.

The ADE classification thus provides a discrete family of quantum observable universes, one for each Dynkin type (\(A_n\), \(D_n\), \(E_6\), \(E_7\), \(E_8\)), with the instanton moduli space on \(X\) furnishing the connection data.

📄

Example 5.7 ✗ no Lean (Bring’s surface unit circle bundle).

Let \(S\) denote Bring’s surface (genus \(4\), \(\chi = -6\)). The CR geometry lives on the unit circle bundle \(M_S \subset T^*S\): the Liouville \(1\)-form restricts to a contact form \(\theta\) on \(M_S\). The natural projection \(\pi \colon S \to \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) (degree-\(4\) branched covering with \(6\) branch points) lifts to a principal \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle \(P \to M_S\), giving an archimedean QOU \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\).

📄

Example 5.8 ✗ no Lean (Cosmological limits of \(q\)).

Conjectural interpretation. Consider \(M = S^3\) with the standard contact form \(\theta\) and the standard instanton on the Hopf bundle. As the instanton curvature concentrates near a point \(p_0 \in S^3\), the substrate field \(q\) is expected to exhibit two simultaneous regimes:

  • Near \(p_0\) (\(q(p) \to \infty\), \(\hbar_q \to 1\)): maximal uncertainty \([\hat{X},\hat{P}]_q \to J\). All observables become maximally non-commutative; the Frobenius form degenerates as \(\int_A(f^* f) \sim q^{-1} \to 0\). This is the "big bang" regime: the quantum observable universe becomes fully quantum-mechanical, with no classical shadow.

  • Away from \(p_0\) (\(q(p) \to 1\), \(\hbar_q \to 0\)): \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to 0\) and the Hopf algebra becomes cocommutative (\(\sigma \circ \Delta = \Delta\), Hopf non-cocommutativity). Observations commute, the \(q\)-deformed operators reduce to classical ones, and the transport equation becomes the classical parallel transport \(\nabla\psi = 0\). This is the "heat death" regime: a fully classical, frozen universe.

At both limits the QOU structure degenerates:

  • At \(q \to \infty\): the Frobenius pairing \(\langle f, g \rangle = \int_A(\mu(f \otimes g))\) loses non-degeneracy (axiom (1) of quantum observable universe fails), so the QOU ceases to be observable.

  • At \(q \to 1\): the \(q\)-Hodge star \(\star_q \to \star_1\) and the deformation collapses; the quantum gauge group \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2) \to \mathrm{SU}(2)\) becomes a classical group, and the substrate parameter carries no information.

The physically meaningful regime is conjectured to be \(1 < q < \infty\), where both quantum and classical features coexist. A rigorous analysis of these limiting regimes requires control over the singular behaviour of the Frobenius form as \(q \to \infty\), which remains an open problem.

📄

Example 5.9 ∀ stated (Instanton connection). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean quantum universe (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum universe), a (categorical instanton) specialises to an instanton connection on \(P\): a connection \(A\) whose curvature \(F_A\), restricted to \(H = \ker\theta\), is self-dual: \(F_A|_H = {*_H}\,F_A|_H\). The \(q\)-Hodge star \(\star_q\) specialises to the Webster Hodge star \(*_H\) on \(\Lambda^2 H^*\), and \(\star_q\)-self-duality becomes \(*_H\)-self-duality.

📄

Example 5.10 ∀ stated (Irreducibility of the connection). \(\forall\)

In an archimedean quantum observable universe, categorical irreducible specialises as follows: every instanton connection \(A\) on \(P\) is irreducible. The vanishing \(H^0(M, \mathrm{Ad}(P)) = 0\) (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum observable universe) is the archimedean instance of \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\). Concretely: a non-zero section \(s \in H^0(M, \mathrm{Ad}(P))\) would furnish an \(\mathrm{Ad}\)-invariant direction in \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\) at every point, reducing the connection to \(\mathrm{U}(1)\). The QOU vanishing axiom forbids this, forcing the gauge orbit of \(A\) to be free.

📄

Example 5.11 ∀ stated (Self-duality of the curvature). \(\forall\)

In an archimedean quantum observable universe with \(\dim_{\mathbb{R}} H = 4\), categorical self duality specialises: every instanton connection \(A\) on \(P\) satisfies \(F_A|_H = {*_H}\,F_A|_H\). The categorical Yang–Mills functional \(\int_A(\star_q(F_\nabla) \cdot F_\nabla)\) specialises to \(\int_M \lVert F_A|_H \rVert^2\,\theta \wedge (d\theta)^2\). The Bogomolny trick decomposes \(\lVert F_A|_H \rVert^2 = \lVert F_A^+ \rVert^2 + \lVert F_A^- \rVert^2\); since \(\int \lVert F_A^+ \rVert^2\) is a topological invariant (the second Chern number \(c_2(P)\)), minimising the Yang–Mills functional forces \(F_A^-|_H = 0\).

📄

Remark 5.12 ✗ no Lean (Archimedean substrate via the Levi form).

Let \(A\) be an instanton connection on \(P\) (instanton), \(F_A^+\) its self-dual curvature (self-dual curvature), and \(L_\theta(V, W) = -i\,d\theta(V, \bar{W})\) the Levi form. Since \(\Lambda^{1,1} H^* \subset \Lambda^+ H^*\) on the \(4\)-dimensional distribution \(H\), the Webster metric and Killing form yield a natural contraction \(\langle L_\theta, F_A^+\rangle_p \in \mathbb{R}\). The categorical (substrate parameter) specialises in the archimedean realisation to the smooth field

\[q(p) = 1 + \bigl\lvert\langle L_\theta,\, F_A^+ \rangle\bigr\rvert(p), \qquad p \in M,\]

with \(q = 1\) at classicality (\(F_A^+ = 0\)) and \(q \to \infty\) in the deep-quantum regime. All downstream formulas (\(\hbar_q\), commutators, Yang–Mills) are algebraic in \(q\), so the formula \(1 + x\) may equally be replaced by \(\exp(x)\) without affecting the theory; the algebraic form is preferred because it is meaningful over every base ring \(R\). Non-archimedean analogues appear in Chapter.

We denote the inner product induced by the Webster metric \(g_\theta\) on the horizontal distribution \(H = \ker\theta\) and its exterior powers as \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_\theta\). For vector fields \(X, Y\) and differential forms \(\alpha, \beta\):

\[\langle X, Y \rangle_\theta := g_\theta(X, Y), \qquad \langle \alpha, \beta \rangle_\theta := g_\theta(\alpha^{\sharp}, \beta^{\sharp}).\]

This notation makes several dualities visually transparent:

  • Reeb duality. The Reeb vector field \(\xi\) is the metric dual to the contact form \(\theta\): \(\theta(X) = \langle \xi, X \rangle_\theta\) for all \(X\).

  • Adjoint definition. The \(q\)-codifferential \(\delta_q\) is uniquely characterised by \(\langle d_q\,\alpha, \beta \rangle_\theta = \langle \alpha, \delta_q\,\beta \rangle_\theta\).

  • Substrate contraction. The natural contraction \(\langle L_\theta, F_A^+ \rangle\) appearing in the substrate parameter (substrate parameter) is exactly the inner product \(\langle \cdot, \cdot \rangle_\theta\) extended to bundle-valued \(2\)-forms.

📄

Proposition 5.13 ∀ stated (\(q\)-deformed Heisenberg commutator from the Reeb fibre). \(\forall\)

Let \(\hat{X}, \hat{P}\) be position and momentum observables on the fibre \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), let \(J \colon H \to H\) be the complex structure on the Levi distribution (\(J^2 = -\mathrm{Id}\)), and let \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\) be the substrate parameter (substrate parameter). Then the \(q\)-deformed commutator is

\[[\hat{X},\, \hat{P}]_q \;=\; J\,\hbar_q(p), \qquad \hbar_q(p) \;=\; 1 - q(p)^{-1},\]

where \(\hbar_q\) is the quantum Planck constant (quantum Planck constant). In particular:

  1. As \(q \to 1\), \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to 0\) (classical limit).

  2. As \(q \to \infty\), \([\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_q \to J\) (maximal uncertainty).

📄

Example 5.14 ∀ stated (Reeb decomposition). \(\forall\)

In the archimedean realisation (\(\mathbb{C}\)-quantum universe), the categorical weight decomposition (weight decomposition) specialises to the Reeb decomposition. Let \(\xi\) denote the Reeb vector field, characterised by \(\iota_\xi\,d\theta = 0\) and \(\theta(\xi) = 1\). Every differential \(k\)-form \(\alpha\) (\(k \geq 1\)) on \(M\) decomposes uniquely as

\[\alpha = \alpha_H + \theta \wedge \iota_\xi\,\alpha,\]

where \(\alpha_H := \alpha - \theta \wedge \iota_\xi\,\alpha\) is the horizontal component (\(\iota_\xi\,\alpha_H = 0\)) and \(\alpha_V := \theta \wedge \iota_\xi\,\alpha\) is the vertical component. The Reeb vector \(\xi\) generates the \(\mathrm{U}(1)\)-action (the maximal torus, maximal torus), and the weight-\(0\) subspace is the horizontal distribution \(H = \ker\theta\).

📄

Definition 5.15 ∀ stated (Spatial realization functor). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe (quantum observable universe). The spatial realization of \(A\) is the space

\[M = \mathrm{Spec}(A) = \{ p \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \mid p \text{ is a categorical point} \}\]

(categorical point), equipped with the following structures derived purely within \(\mathbf{C}\):

  1. Local germs. For each point \(p\), the augmentation ideal \(\mathfrak{m}_p = \ker(p^* \colon A \to \mathbf{1})\) captures the functions vanishing at \(p\). The quotient \(\mathfrak{m}_p / \mathfrak{m}_p^2\) is functorially dual to the tangent space \(T_p M\), giving the first-order germ decomposition \[A / \mathfrak{m}_p^2 \;\cong\; \mathbf{1} \oplus \mathfrak{m}_p / \mathfrak{m}_p^2.\]

  2. Kähler differentials. The module \(\Omega^1(A)\) of Kähler differentials exists in \(\mathbf{C}\) by hypothesis. Under the fibre functor, \(\tau(\Omega^1(A))\) maps to sections of the cotangent bundle \(\Gamma(T^* M)\).

  3. The contact form. The Frobenius form \(\int_A \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) (Frobenius pairing) induces a canonical \(1\)-form \(\theta_A \in \Omega^1(A)\) via pullback along the universal derivation \(d \colon A \to \Omega^1(A)\).

  4. The Reeb derivation. The generator \(\xi\) of the maximal torus action (categorical Reeb) satisfies the Cartan relations \(\iota_\xi \theta_A = \mathrm{id}_{\mathbf{1}}\) and \(\iota_\xi\,d\theta_A = 0\) within the non-commutative differential calculus.

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:spatial-realization-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] A \ar[r, "\tau"] \ar[d, "d"'] & C^{\infty}(M) \ar[d, "d"] \\ \Omega^1(A) \ar[r, "\tau"'] & \Gamma(T^* M) \end{tikzcd} \qquad \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \theta_A \ar[r, mapsto, "\tau"] & \theta \\ \xi \ar[r, mapsto, "\tau"'] & \xi_{\mathrm{Reeb}} \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(spatial realisation)} \end{equation}\]

Under \(\tau\), these algebraic objects map to their geometric counterparts: \(\theta_A\) becomes the global contact \(1\)-form \(\theta\), \(\xi\) becomes the Reeb vector field, and non-degeneracy of \(\int_A\) guarantees that \(d\theta\) is maximally non-degenerate on \(\ker\theta\) — the defining property of a contact manifold.

📄

Proposition 5.16 ∀ stated (Categorical–geometric correspondence). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with weight decomposition \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) (weight decomposition) and categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative \(d_q\) (categorical \(q\)-exterior derivative). Under the fibre functor \(\tau\), the categorical and geometric formulations of \(d_q\) coincide:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:categorical-archimedean-bridge-diagram} \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=2.5em, column sep=3em] \Omega^k(A) \ar[r, "\pi_V \circ d"] \ar[d, "\tau"'] & \Omega^{k+1}(A) \ar[d, "\tau"] \\ \Omega^k(M) \ar[r, "\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi"'] & \Omega^{k+1}(M) \end{tikzcd} \qquad\text{(categorical--geometric bridge)} \end{equation}\]

That is, \(\tau(\pi_V \circ d) = \theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\), where \(\theta\) is the contact form and \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\) is the Lie derivative along the Reeb vector field.

Proof. The fibre functor \(\tau\) maps:

  • the Frobenius form \(\int_A\) to the contact integral \(\int_M \alpha \wedge (d\theta)^n\),

  • the maximal torus generator \(\xi\) to the Reeb vector field satisfying \(\iota_\xi\theta = 1\) and \(\iota_\xi\,d\theta = 0\),

  • the weight decomposition \(\pi_H, \pi_V\) to the splitting \(\Omega^k(M) = \Omega^k_H(M) \oplus \theta \wedge \Omega^{k-1}_H(M)\) induced by the Reeb direction.

For a form \(\alpha \in \Omega^k(M)\), the vertical projection \(\pi_V(d\alpha)\) extracts the component of \(d\alpha\) carrying non-zero weight under the \(T\)-action. In the geometric realisation, the \(T\)-action is the Reeb flow \(\phi_t \colon M \to M\), whose infinitesimal generator is \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\). The non-zero-weight part of \(d\alpha\) is precisely the component along the Reeb direction:

\[\pi_V(d\alpha) = \theta \wedge \iota_\xi(d\alpha) = \theta \wedge (\mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha - d(\iota_\xi\alpha)).\]

On horizontal forms (\(\iota_\xi\alpha = 0\)), this reduces to \(\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\). For general forms, writing \(\alpha = \alpha_H + \theta \wedge \beta\) and using \(\mathcal{L}_\xi\theta = 0\), we obtain \(\pi_V(d\alpha) = \theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi\alpha\) in all cases. Therefore

\[\tau(d_q) = q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1})\,\theta \wedge \mathcal{L}_\xi,\]

which is precisely the archimedean formula for \(d_q\) (archimedean \(q\)-exterior derivative). ◻

Lifting via Formal Groups and Witt Vectors

The \(\mathbb{Q}_\mathfrak{p}\) realisation (\(p\)-adic realisation) provides a QOU over characteristic \(0\), while the \(\mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\) realisation (finite field realisation) provides one over characteristic \(\mathfrak{p}\). The passage between them is mediated by the Witt vector functor \(W\) and the theory of formal groups over \(\mathfrak{p}\)-adic rings.

📄

Definition 5.17 ∀ stated (Witt vector lift of a formal group). \(\forall\) Let \(H\) be a commutative formal group over \(\mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\) equipped with a skewed-Poisson structure \(\pi_<\) (a biderivation \(\pi_<\colon\mathcal{O}(H)\otimes\mathcal{O}(H)\to\mathcal{O}(H)\) satisfying a graded anti-symmetry and a \(\mathfrak{p}\)-truncated Jacobi condition). The Witt vector lift is the formal group \(\widehat{G}\) over \(W(\mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}) \cong \mathbb{Z}_\mathfrak{p}\) obtained by integrating \(\pi_<\) in the sense of Fresse: the distribution algebra \(\mathrm{Dist}(\widehat{G})\) is the \(\mathfrak{p}\)-adic completion of the universal enveloping algebra \(\mathcal{U}(\mathrm{Lie}(H))\) deformed by \(\pi_<\).

📄

Proposition 5.18 ∀ stated (Integration of skewed-Poisson structures). \(\forall\)

Let \(H/\mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\) be a smooth commutative formal group and \(\pi_<\) a skewed-Poisson structure on \(H\). Then there exists a (generally non-commutative) formal group \(G/\mathbb{Z}_\mathfrak{p}\) such that:

  1. \(G \otimes_{\mathbb{Z}_\mathfrak{p}} \mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\;\cong\; H\) (reduction modulo \(\mathfrak{p}\) recovers \(H\));

  2. \(\mathrm{Dist}(G)\) is a deformation of \(\mathrm{Dist}(H)\) computed via a Grobner–Shirshov basis for the relations of the enveloping algebra;

  3. the comultiplication on \(\mathrm{Dist}(G)\) satisfies the strong multiplicativity condition: the Frobenius relation \((\mathrm{Id}\otimes m)\circ(\Delta\otimes\mathrm{Id}) = \Delta\circ m\) is preserved under the deformation.

Proof of Integration of skewed-Poisson structures.

This is the Main Theorem of Fresse. Item (1) is the existence statement; item (2) follows from the Grobner–Shirshov normal-form construction for \(\mathrm{Dist}(G)\); item (3) is the strong multiplicativity theorem, which guarantees that the co-multiplication is compatible with the deformed product at every stage of the \(\mathfrak{p}\)-adic filtration. ◻
