The Algebraic Substrate

The algebraic substrate and the Reeb derivation

Having established the physical observations in the preceding chapter — mass spectra, coupling constants, and the spectral predictions that connect the substrate parameter \(q\) to measurable quantities — we now turn to the algebraic foundations that underpin these results. The goal of this chapter is to exhibit, in full categorical detail, the algebraic object whose internal geometry generates the physics.

The quantum vacuum is formalized as a self-dual Frobenius–Hopf algebra \(A\) living in a rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\). This object carries three layers of structure. First, the Frobenius form \(\lambda \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) and the Hopf comultiplication \(\Delta \colon A \to A \otimes A\) endow \(A\) with both an inner product and a coalgebra structure, related by the Frobenius compatibility condition. Second, a categorical Reeb derivation \(\xi_q \colon A \to A\) encodes the observer drift — the intrinsic time evolution generated by the contact structure on the state bundle \(\mathcal{S}\). Third, the spectral geometry of Bring’s curve \(\mathcal{B}\) provides the coordinate fibers: the \(2g = 8\) independent cycles of this genus-\(4\) curve determine the fundamental modes of the Reeb spectrum.

Self-duality is the conceptual keystone. Yekutieli’s rigid dualizing complex \(\omega_A^\bullet\) provides a canonical duality theory for the non-commutative algebra \(A\). The Frobenius form induces a quasi-isomorphism \(A \xrightarrow{\sim} \omega_A^\bullet\), establishing that the observer trace \(\Phi = \lambda \circ \mu\) and the observed state space are intrinsically paired. This self-duality ensures that the substrate does not require an external arena: it is simultaneously the algebra of observables and the space on which those observables act.

📄

Definition 6.1 ∀ stated (The quantum vacuum as a Frobenius–Hopf algebra). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathbf{C}\) be a rigid monoidal category. A Frobenius–Hopf substrate is a sextuple \((A, \mu, \eta, \Delta, \varepsilon, S)\) in \(\mathbf{C}\) equipped with a Frobenius form \(\lambda \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) satisfying the following axioms.

Algebra structure. The morphisms \(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A\) (multiplication) and \(\eta \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) (unit) make \(A\) into an associative unital algebra object in \(\mathbf{C}\).

Coalgebra structure. The morphisms \(\Delta \colon A \to A \otimes A\) (comultiplication) and \(\varepsilon \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) (counit) make \(A\) into a coassociative counital coalgebra object, with antipode \(S \colon A \to A\) satisfying the Hopf compatibility:

\[\varepsilon \circ \mu = u \circ (\varepsilon \otimes \varepsilon),\]

where \(u \colon \mathbf{1} \otimes \mathbf{1} \xrightarrow{\cong} \mathbf{1}\) is the canonical unit isomorphism, so that \(\varepsilon\) is an algebra map into the monoidal unit.

Frobenius relation. The Frobenius form \(\lambda\) satisfies:

\[\mu \circ \Delta = (\Delta \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \alpha \circ (\mathrm{id} \otimes \mu)\]

where \(\alpha\) is the associator in \(\mathbf{C}\).

Non-degeneracy. The Frobenius pairing \(\langle a, b \rangle_F = \lambda(\mu(a \otimes b))\) is non-degenerate: the induced map \(A \to A^\vee\) is an isomorphism, equivalently the snake identities hold with respect to a coevaluation \(\tilde{\eta} \colon \mathbf{1} \to A \otimes A\).

Self-duality. The algebra \(A\) is self-dual as a substrate: the non-degenerate Frobenius pairing identifies \(A\) with its dual \(A^\vee\) canonically, so that the observer trace \(\Phi = \lambda \circ \mu\) and the observed state space are intrinsically paired.

📄

Definition 6.2 ∀ stated (Substrate parameter and quantum Planck constant). \(\forall\)

The substrate parameter \(q \in \mathbb{C}^*\) is the deformation parameter of the Frobenius–Hopf algebra \(A\). It governs the non-commutativity of the algebraic substrate: when \(q = 1\) the algebra is commutative and the quantum structure degenerates to its classical shadow.

The quantum Planck constant associated to \(q\) is

\[\hbar_q \;=\; 1 - q^{-1} \;=\; \frac{q - 1}{q}.\]

The pair \((q, \hbar_q)\) parametrizes the deviation of \(A\) from commutativity. In the classical limit \(q \to 1\) one has \(\hbar_q \to 0\), recovering the commutative coordinate ring and the smooth manifold geometry of the base space.

Two structural properties follow directly from the definition. First, the invertibility condition \(q \ne 0\) ensures that \(A\) is a genuine Hopf algebra (the antipode is well-defined). Second, \(\hbar_q \ne 0\) whenever \(q \ne 1\), so the non-commutative regime \(q \ne 1\) always carries a non-trivial quantum scale.

In the categorical formulation of Chapter 1, the substrate parameter is an element of \(\mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1}) \cong k^\times\). Here we work with the concrete representative \(q \in \mathbb{C}^*\) obtained by evaluating this endomorphism. In geometric realisations (Chapter 6), \(q\) further specialises to a real parameter \(q > 1\) governing the Descartes universe.

📄

Definition 6.3 ∀ stated (Categorical Reeb derivation). \(\forall\)

Let \(A\) be a Frobenius–Hopf substrate in a rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\). The categorical Reeb derivation is the morphism \(\xi_q \colon A \to A\) uniquely determined by the following two conditions.

Normalization. The derivation is compatible with the contact form \(\theta\):

\[\xi_q \circ \theta \;=\; \theta,\]

so that \(\xi_q\) preserves the contact structure on the state bundle \(\mathcal{S}\).

Derivation property. The morphism \(\xi_q\) satisfies the Leibniz rule with respect to the multiplication \(\mu\) of \(A\):

\[\xi_q \circ \mu \;=\; \mu \circ (\xi_q \otimes \mathrm{id} + \mathrm{id} \otimes \xi_q).\]

The period of the Reeb derivation is the smallest positive integer \(\Omega_q\) (when it exists) such that the iterated composition satisfies

\[\xi_q^{\,\Omega_q} \;=\; \mathrm{id}_A.\]

The derivation \(\xi_q\) encodes the observer drift: the intrinsic time evolution of the substrate as seen from within. The periodicity condition ensures that the Reeb flow closes, yielding a discrete spectrum of frequencies on \(A\). Each eigenvalue of \(\xi_q\) corresponds to a fundamental mode of the substrate, and the full Reeb spectrum is determined by the spectral geometry of Bring’s curve \(\mathcal{B}\).

📄

Definition 6.4 ∀ stated (Non-commutative coordinate ring of Bring’s curve). \(\forall\)

Bring’s curve \(\mathcal{B} \subset \mathbb{P}^4\) is defined as the complete intersection

\[\mathcal{B} \;=\; V\!\bigl( \textstyle\sum x_i,\; \textstyle\sum x_i^2,\; \textstyle\sum x_i^3 \bigr) \;\subset\; \mathbb{P}^4,\]

where \([x_0 : x_1 : x_2 : x_3 : x_4]\) are homogeneous coordinates. This is a smooth algebraic curve of genus \(g = 4\), and it serves as the spectral coordinate fiber of the algebraic substrate.

The non-commutative coordinate ring of \(\mathcal{B}\) is defined as the quotient

\[\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B}) \;=\; \mathcal{O}_q(\mathbb{P}^4) \,\big/\, \bigl( \textstyle\sum x_i,\; \textstyle\sum x_i^2,\; \textstyle\sum x_i^3 \bigr),\]

where \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathbb{P}^4)\) is the quantum polynomial ring with relations \(x_i x_j = q\, x_j x_i\) for \(i < j\).

Symmetry. The symmetric group \(S_5\) acts on \(\mathcal{B}\) by permutation of the homogeneous coordinates. This action descends to an \(S_5\)-action on \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})\) by algebra automorphisms, reflecting the five-fold combinatorial symmetry of the substrate.

Spectral modes. By the Riemann–Hurwitz formula, a smooth curve of genus \(g\) has \(2g\) independent cycles in its first homology. For \(\mathcal{B}\) with \(g = 4\), the \(2g = 8\) fundamental modes of the Reeb spectrum correspond to these \(8\) independent cycles, providing the spectral basis for the derivation \(\xi_q\) acting on \(A\).

📄

Definition 6.5 ∀ stated (Rigid dualizing complex). \(\forall\)

Let \(A\) be the Frobenius–Hopf substrate algebra and let \(D(A)\) denote its derived category of bimodules. A rigid dualizing complex for \(A\) is a complex \(\omega_A^\bullet\) of \(A\)-bimodules satisfying the following conditions.

Finite injective dimension. The complex \(\omega_A^\bullet\) has finite injective dimension on both sides: as a left \(A\)-module and as a right \(A\)-module.

Rigidifying isomorphism. There exists a canonical isomorphism

\[\omega_A^\bullet \;\simeq\; R\mathrm{Hom}_{A^e}(A,\, A^e)\]

in \(D(A^e)\), where \(A^e = A \otimes A^{\mathrm{op}}\) is the enveloping algebra. This isomorphism is the rigidifying structure: it pins down \(\omega_A^\bullet\) up to unique isomorphism, eliminating the ambiguity that afflicts ordinary dualizing complexes.

Van den Bergh duality. For any finitely generated \(A\)-bimodule \(M\), the rigid dualizing complex induces a duality

\[\mathrm{Ext}^i_A(M,\, \omega_A^\bullet) \;\cong\; H^{d-i}(M)^\vee,\]

where \(d\) is the homological dimension of \(A\).

The rigidity condition, introduced by Yekutieli, ensures that the dualizing complex is intrinsic to \(A\) — it does not depend on a choice of base ring or presentation. This makes \(\omega_A^\bullet\) the correct categorical substitute for the canonical sheaf in the non-commutative setting.

📄

Theorem 6.6 ∀ stated (Self-duality of the algebraic substrate). \(\forall\)

The Frobenius form \(\lambda \colon A \to \mathbf{1}\) of the substrate algebra \(A\) induces a quasi-isomorphism between \(A\), viewed as a complex concentrated in degree zero, and its rigid dualizing complex \(\omega_A^\bullet\):

\[A \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}\; \omega_A^\bullet \quad\text{in } D(A).\]

More precisely, the non-degenerate Frobenius pairing \(\langle a, b \rangle_F = \lambda(\mu(a \otimes b))\) defines an \(A\)-bimodule map \(\varphi \colon A \to \omega_A^\bullet\) whose cone is acyclic, establishing a quasi-isomorphism in the derived category of \(A\)-bimodules.

Physical interpretation. Self-duality means that the observer trace \(\Phi = \lambda \circ \mu\) and the observed state space are canonically paired. The algebra \(A\) does not require an external arena: it is simultaneously the algebra of observables and the space on which those observables act. In the language of Yekutieli’s rigidity theory, the Frobenius form \(\lambda\) is the unique trace that makes \(A\) its own dualizing object.

Consequences. The quasi-isomorphism \(A \simeq \omega_A^\bullet\) implies:

  1. Serre-type duality: \(\mathrm{Ext}^i_A(M, A) \cong H^{d-i}(M)^\vee\) for finitely generated \(A\)-modules \(M\), where \(d\) is the homological dimension.

  2. Canonical trace: the composition \(\varepsilon \circ \mu\) factors through the Frobenius form, providing a categorical trace on \(\mathrm{End}(A)\).

  3. Uniqueness: since \(\omega_A^\bullet\) is rigid, the quasi-isomorphism is unique up to unique isomorphism — there is no ambiguity in the self-duality.

The unit particle as a cohomological defect

Having established the self-dual algebraic substrate, we now ask: where does matter arise? The Frobenius structure of \(A\) is globally non-degenerate, but it can fail locally. Matter emerges precisely at the locus of this failure — where a non-degenerate Levi form obstructs the Frobenius pairing. The unit particle is the fundamental cohomological defect, a generator of the local cohomology at the singular point \(z = 1\).

📄

Definition 6.7 ∀ stated (Matter as Frobenius failure via the Levi form). \(\forall\)

Define matter as the failure of the Frobenius structure. At a point \(p\) in the spectral fiber, the Levi form \(\mathcal{L}_p : T_p^{1,0}A \times T_p^{0,1}A \to \mathbb{C}\) measures the non-degeneracy of the contact structure. When \(\mathcal{L}_p \neq 0\), the Frobenius form \(\lambda\) cannot extend smoothly through \(p\), creating a topological defect. The set of such points forms the matter locus \(\mathrm{Sing}(\lambda) \subset \mathrm{Spec}(A)\).

📄

Definition 6.8 ∀ stated (Maximal ideal at the unit coordinate). \(\forall\)

Define the maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}_1 \subset A\) corresponding to the coordinate \(z = 1\) in the spectral fiber. This is the kernel of the evaluation homomorphism \(\mathrm{ev}_1 : A \to k\), \(f \mapsto f(1)\). The point \(z = 1\) is distinguished by the Frobenius structure: it is the fixed point of the antipode \(S\), hence the unique point where the Hopf and Frobenius structures interact maximally. The local ring \(A_{\mathfrak{m}_1}\) captures the algebraic behavior of the substrate near this fundamental singularity.

📄

Definition 6.9 ∀ stated (Local cohomology at the unit defect). \(\forall\)

Define the local cohomology group \(H^1_{\mathfrak{m}_1}(A)\) as the first right derived functor of the \(\mathfrak{m}_1\)-torsion functor \(\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}_1}\):

\[H^1_{\mathfrak{m}_1}(A) = R^1\Gamma_{\mathfrak{m}_1}(A)\]

This group measures the algebraic obstruction to extending sections across the defect at \(z = 1\). In the commutative case, \(H^1_{\mathfrak{m}_1}(A) \cong A_{\mathfrak{m}_1}/A\) captures the "principal parts" supported at the singularity. In our non-commutative setting, Yekutieli’s derived category framework provides the correct generalization.

📄

Definition 6.10 ∀ stated (The unit particle state \(\mathrm{Li}_q(z)\)). \(\forall\)

Define the unit particle state \(\mathrm{Li}_q(z)\) as the fundamental generator of \(H^1_{\mathfrak{m}_1}(A)\). It is the unique (up to scalar) element satisfying the \(q\)-differential equation:

\[d_q \mathrm{Li}_q(z) = \frac{1}{\log_q z}\, dz\]

where \(d_q\) is the Jackson \(q\)-derivative and \(\log_q z = \frac{z^{\hbar_q} - 1}{\hbar_q}\) is the \(q\)-logarithm. The notation \(\mathrm{Li}_q\) reflects that in the classical limit \(q \to 1\), this recovers the classical dilogarithm \(\mathrm{Li}_2(z)\), the fundamental period integral of algebraic geometry.

📄

Theorem 6.11 ∀ stated (Quantization of topological charge). \(\forall\)

The topological charge of the unit particle is quantized. The algebraic residue at \(z = 1\), computed via the observer trace \(\Phi\), equals unity:

\[\mathrm{Res}_q(\omega, 1) = \Phi\bigl(\mathrm{Res}_{\xi}(\omega)\bigr) = 1\]

where \(\omega\) is the canonical differential form on \(A\) and \(\mathrm{Res}_{\xi}\) denotes the residue along the Reeb flow. This result is the algebraic counterpart of the Gauss–Bonnet theorem: the total "curvature" of the defect, as measured by the self-dual pairing, is an integer. The quantization follows from the non-degeneracy of the Frobenius pairing and the periodicity of the Reeb derivation \(\xi_q\).

📄

Proposition 6.12 ∀ stated (The unit defect as a Legendrian knot). \(\forall\)

The unit particle defect is a Legendrian knot restricted to the \(q\)-torsion leaf \(L_q\) where the horizontal contact form \(\theta\) vanishes. Precisely, the support of \(\mathrm{Li}_q(z)\) in the contact manifold \((A, \theta)\) satisfies:

\[\theta\big|_{\mathrm{supp}(\mathrm{Li}_q)} = 0\]

This means the defect is maximally tangent to the contact distribution — it is a Legendrian submanifold. Since \(\dim_{\mathbb{R}} L_q = 3\), Legendrian curves in \(L_q\) are knots, and the unit particle inherits a knot type from its embedding in the \(q\)-torsion leaf. The Legendrian condition ensures that the defect carries no "angular momentum" transverse to the contact planes, consistent with its interpretation as a fundamental scalar particle.

The spectral trace and Tannaka–Krein duality

Having identified the unit particle as a cohomological defect — a maximal ideal of \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})\) at which the local cohomology \(H^2_\mathfrak{m}(A)\) is nonzero — we now turn to the problem of counting these defects across the entire spectral fiber. The maximal ideals of \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})\) are the "primes" of the quantum geometry, and counting them with appropriate weights yields \(q\)-analogs of the classical arithmetic functions of analytic number theory. The key insight is that defect-counting on the geometric side is dual to spectral decomposition on the algebraic side.

Tannaka–Krein duality provides the bridge: the category of localized representations at defects is equivalent to the category of comodules over the Hopf algebra reconstructed from the Reeb spectrum. This equivalence converts the geometric sum over defects into a spectral trace over Reeb eigenvalues, culminating in an explicit formula that equates the geometric and spectral sides — the non-commutative analog of the classical explicit formula of prime number theory.

📄

Definition 6.13 ∀ stated (The \(q\)-von Mangoldt function). \(\forall\)

The \(q\)-von Mangoldt function is defined over the maximal ideals \(\mathfrak{m}\) of the coordinate ring \(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})\). For a maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) with norm \(N(\mathfrak{m})\) (the cardinality of the residue field):

\[\Lambda_q(\mathfrak{m}) = \begin{cases} \dfrac{N(\mathfrak{m})^{\hbar_q} - 1}{\hbar_q} & \text{if } \mathfrak{m} \text{ corresponds to a fundamental defect}, \\[6pt] 0 & \text{otherwise}. \end{cases}\]

A maximal ideal is a fundamental defect if it lies over a prime ideal of the center of \(A\). The weight \(\frac{N(\mathfrak{m})^{\hbar_q} - 1}{\hbar_q}\) is the \(q\)-deformation of \(\log N(\mathfrak{m})\): as \(q \to 1\) (hence \(\hbar_q \to 0\)), L’Hôpital’s rule gives \(\Lambda_q(\mathfrak{m}) \to \log N(\mathfrak{m}) = \Lambda(\mathfrak{m})\), the classical von Mangoldt function.

📄

Definition 6.14 ∀ stated (The \(q\)-Chebyshev function). \(\forall\)

The \(q\)-Chebyshev function is the partial sum of the \(q\)-von Mangoldt function over the geometry:

\[\psi_q(X) = \sum_{\substack{\mathfrak{m} \in \mathrm{MaxSpec}(\mathcal{O}_q(\mathcal{B})) \\ N(\mathfrak{m}) \le X}} \Lambda_q(\mathfrak{m})\]

This is the \(q\)-deformed prime counting function: it accumulates the weights of fundamental defects ordered by norm. The function \(\psi_q(X)\) encodes the distribution of matter across the spectral fiber, weighted by the quantum Planck constant. In the classical limit, \(\psi_q(X) \to \psi(X)\), the classical Chebyshev function of analytic number theory.

📄

Theorem 6.15 ∀ stated (Tannaka–Krein duality for the substrate). \(\forall\)

Tannaka–Krein duality establishes an equivalence between two perspectives on the substrate:

\[\mathbf{Rep}_{\mathrm{loc}}(A) \simeq \mathbf{Comod}(H_\xi)\]

where \(\mathbf{Rep}_{\mathrm{loc}}(A)\) is the category of localized \(A\)-module representations (the "monopoles" — modules supported at maximal ideals) and \(\mathbf{Comod}(H_\xi)\) is the category of comodules over the Hopf algebra \(H_\xi\) reconstructed from the Reeb spectrum. The fibre functor \(\tau\) underlying this equivalence sends each localized module to its fiber at the unit defect.

This is a self-duality: the geometric side (localized representations at defects) and the spectral side (global quantum group symmetries of the Reeb flow) are equivalent descriptions of the same physical content. The reconstruction theorem guarantees that \(H_\xi\) is uniquely determined by the monoidal structure of \(\mathbf{Rep}_{\mathrm{loc}}(A)\) .

📄

Theorem 6.16 ∀ stated (Explicit formula as a spectral–geometric trace identity). \(\forall\)

The Tannaka–Krein self-duality manifests as a discrete Fourier transform over the spectral-geometric space. The explicit formula equates the geometric sum (over defects) to the spectral trace (over Reeb eigenvalues):

\[\psi_q(X) = X - \sum_{\rho \in \mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q)} \frac{X^\rho}{[\rho]_q} - \ln_q(2\pi\Omega_q) - \frac{1}{2}\ln_q(1 - X^{-2})\]

where \([\rho]_q = \frac{q^\rho - q^{-\rho}}{q - q^{-1}}\) is the \(q\)-integer, \(\Omega_q\) is the Reeb period, and \(\ln_q\) is the \(q\)-logarithm.

The leading term \(X\) represents the smooth background growth of defect density. The oscillatory sum over \(\mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q)\) encodes the fluctuations due to the Reeb eigenvalues — each eigenvalue \(\rho\) contributes a wave of amplitude \(X^\rho / [\rho]_q\). The constant and tail terms arise from the trivial eigenvalues and the symmetry of the functional equation. This formula is the non-commutative analog of the classical explicit formula of prime number theory .

Geometric stability via the Weil bound

The explicit formula relates the distribution of defects to the spectrum of the Reeb flow. But is this spectrum stable? If the Reeb eigenvalues stray too far from the critical line, the oscillatory terms in the explicit formula can grow without bound, leading to catastrophic accumulation or rarefaction of defects.

We now prove that the algebraic geometry of Bring’s curve unconditionally constrains the eigenvalues to the critical line \(\mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2\). This is the Weil bound — the finite-field analog of the Riemann hypothesis — applied to the spectral geometry of the substrate.

📄

Definition 6.17 ∀ stated (Local \(q\)-zeta function of Bring’s curve). \(\forall\)

Define the local \(q\)-zeta function of Bring’s curve \(\mathcal{B}\) as the generating function for point counts over finite extensions:

\[Z(\mathcal{B}, t) = \exp\!\left(\sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{|\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})|}{n}\, t^n\right) = \frac{P(t)}{(1-t)(1-qt)}\]

where \(P(t) = \prod_{i=1}^{2g}(1 - \alpha_i t)\) is the characteristic polynomial of the Frobenius endomorphism \(\mathrm{Fr}_q : H^1(\mathcal{B}) \to H^1(\mathcal{B})\), of degree \(2g = 8\) (since \(g = 4\) for Bring’s curve). The roots \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_8\) are the fundamental eigenvalues of the Frobenius action on the first étale cohomology.

The denominator factors \((1-t)\) and \((1-qt)\) correspond to \(H^0\) and \(H^2\) respectively, reflecting the trivial and cyclotomic contributions.

📄

Theorem 6.18 ∀ stated (Hasse–Weil bound for the fundamental eigenvalues). \(\forall\)

The 8 fundamental eigenvalues of the Frobenius endomorphism satisfy the Hasse–Weil bound:

\[|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2} \qquad \text{for all } i = 1, \ldots, 8\]

Proof sketch. The argument proceeds via the Castelnuovo–Severi inequality on the self-product \(\mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{B}\). The diagonal \(\Delta \subset \mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{B}\) defines a correspondence whose intersection number with the graph of \(\mathrm{Fr}_q^n\) counts \(|\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{F}_{q^n})|\). The Hodge index theorem on the surface \(\mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{B}\) implies the Castelnuovo–Severi inequality:

\[\bigl(D \cdot D\bigr) \le 2g \cdot \bigl(D \cdot H\bigr)\]

for any correspondence \(D\) and ample divisor \(H\). Applied to \(D = \mathrm{graph}(\mathrm{Fr}_q^n) - q^n \cdot \Delta\), this yields \(|\alpha_i|^2 \le q\) for all \(i\). The functional equation \(P(t) = q^g t^{2g} P(1/qt)\) then forces \(|\alpha_i|^2 = q\), completing the proof.

This is the Riemann hypothesis for Bring’s curve over \(\mathbb{F}_q\) — an unconditional theorem, not a conjecture, established by Weil’s foundational work on algebraic geometry over finite fields.

📄

Corollary 6.19 ∀ stated (All fundamental Reeb modes lie on the critical line). \(\forall\)

The spectral coordinate mapping \(\alpha_i = q^{\rho_i}\) translates the Hasse–Weil bound into a statement about the Reeb spectrum. Since \(|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}\) and \(|q^{\rho_i}| = q^{\mathrm{Re}(\rho_i)}\), we obtain:

\[\mathrm{Re}(\rho_i) = \frac{1}{2} \qquad \text{for all } \rho_i \in \mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q),\; i = 1, \ldots, 8\]

All 8 fundamental modes of the Reeb spectrum lie exactly on the critical line \(\mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2\). This is the finite-field Riemann hypothesis expressed in the language of the substrate: the spectral oscillations in the explicit formula are perfectly balanced, with each mode contributing fluctuations of amplitude \(|X^{\rho_i}/[\rho_i]_q| = X^{1/2}/|[\rho_i]_q|\) — square-root cancellation.

The classical limit and the macroscopic continuum

The preceding sections established that the algebraic substrate is unconditionally stable at the \(q\)-scale: the Hasse–Weil bound guarantees that all Frobenius eigenvalues lie on the critical circle \(|\alpha_i| = q^{1/2}\), and the Reeb spectrum inherits this alignment through the spectral coordinate mapping. The \(q\)-Chebyshev function satisfies its prime-counting estimate with the optimal square-root error term — a finite-field Riemann hypothesis, proven, not conjectured.

We now ask what happens when we pass to the macroscopic continuum. The classical limit \(q \to 1\) collapses the quantum gap \(\hbar_q \to 0\), smooths the Jackson \(q\)-derivative into the ordinary derivative, and degrades the braided tensor category into a symmetric one. The local \(q\)-geometries at each prime fiber glue into an adelic global object — the classical Riemann zeta function \(\zeta(s)\). Whether the macroscopic continuum inherits the stability of the \(q\)-scale is precisely the content of the Riemann hypothesis.

📄

Definition 6.20 ∀ stated (The classical limit functor \(q \to 1\)). \(\forall\)

Define the classical limit as a monoidal functor

\[\mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}_1\]

from the braided monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}_q\) (at deformation parameter \(q\)) to the symmetric monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}_1\) (at \(q = 1\)). The functor \(\mathcal{L}\) acts on the substrate algebra by:

  1. Quantum gap collapse: \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} \to 0\), so that the non-commutativity vanishes.

  2. Differential smoothing: The Jackson \(q\)-derivative \(d_q f(z) = \frac{f(qz) - f(z)}{(q-1)z}\) converges to the ordinary derivative \(\frac{df}{dz}\).

  3. Braiding trivialization: The braiding \(\sigma_{X,Y} : X \otimes Y \to Y \otimes X\) specializes to the symmetric swap \(\tau_{X,Y}\), since \(R(q) \to \mathrm{id}\) as \(q \to 1\).

The functor \(\mathcal{L}\) is exact (preserves short exact sequences) but not full: quantum information is lost in the limit.

📄

Theorem 6.21 ∀ stated (Collapse of the quantum gap). \(\forall\)

Under the classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L}\), the following degenerations occur simultaneously:

  1. Planck constant: \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1} \to 0\).

  2. \(q\)-differential: \(d_q \to d\) (the Jackson derivative becomes the ordinary derivative).

  3. Braiding: The braided monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}_q\) degenerates to a symmetric monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}_1\), as the \(R\)-matrix \(R(q) \to \mathrm{id} \otimes \mathrm{id}\).

  4. Reeb period: \(\Omega_q \to \infty\) (the discrete Reeb flow becomes a continuous one-parameter group).

Formally, \(\mathcal{L}\) sends the Frobenius–Hopf algebra \(A_q\) to a commutative Hopf algebra \(A_1 = \mathcal{O}(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cl}})\), the coordinate ring of the classical Bring’s curve over \(\mathbb{C}\). The self-duality \(A_q \simeq \omega_{A_q}^\bullet\) descends to the classical Serre duality \(H^i(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cl}}, \mathcal{O}) \cong H^{g-i}(\mathcal{B}_{\mathrm{cl}}, \Omega^1)^\vee\).

📄

Definition 6.22 ∀ stated (The classical limit obstruction of a quantum universe). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum universe over a Noetherian ring \(R\) with substrate parameter \(q\) and classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L} : \mathbf{C}_q \to \mathbf{C}_1\) (classical limit functor).

The classical limit obstruction of the quantum universe is the Hochschild cohomology group

\[\mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \;:=\; HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g}),\, \mathrm{Ad})\]

where \(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{g})\) is the Lusztig integral form of the quantized enveloping algebra associated to \(A\), and \(\mathrm{Ad}\) denotes the adjoint bimodule. Elements of \(\mathrm{Obs}\) are obstructions to extending second-order deformations of the Frobenius–Hopf algebra \(A_q\) across \(q = 1\).

The Hochschild tower. The Hochschild cohomology groups \(HH^n(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad})\) govern the deformation theory of the substrate family \(\{A_q\}_{q \in \mathbb{G}_m}\):

Degree Group Interpretation
\(HH^0(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\mathrm{Ad}^G\) \(G\)-invariant adjoint vectors (hidden symmetries)
\(HH^1(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\mathrm{Der}(\mathcal{U}_q) / \mathrm{Inn}(\mathcal{U}_q)\) Outer derivations (infinitesimal deformations of the family)
\(HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1)\) Obstructions to extending deformations across \(q = 1\)
\(HH^3(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\mathrm{Obs}_2\) Secondary obstructions (Massey products)

A property \(\mathcal{P}(q)\) that holds for \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}\) (generic non-torsion) persists through \(q = 1\) if and only if its obstruction class \([\mathcal{P}] \in HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})\) vanishes.

Why \(HH^2\) controls the classical limit. The classical limit \(q \to 1\) is a deformation-theoretic specialisation: the family \(\{A_q\}_{q \in \mathbb{G}_m}\) is a flat deformation of \(A_1\) over the formal neighborhood of \(q = 1\). The base of the deformation is \(\mathrm{Spf}\, R[[q-1]]\), and the obstructions to flatness at each order in \((q-1)\) live in \(HH^2\).

Concretely: expanding \(A_q = A_1 + (q-1)\,\phi_1 + (q-1)^2\,\phi_2 + \cdots\) (the Drinfeld–Jimbo expansion), the first-order deformation \(\phi_1\) is a Hochschild 2-cocycle (defines \([\phi_1] \in HH^2\)). The second-order term \(\phi_2\) exists iff \([\phi_1] \cup [\phi_1] = 0\) in \(HH^3\). The obstruction tower continues: \(\phi_n\) exists iff a sequence of Massey products vanishes in \(HH^{n+1}\).

The total obstruction to the classical limit is the formal sum:

\[\mathrm{obs}_\infty \;=\; \sum_{n \geq 1} (q-1)^n\, [\phi_n] \;\in\; HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})[[q-1]].\]

This formal power series converges (is a well-defined formal obstruction) iff all Massey products vanish through the tower.

For a general quantum universe: the obstruction space \(HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})\) has no a priori bound on its dimension. With \(m = \dim HH^0(\mathrm{Ad})\) hidden symmetries, the space of obstructions can be at least \(m\)-dimensional (by the cup product \(HH^0 \otimes HH^2 \to HH^2\), the hidden symmetries act on the obstruction space). Each independent obstruction class corresponds to a distinct way the classical limit can fail.

Connection to the Yekutieli tower. The Hochschild obstruction \([\phi_n] \in HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})\) maps to the quantum characteristic class \(\kappa_n \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B})\) (quantum characteristic classes) under the Hochschild-to-sheaf comparison map:

\[HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{HKR}\;} H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B}).\]

For smooth algebras this is the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg isomorphism; for the quantum group it is a filtered quasi-isomorphism . The upshot: the abstract Hochschild obstruction is computed concretely by the Euler class \(\kappa_0 = e(\xi)\) and its Kummer filtration.

📄

Theorem 6.23 ∀ stated (In a QOU the classical limit obstruction is one-dimensional). \(\forall\)

Theorem. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with gauge group \(G = \mathrm{Aut}^{\otimes}(\tau)\) of dimension \(d = \dim G\). Then:

(a) The classical limit obstruction (classical limit obstruction) is one-dimensional:

\[\dim_k \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \;=\; \dim_k HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) \;=\; 1.\]

(b) The unique obstruction class is the image of the Euler characteristic under the trace map:

\[\mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \;\cong\; k, \qquad [\phi_1] \;\mapsto\; \chi(A) \in R.\]

(c) The obstruction vanishes at Kummer level \(n\) iff \(n \mid \chi(A)\):

\[\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n \mid \chi(A).\]

Contrast with a general QU.

QU (no observability) QOU (observability)
\(HH^0(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\dim \geq 0\) (hidden symmetries) \(= 0\)
\(HH^1(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\dim \geq 1\) (deformation params) \(= 1\) (just \(q\))
\(HH^2(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\dim \geq 1\) (multiple obstructions) \(= 1\) (single scalar)
\(HH^3(\mathrm{Ad})\) \(\dim \geq 0\) (secondary obstructions) \(= 0\)
Obstruction multi-dimensional single integer \(\chi(A)\)
Classical limit may fail in independent ways controlled by Kummer divisibility

Proof of (a). Three ingredients combine:

Step 1: Observability kills \(HH^0\). The QOU axiom \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) (observability) is the statement

\[HH^0(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) = \mathrm{Ad}^G = 0.\]

The adjoint representation of a semisimple group has no invariant vectors (equivalently: \(\mathfrak{g}\) has trivial center).

Step 2: Frobenius duality relates \(HH^0\) and \(HH^d\). The Frobenius–Hopf self-duality \(A \cong A^\vee\) (the non-degenerate pairing from Frobenius–Hopf data) induces a Poincare duality on Hochschild cohomology :

\[HH^n(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad}) \;\cong\; HH^{d-n}(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad})^\vee, \qquad d = \dim G.\]

This is the Van den Bergh duality for Frobenius algebras: the dualizing bimodule is trivialized by the Frobenius form \(\lambda : A \to \mathbf{1}\).

Step 3: Dimension count for \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\). With \(d = \dim \mathrm{SU}(2) = 3\):

\(n\) \(HH^n\) Dimension Source
\(0\) \(\mathrm{Ad}^G\) \(0\) QOU observability
\(1\) Outer derivations \(1\) Single parameter \(q\)
\(2\) Obstructions \(1\) Dual to \(HH^1\) (\(d - 2 = 1\))
\(3\) Secondary \(0\) Dual to \(HH^0\) (\(d - 3 = 0\))

The key: \(HH^2 \cong (HH^{d-2})^\vee = (HH^1)^\vee\). The outer derivation space is one-dimensional because the Lusztig integral form \(\mathcal{U}^{\mathbb{Z}}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\) is a one-parameter family — \(q\) itself is the unique deformation direction. There are no other independent deformation parameters (this is a theorem of Drinfeld: the quantized enveloping algebra is the unique deformation of \(\mathcal{U}(\mathfrak{g})\) for simple \(\mathfrak{g}\)).

Therefore \(HH^2 \cong k\): the obstruction space is one-dimensional. \(\square\)

Proof of (b). The HKR comparison map sends the generator of \(HH^2\) to the Euler class \(\kappa_0 = e(\xi) \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B})\), whose trace is \(\chi(A)\) (QU-to-QOU theorem, item 2). Since \(HH^2 \cong k\) is one-dimensional, the entire obstruction is determined by the single scalar \(\chi(A)\). \(\square\)

Proof of (c). This is the Kummer specialisation (Kummer): \(\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0\) in \(H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m) / n\,H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) iff \(n\) divides the trace \(\chi(A)\). \(\square\)

The obstruction as a function on \(\mathbb{P}^1\).

The obstruction \(\chi(A) \bmod n\) varies over the Kummer tower \(\{\mu_n\}_{n \geq 1}\) inside \(\mathbb{G}_m \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1\):

\[\mathrm{obs}(n) := \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } n \mid \chi(A), \\ \chi(A) \bmod n & \text{otherwise.} \end{cases}\]

For the Descartes universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\):

Kummer level \(n\) \(\mathrm{obs}(n)\) Obstruction?
\(1\) \(0\) vanishes (trivially)
\(2\) \(0\) vanishes (\(2 \mid 6\))
\(3\) \(0\) vanishes (\(3 \mid 6\))
\(4\) \(-6 \bmod 4 = 2\) persists
\(5\) \(-6 \bmod 5 = 4\) persists
\(6\) \(0\) vanishes (\(6 \mid 6\))
\(7\) \(-6 \bmod 7 = 1\) persists
\(p > 3\) prime \(\neq 0\) persists

The obstruction vanishes at only finitely many levels (the divisors of \(|\chi(A)| = 6\), namely \(\{1, 2, 3, 6\}\)) and persists at all levels \(n\) with \(\gcd(n, 6) \neq n\) — in particular at all primes \(> 3\).

Physical consequence: the classical limit \(q \to 1\) must pass through infinitely many Kummer levels where the obstruction is nonzero. The density of non-vanishing levels in the Kummer tower is

\[\delta \;=\; 1 - \frac{|\{n : n \mid 6\}|}{N} \;\xrightarrow{N \to \infty}\; 1.\]

In the limit: the obstruction is nonzero at density-\(1\) set of levels. The classical limit cannot avoid the obstruction.

The three millennium problems as specializations. Each millennium problem is a property \(\mathcal{P}\) that holds unconditionally at the \(q\)-scale, with obstruction class \([\mathcal{P}] \in \mathrm{Obs}(\mathbf{C}, q \to 1) \cong k\). In the QOU, the single obstruction scalar controls all three:

Problem Property \(\mathcal{P}(q)\) \(q\)-scale status Classical obstruction
RH \(\mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2\) (spectral half-line) Proved (Hasse–Weil) Phase coherence of adelic assembly
NS \(q\)-NS global regularity Proved (exp. damping) Levi non-degeneracy at collision
BSD \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \neq 0\) (\(r_q = 0\)) Proved (Tannaka–Krein) \(L\)-value non-vanishing through assembly

All three obstructions are images of the same class \(\chi(A) \in HH^2 \cong k\) under different evaluation maps:

  • RH: evaluate \(\chi(A)\) on the spectral localization map \(HH^2 \to H^2(\mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q))\)

  • NS: evaluate \(\chi(A)\) on the collision restriction map \(HH^2 \to H^2(\Sigma, \mathcal{B}|_\Sigma)\)

  • BSD: evaluate \(\chi(A)\) on the elliptic restriction map \(HH^2 \to H^2(\mathcal{E}_q, \mathcal{B}|_{\mathcal{E}_q})\)

The one-dimensionality of \(HH^2\) means these three evaluations are proportional: there is a single real number (the Euler characteristic \(\chi(A) = -6\)) that controls whether all three millennium problems persist through the classical limit.

Corollary. If any one of the three millennium problems is resolved (in either direction), the resolution constrains the other two. Specifically: if the classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L}\) preserves the property \(\mathcal{P}\) for one problem, then the same functor either preserves or violates \(\mathcal{P}\) for the other two — the mechanism is the same, only the evaluation map differs.

Definition 6.24 ∀ stated (Classical Riemann zeta function as adelic limit). \(\forall\)

Define the classical Riemann zeta function \(\zeta(s)\) as the adelic global limit of the local \(q\)-geometries. As \(q \to 1\), the local zeta functions \(Z(\mathcal{B}, q^{-s})\) at each prime fiber assemble into the Euler product:

\[\zeta(s) = \prod_{p \text{ prime}} \frac{1}{1 - p^{-s}} = \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{n^s}, \qquad \mathrm{Re}(s) > 1\]

The passage from \(Z(\mathcal{B}, t)\) to \(\zeta(s)\) can be understood as follows: each maximal ideal \(\mathfrak{m}\) of norm \(N(\mathfrak{m}) = p^f\) contributes a local factor to the product. The adelic completion — taking the product over all primes simultaneously — yields the global zeta function.

The non-trivial zeros of \(\zeta(s)\) are the classical shadows of the Reeb eigenvalues: under the spectral coordinate mapping, \(\alpha_i = q^{\rho_i} \to e^{-\rho_i \log p}\) at each prime \(p\), and the global zeros arise from the coherent alignment of the local spectra.

📄

Conjecture 6.25 ✗ no Lean (The Riemann hypothesis).

Conjecture (Riemann, 1859). All non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function \(\zeta(s)\) satisfy

\[\mathrm{Re}(s) = \frac{1}{2}\]

In the language of the substrate, this asserts that the critical-line property established unconditionally at the \(q\)-scale (Corollary, §4) persists through the classical limit \(q \to 1\). The Hasse–Weil bound guarantees \(\mathrm{Re}(\rho) = 1/2\) for each local geometry individually; the Riemann hypothesis asserts that this alignment survives the adelic assembly into the global zeta function.

The gap between the local and global statements is precisely the gap between the proven Weil conjectures and the unproven Riemann hypothesis.

📄

Theorem 6.26 ∀ stated (Macroscopic stability is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis). \(\forall\)

The stability of the macroscopic spacetime continuum is equivalent to the Riemann hypothesis. Precisely:

Theorem. The following are equivalent:

  1. Macroscopic stability: The classical Chebyshev function satisfies \(\psi(X) = X + O(X^{1/2 + \varepsilon})\) for all \(\varepsilon > 0\).

  2. Riemann hypothesis: All non-trivial zeros of \(\zeta(s)\) satisfy \(\mathrm{Re}(s) = 1/2\).

  3. Spectral persistence: The critical-line property of the Reeb spectrum is preserved under the classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L}\).

The implication \((2) \Leftrightarrow (1)\) is classical (the prime number theorem with optimal error term). The implication \((2) \Leftrightarrow (3)\) follows from the spectral coordinate mapping and the explicit formula.

Crucially, the \(q\)-scale analog of statement (1) — namely, \(\psi_q(X) = X + O(X^{1/2})\) — is an unconditional theorem, guaranteed by the Hasse–Weil bound (Theorem, §4). The obstacle to extending this to the macroscopic scale is that the classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L}\) is not full: information about the relative phases of the local spectra is lost in the limit. Whether this information loss preserves the critical-line alignment is exactly the content of the Riemann hypothesis.

The algebraic substrate thus provides a conditional framework: \(q\)-scale stability is proven; macroscopic stability requires the Riemann hypothesis.

Conjecture 6.27 ✗ no Lean (The \(q\)-deformed Birch and Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture).

Conjecture (\(q\)-BSD). Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be a QOU with substrate parameter \(q\) and Descartes elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_q\) (Descartes elliptic curve). Define the categorical Mordell–Weil group as the abelian group of \(\mathbf{1}\)-rational points:

\[\mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1}) \;:=\; \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1},\, E_q)\]

where \(E_q \in \mathrm{Ob}(\mathbf{C})\) is the object whose fibre functor image \(\tau(E_q) = H^1(\mathcal{E}_q, \mathbb{Z})\) is the first cohomology of the elliptic fiber, and the group law is induced by the chord-tangent addition on \(\mathcal{E}_q\). Set \(r_q := \mathrm{rank}\,\mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1})\).

Categorical determination of the rank. The Tannaka–Krein equivalence (reconstruction) identifies \(\mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(G)\), so the categorical Mordell–Weil group is the \(G\)-invariant subspace:

\[\mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1}) \;\cong\; \tau(E_q)^G \;=\; H^1(\mathcal{E}_q)^G.\]

The rank \(r_q\) is the multiplicity of the trivial representation \(\mathbf{1}\) in the \(G\)-module \(H^1(\mathcal{E}_q)\). This depends critically on the categorical axioms:

Axioms Gauge group \(H^1(\mathcal{E}_q)\) as \(G\)-rep \(r_q\)
QU only unconstrained may contain \(\mathbf{1}\) \(\geq 0\)
QOU (+ observability) semisimple (\(\mathfrak{g}^G = 0\)) non-trivial if color-charged \(= 0\)
Descartes QOU (\(\chi = -6\)) \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) \(V_{1/2} \cong \mathbb{C}^2\) (fundamental) \(= 0\)

Proof that \(r_q = 0\) in the Descartes QOU. The Descartes elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_q\) is a coral fiber of the color fibration (coral elliptic), so \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) acts non-trivially on it. The first cohomology \(H^1(\mathcal{E}_q) \cong \mathbb{C}^2\) is two-dimensional (genus \(1\)). The only two-dimensional irreducible representation of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) is the fundamental \(V_{1/2}\). Since

\[V_{1/2}^{\,\mathrm{SU}(2)} = 0\]

(no nonzero vector in \(\mathbb{C}^2\) is fixed by all of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)), the categorical Mordell–Weil group is trivial: \(\mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1}) = 0\) and \(r_q = 0\).

Remark. This vanishing is forced by the QOU axioms, not by arithmetic accident. The observability axiom \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) forces \(G\) to be semisimple (the Lie algebra has no \(G\)-fixed vectors). For any semisimple \(G\), every non-trivial irreducible representation \(V\) satisfies \(V^G = 0\). The elliptic fiber carries a non-trivial representation because it lies in the color directions — the same directions on which \(G\) acts. A QU without observability could have \(G\) with a center (e.g. \(\mathrm{U}(2)\)), but even then \(V_{1/2}^{U(2)} = 0\) since the center scales all vectors. The only way to achieve \(r_q > 0\) would be an elliptic curve in the spacetime directions (on which \(G\) acts trivially), but \(\mathcal{E}_q\) is categorically determined as a color fiber.

The substrate family over \(\mathbb{P}^1\). The substrate parameter \(q\) is a section of \(\mathbb{G}_m\) (substrate \(\mathbb{G}_m\) torsion). The \(q\)-BSD conjecture is a statement about a family of \(L\)-functions parametrised by \(\mathbb{G}_m\), and its behavior at the boundary and torsion points of \(\mathbb{P}^1\) reveals the arithmetic content.

Embed \(\mathbb{G}_m \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^1\) via \(k^\times \hookrightarrow k \cup \{\infty\}\). The \(q\)-BSD data extends to a family over \(\mathbb{P}^1\) with three regimes:

(I) Generic \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}\) (non-torsion locus). The QOU axioms hold. The representation category \(\mathbf{C} \simeq \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) has infinitely many simple objects \(V_j\), \(j = 0, \tfrac{1}{2}, 1, \ldots\), with positive quantum dimensions \([2j+1]_q > 0\). The \(q\)-BSD data is:

  • \(r_q = 0\) (by the argument above)

  • \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \neq 0\) (computable from Frobenius eigenvalues; the Hasse–Weil bound gives \(|\alpha_\mathcal{E}| = q^{1/2}\), so the Euler factors are bounded away from zero)

  • The weak \(q\)-BSD reduces to \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \neq 0\), which is an unconditional theorem at the \(q\)-scale

(II) \(\mathbb{G}_m\) torsion: roots of unity \(q = \zeta_n\). At the torsion points (root-of-unity truncation), the representation category truncates to finitely many simple objects \(V_0, V_{1/2}, \ldots, V_{(n-2)/2}\), forming a modular tensor category (Chern–Simons TQFT at level \(n\)). The \(q\)-BSD data undergoes a phase transition:

  • The categorical rank remains zero: \(V_{1/2}\) is still non-trivial in the truncated category, so \(V_{1/2}^G = 0\) and \(r_q = 0\) persists at all roots of unity.

  • The \(q\)-integers degenerate: \([n]_{\zeta_n} = 0\), so the \(q\)-factorial \([r]_q!\) and the explicit formula have poles/zeros at the torsion points.

  • The \(L\)-function truncates: the Euler product over \(\mathrm{Spec}(R_q)\) reduces to a finite product (only finitely many representations contribute to the trace), giving a rational function in \(\zeta_n\) rather than an infinite product.

  • The Kummer obstruction (Kummer specialisation) controls the behavior: \(\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0\) iff \(n \mid \chi(A)\). For \(\chi(A) = -6\), the obstruction vanishes only at \(n \in \{1, 2, 3, 6\}\) and persists for all other \(n\). At levels where the obstruction persists, the \(L\)-function carries non-trivial arithmetic information from the Euler class.

(III) Boundary points \(q = 0\) and \(q = \infty\). At the boundary of \(\mathbb{P}^1\):

  • \(q = 0\): the operator \(d_q = q^{-1} d + (1 - q^{-1}) \pi_V d\) has a pole. The elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_q\) degenerates (the Weierstrass coefficients \(p(q), r(q)\) diverge). The \(L\)-function has an essential singularity.

  • \(q = \infty\): \(d_q \to \pi_V \circ d\) (pure Reeb direction). The \(j\)-invariant \(j(\mathcal{E}_q) \to 0\): the curve approaches a CM curve with complex multiplication. The \(L\)-function acquires Hecke \(L\)-function structure (Deuring’s theorem).

The \(q\)-deformed \(L\)-function. The Frobenius eigenvalues \(\alpha_1, \ldots, \alpha_8\) of the local \(q\)-zeta function (local \(q\)-zeta) act on \(H^1(\mathcal{B})\), the first étale cohomology of Bring’s curve. The elliptic fiber \(\mathcal{E}_q \hookrightarrow \mathcal{B}\) is a genus-\(1\) sub-curve, so the restriction of Frobenius to \(H^1(\mathcal{E}_q) \subset H^1(\mathcal{B})\) yields a conjugate pair \(\alpha_{\mathcal{E}}, \bar{\alpha}_{\mathcal{E}}\) with \(|\alpha_{\mathcal{E}}| = q^{1/2}\) (by the Hasse–Weil bound). Define:

\[L(\mathcal{E}_q, s) \;:=\; \prod_{\mathfrak{m} \in \mathrm{Spec}(R_q)} \frac{1}{1 - \alpha_{\mathcal{E}}(\mathfrak{m})\, N(\mathfrak{m})^{-s} + N(\mathfrak{m})^{1-2s}}\]

where the product runs over the maximal ideals of the coordinate ring \(R_q\) of Bring’s curve and \(N(\mathfrak{m}) = q^{f(\mathfrak{m})}\) is the norm.

The \(q\)-Tate–Shafarevich group. The fibre functor atlas of the QOU forms a \(G\)-gerbe over the spectral base. For each Reeb eigenvalue \(\rho \in \mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q)\), let \(\mathbf{C}_\rho\) be the localization of \(\mathbf{C}\) at \(\rho\) (the full subcategory of objects whose spectral support contains \(\rho\)). Define the \(q\)-Tate–Shafarevich group as the kernel of the local-global map:

\[\mathrm{Sha}_q(\mathcal{E}_q) \;:=\; \ker\!\left( H^1_{\otimes}(\mathbf{C},\, E_q) \;\longrightarrow\; \prod_{\rho \,\in\, \mathrm{Spec}(\xi_q)} H^1_{\otimes}(\mathbf{C}_\rho,\, E_q) \right)\]

where \(H^1_{\otimes}\) denotes the first cohomology of the monoidal category (classifying torsors under \(\mathcal{E}_q\) in \(\mathbf{C}\)). This measures the failure of the local-global principle at the \(q\)-scale: torsors that are trivial at every spectral localization but globally non-trivial.

Statement. The conjecture has two parts, mirroring the classical BSD:

(Weak \(q\)-BSD). The order of vanishing of \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, s)\) at \(s = 1\) equals the categorical rank:

\[\mathrm{ord}_{s=1}\, L(\mathcal{E}_q, s) \;=\; r_q\]

For the Descartes QOU: since \(r_q = 0\), this reduces to \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \neq 0\), which is an unconditional theorem at the \(q\)-scale (the Hasse–Weil bound ensures the Euler factors are bounded away from zero).

(Full \(q\)-BSD). Since \(r_q = 0\), the regulator is \(\mathrm{Reg}_q = 1\) (determinant of the empty matrix), the torsion subgroup is trivial, and the formula collapses to:

\[L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1) \;=\; \Omega_q \;\cdot\; |\mathrm{Sha}_q(\mathcal{E}_q)| \;\cdot\; \prod_{\mathfrak{m}} c_{\mathfrak{m}}(q)\]

This is a computable identity at the \(q\)-scale: the left side comes from Frobenius eigenvalues, the right side from the Reeb period, the \(q\)-Tate–Shafarevich group, and the Tamagawa numbers.

In the general formulation (for categories where \(r_q > 0\)), the leading Taylor coefficient satisfies:

\[\frac{L^{(r_q)}(\mathcal{E}_q, 1)}{[r_q]_q!} \;=\; \frac{\Omega_q \;\cdot\; \mathrm{Reg}_q(\mathcal{E}_q) \;\cdot\; |\mathrm{Sha}_q(\mathcal{E}_q)| \;\cdot\; \displaystyle\prod_{\mathfrak{m}} c_{\mathfrak{m}}(q)} {|\mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1})_{\mathrm{tors}}|^2_q}\]

where \([r_q]_q! = [1]_q \cdot [2]_q \cdots [r_q]_q\) is the \(q\)-factorial, \(\Omega_q\) is the Reeb period, \(\mathrm{Reg}_q\) is the \(q\)-regulator (determinant of the \(q\)-Neron–Tate height pairing), and \(c_\mathfrak{m}(q)\) are the Tamagawa numbers.

Kummer tower and the \(q \to 1\) obstruction. The Kummer exact sequence (Kummer specialisation)

\[1 \to \mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n} \mathbb{G}_m \to 1\]

controls the specialisation of \(L(\mathcal{E}_q, 1)\) to the classical limit. The Euler class \(\kappa_0 = e(\xi)\) with \(\mathrm{tr}(\kappa_0) = \chi(A) = -6\) satisfies:

\[\kappa_0 \bmod n \neq 0 \qquad\text{for } n \nmid 6.\]

This means: the topological obstruction class \(\kappa_0 \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) is not \(n\)-divisible for \(n = 5, 7, 11, 13, \ldots\) (all primes \(> 3\) and their multiples). At each such level of the Kummer tower, the \(q\)-BSD formula carries non-trivial arithmetic content that cannot be cancelled by torsion.

The parallel with the NS obstruction (NS Kummer) is exact:

Millennium problem \(q\)-scale Classical limit \(q \to 1\) Obstruction
Riemann hypothesis Hasse–Weil (proved) \(\mathrm{Re}(s) = 1/2\) (open) Phase coherence of local spectra
Navier–Stokes \(q\)-NS regular (proved) NS regularity (open) \(\kappa_0 \bmod 2\kappa \neq 0\) for \(\kappa \geq 4\)
Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer \(r_q = 0\), \(L \neq 0\) (proved) \(r_1 = 0\), \(L(E_1, 1) \neq 0\) (open) \(\kappa_0 \bmod n \neq 0\) for \(n \nmid 6\)

All three millennium problems share the same structure in the QOU framework: an unconditional theorem at the \(q\)-scale whose persistence through the \(q \to 1\) limit is controlled by the Kummer divisibility of the Euler class \(\chi(A) = -6\).

Classical limit. As \(q \to 1\) (the adelic assembly), the \(q\)-BSD formula recovers the classical Birch–Swinnerton-Dyer conjecture for \(E_1 : y^2 = x^3 + \frac{2}{3}x + \frac{20}{27}\). The representation category deforms from \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) to \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\), but the rank \(r_1 = 0\) persists (the fundamental of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) still has no invariants). So the classical prediction is: the classical curve \(E_1\) has rank \(0\) and \(L(E_1, 1) \neq 0\).

The passage from the \(q\)-scale theorem (\(L \neq 0\)) to the classical statement (\(L(E_1, 1) \neq 0\)) is obstructed by the same mechanism as the Riemann hypothesis: the classical limit functor \(\mathcal{L}\) is not full, and information about the relative phases of local \(L\)-factors is lost in the adelic assembly.

The \(q\)-height pairing (general \(r_q\)). For categories where \(r_q > 0\) (non-observable universes or spacetime-direction elliptic curves), the Neron–Tate height admits a \(q\)-deformation via the spectral trace. For \(P, Q \in \mathcal{E}_q(\mathbf{1})\):

\[\langle P, Q \rangle_q \;:=\; \lim_{n \to \infty} \frac{\hat{h}_q([n]_q P,\, Q)}{[n]_q^2}\]

where \(\hat{h}_q\) is the naive \(q\)-Weil height and \([n]_q P\) denotes scalar multiplication by the \(q\)-integer \([n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1})\). At \(\mathbb{G}_m\) torsion points \(q = \zeta_n\), the denominator \([n]_{\zeta_n}^2 = 0\) and the height pairing degenerates — a reflection of the category truncation. The regulator \(\mathrm{Reg}_q = \det(\langle P_i, P_j \rangle_q)\) has poles at the torsion locus, matching the zeros of \([r_q]_q!\) in the denominator of the full BSD formula.

Conjecture 6.28 ✗ no Lean (The \(q\)-Collatz conjecture: Skein-module crossing resolution).

Conjecture (\(q\)-Collatz). Let \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k)\) be a substrate parameter (torsion avoidance) and let \(\mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) be the Skein module of the Reeb bundle \(\mathcal{R}_p = (S^3 \to S^2, \xi_q)\) (Reeb bundle).

Convention. This section uses the combinatorial \(q\)-integer \([n]_q = (q^n - 1)/(q - 1)\), giving \([2]_q = q + 1\) and \([3]_q = q^2 + q + 1\). The paper’s Iwahori–Hecke algebra convention \([n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1})\) (symmetric, giving \([2]_q = q + q^{-1}\)) differs by a factor of \(q^{(n-1)/2}\). The combinatorial convention is used here because the Skein divisibility identity \([3]_q = q[2]_q + 1\) and the contraction gap \([2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q\) require it.

\(q\)-parity in the Skein module

An element \(P \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) is \(q\)-even if \([2]_q \mid P\) and \(q\)-odd if \([2]_q \mid (P + 1)\). At \(q = 1\): \([2]_1 = 2\), and these recover integer parity.

The Skein-Collatz map

Define \(\mathcal{C}_q \colon \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}] \to \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) by:

\[\mathcal{C}_q(P) \;=\; \begin{cases} P \,/\, [2]_q & P \text{ is } q\text{-even},\\[4pt] \bigl([3]_q\, P + 1\bigr) \,/\, [2]_q & P \text{ is } q\text{-odd}. \end{cases}\]

The odd branch is well-defined by the Skein divisibility identity:

\[[3]_q \;=\; q\,[2]_q + 1,\]

which gives \([3]_q\, P + 1 = q\,[2]_q\, P + (P + 1)\). Since \(P\) is \(q\)-odd (\([2]_q \mid P + 1\)), the numerator is divisible by \([2]_q\). Writing \(P + 1 = [2]_q\, Q\):

\[\mathcal{C}_q(P) \;=\; q\,P + Q \;=\; [3]_q\,Q - q.\]

Classical limit. At \(q = 1\): \(\mathcal{C}_1(n) = n/2\) (even) or \((3n+1)/2\) (odd) — the Syracuse map.

Skein-theoretic interpretation

Each application of \(\mathcal{C}_q\) corresponds to a crossing resolution in the Skein module (skein generation):

  • Even branch (\(P/[2]_q\)): Markov destabilization — remove one strand from the braid closure, dividing the Jones polynomial by the Markov parameter. This is the \(q\)-analog of "halving."

  • Odd branch (\(([3]_q P + 1)/[2]_q\)): apply the Hecke relation \(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\) to reduce a quadratic crossing word to linear, then destabilize. The three generators in \(T^3 = [3]_q \cdot T + \cdots\) reduce to one via the Hecke relation, then the Markov move removes it.

The Skein relation \(q\,L_+ - q^{-1}\,L_- = (q - q^{-1})\,L_0\) ensures each resolution step is a convex combination:

\[J(L_+) = q^{-2}\,J(L_-) + (1 - q^{-2})\,J(L_0).\]

For \(q > 1\) both coefficients are positive and sum to \(1\). The crossing resolution is non-expansive on the Jones polynomial.

The contraction estimate

The algebraic identity \([2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q\) gives the contraction. Over one Collatz cycle (one odd step followed by enough even steps to exhaust \([2]_q\)-divisibility):

  • The odd step maps \(P \mapsto [3]_q\,Q - q\), where \(Q = (P+1)/[2]_q\). The ratio \(|P|/|Q| \approx [2]_q\).

  • The subsequent even steps divide by \([2]_q\) as many times as \([2]_q\) divides the result.

If each tripling is followed by at least two halvings on average, the orbit contracts. Two halvings multiply by \(1/[2]_q^2\); one tripling multiplies by \([3]_q/[2]_q\). The net factor per cycle is \([3]_q / [2]_q^3 < 1\), with margin:

\[[2]_q^2 - [3]_q \;=\; q.\]

The margin is the substrate parameter itself. Two halvings beat one tripling by a factor \([2]_q^2 / [3]_q = 1 + q/[3]_q \approx 4/3\).

The conjecture

\[\boxed{ \text{For all } q > 1 \text{ and all } P \in \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]_{>0},\; \text{the orbit } \{\mathcal{C}_q^k(P)\}_{k \geq 0} \text{ reaches } 1. }\]

Connection to the obstruction framework

The Collatz obstruction \(\kappa_C := \mathrm{res}_{C_q}(\kappa_0) \in H^2(\mathcal{S}_{C_q}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) (classical limit obstruction, QOU obstruction reduction) measures the failure of Skein-Collatz orbits to converge.

The conjecture \(\kappa_C = 0\) is equivalent to: every element of the Skein module \(\mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) reduces to the unknot polynomial \(1\) under iterated crossing resolution via \(\mathcal{C}_q\).

Proposition 6.29 (The \([2]_q\)-contact boundary on the Reeb bundle).

Proposition (\([2]_q\)-contact boundary). Let \(\mathcal{R}_p = (S^3 \xrightarrow{\pi_H} S^2, \xi_q)\) be the Reeb bundle (Reeb bundle) with \(U(1)\) fiber parametrized by \(q = e^{i\theta}\), \(\theta \in [0, 2\pi)\).

From integer parity to the \([2]_q\)-divisor

Classical Collatz hinges on a single question: is \(n\) even or odd? Parity is residue mod \(2\). The number \(2\) is special: it is the smallest prime, the only even prime, and the denominator of the halving step \(n/2\).

In the QOU, the integer \(2\) lifts to the quantum integer \([2]_q = q + 1\) (combinatorial convention; see q-Collatz conjecture). The \([2]_q\)-divisor is the locus where \([2]_q = 0\), i.e. \(q = -1\):

\[D_{[2]} \;:=\; \{q : [2]_q = 0\} \;=\; \{-1\}.\]

This is where the \(q\)-analog of "dividing by \(2\)" degenerates — where the halving step ceases to exist.

Kummer obstruction at the divisor. The point \(q = -1\) belongs to \(\mu_2\) (the 2nd roots of unity). The Kummer obstruction (root-of-unity truncation) at level \(n = 2\) asks: does \(2\) divide \(\chi(A) = -6\)? Yes — \(6/2 = 3\). The obstruction vanishes. This means the \([2]_q\)-divisor is removable: the QOU axioms can resolve the singularity. At \(q = -1\), the residue ring is \(\mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]/(q+1) \cong \mathbb{Z}\) (setting \(q = -1\)), and the \([2]_q\)-adic valuation specializes to the ordinary \(2\)-adic valuation.

The \([2]_q\)-adic valuation as contact order

For an element \(P \in \mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) of the Skein module, define the \([2]_q\)-adic valuation:

\[v_{[2]}(P) \;:=\; \max\bigl\{k \geq 0 : [2]_q^k \mid P \text{ in } \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\bigr\}.\]

This counts how many times \([2]_q\) divides \(P\) in the Laurent polynomial ring — the \(q\)-analog of the \(2\)-adic valuation \(v_2(n)\) that counts trailing zeros in the binary expansion of an integer.

Geometric meaning. The value \(v_{[2]}(P)\) is the contact order of \(P\) with the divisor \(D_{[2]}\): the order to which \(P(q)\) vanishes at \(q = -1\). High contact order means the orbit "grazes" the divisor closely — it is very divisible by \([2]_q\), meaning many halvings can be extracted.

At \(q = 1\): \([2]_1 = 2\), and \(v_{[2]}(n) = v_2(n)\) recovers ordinary \(2\)-adic valuation. The number \(n = 24 = 2^3 \cdot 3\) has \(v_2(24) = 3\): three halvings before hitting an odd number.

Why the orbit needs to touch the divisor

The Skein-Collatz map (conj:q-collatz) has two branches:

  • Even branch (\(P/[2]_q\)): each application decreases \(\log|P|\) by \(\log [2]_q\). This is a halving — the orbit moves toward \(1\).

  • Odd branch (\(([3]_q P + 1)/[2]_q\)): the multiplication by \([3]_q\) increases \(\log|P|\) by \(\log([3]_q/[2]_q)\), despite the single division by \([2]_q\) built into the accelerated step.

The competition: each tripling (odd step) inflates the orbit, and each subsequent halving deflates it. The orbit converges only if the halvings win on average.

After each odd step, the result \(\mathcal{C}_q(P)\) is \(q\)-even — the Skein divisibility identity \([3]_q = q[2]_q + 1\) guarantees this. But how even is it? The number \(v_{[2]}(\mathcal{C}_q(P))\) — the contact order with \(D_{[2]}\) — determines how many consecutive halvings follow before the next odd step.

The contact threshold

Proposition. The orbit converges if and only if the average contact order exceeds a critical threshold.

Define the orbit contact average: over the first \(N\) steps, restrict to the odd steps (there are \(N_{\mathrm{odd}}\) of them), and average the \([2]_q\)-adic valuation of the results:

\[\langle v_{[2]} \rangle_N(P) \;:=\; \frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{odd}}} \sum_{\substack{0 \leq k < N \\ \mathcal{C}_q^k(P) \text{ is } q\text{-odd}}} v_{[2]}\bigl(\mathcal{C}_q^{k+1}(P)\bigr).\]

The condition is simplest without logarithms. Since \(1 < v^*(q) < 2\) (proved: \([2]_q < [3]_q < [2]_q^2\)), the orbit converges whenever each tripling is followed by at least two halvings on average:

\[\text{orbit converges} \quad\Longleftarrow\quad \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) \;\geq\; 2.\]

Two halvings multiply by \([2]_q^{-2}\); one tripling multiplies by \([3]_q / [2]_q\). The net factor per cycle (one tripling + two halvings) is:

\[\frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q} \cdot \frac{1}{[2]_q^2} \;=\; \frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^3}.\]

This is contractive because \([3]_q < [2]_q^2 < [2]_q^3\). The contraction ratio is:

\[\frac{[3]_q}{[2]_q^3} \;=\; \frac{[2]_q^2 - q}{[2]_q^3} \;=\; \frac{1}{[2]_q} - \frac{q}{[2]_q^3},\]

so the orbit shrinks by slightly more than \(1/[2]_q\) per cycle. The margin — the gap between two halvings and the minimum needed — is:

\[[2]_q^2 - [3]_q \;=\; q.\]

The margin is the substrate parameter itself.

The sharp threshold (for the record) is \(v^* = \log [3]_q / \log [2]_q\), but since \(v^* < 2\) is proved algebraically, the integer condition \(\langle v \rangle \geq 2\) is sufficient and avoids transcendental quantities.

Classical verification. At \(q = 1\): the average \(2\)-adic valuation of \(3n+1\) for odd \(n\) is exactly \(2\) (a theorem: the probability \(\Pr(v_2(3n+1) = k) = 2^{-k}\) gives \(\mathbb{E}[v_2] = 2\)). Two halvings per tripling, exactly at the integer threshold.

The boundary

The Collatz contact boundary is the codimension-\(1\) locus where the orbit’s contact with \(D_{[2]}\) is exactly critical:

\[\mathcal{H}_{Col}(q) \;=\; \bigl\{P \in \mathcal{S}(q) : \langle v_{[2]} \rangle(P) = v^*(q)\bigr\}.\]

Elements above the boundary (high contact, many halvings) converge. Elements below (insufficient contact, too few halvings) diverge. The conjecture says no element is below.

Two halvings beat one tripling? \([2]_q^2 > [3]_q\) \(4 > 3\) \(4.45 > 3.34\)
Margin \([2]_q^2 - [3]_q = q\) \(1\) \(1.110\)
Relative margin \(q / [3]_q\) \(1/3\) \(0.332\)

Two halvings overpower one tripling by a factor \([2]_q^2 / [3]_q = 1 + q/[3]_q \approx 4/3\). The margin \(q/[3]_q \approx 1/3\) is the substrate parameter divided by the tripling factor — clean and algebraic.

The conjecture as contact condition

The \(q\)-Collatz conjecture (conj:q-collatz) is equivalent to:

\[\boxed{ \bigl\langle v_{[2]}([3]_q P + 1) \bigr\rangle \;\geq\; 2 \quad\text{for all } P \in \mathcal{S}(q)_{>0}. }\]

Two halvings per tripling, on average over every orbit.

Proposition 6.30 (No periodic Collatz cycles: coprimality of \([2]_q\) and \([3]_q\)).

Proposition (no periodic Collatz cycles). The Skein-Collatz map \(\mathcal{C}_q\) on \(\mathcal{S}(q) \cong \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\) has no periodic orbits other than the fixed point \(P = 1\).

Proof. A periodic orbit of length \(k\) with \(k_{\mathrm{odd}}\) odd steps and \(k_{\mathrm{even}}\) even steps satisfies \(\mathcal{C}_q^k(P) = P\). The odd steps multiply by \([3]_q / [2]_q\) and the even steps multiply by \(1/[2]_q\), so the return condition requires:

\[\frac{[3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}}}{[2]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}} + k_{\mathrm{even}}}} \;=\; 1, \qquad\text{i.e.,}\qquad [3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} \;=\; [2]_q^k \quad (k = k_{\mathrm{odd}} + k_{\mathrm{even}}).\]

But \([2]_q\) and \([3]_q\) are coprime in \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\). The Skein divisibility identity gives the proof in one line:

\[[3]_q - q\,[2]_q = 1,\]

so \(\gcd([2]_q,\, [3]_q) = 1\) by Bézout. Since \([3]_q\) is a unit modulo \([2]_q\):

\[[3]_q^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} \;\equiv\; 1^{k_{\mathrm{odd}}} \;\equiv\; 1 \pmod{[2]_q},\]

while \([2]_q^k \equiv 0 \pmod{[2]_q}\) for \(k \geq 1\). These are never equal for \(k_{\mathrm{odd}} \geq 1\). A cycle with \(k_{\mathrm{odd}} = 0\) (all even steps) would be \(P \mapsto P / [2]_q^k = P\), forcing \(P = 0\).

Therefore the only periodic orbit is \(P = 1\) (the unknot). \(\square\)

Classical limit. At \(q = 1\): \(\gcd(2, 3) = 1\) and \(3^a \neq 2^b\) for \(a, b > 0\) (unique prime factorization). The \(q\)-deformation lifts this to polynomial coprimality.

The full \((a, a+1)\) family. The identity \(\gcd([a]_q, [b]_q) = [\gcd(a,b)]_q\) shows that all Collatz-type maps \((a, a+1)\) exclude periodic cycles, since \(\gcd(a, a+1) = 1\) for all \(a\). Cycle exclusion is a consequence of consecutive integers being coprime — a fact that lifts from \(\mathbb{Z}\) to \(\mathbb{Z}[q]\) via the \(q\)-integer functor.

What remains. This proposition settles half the Collatz conjecture: no periodic cycles other than \(\{1\}\). The other half — no divergent orbits — is the contact condition \(\langle v_{[2]} \rangle \geq 2\) (contact boundary).

Fluid Dynamics of the Brane

\(q\)-deformed hydrodynamics

The brane of a quantum observable universe carries a natural fluid dynamics. The substrate parameter \(q\) sets the effective brane thickness: at \(q = 1\) the brane is infinitely thin (classical vacuum); at \(q > 1\) it acquires a finite transverse extent controlled by the \(q\)-deformed contact geometry. The resulting dynamics inherits three features absent from ordinary Navier–Stokes theory:

  1. Algebraic viscosity. The \(q\)-Laplacian \(\Delta_q\) (q-Laplacian interpretation) replaces the classical Laplacian, and its eigenvalues are \(q\)-integers \([k]_q\). The viscous dissipation rate is therefore algebraically quantised rather than continuously variable.

  2. Gauge-covariant advection. The velocity field \(v = \nabla_A S\) is defined via the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) connection \(A\) rather than a flat gradient. Advection along \(v\) preserves the horizontal self-duality \(F_A|_H = {*_H}F_A|_H\), coupling the fluid motion to the gauge structure.

  3. Topological vortex quantisation. The circulation around any closed vortex filament \(\varrho\) is constrained by the \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) holonomy to discrete values \([j]_q[j+1]_q\), producing the discrete vortex spectrum.

📄

Definition 7.1 ∀ stated (\(q\)-deformed Navier–Stokes equation). \(\forall\)

The quantum Euler equation describes inviscid flow in the brane fluid. To account for dissipation — the irreversible transfer of kinetic energy from coherent vortex motion to incoherent thermal fluctuations — we introduce the \(q\)-deformed Navier–Stokes equation, first in categorical language and then in coordinates.

Categorical formulation. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a QOU with substrate parameter \(q \in \mathrm{End}(\mathbf{1})\), \(q > 1\). Let \(\Omega^k(A)\) denote the differential forms on the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\), with q-exterior derivative \(d_q \colon \Omega^k(A) \to \Omega^{k+1}(A)\) and its adjoint \(\delta_q \colon \Omega^{k+1}(A) \to \Omega^k(A)\) with respect to the Frobenius pairing. The \(q\)-Laplacian is \(\Delta_q = d_q\delta_q + \delta_q d_q\).

The \(q\)-Navier–Stokes system is the pair of morphisms in \(\mathbf{C}\):

\[\partial_t v + \mu \circ (v \otimes \nabla_q v) \;=\; -\rho^{-1}\,d_q\,p \;-\; d_q\,Q_q \;+\; \tfrac{1}{2}(1 - q^{-1})\,\Delta_q\,v \;+\; \rho^{-1}\,\delta_q\,\boldsymbol{\sigma}_q,\]

\[\partial_t\,\rho + \delta_q(\rho \cdot v) = 0,\]

where:

  • \(v \in \Omega^1(A)\) is the velocity 1-form,

  • \(\rho \in A\) is the density (a 0-form),

  • \(p \in A\) is the pressure,

  • \(\nabla_q\) is the q-connection,

  • \(\mu \colon A \otimes A \to A\) is the multiplication on \(A\),

  • \(Q_q = -\tfrac{1}{2}(1-q^{-1})^2\, \Delta_q(\rho^{1/2}) \cdot \rho^{-1/2} \in A\) is the quantum pressure,

  • $\{}boldsymbol{\{}sigma}_q = (1-q^{-1}),\{}rho, \{}bigl(d_q v + (d_q v)^\{}dagger

    • \{}tfrac{2}{3},(\{}delta_q v),\{}mathrm{id}_A\{}bigr) \{}in \{}Omega^2(A)$ is the viscous stress,

  • and the dagger \((-)^\dagger\) uses the Frobenius pairing.

The kinematic viscosity \(\nu_q = \frac{1}{2}(1 - q^{-1}) = \hbar_q/2\) arises from the substrate parameter alone — it is not an independent physical constant.

Incompressibility. The constraint \(\delta_q v = 0\) (divergence-free, i.e. \(v \in \ker(\delta_q|_{\Omega^1})\)) replaces the classical \(\nabla \cdot v = 0\). The observability condition \(\mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{C}}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) ensures this constraint is non-degenerate: there are no gauge modes that could trivially satisfy it.

Archimedean realisation. Under the categorical–archimedean bridge, the fibre functor \(\tau\) sends the categorical system to coordinates on the state bundle \(\mathcal{S}\):

\[\partial_t v + (v \cdot \nabla_A)v \;=\; -\frac{1}{\rho}\,\nabla_A p \;-\; \nabla_A Q_q \;+\; \nu_q\,\Delta_q v \;+\; \frac{1}{\rho}\, \nabla_A \cdot \boldsymbol{\sigma}_q,\]

where \(\nabla_A\) is the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) covariant derivative (the geometric image of \(\nabla_q\) under \(\tau\)), and the \(q\)-deformed viscous stress tensor in coordinates is

\[(\boldsymbol{\sigma}_q)_{ij} \;=\; \nu_q\,\rho\, \bigl( \nabla_{A,i}\,v_j + \nabla_{A,j}\,v_i - \tfrac{2}{3}\,(\nabla_A \cdot v)\,\delta_{ij} \bigr),\]

with the continuity equation \(\partial_t\rho + \nabla_A \cdot (\rho v) = 0\).

Properties.

  1. Algebraic dissipation spectrum. The viscous term \(\nu_q\,\Delta_q v\) damps mode \(k\) at rate \(\nu_q\,[k]_q^2 / L_q^2\). Because the \(q\)-integers grow as \([k]_q \sim q^k / (q - q^{-1})\) for large \(k\), high-wavenumber modes are damped exponentially rather than polynomially, providing a natural UV regularisation absent from classical Navier–Stokes.

  2. Gauge-covariant diffusion. The connection \(A\) appears in every derivative. Viscous diffusion transports not only momentum but also colour charge: a vortex filament that decays by viscous damping radiates its \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) quantum numbers into neighbouring filaments via the connection.

  3. Quantum pressure as negative viscosity. The \(Q_q\) term acts as a negative viscosity at short wavelengths: it opposes compression of the fluid below the scale \(\ell_q = (q-1)/q\). The balance between \(\nu_q\,\Delta_q v\) (dissipation) and \(\nabla_A Q_q\) (quantum repulsion) determines the minimum vortex core radius.

Energy dissipation rate. The global energy dissipation rate of the \(q\)-Navier–Stokes equation is

\[\varepsilon_q \;=\; \nu_q \int_{\mathcal{S}} \rho\,\lVert\nabla_A v\rVert^2\,d\mu \;=\; \nu_q \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} [k]_q^2\,|v_k|^2,\]

where \(v_k\) are the Fourier coefficients in the \(q\)-integer eigenbasis. For \(q > 1\), the sum converges absolutely (exponential damping of high modes), resolving the classical difficulty of proving energy estimates for 3d Navier–Stokes.

Classical and quantum limits.

Limit \(\nu_q\) \(Q_q\) Equation reduces to
\(q \to 1\) \(0\) \(0\) Euler equation (inviscid, no quantum pressure)
\(q \to 1^+\) with \(\hbar_q\) held \(\hbar_q/2\) \(-\hbar^2\Delta\sqrt{\rho}/(2\sqrt{\rho})\) Ordinary Navier–Stokes + Bohm potential
\(q \gg 1\) \((1 - 1/q)/2\) Dominant Quantum pressure dominates; flow frozen to ground state

Well-posedness. The exponential damping of high-wavenumber modes by the \(q\)-Laplacian ensures that the \(q\)-Navier–Stokes equation is globally well-posed in 3d for any \(q > 1\): the energy estimate \(\frac{d}{dt}\lVert v\rVert^2 \leq -\nu_q\,[1]_q^2\,\lVert v\rVert^2\) gives exponential decay of the total kinetic energy, and the \(q\)-integer growth prevents the enstrophy blowup that obstructs classical regularity proofs. The classical 3d Navier–Stokes regularity problem is thus an artefact of the \(q \to 1\) degeneration.

Vortex spectrum and helicity

Proposition 7.2 ✗ no Lean (Discrete vortex mode spectrum).

Let \(\varrho\) be a stable vortex filament of length \(L\) in the brane fluid with substrate parameter \(q > 1\), and let \(\Delta_q\) be the \(q\)-Laplacian acting on sections of the normal bundle \(N_\varrho\). Then:

  1. The eigenvalues of \(\Delta_q\) restricted to \(\varrho\) form a discrete spectrum \(\{\lambda_k^{(q)}\}_{k \geq 1}\) with \[\lambda_k^{(q)} \;=\; [k]_q^2 \cdot \frac{\hbar_q}{L_q^2},\] where \([k]_q = (q^k - q^{-k})/(q - q^{-1})\) is the \(q\)-integer and \(L_q\) is the \(q\)-deformed filament length.

  2. The intensity levels of the vortex are indexed by the spin label \(j \in \frac{1}{2}\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}\) of the \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) representation carried by the holonomy around \(\varrho\). The vortex energy at level \(j\) is \[E_j^{(q)} \;=\; \frac{\hbar_q}{2I_q}\,[j]_q\,[j+1]_q,\] where \(I_q\) is the \(q\)-deformed moment of inertia of the filament cross-section.

  3. Transitions between intensity levels \(j \to j'\) are mediated by the ladder modes \(E_\pm\) of the weight-space decomposition, with selection rule \(|j - j'| = 1\). The energy released or absorbed is \[\Delta E_{j \to j'} \;=\; \frac{\hbar_q}{2I_q} \bigl([j']_q[j'+1]_q - [j]_q[j+1]_q\bigr).\]

  4. In the classical limit \(q \to 1\):

    • \([k]_q \to k\) and the Kelvin-wave spectrum is recovered.

    • \([j]_q[j+1]_q \to j(j+1)\) and the energy levels reduce to the rigid-rotor spectrum of angular momentum theory.

    • The selection rule \(\Delta j = \pm 1\) reduces to the standard dipole selection rule.
