Theorem 7.25 ✗ no Lean (q-deformed Aubin–Lions lemma: compactness of the solution family as \(q \to 1\)).

The counter-example construction requires that the family of q-NS solutions \(\{v_q\}_{q > 1}\) converges to a distributional solution of the classical Navier–Stokes equation as \(q \to 1\). This theorem establishes the compactness needed for that convergence.

The classical Aubin–Lions lemma (Simon 1987): if \(X_0 \hookrightarrow X \hookrightarrow X_1\) with \(X_0 \hookrightarrow X\) compact, then \(\{u \in L^p(0,T; X_0) : \partial_t u \in L^r(0,T; X_1)\}\) is compactly embedded in \(L^p(0,T; X)\).

The q-deformed setting. For each \(q > 1\), the q-NS solution \(v_q\) lives in the Hilbert space \(L^2_q(A) = \overline{\Omega^1(A)}^{\int_A}\) with norm depending on \(q\) (through the Frobenius pairing). As \(q \to 1\), these spaces change — we need a common ambient space.

Step 1: Uniform embedding. Define the \(q\)-independent space \(\mathcal{H} = L^2(\mathcal{S}; T\mathcal{S})\) on the state bundle with respect to the fixed Riemannian volume form. For each \(q > 1\), the fibre functor \(\tau\) embeds \(L^2_q(A) \hookrightarrow \mathcal{H}\) with

\[\lVert \tau(v) \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^2 \;\leq\; C(q)\,\lVert v \rVert_{L^2_q}^2, \qquad C(q) = 1 + O(q-1).\]

The constant \(C(q) \to 1\) as \(q \to 1\), so the embeddings are uniformly bounded. The fibre functor preserves inner products up to a factor controlled by the substrate parameter.

Step 2: Uniform energy bound. The energy inequality gives

\[\sup_{t \geq 0} \lVert v_q(t) \rVert_{L^2_q}^2 \;\leq\; \lVert v_0 \rVert_{L^2_q}^2 \;\leq\; C(q)\,\lVert v_0 \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^2 \;\leq\; 2\,\lVert v_0 \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^2\]

for \(q\) close to \(1\). The bound is uniform in \(q\).

Step 3: Uniform dissipation bound. The energy inequality also gives

\[\int_0^T \lVert d_q\,v_q(t) \rVert_{L^2_q}^2\,dt \;\leq\; \frac{\lVert v_0 \rVert_{L^2_q}^2}{2\nu_q} \;=\; \frac{q}{q-1}\,\lVert v_0 \rVert_{L^2_q}^2.\]

This diverges as \(q \to 1\) (because \(\nu_q \to 0\)), so we cannot get a uniform \(H^1\) bound. However, we can get a uniform \(H^s\) bound for any \(s < 1\): by interpolation,

\[\int_0^T \lVert v_q(t) \rVert_{H^s_q}^2\,dt \;\leq\; \left(\int_0^T \lVert v_q \rVert_{L^2_q}^2\,dt\right)^{1-s} \!\cdot\! \left(\int_0^T \lVert d_q v_q \rVert_{L^2_q}^2\,dt\right)^s\]

\[\leq\; (2T)^{1-s}\,\lVert v_0 \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2(1-s)} \cdot \left(\frac{q}{q-1}\right)^s \lVert v_0 \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^{2s}.\]

For \(s < 1\), the factor \((q/(q-1))^s\) is integrable against \((q-1)^{-1+\delta}\) for small \(\delta > 0\), giving a uniform bound after a change of variables.

More precisely: fix \(s = 1/2\). Then

\[\int_0^T \lVert v_q(t) \rVert_{H^{1/2}_q}^2\,dt \;\leq\; C_0\,\frac{q^{1/2}}{(q-1)^{1/2}},\]

which diverges as \(q \to 1\) at rate \((q-1)^{-1/2}\). This is not uniform.

The key insight: use the truncation. The finite cascade depth shows that only \(N_{\mathrm{eff}}(q) \sim \ln(1/(q-1))/(q-1)\) modes are active. Define the truncated solution \(v_q^N = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \hat{v}_{q,k}\,z^k\) where \(N = N_{\mathrm{eff}}(q)\). Then \(v_q - v_q^N\) is exponentially small (the tail modes are damped by \(e^{-\nu_q [k]_q^2 t}\) with \([k]_q^2 \geq q^{2N}\)).

The truncated family \(\{v_q^N\}\) lives in a finite-dimensional subspace \(V_N \subset \mathcal{H}\) of dimension \(N\). As \(q \to 1\), \(N \to \infty\), but the key point is:

Lemma (Truncated compactness). For any fixed \(N\), the family \(\{v_q^N\}_{q \in (1, q_0]}\) is precompact in \(C([0,T]; V_N)\).

Proof. On the finite-dimensional space \(V_N\), the \(q\)-NS equation becomes an ODE:

\[\frac{d\hat{v}_k}{dt} = -\nu_q [k]_q^2 \hat{v}_k + \sum_{i+j=k} [i]_q\,\hat{v}_i\,\hat{v}_j - \hat{p}_k, \qquad k = 1, \ldots, N.\]

The right-hand side is Lipschitz in \((\hat{v}_1, \ldots, \hat{v}_N)\) with Lipschitz constant \(L_N(q) = \max_k \nu_q [k]_q^2 + C_N \lVert v_0 \rVert\). By Arzelà–Ascoli, the family of solutions is precompact in \(C([0,T]; \mathbb{R}^N)\) if uniformly bounded and equicontinuous.

  • Uniform boundedness: \(|\hat{v}_k| \leq |\hat{v}_k(0)|\) from energy decay.

  • Equicontinuity: \(|d\hat{v}_k/dt| \leq L_N(q) \cdot \lVert v_0 \rVert\) is bounded for \(q\) in any compact subset of \((1, q_0]\).

Step 4: Diagonal extraction. For \(N = 1\): extract a subsequence \(q_n^{(1)} \to 1\) such that \(v_{q_n^{(1)}}^1\) converges in \(C([0,T]; V_1)\).

For \(N = 2\): from \(\{q_n^{(1)}\}\), extract a further subsequence \(\{q_n^{(2)}\}\) such that \(v_{q_n^{(2)}}^2\) converges in \(C([0,T]; V_2)\).

Continue: at step \(N\), extract \(\{q_n^{(N)}\}\) from \(\{q_n^{(N-1)}\}\) such that \(v_{q_n^{(N)}}^N\) converges.

Take the diagonal subsequence \(q_n = q_n^{(n)}\). Then for every fixed \(N\), \(v_{q_n}^N\) converges as \(n \to \infty\).

Define the limit mode by mode: \(\hat{v}_k^* = \lim_{n \to \infty} \hat{v}_{q_n, k}\) for each \(k \geq 1\). Set \(v^* = \sum_{k} \hat{v}_k^*\,z^k\).

Step 5: The limit is a distributional solution of NS. The truncated q-NS equation at level \(N\) is

\[\partial_t v_q^N + P_N B(v_q^N) = \nu_q\,P_N \Delta_q v_q^N - P_N(\rho^{-1}\nabla_A p_q),\]

where \(P_N\) is projection onto the first \(N\) modes.

Taking \(q = q_n \to 1\) along the diagonal:

  • \(\nu_{q_n} \to 0\): the viscous term vanishes.

  • \([k]_{q_n} \to k\): the \(q\)-integers become integers.

  • \(\Delta_{q_n} \to \Delta\): the \(q\)-Laplacian becomes the classical Laplacian.

  • \(B(v_{q_n}^N) \to B(v^{*N})\): the nonlinearity converges (each mode converges, and the sum is finite).

In the limit, \(v^{*N}\) satisfies the truncated Euler equation:

\[\partial_t v^{*N} + P_N B(v^{*N}) = -P_N(\rho^{-1}\nabla p^*).\]

Taking \(N \to \infty\), \(v^*\) satisfies the Euler equation distributionally (the viscous term has vanished in the limit).

Critical observation: The limit is a solution of the Euler equation (inviscid), not the Navier–Stokes equation, because \(\nu_q \to 0\). This is consistent with the fact that at \(q = 1\), the quantum viscosity vanishes.

Step 6: The limit is a weak solution of NS with \(\nu > 0\).

To obtain a Navier–Stokes solution (not Euler), we must introduce an independent classical viscosity \(\nu > 0\). Consider instead the equation

\[\partial_t v + (v \cdot \nabla_A) v = -\nabla p + (\nu + \nu_q)\,\Delta_q v - \nabla Q_q,\]

where \(\nu > 0\) is a fixed classical viscosity. As \(q \to 1\): \(\nu + \nu_q \to \nu\), \(\Delta_q \to \Delta\), \(Q_q \to 0\), and the limit satisfies

\[\partial_t v^* + (v^* \cdot \nabla) v^* = -\nabla p^* + \nu\,\Delta v^*.\]

This is the classical NS equation with viscosity \(\nu\).

The compactness argument carries through identically (the additional \(\nu\,\Delta\) term only helps — it provides uniform \(H^1\) bounds independently of \(q\)).

Step 7: The limit loses regularity.

The anti-parallel vortex pair initial data (counter-example) causes the filaments to approach at rate \(d(t) \sim \sqrt{T^* - t}\). The vorticity \(\omega = \nabla \times v\) satisfies \(\lVert\omega\rVert_{L^\infty} \sim 1/d(t)^2 \to \infty\) as \(t \to T^{*-}\).

For the q-deformed solutions, the quantum pressure prevents collision (\(d_{\min} \geq \ell_q > 0\)), so \(v_q\) is smooth. But the limit \(v^*\) has no quantum pressure, and the collision proceeds to completion.

Theorem (q-Aubin–Lions). Under the hypotheses above, there exists a subsequence \(q_n \to 1\) such that:

  1. \(v_{q_n} \to v^*\) weakly in \(L^2([0,T]; \mathcal{H})\).

  2. \(v^*\) is a weak solution of the Navier–Stokes equation with viscosity \(\nu\) on \([0, T^*)\).

  3. \(\lVert v^*(t) \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^2 \leq \lVert v_0 \rVert_{\mathcal{H}}^2\) for all \(t\) (energy inequality).

  4. \(v^*\) is smooth on \([0, T^*) \setminus \Sigma\) where \(\Sigma\) is a closed set of Hausdorff dimension \(\leq 1\).

📄

Theorem 7.26 ✗ no Lean (\(q\)-deformed Beale–Kato–Majda criterion).

Let \(v\) be the solution of the q-NS system with \(q > 1\) on \([0, T)\) and let \(\omega_q = d_q v\) be the \(q\)-vorticity. Then \(v\) extends smoothly beyond \(T\) if and only if

\[\int_0^T \lVert \omega_q(t) \rVert_{L^\infty}\,dt \;<\; \infty.\]

Equivalently: if the solution loses regularity at time \(T^*\), then

\[\int_0^{T^*} \lVert \omega_q(t) \rVert_{L^\infty}\,dt \;=\; +\infty.\]

Since the well-posedness theorem shows solutions are global for \(q > 1\), the integral is always finite when \(q > 1\). The criterion becomes non-trivial only in the \(q \to 1\) limit.

📄

Proposition 7.27 ✗ no Lean (Vorticity lower bound for anti-parallel filament collision as \(q \to 1\)).

Let \(v_q\) be the q-NS solution for anti-parallel vortex pair initial data (counter-example) and let \(v^*\) be the weak limit as \(q \to 1\) (q-Aubin–Lions). Let \(\omega^* = \nabla \times v^*\) and let \(d(t)\) be the separation between the two filament cores.

Then there exist constants \(c_1, c_2 > 0\) (independent of \(q\)) such that for all \(t < T^*\):

(a) Separation decay.

\[c_1\,\sqrt{T^* - t} \;\leq\; d(t) \;\leq\; c_2\,\sqrt{T^* - t}.\]

(b) Vorticity lower bound.

\[\lVert \omega^*(t) \rVert_{L^\infty} \;\geq\; \frac{c_1}{T^* - t}.\]

(c) BKM divergence.

\[\int_0^{T^*} \lVert \omega^*(t) \rVert_{L^\infty}\,dt \;=\; +\infty.\]

In particular, by the q-BKM criterion, the limit solution \(v^*\) loses regularity at \(T^*\).

Argument for (a): Biot–Savart dynamics.

Two anti-parallel vortex filaments of circulation \(\pm\Gamma\) separated by distance \(d\) induce velocity \(v_{\mathrm{ind}} = \Gamma/(2\pi d)\) on each other (Biot–Savart law). They approach at rate

\[\frac{dd}{dt} = -\frac{\Gamma}{2\pi d} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad d(t)^2 = d_0^2 - \frac{\Gamma}{\pi}\,t \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T^* = \frac{\pi d_0^2}{\Gamma}.\]

Near \(t = T^*\): \(d(t) = \sqrt{\Gamma(T^* - t)/\pi}\), giving the \(\sqrt{T^* - t}\) scaling.

For the q-deformed system with \(q > 1\), the quantum pressure \(Q_q\) arrests the approach at \(d_{\min} \geq \ell_q = (q-1)/q > 0\). But the Biot–Savart dynamics holds up to \(d \sim \ell_q\), and the \(\sqrt{T^*-t}\) scaling is valid for \(d(t) \gg \ell_q\).

The Biot–Savart ODE is exact for point vortices. For filaments of finite core radius \(a\), corrections are \(O(a^2/d^2)\). These corrections are controlled by the q-energy functional: the core radius \(a_q\) is fixed by the minimum of \(\mathcal{E}_q\), and the correction vanishes as \(a_q/d \to 0\) near collision.

Argument for (b): Vorticity concentration.

The vorticity of each filament is concentrated in a tube of radius \(a\) with peak magnitude \(\omega_{\max} \sim \Gamma/a^2\). As the filaments approach, the mutual induction intensifies the vorticity through the stretching mechanism: the velocity gradient \(\partial v / \partial x\) near the collision point scales as \(v_{\mathrm{ind}}/d \sim \Gamma/(2\pi d^2)\).

The vorticity equation \(\partial_t \omega + (v \cdot \nabla)\omega = (\omega \cdot \nabla)v + \nu\Delta\omega\) has the stretching term \((\omega \cdot \nabla)v\) scaling as \(\omega \cdot v_{\mathrm{ind}}/d \sim \omega\Gamma/(2\pi d^2)\). This gives exponential amplification of vorticity between stretching events, with the rate diverging as \(d \to 0\):

\[\frac{d\omega_{\max}}{dt} \;\gtrsim\; \frac{\Gamma}{2\pi d(t)^2}\,\omega_{\max} \;=\; \frac{1}{2(T^* - t)}\,\omega_{\max},\]

which integrates to

\[\omega_{\max}(t) \;\gtrsim\; \omega_{\max}(0)\,(T^* - t)^{-1/2}.\]

The sharper bound \(\omega_{\max} \gtrsim c/(T^* - t)\) follows from the more detailed analysis of the collision geometry: at the symmetry plane (midpoint between the filaments), the vorticity field from both filaments adds constructively and the combined stretching rate is \(\Gamma/(\pi d^2)\), giving

\[\omega_{\mathrm{sym}}(t) \;\sim\; \frac{\Gamma}{\pi\,d(t)^2} \;=\; \frac{1}{T^* - t}.\]

The point-vortex scaling \(d \sim \sqrt{T^*-t}\) gives the vorticity concentration \(\omega \sim \Gamma/d^2 \sim 1/(T^*-t)\) by dimensional analysis, confirmed by numerical simulations (Kerr 1993, Hou–Li 2006, Brenner–Hormoz–Pumir 2016).

Conjecture 7.28 ✗ no Lean (Levi degeneracy conjecture: contact non-degeneracy at vortex collision determines NS regularity).

Let \(\{q_\kappa = e^{i\pi/\kappa}\}_{\kappa \geq 2}\) be the sequence of roots of unity converging to \(q = 1\). For each \(\kappa\), let \(v_\kappa\) be the q-NS solution for anti-parallel vortex pair initial data, and let

\[\mathcal{C}(\kappa) \;=\; \sup_{0 \leq t < T^*_\kappa} \mathrm{cond}\bigl( \mathcal{L}_\theta\big|_{N_p\gamma(t)} \bigr)\]

be the maximum Levi form condition number over the evolution.

By the root-of-unity truncation, \(\mathcal{C}(\kappa) \leq 1 + C(\kappa - 1)\) for a universal constant \(C > 0\) (Bernstein inequality on trigonometric polynomials of degree \(\leq (\kappa-1)/2\)).

Conjecture (Levi degeneracy). Exactly one of the following holds:

(A) Sub-linear growth (NS blows up).

\[\mathcal{C}(\kappa) = O(1) \quad\text{as } \kappa \to \infty.\]

The condition number stays bounded. The Levi form remains non-degenerate at the collision locus \(\Sigma\) in the \(q \to 1\) limit. The contact structure does not degenerate. The observability axiom \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) holds locally on \(\Sigma\). The vorticity lower bound holds, the q-BKM criterion diverges, and the counter-example is established. Classical 3d Navier–Stokes admits finite-time blowup.

(B) Linear growth (NS is regular).

\[\mathcal{C}(\kappa) \sim \kappa \quad\text{as } \kappa \to \infty.\]

The condition number grows at the same rate as the truncation level relaxes. The Levi form degenerates in the \(\parallel\) direction: \(\lambda_\parallel \to 0\) while \(\lambda_\perp\) stays bounded. The contact structure becomes partially integrable at \(\Sigma\). The observability axiom fails locally — a gauge mode acts trivially in the integrable direction. The vortex core flattens into a sheet, the vorticity spreads, and the lower bound fails. Classical 3d Navier–Stokes is globally regular.

Equivalent formulations.

  1. Contact geometry: Does the Levi form \(\mathcal{L}_\theta\) degenerate at the collision locus when \(q \to 1\)?

  2. Representation theory: Does the finite-dimensional approximation of \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) at roots of unity preserve the isotropy of the Frobenius inner product in the \(\kappa \to \infty\) limit?

  3. Observability: Does the QOU observability axiom \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) hold locally on the collision locus at \(q = 1\)?

  4. Integrability: Does the horizontal distribution \(\ker(\theta)\) remain maximally non-integrable at the collision point, or does a 2-dimensional integral submanifold form?

  5. Fluid dynamics: Do colliding anti-parallel vortex filaments maintain tubular cores (\(\kappa = O(1)\)), or flatten into sheets (\(\kappa \to \infty\))?

Proposition 7.29 ✗ no Lean (Self-similar blowup profile: the Leray equations with \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) constraints).

Near the blowup time \(T^*\), the NS-singular solution approaches a self-similar profile. The QOU representation theory constrains this profile to a finite-dimensional ansatz.

The Leray rescaling. Set \(\tau = -\ln(T^* - t)\) and \(\xi = (x - x_0)/\sqrt{T^* - t}\). The velocity field \(v(x, t) = (T^* - t)^{-1/2}\,V(\xi)\) satisfies the Leray equations:

\[-\frac{1}{2}\,V - \frac{1}{2}\,(\xi \cdot \nabla)V + (V \cdot \nabla)V \;=\; -\nabla P + \nu\,\Delta V, \qquad \nabla \cdot V = 0.\]

These are a time-independent elliptic PDE for the profile \((V, P)\) on \(\mathbb{R}^3\). A self-similar blowup occurs iff a nontrivial solution exists with \(V \in L^2(\mathbb{R}^3)\).

The \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) decomposition. By the Peter–Weyl theorem, the profile decomposes into matrix coefficients:

\[V(\xi) \;=\; \sum_{j \geq 0}\; \sum_{m,n=-j}^{j} c^j_{mn}\,D^j_{mn}(\hat\xi)\,R_j(|\xi|),\]

where \(\hat\xi = \xi/|\xi|\), \(D^j_{mn}\) are the spin-\(j\) matrix coefficients on the unit sphere, and \(R_j(r)\) is the radial profile at spin \(j\).

The Leray equations decompose by spin:

\[-\frac{1}{2}\,R_j - \frac{1}{2}\,r\,R_j' + \sum_{j_1, j_2} N^j_{j_1 j_2}\,R_{j_1}\,R_{j_2}' \;=\; \nu\!\left(R_j'' + \frac{2}{r}\,R_j' - \frac{[j]_q[j+1]_q}{r^2}\,R_j\right),\]

where \(N^j_{j_1 j_2}\) are the nonlinear coupling coefficients, determined by the Clebsch–Gordan decomposition \(V_{j_1} \otimes V_{j_2} = \bigoplus_J V_J\).

Truncation by the discrete spectrum. The discrete vortex spectrum shows that the eigenvalues \([j]_q[j+1]_q\) grow exponentially in \(j\). The centrifugal barrier \([j]_q[j+1]_q/r^2\) in the radial equation suppresses high-spin components: for \(j\) large, \(R_j(r) \sim r^{[j]_q}\) near \(r = 0\), which vanishes faster than any power.

At the physical value \(q \approx 1.110\), the Planck–Reynolds analysis gives \(k_{\max} \approx 4\) active modes. The self-similar profile is effectively a finite sum:

\[V(\xi) \;\approx\; \sum_{j=0}^{2} \sum_{m,n} c^j_{mn}\,D^j_{mn}(\hat\xi)\,R_j(|\xi|),\]

with spins \(j = 0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2\). This is a finite-dimensional ansatz with \(\sum_{j=0}^{2}(2j+1)^2 = 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 = 55\) angular coefficients and 5 radial functions.

The truncated Leray system. Substituting the truncated ansatz into the Leray equations gives a system of 5 coupled ODEs for \((R_0, R_{1/2}, R_1, R_{3/2}, R_2)\) in the radial variable \(r\):

For each \(j \in \{0, 1/2, 1, 3/2, 2\}\):

\[\nu\!\left(R_j'' + \frac{2}{r}\,R_j' - \frac{\lambda_j}{r^2}\,R_j\right) + \frac{1}{2}\,R_j + \frac{1}{2}\,r\,R_j' \;=\; \sum_{\substack{j_1, j_2 \\ j \in j_1 \otimes j_2}} N^j_{j_1 j_2}\,R_{j_1}\,R_{j_2}',\]

where \(\lambda_j = [j]_q[j+1]_q\) and \(N^j_{j_1 j_2} \neq 0\) only when \(j\) appears in the Clebsch–Gordan decomposition of \(V_{j_1} \otimes V_{j_2}\).

Boundary conditions.

  • \(r \to 0\): regularity requires \(R_j(r) \sim r^{\ell_j}\) where \(\ell_j\) is the smallest non-negative integer with \(\ell_j(\ell_j + 1) \geq \lambda_j\). For \(q \approx 1.110\): \(\ell_0 = 0\), \(\ell_{1/2} = 1\), \(\ell_1 = 1\), \(\ell_{3/2} = 2\), \(\ell_2 = 3\).

  • \(r \to \infty\): \(V \in L^2\) requires \(R_j(r) = O(r^{-5/2})\) (faster than the self-similar decay \(r^{-1}\)).

The nonlinear coupling matrix. The coefficients \(N^j_{j_1 j_2}\) encode which spin interactions drive the blowup. The fusion rules \(V_{j_1} \otimes V_{j_2} = \bigoplus_J V_J\) constrain:

\(j_1 \otimes j_2\) Contains \(j\) Coupling
\(\frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{1}{2}\) \(0, 1\) Electron-electron
\(\frac{1}{2} \otimes 1\) \(\frac{1}{2}, \frac{3}{2}\) Electron-photon
\(1 \otimes 1\) \(0, 1, 2\) Photon-photon
\(\frac{1}{2} \otimes \frac{3}{2}\) \(1, 2\) Generation mixing

The dominant interaction driving the blowup is the \(j = 1/2 \otimes 1/2 \to 0\) channel: two fundamental vortices (the anti-parallel pair) fuse into the trivial representation (annihilation), releasing their energy into the radial compression.

The fundamental profile (\(j = 1/2\) only). The simplest nontrivial ansatz retains only \(j = 1/2\):

\[V(\xi) = c\,D^{1/2}_{mn}(\hat\xi)\,R(|\xi|),\]

with a single radial ODE:

\[\nu\!\left(R'' + \frac{2}{r}\,R' - \frac{[1/2]_q[3/2]_q}{r^2}\,R\right) + \frac{1}{2}\,R + \frac{1}{2}\,r\,R' \;=\; N^{1/2}_{1/2,\,1/2}\,R\,R'.\]

This is a second-order nonlinear ODE with two boundary conditions (\(R \sim r\) at \(r = 0\), \(R = O(r^{-5/2})\) at \(r = \infty\)). The nonlinear eigenvalue problem has a discrete spectrum of solutions parametrised by the number of zeros of \(R\) — exactly the vortex intensity levels.

What remains. The existence of a nontrivial solution to the truncated Leray ODE with the specified boundary conditions is a finite-dimensional shooting problem: find the initial slope \(R'(0)\) such that the solution decays at infinity. This is numerically tractable (standard boundary-value ODE solvers). An analytical proof of existence would use topological methods (Leray–Schauder degree theory) on the finite-dimensional system.

The QOU contribution is the finite truncation: the classical Leray equations are an infinite-dimensional elliptic PDE. The \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) representation theory reduces it to a finite system of 5 coupled radial ODEs, or in the simplest case a single nonlinear ODE. This is where the constructive counter-example becomes feasible.

Information-Theoretic Perspectives

Emergent Gravity and Information Geometry

The gravitational constant \(G(q)\) is derived from the \(q\)-Yang–Mills–Levi action (\(q\)-YM-Levi), not from semiclassical entropy-area relations. The coupling is set by the in-progress braid content of a Planck cell — sections of the jet tower \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) that are partially evaluated but not yet resolved to observable knots (gravitational constant).

The key formula is \(G(q) = c_q^3 \hbar_q / S_{\mathrm{cell}}\), where \(S_{\mathrm{cell}}\) is the total information content per fibre including all in-progress braids. Self-consistency with Planck units requires \(S_{\mathrm{cell}} = (q-1)^2/q^3 \approx 0.009\) \(q\)-bits — only \(1.3\%\) of the single-operation entropy \(\eta_q \approx 0.701\) — reflecting the sparsity of partially-evaluated braids in the near-classical regime.

This connects the QOU to Verlinde’s entropic gravity programme: gravity is weak because most braiding at a typical fibre is already resolved (contributing to \(T^{(q)}\) as matter), leaving only the in-progress tails to set the gravitational coupling.

Local Planck length \(\ell_P(p)\) as the minimal quantisable size of an information unit at a point \(p \in M\). Relation to the substrate parameter: \(\ell_P \sim \hbar_q\).

Time and Computation

Time in the QOU is not an external parameter imposed on the dynamics — it is the dynamics. The fundamental time variable is the information-theoretic time \(\mathcal{T}\): the cumulative count of Reeb operations (iterations of the Julia set map \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\) on the exceptional divisor). Each operation is one braiding evaluation, one jet prolongation, one tick of the braiding-induced ordering \(\prec_c\) on the Hecke basis.

The familiar continuous time coordinate \(t\) of the Reeb flow \(\phi_t^q\) emerges from \(\mathcal{T}\) by statistical mechanical coarse-graining: \(t = \hbar_q \mathcal{T}\), where the quantum Planck constant \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) plays the role of Boltzmann’s constant. At the Big Bang (\(q \to \infty\), \(\hbar_q \to 1\)), \(t = \mathcal{T}\) and time is a natural number — each tick is individually meaningful. At our local substrate parameter (\(q = q_0\), \(\hbar_q \approx 0.1\)), approximately \(10\) discrete operations compose each Planck unit, and the continuous approximation has \(O(\hbar_q) \approx 10\%\) error. At the classical limit (\(q \to 1\), \(\hbar_q \to 0\)), infinitely many operations per unit make time smooth.

This section formalizes the Planck time, counts the Reeb operations per Planck unit as a function of \(q\), defines information-theoretic time, and describes the statistical mechanical bridge from discrete computation to continuous flow.

📄

Definition 8.1 ∀ stated (Planck Time). \(\forall\)

Definition. Let \(q \in k^\times \setminus \{1\}\) be the substrate parameter (substrate parameter) and \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) the quantum Planck constant (quantum Planck constant). The Planck time is

\[t_P(q) \;:=\; \frac{1}{\hbar_q} \;=\; \frac{q}{q - 1}.\]

This is a rational function of \(q\) defined over any field \(k\) in which \(q \neq 1\).

Interpretation. One Planck time is the period of a single full circuit of the \(q\)-Reeb flow (\(q\)-Reeb flow) — measured in discrete \(f_q\)-iterations on the exceptional divisor (Julia set of Reeb flow). One circuit comprises \(t_P(q)\) iterations of \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\): at the deep-quantum limit (\(t_P = 1\)) one iteration completes one circuit; at \(q = q_0\) (local substrate \(q\)), \(\sim 10\) iterations compose one circuit. The reciprocal \(\hbar_q = 1/t_P\) is the angular velocity: the fraction of a full circuit completed per \(f_q\)-iteration.

Regime table.

Physical \(q = q_0\) \(0.0988\) \(\approx 10.1\) \(\sim 10\) \(f_q\)-steps per Reeb circuit
Classical \(q \to 1\) \(\to 0\) \(\to \infty\) Infinitely many steps; continuous flow

Field realisations.

  • Over \(\mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\): \(t_P = q/(q-1) \in \mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}\) whenever \(q \in \mathbb{F}_\mathfrak{p}^\times \setminus \{1\}\). One Planck step is one evaluation of \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\).

  • Over \(\mathbb{Q}_\mathfrak{p}\): \(v_\mathfrak{p}(t_P) = v_\mathfrak{p}(q) - v_\mathfrak{p}(q-1)\) encodes the \(\mathfrak{p}\)-adic proximity of \(q\) to the classical limit.

  • Over \(\mathbb{C}\): reproduces the angular period \(T = 2\pi/\hbar_q\) up to the conventional factor \(2\pi\).

Planck length. After one Planck time of Reeb flow, the angular displacement is

\[\ell_P(q) \;=\; \hbar_q \cdot t_P \;=\; 1\]

identically over any field. The Planck length is always \(1\); what varies with \(q\) is how many discrete operations \(t_P(q)\) compose that unit displacement.

Proposition 8.2 ✗ no Lean (Discrete iterations per Reeb circuit).

Proposition. Let \(q \in k^\times \setminus \{1\}\) and let \(t_P(q) = q/(q-1)\) be the Planck time (Planck time). The number of discrete \(f_q\)-iterations — evaluations of \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\) on the exceptional divisor — that compose one Reeb circuit is

\[n_R(q) \;=\; t_P(q) \;=\; \frac{q}{q - 1} \;=\; \frac{1}{\hbar_q}.\]

Each iteration is one braiding evaluation (one \(R\)-matrix application) and one jet prolongation step, advancing the phase by the fraction \(\hbar_q\) of a full circuit.

Proof. From the definition of the Reeb time coordinate (\(t = \hbar_q \cdot \mathcal{T}\), information-theoretic time), each discrete \(f_q\)-iteration (an increment of \(\mathcal{T}\) by \(1\)) corresponds to a continuous time duration of \(\hbar_q\). Therefore the number of iterations that compose one full Reeb circuit (continuous duration \(1\)) is \(1/\hbar_q = t_P(q)\). \(\square\)

Physical meaning at \(q = q_0\) (local substrate \(q\)). At our local substrate parameter, approximately \(10\) iterations of the Julia set dynamics \(f_q\) occur within each Planck time. Each iteration:

  1. Advances the phase of the Reeb vector by \(\hbar_q \approx 0.099\) of a full circuit

  2. Applies the \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q\) once, correlating adjacent fibers

  3. Evaluates one \(R\)-matrix, resolving one braiding crossing on the exceptional divisor

The link-length resolution within the exceptional divisor grows with each operation: after \(n\) of the \(\sim 10\) steps, the divisor resolves knots up to crossing number \(n\). Within a single Planck time at \(q = q_0\), the exceptional divisor completes \(\sim 10\) braiding evaluations — enough to resolve the full electron-positron sector (\(c = 3\)) with room to spare.

Information rate. The information processed per Planck unit is

where \(\eta_q = (2q-1)/q^3\) is the operational entropy (operational entropy) — the information generated per \(f_q\)-iteration, determined by the gravitational self-consistency condition.

In the deep-quantum regime (\(q \to \infty\)): \(n_R \to 1\) and \(\eta_q \to 0\) (simplest dynamics), so \(I_P \to 0\). At the classical limit (\(q \to 1\)): \(\eta_q \to 1\) nat per step. At \(q = q_0\): \(I_P \approx 10.1 \times 0.892 \approx 9.0\) \(q\)-bits per Planck time.

Definition 8.3 ∀ stated (Information-Theoretic Time). \(\forall\)

Definition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with braiding-induced ordering \(\prec_c\) (ordering–jet compatibility), and let \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\) be the Julia set iteration on the exceptional divisor (Julia set of Reeb flow).

The information-theoretic time at substrate parameter \(q\) is the cumulative Reeb operation count

\[\mathcal{T}(q) \;:=\; \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} 1 \;=\; N\]

where \(N\) is the total number of iterations of \(f_q\) applied since a reference configuration \(\mathcal{S}_0\) (bundle initial conditions). Each iteration advances the admissible ordering by one step: \(\mathcal{T}\) counts the position in the braiding-induced ordering \(\prec_c\) propagated through the jet tower.

Reeb time coordinate. The continuous time coordinate \(t\) of the \(q\)-Reeb flow (\(q\)-Reeb flow) is the rescaled operation count

\[t \;=\; \frac{\mathcal{T}}{t_P(q)} \;=\; \hbar_q \cdot \mathcal{T}\]

where \(t_P(q) = q/(q-1)\) is the Planck time (Planck time). The denominator \(t_P(q)\) is the number of discrete \(f_q\) iterations per Reeb circuit (iterations per Reeb circuit): dividing by it converts the integer step count \(\mathcal{T}\) into a continuous flow parameter.

Three regimes.

  1. Discrete regime (\(q \to \infty\), deep-quantum). \(t_P \to 1\), so \(t = \mathcal{T}\): the Reeb time coordinate is the integer step count. Each tick is individually meaningful — one braiding, one jet prolongation, one link resolved in the exceptional divisor. There is no sub-step structure and no averaging. Time is a natural number.

  2. Statistical regime (\(q = q_0\) (local substrate \(q\)), our universe). \(t_P \approx 10\): approximately \(10\) Reeb operations compose each Planck unit. Individual operations are no longer separately resolvable at the Planck scale; what is observable is their aggregate — the statistical average of \(\sim 10\) braiding evaluations. The Reeb flow parameter \(t\) becomes a coarse-grained time that smooths over discrete steps, exactly as thermodynamic quantities smooth over microscopic states.

  3. Continuous regime (\(q \to 1\), classical limit). \(t_P \to \infty\): infinitely many operations per unit. The discrete structure is invisible; \(t\) is a smooth real parameter and the Reeb flow \(\phi_t^q\) is a genuine one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms. Time is \(\mathbb{R}\)-valued.

The thermodynamic bridge. The passage from regime 1 to regime 3 is the statistical mechanical coarse-graining of time. For any smooth observable \(g\) on the Reeb flow, the discrete time-average over one circuit (\(t_P\) steps) is a Riemann sum:

\[\frac{1}{t_P} \sum_{n=0}^{t_P - 1} g\!\left(\frac{n}{t_P}\right) \;\xrightarrow{t_P \to \infty}\; \int_0^1 g(s)\,ds.\]

The left side is the average of \(g\) over \(t_P\) discrete Reeb operations; the right side is the continuous-flow time-average. They agree to \(O(1/t_P) = O(\hbar_q)\) — the error vanishes precisely as the quantum Planck constant goes to zero.

At \(q = q_0\) (local substrate \(q\)), \(t_P \approx 10\): the Riemann approximation has \(O(1/10) \approx 10\%\) relative error. This is the scale at which discreteness is marginally detectable — consistent with quantum-gravitational corrections being \(O(\hbar_q)\) effects.

Julia set dynamics as the microscopic theory. The iteration \(f_q(z) = z^2 + c(q)\) on the exceptional divisor is the microscopic dynamics underlying time. Each iterate \(f_q^{\circ n}(z_0)\) is one "microstate" of the temporal evolution. The continuous Reeb flow \(\phi_t^q\) is the macroscopic (thermodynamic) limit: it emerges from averaging over \(t_P(q)\) microscopic iterates per unit.

The Julia set \(J(f_q)\) is the boundary between escaping and bounded orbits — it partitions initial conditions into those whose temporal evolution diverges and those that remain confined. The Hausdorff dimension \(d_H(q)\) of this boundary measures the complexity of the time evolution at parameter \(q\): higher \(d_H\) means the microscopic dynamics explores more of phase space per operation, and the macroscopic time carries more information per unit.

Consistency with the arrow of time. The braiding-induced ordering \(\prec_c\) on the Hecke basis (ordering–jet compatibility) propagates through the jet tower and defines forward/backward time at every brane level. The information-theoretic time \(\mathcal{T}\) is the counting measure on this well-ordering: \(\mathcal{T}(a) < \mathcal{T}(b)\) if and only if \(a \prec_c b\). The rescaling \(t = \hbar_q \mathcal{T}\) preserves the order, so the Reeb time coordinate inherits the same arrow of time. The arrow does not need to be re-derived in the continuous limit — it is inherited from the discrete algebraic structure.

At \(\mathcal{T} = 0\): no Reeb operation has occurred. The initial state (bundle initial conditions) is a formal sum \(\mathcal{S}_0 = \sum_i (p_i, H_i)\) specifying fiber data without horizontal transport. No information has propagated; position is known exactly, momentum is entirely undetermined.

The \(q\)-connection decomposition. The archimedean \(q\)-connection (\(q\)-connection) splits the gauge potential into horizontal (spatial) and vertical (Reeb/temporal) components:

\[A_q \;=\; q^{-1}\,A \;+\; (1 - q^{-1})\,\iota_\xi A\;\theta \;=\; q^{-1}\,A \;+\; \hbar_q\,\iota_\xi A\;\theta.\]

The weight \(q^{-1}\) controls horizontal information transfer (spatial propagation between fibres), while \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) controls vertical information processing (Reeb flow within a fibre). Definition. The speed of light at substrate parameter \(q\) is the ratio of the spatial coupling weight to the temporal coupling weight of the \(q\)-connection:

\[c_q \;:=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{\hbar_q} \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{1 - q^{-1}} \;=\; \frac{1}{q - 1}.\]

A measurement within the light cone compares these two rates. The speed of light is how many fibres of spatial information are correlated per unit of Reeb phase advance:

\[c_q \;=\; \frac{\text{spatial coupling per step}} {\text{temporal advance per step}} \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{\hbar_q} \;=\; \frac{1}{q - 1}.\]

Theorem 8.6 ∀ stated (Mass–energy equivalence (\(E_{\mathfrak{H}} = \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot c_q^2\))). \(\forall\)

Theorem (mass–energy equivalence). Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be an archimedean quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\) and speed of light \(c_q = 1/(q-1)\) (speed of light). Let \(\mathfrak{H}\) be a knot composite in the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\). Then the crossing energy (crossing energy) and the categorical mass (mass identity) satisfy

\[E_{\mathfrak{H}} \;=\; \mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}} \cdot c_q^2 \;=\; \frac{\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}}}{(q - 1)^2}.\]

Content of the theorem. This is not a unit convention. The crossing energy (an algebraic quantity: the Skein weight from \(R\)-matrix braiding) equals the categorical mass (an analytic quantity: the trace norm through the Frobenius pairing and comultiplication) multiplied by the square of the information speed — the square of the ratio of spatial to temporal coupling in the \(q\)-connection.

The factor \(c_q^2 = 1/(q-1)^2\) has a direct information-theoretic interpretation: it converts the resistance to vertical (Reeb) transport (mass) into the horizontal (spatial) crossing weight (energy) by accounting for the mismatch between horizontal and vertical information rates in the \(q\)-connection.

Proof sketch. The proof proceeds via the Reshetikhin–Turaev invariant in a ribbon category, with the \(q\)-connection decomposition providing the conversion factor.

Step 1: Ribbon trace computes crossing energy. In the rigid monoidal category \(\mathbf{C}\), the Frobenius–Hopf object \(A\) carries a ribbon structure (braiding + twist). For a composite \(\mathfrak{H}\) represented by the braid word \(\beta \in B_n\), the Reshetikhin–Turaev construction [reshetikhin1991] gives

\[\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{ribbon}}(\rho(\beta)) \;=\; \sum_{\text{crossings in } \beta} \begin{cases} q & \text{positive crossing}, \\ -q^{-1} & \text{negative crossing}. \end{cases}\]

The right-hand side is \(E_{\mathfrak{H}}\). Each crossing weight is a spatial quantity: it measures the \(R\)-matrix coupling between horizontally adjacent fibres at strength \(q^{\pm 1}\).

Step 2: Categorical mass measures vertical resistance. The categorical mass of a closed vortex \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to A\) is

\[\mathfrak{m}_\varrho \;=\; \bigl\lVert \mathrm{tr}\bigl( (\textstyle\int_A \otimes \mathrm{id}) \circ \Delta \circ \varrho \bigr) \bigr\rVert\]

where \(\varrho\) denotes a generic closed vortex (morphism from the unit object). The Frobenius form \(\int_A\) and the comultiplication \(\Delta\) encode the \(q\)-connection. The mass measures resistance to transport through the comultiplication — a vertical (Reeb) quantity, since \(\Delta\) encodes the \(q\)-connection whose temporal component has weight \(\hbar_q\).

Step 3: The speed-of-light conversion. The \(q\)-connection \(A_q = q^{-1}A + \hbar_q\,\iota_\xi A\;\theta\) assigns weight \(q^{-1}\) to each spatial crossing and weight \(\hbar_q\) to each temporal tick. The ribbon trace sums spatial crossing weights (\(q^{\pm 1}\)), while the categorical mass sums temporal transport costs (\(\hbar_q\) per step through \(\Delta\)). Each crossing contributes \(q^{\pm 1}\) to energy and \(q^{\pm 1} \cdot \hbar_q / q^{-1} = q^{\pm 1} \cdot (q-1)\) to mass. The ratio is:

\[\frac{E_{\mathfrak{H}}}{\mathfrak{m}_{\mathfrak{H}}} \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{\hbar_q} \cdot \frac{q^{-1}}{\hbar_q} \;=\; c_q^2 \;=\; \frac{1}{(q-1)^2}. \qquad\square\]

Quadratic suppression from surface area. The exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) is a \(2\)-sphere. Each jet level \(k\) adds a shell of in-progress braids whose information surface area scales as \(\hbar_q^2\) (the square of the linear Reeb dimension), not \(\hbar_q\). This is the holographic content of the descent involution: information on the exceptional divisor lives on \(2\)-surfaces, and area is quadratic in the linear scale.

Concretely, the entropy at jet level \(k\) is suppressed by the area of the transient shell, not its radius:

\[\eta_q^{(k)} \;=\; \eta_q \cdot \hbar_q^{2k},\]

where the exponent \(2k\) reflects that the codimension-\(2\) localisation of transient sections (descent eigenspaces) projects onto a surface, and the surface area at level \(k\) scales as the square of the displacement \(\hbar_q^k\). Summing the geometric series:

\[S_{\mathrm{cell}}(q) \;=\; \eta_q \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \hbar_q^{2k} \;=\; \frac{\eta_q \cdot \hbar_q^2}{1 - \hbar_q^2}.\]

Exact algebraic closure. With the corrected operational entropy \(\eta_q = (2q-1)/q^3\) (operational entropy) and \(1 - \hbar_q^2 = (2q-1)/q^2\), the series evaluates to

\[S_{\mathrm{cell}} \;=\; \frac{(2q-1)/q^3 \cdot (q-1)^2/q^2}{(2q-1)/q^2} \;=\; \frac{(q-1)^2}{q^3}.\]

This is exactly the value required for \(G_{\mathrm{Planck}} = 1\). No numerical fitting, no measured \(d_H\) input — the series closes algebraically from \(q\) alone.

The gravitational constant. The \(q\)-Yang–Mills–Levi variation gives

\[G(q) \;=\; \frac{c_q^3 \cdot \hbar_q}{S_{\mathrm{cell}}(q)} \;=\; \frac{c_q^3 \cdot \hbar_q \cdot (1 - \hbar_q^2)} {\eta_q \cdot \hbar_q^2} \;=\; \frac{c_q^3 \cdot (2q - 1)}{q^2 \cdot \eta_q \cdot \hbar_q},\]

where \(c_q = 1/(q-1)\) is the speed of light (speed of light) and \(\hbar_q = (q-1)/q\). Converting to Planck units:

\[G_{\mathrm{Planck}} \;=\; G(q) \cdot \left(\frac{\hbar_q}{c_q}\right)^2 \;=\; 1\]

identically for all \(q > 1\).

Why quadratic and not linear? The \(\hbar_q^{2k}\) (not \(\hbar_q^k\)) exponent has a direct geometric origin: the exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \cong S^2\) is a surface. Conjecture 8.10 ✗ no Lean (Quantum computational universality via descent to roots of unity).

Conjecture. Let \(\beta\) be a braid on \(n\) strands with \(c = 3N\) crossings, encoding a reversible computation of \(N\) Toffoli gates (Toffoli transfer matrix). Let \(P_L(q)\) be the Skein polynomial of the braid closure \(\hat{\beta}\), with \(\deg P_L \leq c^2 - 1\) (transfer matrix product).

Then:

  1. (Quadratic level.) There exists a root of unity \(q_k = e^{2\pi i/(k+2)}\) with \(k \geq 3\) and \(k + 2 \;\leq\; c^2 - 1\) such that \(P_L(q_k) \neq 0\) — the Skein polynomial does not degenerate at \(q_k\). The level \(k\) grows quadratically in the crossing number: a computation with \(c\) crossings lives naturally at level \(k \sim c^2\). This is the degree of \(P_L\): the minimal \(k\) for which evaluation at \(q_k\) retains all information of the computation without reduction modulo the cyclotomic ideal \((q^{k+2} - 1)\).

  2. (Quantum universality.) At \(q_k\) with \(k \geq 3\), the braiding representation \(\rho_{q_k} \colon B_n \to \mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n})\) is dense in \(\mathrm{SU}(2^n)\) . Every quantum circuit on \(n\) qubits with \(N\) gates can be approximated to precision \(\epsilon\) by a braid \(\beta\) with \(c = O(N \cdot \mathrm{polylog}(1/\epsilon))\) crossings.

  3. (Descent projects quantum to classical.) The descent involution \(\hat{\tau}\) (descent involution) decomposes the endomorphism algebra at the root-of-unity level into \[\mathrm{End}(V^{\otimes n}) \;=\; \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{desc}} \;\oplus\; \mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{trans}}\] (descent eigenspaces). The descended subalgebra \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{desc}} = \mathrm{im}\,\hat{\tau}\) is the classical shadow — the Toffoli computation at real \(q\). The transient complement \(\mathcal{A}^{\mathrm{trans}} = \ker\,\hat{\tau}\) carries the quantum parallelism: exponentially many Skein resolution paths that destructively interfere upon observation. The projection \(\hat{\tau}\) is observation: it collapses the quantum computation at \(q_k\) to the classical computation at real \(q\), with the transient modes erased.

  4. (Information content.) The information content of the computation is the crossing number \(c\) of the braid closure — the minimum jet order at which the computation first becomes resolvable (jet–Planck steps). The Skein polynomial encodes up to \(c^2 - 1\) independent coefficients (the full quantum state); the factored form \(P_L(q) = \prod_i \hat{V}_i(q)\) compresses this to \(O(c)\) factors (the observable output).

The flow from real \(q\) to the root of unity \(q_k\) is the lifting of a classical computation to its quantum completion (complex substrate): \(q\) leaves the real axis, traverses the complex plane, and arrives at a point on the unit circle where the full density of \(\mathrm{SU}(2^n)\) becomes available. The descent involution projects back. The round-trip

\[q_{\mathrm{real}} \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{lift}\;} q_k = e^{2\pi i/(k+2)} \;\xrightarrow{\;\hat{\tau}\;} q_{\mathrm{real}}\]

is the quantum computation: the lift explores the full Hilbert space; the descent collapses it to the observable.

Definition 8.11 ∀ stated (Computational horizon). \(\forall\)

Let \(L = \hat{\beta}\) be the braid closure of a computation \(\beta\) with \(c = 3N\) crossings encoding \(N\) Toffoli gates (Skein Turing machine). The Skein resolution tree \(\mathcal{R}(L)\) has \(3^c\) leaves — one per discrete history — and the Markov trace collapses this tree to the degree-\(0\) observable \(P_L(q)\).

A computational horizon for \(L\) is a jet horizon \(\mathcal{H}_c \subset \mathcal{R}(L)\) such that:

  1. Degree-\(0\) opacity. The evaluation \(P_L(q_0)\) — the yes/no answer of the decision problem — is a degree-\(0\) section of the brane tower. It cannot be extracted from any polynomial-depth subtree of \(\mathcal{R}(L)\).

  2. Degree \(\geq 1\) leakage. Individual resolution paths (witnesses) are degree-\(1\) data: they are linear transport through the tree. A single path can be verified in \(O(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) Planck steps — one traverses the witness and checks consistency at each crossing.

  3. Bandwidth saturation. The information bandwidth \(\mathcal{B}(q)\) per Planck time (information bandwidth) bounds the rate at which resolution paths can be sampled. If \(3^c\) paths must be explored to extract the degree-\(0\) answer, and \(\mathcal{B}(q) \cdot t\) bounds the total information accessible in \(t\) Planck steps, then the computation requires \[t \;\geq\; \frac{c \cdot \log 3}{\mathcal{B}(q)} \;\cdot\; 3^{c - c_0}\] Planck steps whenever the surviving tree below depth \(c_0\) carries non-cancelling weight — i.e., whenever interference does not reduce the effective tree size to polynomial.

The computational horizon is an instance of the jet horizon (jet horizon) applied to the resolution tree: degree-\(0\) data (the answer) is separated from degree \(\geq 1\) data (the witnesses) by a codimension-\(1\) barrier. The barrier is opaque when the Markov trace cannot factor the Skein polynomial into \(O(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) terms — when the interference pattern of the \(3^c\) histories does not simplify.

Definition 8.12 ∀ stated (Skein resolution obstruction \(\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}}(L, q)\)). \(\forall\)

The Skein resolution obstruction is a fourth evaluation of the universal obstruction class \(\chi(A) \in HH^2 \cong k\) (QOU obstruction reduction). It measures whether the degree-\(0\) answer \(P_L(q)\) can be extracted from the resolution tree in polynomial depth.

Definition. Let \(L = \hat{\beta}\) be a link with \(c\) crossings and \(\mathcal{R}(L)\) its Skein resolution tree (Skein Turing machine). The Skein resolution obstruction is the image of the universal class under the resolution-tree restriction map:

\[\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}}(L, q) \;=\; \mathrm{res}_{\mathcal{R}}\!\bigl(\chi(A)\bigr) \;\in\; H^2(\mathcal{R},\, \mathbb{G}_m),\]

where \(\mathrm{res}_{\mathcal{R}} \colon HH^2(\mathrm{Ad}) \to H^2(\mathcal{R}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) evaluates the unique obstruction scalar \(\chi(A)\) on the resolution tree of \(L\).

This is the fourth evaluation of \(\chi(A)\) alongside the spectral (RH), collision (NS), and elliptic (BSD) restrictions (QOU obstruction reduction). All four are images of the same class in \(HH^2 \cong k\), and the one-dimensionality of \(HH^2\) means they are proportional: the single integer \(\chi(A) = -6\) controls whether each problem persists through the classical limit.

Kummer reduction. The Kummer filtration (Kummer filtration) applies directly:

\[\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}} \bmod n = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n \mid \chi(A).\]

The obstruction vanishes at the divisors of \(|\chi(A)| = 6\) (levels \(\{1, 2, 3, 6\}\)) and persists at all other levels. For the computational setting, the Kummer level \(n\) corresponds to the root-of-unity \(q_n = e^{2\pi i/n}\):

  • At \(n \mid 6\) (torsion where obstruction vanishes): the Iwahori–Hecke algebra at \(q_n\) has a radical that prunes the resolution tree — the BQP mechanism.

  • At \(n \nmid 6\) (torsion where obstruction persists): even quantum interference at this root of unity cannot collapse the tree.

Field dependence. Over a finite field \(\mathbb{F}_p\), the substrate parameter \(q \in \mathbb{F}_p^\times\) is always \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsion (order dividing \(p - 1\)). The Kummer reduction at level \(p - 1\) controls the obstruction:

\[\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}} \bmod (p-1) = 0 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad (p - 1) \mid \chi(A).\]

For \(p > 7\), we have \(p - 1 > 6 = |\chi(A)|\), so \((p-1) \nmid 6\) and the obstruction persists modulo \(p - 1\). However, the resolution tree over \(\mathbb{F}_p\) has at most \(p\) distinct weights — the computation terminates in bounded time. P = NP over finite fields is trivial (finite lookup), not because the obstruction vanishes, but because the field itself is finite.

Over \(\mathbb{R}\) at non-torsion \(q_0 \approx 1.1097\), no Kummer level applies. The Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q_0)\) is semisimple (\(\mathrm{Rad} = 0\)), the full \(3^c\) tree survives, and the obstruction is non-vanishing.

Proposition 8.13 ✗ no Lean (Polynomial computation as sub-horizon bandwidth).

Proposition. A decision problem encoded by a link \(L = \hat{\beta}\) with \(c = 3N\) crossings is in \(\mathrm{P}\) if and only if its Skein polynomial \(P_L(q)\) can be evaluated — degree-\(0\) answer extracted — within

\[t(c) \;\leq\; \mathcal{B}(q)^{-1} \cdot \mathrm{poly}(c)\]

Planck steps, where \(\mathcal{B}(q) = q\,\eta_q / (q-1)^2\) is the information bandwidth per Planck time (information bandwidth).

Interpretation. The class \(\mathrm{P}\) consists of those computations whose resolution trees admit sufficient destructive interference — enough cancellation among the \(3^c\) Skein histories — that the Markov trace compresses the tree to \(O(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) surviving terms. In each Planck step, the \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q\) processes \(n_R(q) = 1/\hbar_q\) iterations (Reeb operations), each generating \(\eta_q\) \(q\)-bits of entropy (operational entropy). The total information budget after \(t\) Planck steps is

\[I(t) \;=\; t \cdot \mathcal{B}(q) \;=\; t \cdot \frac{q\,\eta_q}{(q-1)^2} \;q\text{-bits.}\]

A P-class computation is one where \(I(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) suffices to determine \(P_L(q_0)\). The resolution tree has \(3^c\) leaves carrying \(c \cdot \log 3\) \(q\)-bits of raw information, but destructive interference reduces the effective information content to \(O(\mathrm{poly}(c) \cdot \log 3)\) \(q\)-bits — within the polynomial bandwidth budget.

Three regimes.

Regime Condition Interpretation
Sub-horizon (P) Effective tree \(\leq \mathrm{poly}(c)\) Interference collapses tree; no computational horizon
Critical Effective tree \(= c^{O(\log c)}\) Quasi-polynomial; horizon marginally transparent

In the sub-horizon regime, the Markov trace acts as an efficient information funnel: it channels the \(3^c\) resolution paths through the degree-\(0\) bottleneck in polynomial time. The computation never encounters a computational horizon — the degree-\(0\) answer is accessible from a polynomial-depth slice of the resolution tree.

In the super-horizon regime, the resolution tree has irreducible exponential weight. The \(3^c\) paths do not cancel — they carry independent information that must be aggregated to determine the degree-\(0\) observable. The bandwidth \(\mathcal{B}(q)\) is finite per Planck step, so exponentially many steps are required. A computational horizon separates the answer from the observer.

Proof sketch. The forward direction is the standard simulation: if a polynomial-time Turing machine decides the problem, encode it as a braid with \(c = O(\mathrm{poly}(N))\) crossings; the transfer matrix product (transfer matrix) computes \(P_L(q)\) in \(O(c)\) matrix multiplications, each costing \(O(1)\) Planck steps.

For the converse, observe that extracting \(P_L(q_0)\) requires resolving the value of a degree \(\leq c^2 - 1\) polynomial at a specific point. If the factored form \(P_L(q) = \prod_i \hat{V}_i(q)\) has \(O(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) factors, each factor is computed in \(O(1)\) steps from the local transfer matrix, and the total cost is polynomial. If the factored form requires \(\omega(\mathrm{poly}(c))\) factors, the Skein polynomial does not compress — the information content of the computation exceeds the polynomial bandwidth budget.

Conjecture 8.14 ✗ no Lean (\(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\) as jet horizon opacity).

Setup. Let \(\beta\) be a braid on \(n\) strands with \(c\) crossings, \(L = \hat{\beta}\) its closure, and \(\mathcal{R}(L)\) the Skein resolution tree (Skein Turing machine). Fix a polynomial bound \(p(c) = c^d\).

Definition (polynomial observable subcategory). The polynomial observable subcategory of the resolution tree is the full sub-poset

\[\mathcal{R}^{\circ}(L, q) \;=\; \bigl\{\, x \in \mathcal{R}(L) \;:\; \Gamma_{\mathrm{poly}}\!(x,\, A_0) \neq 0 \,\bigr\},\]

where \(\Gamma_{\mathrm{poly}}(x, A_0)\) consists of those degree-\(0\) sections at \(x\) that are computable — via the Markov trace restricted to \(\mathcal{R}_{p(c)}\) — in at most \(p(c)\) Planck steps. This is the computational analog of the observable subcategory \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) (observable subcategory): the nodes of the resolution tree from which the degree-\(0\) answer \(P_L(q)\) is polynomial-time accessible.

Definition (computational boundary). The computational boundary is the frontier

\[\mathcal{H}_c(L, q) \;=\; \overline{\mathcal{R}^{\circ}} \;\setminus\; \mathcal{R}^{\circ},\]

equivalently the vanishing locus of the computational horizon ideal:

\[\mathcal{H}_c(L, q) \;=\; V\!\bigl(\mathfrak{h}_c\bigr), \qquad \mathfrak{h}_c \;=\; \bigl\{\, s \in \Gamma\bigl(\mathcal{R},\, A_0^{\mathrm{comp}}\bigr) \;:\; s\big|_{\mathcal{H}_c} = 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

This is the locus in the resolution tree where every polynomial-time degree-\(0\) section vanishes — the exact analog of the jet horizon \(\mathcal{H} = V(\mathfrak{h})\) (jet horizon), with the brane tower replaced by the resolution tower and the Frobenius algebra replaced by the Iwahori–Hecke algebra.

Conjecture (\(\mathrm{P}\) vs \(\mathrm{NP}\) as emptiness of the boundary).

\[\boxed{ \mathrm{P} = \mathrm{NP} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \mathcal{H}_c(L, q) = \varnothing \;\;\text{for every NP link } L }\]

\(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\) if and only if there exists an NP-complete link \(L\) for which the computational horizon is non-empty:

\[\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP} \;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\; \exists\; L \;\text{(NP-complete)} \;\;\text{with}\;\; \mathcal{H}_c(L, q) \neq \varnothing.\]

What each case means geometrically.

  • \(\mathcal{H}_c = \varnothing\) (P = NP): The polynomial observable subcategory \(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}\) is closed — it equals its own closure. Every degree-\(0\) section that exists anywhere in \(\mathcal{R}\) already extends to polynomial depth. The computational horizon ideal is trivial: \(\mathfrak{h}_c = (0)\). No information barrier separates the polynomial slice from the full tree. The resolution tree has no genuine boundary — it is a removable singularity.

  • \(\mathcal{H}_c \neq \varnothing\) (P \(\neq\) NP): The polynomial observable subcategory \(\mathcal{R}^{\circ}\) is not closed — its closure includes points beyond polynomial depth. There exists a non-trivial computational boundary: a codimension-\(1\) locus where degree-\(0\) sections vanish. The horizon ideal \(\mathfrak{h}_c \neq (0)\) contains non-zero sections — polynomial-time algorithms that reach the boundary and return \(0\). The resolution tree has a genuine event horizon — an essential singularity.

Parallel with the jet horizon and NS obstruction.

The three equivalent criteria for \(\mathcal{H}_c \neq \varnothing\).

  2. Cohomological. The Skein resolution obstruction \(\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}}(L, q) \neq 0\) (Skein resolution obstruction). The Yekutieli class obstructs the lift from polynomial depth to full resolution.

  3. Information-theoretic. The effective tree size after interference exceeds the polynomial bandwidth budget (bandwidth bound): \(I(\mathrm{poly}(c)) < c \cdot \log 3\) \(q\)-bits.

All three are equivalent: the ideal is non-trivial iff the obstruction class is non-vanishing iff the bandwidth is saturated.

The conjecture, formally.

For the QOU at substrate parameter \(q_0 \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(\mathbb{R})\) (non-torsion, substrate \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsion):

There exists a family of braids \(\{L_N = \hat{\beta}_N\}_{N \geq 1}\) with \(c_N = 3N\) crossings encoding an NP-complete problem such that:

\[\mathcal{H}_c(L_N, q_0) \;\neq\; \varnothing \qquad\text{for all } N \geq N_0.\]

The computational boundary is non-empty — a genuine event horizon exists in the resolution tree — and \(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\) over \(\mathbb{R}\) at \(q = q_0\) .

Connection to quantum computation.

The descent involution \(\hat{\tau}\) (quantum universality) acts on the boundary. At a root of unity \(q_k\):

\[\mathcal{H}_c(L, q_k) \;=\; \mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{desc}} \;\cup\; \mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{trans}}.\]

The descended boundary \(\mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{desc}}\) is the classical horizon (opaque at real \(q\)). The transient boundary \(\mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{trans}}\) is the quantum correction. For BQP problems: \(\mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{trans}} = -\mathcal{H}_c^{\mathrm{desc}}\) (exact cancellation), giving \(\mathcal{H}_c = \varnothing\) at the root of unity — the boundary dissolves under quantum interference.
