Conjecture 8.15 ✗ no Lean (\(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\) at non-torsion \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m\)).

Conjecture. At the physical substrate parameter \(q_0 \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(\mathbb{R})\) (substrate \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsion), \(\mathrm{P} \neq \mathrm{NP}\).

Equivalently: the resolution-tree evaluation of the universal obstruction class \(\chi(A)\) is non-vanishing:

\[\mathrm{res}_{\mathcal{R}}\!\bigl(\chi(A)\bigr) \;\neq\; 0 \qquad\text{at } q = q_0.\]

This is the fourth millennium evaluation. The QOU obstruction reduction shows that all classical-limit obstructions in the QOU are images of the single scalar \(\chi(A) \in HH^2 \cong k\). P vs NP joins RH, NS, and BSD as a fourth restriction of the same class — via the resolution-tree evaluation map. All four evaluations are proportional, controlled by \(\chi(A) = -6\).

The \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsion dichotomy.

At torsion \(q\) (root of unity): the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\) has a non-trivial radical. The radical annihilates exponentially many resolution paths, pruning the tree to polynomial effective size. This is BQP — some computational horizons become transparent.

At non-torsion \(q\) (including \(q_0\)): the Iwahori–Hecke algebra is semisimple (\(\mathrm{Rad} = 0\)), no paths are pruned, and the full \(3^c\) resolution tree survives. The computational horizon \(\mathcal{H}_c(L, q_0) \neq \varnothing\) for NP-complete links.

Kummer persistence. By the Kummer filtration (Kummer filtration): \(\kappa_c^{\mathrm{comp}} \bmod n = 0\) iff \(n \mid 6\). Since \(q_0\) is non-torsion (\(q_0^k \neq 1\) for all \(k \geq 1\)), no finite Kummer level applies, and the obstruction is perpetual.

Corollary (from the reduction theorem). If P \(=\) NP is resolved (in either direction), the resolution constrains the other three millennium problems. Conversely, a resolution of RH, NS, or BSD constrains P vs NP — the evaluation maps differ, but the obstruction class is the same.

Statistical Mechanics

The statistical mechanical structure of the QOU is not an analogy — it is the mechanism by which continuous physics emerges from discrete Reeb dynamics. The Planck time \(t_P(q) = q/(q-1)\) (Planck time) plays the role of inverse temperature \(\beta\): it counts the number of microscopic operations (Julia set iterations on the exceptional divisor) that compose each macroscopic time unit.

The thermodynamic limit \(\beta \to \infty\) (\(q \to 1\)) is the classical limit: infinitely many discrete operations average into smooth Reeb flow, just as infinitely many molecular collisions average into thermodynamic equilibrium. The corrections to the continuous approximation are \(O(1/\beta) = O(\hbar_q)\) — quantum-gravitational effects are literally finite-size corrections to the thermodynamic limit of time.

This section develops the partition function, entropy, and free energy of the Reeb dynamics, establishing the statistical mechanical framework for the information-theoretic time (information-theoretic time).

📄

Definition 8.16 ∀ stated (Quantum temperature). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\) and Planck time \(t_P(q) = q/(q-1) = 1/\hbar_q\) (Planck time). The quantum temperature of a region \(U \subset M\) is

\[T_q(U) \;:=\; \hbar_q \;=\; \frac{q - 1}{q},\]

with inverse temperature \(\beta_q := 1/T_q = t_P(q)\).

The quantum entropy of \(U\) is the non-abelian surface integral

\[S_q(U) \;:=\; -\,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}} \!\oint_{\partial U} \omega_{\mathcal{F}} \,\wedge\, *\eta_q,\]

where \(\mathcal{F} = \mathrm{Ad}(A)\) is the adjoint bundle, \(\omega_{\mathcal{F}}\) is the adjoint connection, \(\eta_q = (2q-1)/q^3\) is the operational entropy density (operational entropy), and \(*\) is the Hodge star on \(\partial U\).

The measurability conditions \(c_1(\mathcal{F}) = 0\), \(c_2(\mathcal{F}) = 0\) (quantum observable universe) ensure that the surface integral is independent of the choice of bounding surface via the Yekutieli non-abelian Stokes theorem (Yekutieli triple).

The quantum temperature is the thermodynamic conjugate:

\[\frac{1}{T_q} \;=\; \frac{\partial S_q}{\partial \mathbf{E}_q}\bigg|_V \;=\; \frac{1}{\hbar_q}.\]

📄

Definition 8.17 ∀ stated (Quantum pressure). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with quantum temperature \(T_q = \hbar_q\) (quantum temperature). Let \(U \subset M\) be a region of the brane with boundary \(\partial U\), and let \(S_q(K)\) denote the categorical action of a knot configuration \(K\) in \(U\) (categorical action). The quantum pressure on \(\partial U\) is

\[P_q(U) \;:=\; -\,\frac{\partial F_q}{\partial V_q}\bigg|_{T_q},\]

where \(F_q = -T_q \ln Z_q\) is the quantum free energy and

\[Z_q(U) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}} \!\sum_{K \,\in\, \mathrm{Conf}(U)} e^{-\beta_q \, S_q(K)}\]

is the partition function over the configuration space \(\mathrm{Conf}(U)\) of knot states in \(U\), with \(\beta_q = 1/\hbar_q = t_P(q)\).

The pressure decomposes as

\[P_q \;=\; P_q^{(\mathrm{bulk})} \;+\; P_q^{(\mathrm{boundary})},\]

where the bulk term is the volume derivative of \(\ln Z_q\) at fixed boundary conditions, and the boundary term arises from the \(q\)-anomaly (\(d_q^2 \neq 0\)):

\[P_q^{(\mathrm{boundary})} \;=\; \frac{\hbar_q^2}{V_q} \,\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}} \!\oint_{\partial U} \langle d_q K \,,\, d_q K \rangle_A,\]

where \(\langle\,\cdot\,,\,\cdot\,\rangle_A\) is the Frobenius pairing (Frobenius pairing).

📄

Definition 8.18 ∀ stated (Quantum volume). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe and \(\mathcal{S} \to M\) the state bundle with Reeb bundle \(S^3 \to \mathcal{S}_p\) at each brane point \(p\) (Reeb bundle). The quantum volume of a region \(U \subset M\) is

\[V_q(U) \;:=\; \int_U \mathrm{Vol}_{S^3}(\mathcal{S}_p)\; \epsilon_q(p),\]

where \(\epsilon_q\) is the categorical volume form on \(\Lambda^2 V\) preserved by the rigid duality of \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) (quantum observable universe).

For a homogeneous gas (uniform \(q\) throughout \(U\)), all fibres are isometric and

\[V_q(U) \;=\; |U| \cdot \mathrm{Vol}(S^3_q),\]

where \(|U|\) is the number of brane points in \(U\) and

\[\mathrm{Vol}(S^3_q) \;=\; \pi^2 \cdot [2]_q \;=\; \pi^2(q + q^{-1})\]

is the volume of \(S^3\) in the \(q\)-deformed metric. At \(q = 1\) this recovers \(\mathrm{Vol}(S^3) = 2\pi^2\).

📄

Proposition 8.19 ∀ stated (Quantum ideal gas law). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(N\) non-interacting particle knots in a region \(U \subset M\). Let \(P_q\), \(V_q\), \(T_q\) be the quantum pressure, volume, and temperature of \(U\) (quantum pressure, quantum volume, quantum temperature). Then the equation of state is

\[P_q \, V_q \;=\; N \, T_q \left( 1 \;+\; \frac{\hbar_q^2}{[2]_q} \,\langle S_q \rangle \right),\]

where \(\langle S_q \rangle\) is the thermal expectation of the categorical action (categorical action) and \([2]_q = q + q^{-1}\).

Proof. The single-particle partition function in a single \(S^3\) fibre is

\[z_q \;=\; \sum_{K \,\in\, \mathrm{Conf}_p} e^{-\beta_q \, S_q(K)}.\]

For \(N\) non-interacting knots across \(|U|\) brane points:

\[Z_q \;=\; \frac{1}{N!} \left( |U| \cdot z_q \right)^N,\]

where \(1/N!\) arises from the braid group action on \(\mathrm{Conf}(U)\) (isotopy-indistinguishability). The free energy \(F_q = -T_q \ln Z_q\) gives, via Stirling and \(V_q = |U| \cdot \pi^2 [2]_q\):

\[P_q \, V_q \;=\; -V_q\,\frac{\partial F_q}{\partial V_q}\bigg|_{T_q} \;=\; N \, T_q\]

at leading order. The \(q\)-anomaly correction from \(d_q^2 \neq 0\) at \(\partial U\) shifts the single-fibre partition function by \(\delta \ln z_q = \hbar_q^2 \langle S_q \rangle / [2]_q\), producing the full equation of state. \(\square\)

📄

Proposition 8.20 ∀ stated (Boltzmann constant as quantum Planck constant). \(\forall\)

The Boltzmann constant is the quantum Planck constant:

\[k_B \;=\; \hbar_q \;=\; \frac{q - 1}{q}.\]

Proof. The quantum ideal gas law (quantum ideal gas law) gives \(P_q V_q = N T_q = N \hbar_q\) at leading order. Comparing with the classical form \(PV = N k_B T\), and using \(T_q = \hbar_q\) (quantum temperature):

\[N \, k_B \, T_q \;=\; N \, \hbar_q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k_B \, \hbar_q \;=\; \hbar_q \quad\Longrightarrow\quad k_B \;=\; 1.\]

But the QOU temperature \(T_q = \hbar_q\) already absorbs what is classically the factor \(k_B T\). The structural identification is: in the QOU, the role of \(k_B T\) in classical physics is played by \(\hbar_q\) alone. The "Boltzmann constant" is not a separate quantity — it is \(\hbar_q\) itself, in the sense that \(k_B T_{\mathrm{phys}} = \hbar_q\) where \(T_{\mathrm{phys}}\) is physical temperature in SI units. \(\qquad\square\)

Phase Transitions and Sublimation

📄

Proposition 8.21 ∀ stated (Phase transitions as \(S^3\) boundary actions). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(N\) particle knots in a region \(U\). A phase transition occurs at a critical temperature \(T_q^{(c)}\) where the dominant saddle point of the partition function \(Z_q\) jumps discontinuously between topologically distinct sectors of \(\mathrm{Conf}(U)\).

The critical temperatures are determined by the \(S^3\) boundary action: the restriction of the categorical action \(S_q\) to the Hopf base \(S^2\) of the fibration \(S^1 \hookrightarrow S^3_q \to S^2\),

\[S_q^{(\partial)} \;:=\; \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Ad}} \!\oint_{S^2} \omega_{\mathcal{F}} \,\wedge\, *\eta_q,\]

where the integral is the non-abelian Stokes surface integral of the adjoint connection (Yekutieli triple).

The gas–liquid critical temperature is

\[T_q^{(g \to l)} \;=\; \frac{S_q^{(\partial)}}{[2]_q}.\]

The liquid–solid critical temperature is

\[T_q^{(l \to s)} \;=\; \frac{S_q^{(\partial)}}{[2]_q \cdot [n_K]_q},\]

where \(n_K\) is the crossing number of the particle knot.

The direct solid–gas transition (sublimation) occurs when the intermediate liquid phase is topologically obstructed: the Hecke representation at the mixed-channel temperature admits a non-split extension

\[0 \;\to\; V_{\mathrm{sym}} \;\to\; V_{\mathrm{mixed}} \;\to\; V_{\mathrm{asym}} \;\to\; 0\]

classified by \(\mathrm{Ext}^1_{H_n(q)}(V_{\mathrm{asym}}, V_{\mathrm{sym}}) \cong \mathbb{Z}\), generated by the Hopf invariant of \(\pi_3(S^2) = \mathbb{Z}\).

📄

Proposition 8.22 ∀ stated (Sublimation from shell-filling representation theory). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{A}(Z, N)\) be a stable atom with electron configuration occupying shells \(S_1, \ldots, S_k\). The complete decomposition (knot eigenbasis)

\[V^{\otimes n} \cong \bigoplus_{\lambda \vdash n,\, \ell(\lambda) \leq 2} V_\lambda \otimes S_\lambda\]

determines both the nuclear shell structure (shell eigenvalues) and the thermodynamic phase behavior (phase transitions) through the same Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\).

Sublimation criterion. An atom sublimes (bypasses the liquid phase) when the Hecke module at the mixed-channel temperature admits a non-split extension (phase transitions). This extension is classified by

\[\mathrm{Ext}^1_{H_n(q)}(S_{\mathrm{asym}}, S_{\mathrm{sym}}) \;\cong\; \mathbb{Z},\]

and it splits (liquid phase is stable) if and only if the outermost electron shell is closed or nearly closed — i.e., the partition \(\lambda_{\mathrm{outer}}\) labelling the dominant representation of the valence electrons satisfies \(\lambda_1 - \lambda_2 \leq 1\).

Equivalently: the extension splits when the valence shell sits in the symmetric or near-symmetric sector of the Schur–Weyl decomposition. It is non-split when the valence shell is in a half-filled partition (\(\lambda_1 \approx \lambda_2 + n/2\)), which corresponds to the mixed Hecke channel having maximal dimension.

Crossing parity (coarse form). The composite crossing number satisfies \(n_K(\mathcal{A}) \equiv Z \pmod{2}\) (from the crossing budget \(A^2 + 7A + 5Z\) and the identity \(A(A+1) \equiv 0 \pmod{2}\)). This parity is a necessary but not sufficient condition for sublimation: it detects the mod-2 shadow of the Young diagram structure but cannot distinguish closed shells from half-filled ones.

Full criterion. Let \(\ell_v\) denote the number of valence electrons beyond the last closed shell (noble gas characterization). Let \(\ell_{\max}\) be the capacity of the valence shell (\(\ell_{\max} = 2n^2\) for principal quantum number \(n\)). Then:

  1. Closed shell (\(\ell_v = 0\) or \(\ell_v = \ell_{\max}\)): extension splits. Stable liquid.

  2. Near-closed shell (\(\ell_v = 1\) or \(\ell_v = \ell_{\max} - 1\)): extension splits via the closed-core trivializing section. Stable liquid.

  3. Half-filled shell (\(\ell_v \approx \ell_{\max}/2\)) with odd \(Z\): extension is non-split. Sublimation-prone.

  4. Metallic band (delocalized electrons): the single-atom Hecke module \(S_\lambda\) is replaced by the band-structure module \(\bigoplus_k S_{\lambda(k)}\) over crystal momenta \(k\). The direct sum generically contains both split and non-split extensions, and the majority (split) wins. Stable liquid.

Horizons and Aeons

📄

Definition 8.23 ∀ stated (Jet horizon (degree-\(0\) vanishing locus)). \(\forall\)

Let \(U \subset M_0\) be an open subset of the descended universe carrying an affine chart, and let \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) be the brane tower (jet prolongation).

A jet horizon in \(U\) is a closed codimension-\(1\) subset \(\mathcal{H} \subset U\) such that every section of \(A_0\) that extends continuously across \(\mathcal{H}\) vanishes on \(\mathcal{H}\):

\[\mathcal{H} \;=\; V\!\bigl(\mathfrak{h}\bigr), \qquad \mathfrak{h} \;=\; \bigl\{\, s \in \Gamma(U, A_0) \;:\; s|_{\mathcal{H}} = 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

The ideal \(\mathfrak{h} \subset \Gamma(U, A_0)\) is the horizon ideal. At degree \(0\), no fibre data crosses \(\mathcal{H}\): photons (\(K = \varnothing\), step \(0\)) cannot propagate across the horizon, and no zeroth-order observable distinguishes one side from the other.

Higher-degree leakage. The horizon ideal lives in \(A_0\) only. The quotient algebras \(A_k / A_0\) for \(k \geq 1\) are not constrained by \(\mathfrak{h}\): first-order (linear) and second-order (curvature) jet data can carry non-trivial sections across \(\mathcal{H}\). Concretely:

Jet degree Data type Crosses \(\mathcal{H}\)?
\(0\) Fibre value (photon identity) No
\(1\) Linear transport (winding number) Yes
\(2\) Curvature (linking number) Yes
\(\geq 3\) Higher-order topology Yes

The information that leaks through a jet horizon is precisely the degree \(\geq 1\) jet data — the Taylor coefficients of the energy function beyond the constant term. This is thermal in character: it carries no particle identity (degree \(0\)), only statistical correlations (degrees \(1\) and \(2\)).

📄

Definition 8.24 ∀ stated (Big bang state (degree-\(0\) trivial configuration)). \(\forall\)

Let \(U \subset M_0\) be an affine chart carrying a bundle initial condition \(\mathcal{S}_0 = \sum_i (p_i, H_i)\) (bundle initial conditions).

A big bang state is a bundle initial condition in which the degree-\(0\) algebra is trivial:

\[\mathcal{S}_0 \text{ is a big bang state} \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \Gamma\!\bigl(U,\, A_0|_{\mathcal{S}_0}\bigr) = 0.\]

Equivalently, every constituent satisfies \(H_i = \varnothing\) (photon with zero fibre data) and the section \(s_0 \in \Gamma(U, A_0)\) encoding their identity vanishes: there are no degree-\(0\) observables at \(\mathcal{S}_0\). What remains is the higher-jet data: sections of \(A_1/A_0\) (linear transport) and \(A_2/A_0\) (curvature), which provide the seed for the forward light cone \(\mathcal{S}_1, \mathcal{S}_2, \ldots\)

Relation to the jet horizon. A big bang state is algebraically identical to the data on one side of a jet horizon (jet horizon): both are characterised by the vanishing of \(A_0\). The difference is contextual:

Concept Algebraic condition Role
Jet horizon \(A_0\vert_{\mathcal{H}} = 0\) Boundary within an affine chart
Big bang state \(A_0\vert_{\mathcal{S}_0} = 0\) Reference configuration of an affine chart

A jet horizon is a boundary; a big bang state is an initial condition. The same vanishing ideal \(\mathfrak{h}\) describes both.

Existence is not assumed. Whether any affine chart in the descended universe admits a big bang state is a dynamical question, not an axiom. It is consistent with the framework that:

  • every affine chart has a big bang state (global initial singularity),

  • some charts do and others do not,

  • no chart does (the backward light cone extends indefinitely).

📄

Definition 8.25 ∀ stated (CMB as boundary datum of a big bang state). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{S}_0\) be a big bang state (big bang state) in an affine chart \(U\), and let \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) be the brane tower (jet prolongation).

The cosmic microwave background (CMB) of \(\mathcal{S}_0\) is the boundary datum

\[\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0) \;=\; \bigl(\, \Gamma(U,\, A_1/A_0)|_{\mathcal{S}_0},\;\; \Gamma(U,\, A_2/A_0)|_{\mathcal{S}_0} \,\bigr)\]

— the pair of degree-\(1\) (linear transport) and degree-\(2\) (curvature) jet data at \(\mathcal{S}_0\). Since \(A_0|_{\mathcal{S}_0} = 0\) (the defining condition of a big bang state), the CMB is equivalently the restriction of \(A_1 \oplus A_2\) to \(\mathcal{S}_0\):

\[\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0) \;\cong\; \bigl(A_1 \oplus A_2\bigr)\big|_{\mathcal{S}_0}.\]

What the CMB contains.

Degree Jet data Physical content
\(1\) \(A_1/A_0\): linear transport Photon polarization modes (\(\sigma_0, \sigma_1\)), winding numbers, first-order correlations
\(2\) \(A_2/A_0\): curvature Hopf-link cross-terms (\(L_{\pm}\)), linking numbers, power spectrum

What the CMB does not contain.

Degree-\(0\) data (\(A_0\)) is absent: no photon identity \(\mathbf{1}\), no particle labels, no knot types. The CMB is thermal in the precise sense that it carries the color content \((\varphi_0, \varphi_1)\) of the boundary photons (photon color content) without their individual identities (degree \(0\)).

Role in aeon structure. If \(\mathcal{S}_0\) is the past boundary of an aeon \(\mathcal{A}\) (aeon), then \(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0)\) is the seed from which the aeon’s forward light cone unfolds. The first Planck step \(\mathcal{S}_0 \to \mathcal{S}_1\) regenerates non-trivial degree-\(0\) data by applying the Reeb flow \(f_q\) to the degree-\(1\) transport data — the CMB "condenses" into particles.

If \(\mathcal{S}_0\) is also the future boundary of a preceding aeon \(\mathcal{A}'\), then \(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0)\) is inherited from the terminal horizon of \(\mathcal{A}'\) (aeon boundary generates chart): the CMB of one aeon is the thermal remnant of the previous aeon’s final state.

📄

Definition 8.26 ∀ stated (Observable subcategory \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\)). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) be the category of finite bundles over the projective line (bundle category), with objects the bundle initial conditions (bundle initial conditions) and morphisms the permutation-isotopy pairs.

The observable subcategory \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) is the full subcategory on objects where the degree-\(0\) algebra is non-trivial:

\[\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \;=\; \bigl\{\, \mathcal{S} \in \mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \;:\; \Gamma(\mathcal{S},\, A_0) \neq 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

Why "observable". The observability axioms of the QOU (observation) require a non-degenerate Frobenius pairing to define degree-\(0\) measurements. When \(A_0|_{\mathcal{S}} = 0\), the pairing degenerates on the lowest floor of the brane tower and no degree-\(0\) observable is well-defined. The subcategory \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\) is precisely the regime where the full observational apparatus functions.

Complement. The complement \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \setminus \mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) consists of configurations with \(A_0 = 0\) — the jet horizons (jet horizon) and big bang states (big bang state).

Connected components. The connected components \(\pi_0(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ})\) are the aeons (aeon). Each aeon is a maximal connected full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\), encompassing all light cones that can be reached from one another without crossing a jet horizon.

📄

Definition 8.27 ∀ stated (Aeon). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) be the category of finite bundles over the projective line (bundle category), and let \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) be the brane tower (jet prolongation).

The observable subcategory. Define the observable subcategory \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) as the full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) on objects \(\mathcal{S}\) for which the degree-\(0\) algebra is non-trivial:

\[\mathrm{Ob}\bigl(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\bigr) \;=\; \bigl\{\, \mathcal{S} \in \mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \;:\; \Gamma(\mathcal{S},\, A_0) \neq 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

This is the subcategory where degree-\(0\) observations are well-defined — where the Frobenius pairing is non-degenerate on \(A_0\).

Definition. An aeon is a connected component of \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\).

Concretely, an aeon \(\mathcal{A}\) is a maximal full subcategory of \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\) such that any two objects \(\mathcal{S}\), \(\mathcal{S}'\) in \(\mathcal{A}\) are connected by a zigzag of morphisms (flow maps, inclusions, or their inverses) that stays entirely within \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\). Each light cone is a directed diagram within the aeon; the aeon is the union of all light cones that can be connected without crossing a jet horizon (jet horizon).

Boundary. The boundary \(\partial\mathcal{A}\) of an aeon is the set of objects \(\mathcal{S} \in \mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) that are limits of diagrams in \(\mathcal{A}\) but do not themselves lie in \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\):

\[\partial\mathcal{A} \;=\; \overline{\mathcal{A}} \setminus \mathcal{A}^{\circ} \;\subset\; \bigl\{\, \mathcal{S} : \Gamma(\mathcal{S}, A_0) = 0 \,\bigr\}.\]

Each boundary object is a jet horizon or a big bang state (big bang state). The boundary datum at \(\mathcal{S} \in \partial\mathcal{A}\) is the colimit of the degree \(\geq 1\) data over all diagrams in \(\mathcal{A}\) approaching \(\mathcal{S}\):

\[\mathrm{CMB}(\partial\mathcal{A}) \;=\; \varinjlim_{\mathcal{S}' \to \mathcal{S}} \bigl(A_1/A_0 \oplus A_2/A_0\bigr)\big|_{\mathcal{S}'}\]

(CMB boundary datum).

Aeon adjacency. Two aeons \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) are adjacent if their boundaries share a common object: \(\partial\mathcal{A} \cap \partial\mathcal{A}' \neq \varnothing\). The shared boundary object is simultaneously the terminal horizon of one aeon and the initial configuration of the next.

Maximality. The connected-component definition automatically gives maximality: no larger subcategory of \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\) containing \(\mathcal{A}\) is connected. This avoids the need for an explicit interval \((a, b) \subset \mathbb{Z}\) — the aeon is defined over the full structure of the category, encompassing all intersecting light cones.

📄

Definition 8.28 ∀ stated (Horizon functor). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\) be the observable subcategory (observable subcategory) and let \(\pi_0(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ})\) denote its set of connected components (the aeons, aeon).

The horizon functor is the map

\[\partial \;\colon\; \pi_0\!\bigl(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\bigr) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathcal{P}\!\bigl( \mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \setminus \mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V)) \bigr)\]

that sends each aeon \(\mathcal{A}\) to its boundary — the set of configurations \(\mathcal{S}\) that are limits of diagrams in \(\mathcal{A}\) but have \(A_0|_{\mathcal{S}} = 0\):

\[\partial(\mathcal{A}) \;=\; \bigl\{\, \mathcal{S} \in \mathrm{Bun} \setminus \mathrm{Bun}^{\circ} \;:\; \mathcal{S} = \varinjlim\, D \text{ for some directed diagram } D \subset \mathcal{A} \,\bigr\}.\]

Each element of \(\partial(\mathcal{A})\) is a jet horizon (jet horizon).

Functoriality. If \(\mathcal{A} \hookrightarrow \mathcal{A}'\) is an inclusion of connected components (i.e.\{} \(\mathcal{A} = \mathcal{A}'\), since connected components are maximal), then \(\partial\) acts as the identity. The non-trivial content is for adjacent aeons: if \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) are adjacent (aeon adjacency), then \(\partial(\mathcal{A}) \cap \partial(\mathcal{A}') \neq \varnothing\) and the shared boundary objects are the loci where the CCC transition occurs.

Relation to the torsion flow. The torsion flow \(\Phi_t^q\) (torsion-driven knot flow) is an endofunctor of \(\mathrm{Bun}(\mathbb{P}(V))\). Within an aeon, \(\Phi_t^q\) restricts to an endofunctor of \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\) (it preserves \(A_0 \neq 0\)). The horizon \(\partial(\mathcal{A})\) is the set of fixed points of the limiting behaviour \(\Phi_t^q \to \partial\) as \(t\) approaches the aeon boundary.

📄

Definition 8.29 ∀ stated (CMB functor). \(\forall\)

Let \(\partial\) be the horizon functor (horizon functor) and let \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) be the brane tower (jet prolongation).

The CMB functor is the composition

\[\mathrm{CMB} \;\colon\; \pi_0\!\bigl(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{\;\partial\;} \mathcal{P}\!\bigl(\mathrm{Bun} \setminus \mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\bigr) \;\xrightarrow{\;\varinjlim (A_1/A_0 \oplus A_2/A_0)\;} \mathbf{Mod}_R\]

that sends each aeon \(\mathcal{A}\) to the colimit of the degree \(\geq 1\) jet quotients over its boundary:

\[\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{A}) \;=\; \varinjlim_{\mathcal{S} \in \partial(\mathcal{A})} \bigl(A_1/A_0 \oplus A_2/A_0\bigr)\big|_{\mathcal{S}}.\]

The target category \(\mathbf{Mod}_R\) is the category of \(R\)-modules (sections of the jet quotient sheaves over the boundary).

Components.

Factor Jet degree Content
\(\varinjlim\, (A_1/A_0)\vert_{\partial\mathcal{A}}\) \(1\) Linear transport: winding modes, first-order correlations
\(\varinjlim\, (A_2/A_0)\vert_{\partial\mathcal{A}}\) \(2\) Curvature: linking modes, power spectrum

The colimit is taken over the directed system of all diagrams in \(\mathcal{A}\) that converge to boundary objects. It aggregates the degree \(\geq 1\) data from every light cone within the aeon that reaches the boundary — not just one computation sequence.

Relation to the pointwise CMB. For a single boundary object \(\mathcal{S}_0 \in \partial(\mathcal{A})\), the pointwise CMB (CMB boundary datum) \(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0) = (A_1/A_0, A_2/A_0)|_{\mathcal{S}_0}\) is the stalk of the CMB functor at \(\mathcal{S}_0\). The full CMB functor is the sheafification over the entire boundary.

Conformal invariance. By conformal invariance at the jet horizon, the CMB functor is independent of the choice of generator of the horizon ideal \(\mathfrak{h} \subset A_0\). It depends only on the vanishing locus — the conformal class of \(A_0\).

📄

Conjecture 8.30 ∀ stated (Aeon recycling: \(\Phi_1^q \circ \mathrm{CMB}\) lands in \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\)). \(\forall\)

Conjecture (Aeon recycling). Let \(\mathrm{CMB}\) be the CMB functor (CMB functor), let \(\Phi_1^q\) denote the first Planck step of the torsion flow (torsion-driven knot flow), and let \(\nabla_q\) be the \(q\)-connection.

If the degree-\(1\) component of \(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{A})\) satisfies the integrability condition of \(\nabla_q\), then the composition

\[\Phi_1^q \circ \mathrm{CMB} \;\colon\; \pi_0\!\bigl(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\bigr) \;\longrightarrow\; \mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}(\mathbb{P}(V))\]

is well-defined — i.e.\{} the first Planck step applied to the CMB of an aeon produces an object with \(A_0 \neq 0\), landing back inside \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\).

What the conjecture says.

  1. The CMB regenerates particles. The degree-\(1\) transport data (winding modes) in \(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{A})\), when iterated once by the Reeb flow \(f_q\), produces non-trivial degree-\(0\) fibre data. This is the "condensation" of thermal radiation into particle states.

  2. The recycling map lands in a new aeon. The output \(\Phi_1^q(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{A}))\) lies in \(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}\), hence in some connected component — a (possibly new) aeon \(\mathcal{A}'\).

  3. Adjacent aeons are connected by the recycling map. If \(\mathcal{A}\) and \(\mathcal{A}'\) are adjacent (aeon), then \(\Phi_1^q(\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{A})) \in \mathcal{A}'\).

The integrability condition. The \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q\) defines parallel transport along the Reeb flow. The integrability condition is \(\nabla_q^2 = F_{\nabla_q}\) — the curvature of the connection controls whether degree-\(1\) data can be iterated coherently. When \(F_{\nabla_q}\) is compatible with the degree-\(2\) component of the CMB, the transport data fits together globally and the recycling map is well-defined.

Categorical formulation. If the conjecture holds for all aeons, then \(\Phi_1^q \circ \mathrm{CMB}\) extends to a functor

\[\mathcal{R} \;\colon\; \pi_0(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ}) \;\longrightarrow\; \pi_0(\mathrm{Bun}^{\circ})\]

— the recycling functor — that sends each aeon to its successor. A fixed point of \(\mathcal{R}\) would be a self-recycling aeon: one whose CMB regenerates itself.

📄

Proposition 8.31 ∀ stated (Conformal invariance at the jet horizon). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{H}\) be a jet horizon (jet horizon) in an affine chart \(U\), and let \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) be the brane tower.

The boundary datum \(\partial\mathcal{A} = (A_1/A_0, A_2/A_0)|_{\mathcal{H}}\) that survives the horizon is invariant under rescaling of \(A_0\): for any \(\lambda \in \mathcal{O}(U)^{\times}\),

\[(A_1 / \lambda A_0,\; A_2 / \lambda A_0)\big|_{\mathcal{H}} \;=\; (A_1 / A_0,\; A_2 / A_0)\big|_{\mathcal{H}}.\]

In particular, the boundary datum depends only on the conformal class of \(A_0\) (its zero locus), not on the specific generator of the horizon ideal \(\mathfrak{h}\).

Proof sketch. On \(\mathcal{H}\), the ideal \(\mathfrak{h}\) vanishes: \(s|_{\mathcal{H}} = 0\) for all \(s \in A_0\). The quotient \(A_k/A_0\) restricted to \(\mathcal{H}\) depends only on the equivalence class of sections modulo \(\mathfrak{h}\). Rescaling \(A_0 \mapsto \lambda A_0\) with \(\lambda|_{\mathcal{H}} \neq 0\) does not change the ideal \(\mathfrak{h}\) (since \(\lambda s\) vanishes on \(\mathcal{H}\) iff \(s\) does). Therefore the quotients are identical on \(\mathcal{H}\). \(\square\)

Interpretation. This is the QOU analogue of conformal invariance in Penrose’s CCC . In CCC, massless particles are conformally invariant: they do not see the conformal factor \(\Omega\). Here, the degree \(\geq 1\) jet data does not see the "size" of \(A_0\) — only its vanishing locus matters.

The observability axioms of the QOU (observation) require a non-degenerate Frobenius pairing to detect degree-\(0\) data. At the horizon, \(A_0 = 0\) and the Frobenius pairing degenerates on that component. The surviving observations are those that act on \(A_k/A_0\) — the higher-jet conformal data. Conformal invariance at the horizon is a consequence of the observability axioms, not an additional assumption.

📄

Proposition 8.32 ∀ stated (A QOU with aeons is a conformal cyclic cosmology). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be a QOU and let \(U \subset M_0\) be an affine chart admitting a chain of adjacent aeons \(\ldots, \mathcal{A}_{-1}, \mathcal{A}_0, \mathcal{A}_1, \ldots\) (aeon). Then the aeon chain satisfies the three defining properties of a conformal cyclic cosmology :

(CCC-1) Conformal invariance at boundaries. At each aeon boundary \(\mathcal{S}_b\), the boundary datum \(\partial\mathcal{A}|_b = (A_1/A_0, A_2/A_0)|_{\mathcal{S}_b}\) is invariant under rescaling of \(A_0\) (conformal invariance). The surviving data depends only on the conformal class of the horizon ideal \(\mathfrak{h}\) — its vanishing locus, not the specific generator.

(CCC-2) Boundary data inheritance. The CMB of aeon \(\mathcal{A}_{k+1}\) (CMB boundary datum) equals the terminal boundary datum of aeon \(\mathcal{A}_k\):

\[\mathrm{CMB}(\mathcal{S}_0^{(k+1)}) \;=\; \partial\mathcal{A}_k\big|_b.\]

The degree \(\geq 1\) jet data that survives the terminal horizon of one aeon is identically the seed of the next.

(CCC-3) Only conformally invariant data crosses. At each boundary, the degree-\(0\) algebra vanishes: \(A_0|_{\mathcal{S}_b} = 0\). By the observability axioms (observation), the Frobenius pairing degenerates on \(A_0\) at the boundary, so no degree-\(0\) observable can detect a difference between the two sides. The only data that crosses is the degree \(\geq 1\) quotient — the conformal data.

Proof. (CCC-1) is the content of conformal invariance at the jet horizon.

(CCC-2) follows from the definition of aeon adjacency (aeon): adjacent aeons share the boundary \(\mathcal{S}_b\), and the CMB of the successor aeon is by definition the degree \(\geq 1\) data at its past boundary, which is the same locus \(\mathcal{S}_b\).

(CCC-3) follows from the definition of a jet horizon (jet horizon): \(A_0|_{\mathcal{H}} = 0\) is the defining condition, and the Frobenius non-degeneracy axiom requires \(A_0 \neq 0\) for degree-\(0\) observations to be well-defined. At the boundary where \(A_0 = 0\), the pairing degenerates and degree-\(0\) data is unobservable. \(\square\)

What the proposition does not claim. The proposition establishes that a QOU with aeons is structurally a CCC. It does not claim:

  • that any particular affine chart admits aeons (this is dynamical),

  • that the aeon chain is infinite in either direction,

  • that Penrose’s specific conformal rescaling \(g \mapsto \Omega^2 g\) is the mechanism (the QOU mechanism is ideal vanishing, not metric rescaling).

The content is that the CCC structure is a theorem of the QOU axioms, not an additional postulate: conformal invariance at boundaries, data inheritance, and the restriction to conformally invariant observables all follow from the observability axioms and the brane tower structure.

Quantum Geometry Variants

This section will develop the quantum version of the commutator relations in the group relations and Bring’s formulas. In particular, the classical commutator \([e_a,e_b] = \epsilon_{abc} e_c\) will be replaced with the \(q\)-deformed commutator from \(U_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\), describing how the Bring’s surface equations transform under the \(q\)-deformed action and relating the non-commutative geometry to the quantum substrate parameter \(q(p)\).

This section will investigate Bring’s surface and its analogues for Euler characteristics other than \(\chi = -6\), classifying surfaces for \(\chi = -2, -4, -8, \ldots\), determining which automorphism groups arise, and connecting to the varying Euler characteristic discussion.

The Descartes Universe

Why this universe

We inhabit a universe in which three facts are immediately apparent to any observer:

  1. Three colors. The strong interaction is mediated by exactly three color charges — red, green, blue — corresponding to the three coral tubes of Bring’s surface (color tube coordinates).

  2. A sense of time passing. Time pushes us forward just as water flows down a stream — always flowing, never still. The Reeb vector field (categorical Reeb) endows the Frobenius–Hopf object with precisely this preferred flow direction: the substrate parameter \(q\) distinguishes past from future, and the contact structure underlying \(A\) generates an arrow of time.

  3. Rotation on a sphere. Spatial rotations are governed by \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\), the symmetry group of the \(2\)-sphere. In the categorical framework, this emerges from the fiber adjoint involution (fiber adjoint involution) acting on the weight decomposition of \(A\): the three real generators of \(\mathfrak{so}(3)\) correspond to the three independent Reeb degrees on the genus-\(4\) surface.

These three observations — color, time, and spatial isotropy — are not independent. They are consequences of a single topological constraint: the Euler characteristic \(\chi(A) = -6\). The Bring surface, with genus \(g = 4\) and \(\chi = 2 - 2g = -6\), is the unique algebraic surface that realises all three simultaneously. This chapter develops the geometry of this surface and derives the Descartes condition that forces \(\chi = -6\).

Bring’s surface as a QOU

📄

Definition 9.1 ∀ stated (Bring’s surface). \(\forall\) Let \(R\) be a commutative ring with \(30 \in R^{\times}\) (i.e. \(\mathrm{char}(R) \nmid 30\)). Let \(x_j\), \(j\in\{0,\dots,4\}\), be homogeneous coordinates on \(\mathbb{P}^4_R\). Bring’s surface is the algebraic variety

\[\Sigma_4 \;=\; \mathrm{Proj}\!\left( R[x_0,\dots,x_4]\Big/\bigl(\textstyle\sum x_j,\; \textstyle\sum x_j^2,\; \textstyle\sum x_j^3\bigr) \right),\]

defined by the vanishing of the first three power sums. Over any algebraically closed field \(K \supseteq R\), \(\Sigma_4\) is a smooth projective curve of genus \(4\) with automorphism group \(\mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma_4) \cong S_5\) (\(\lvert\mathrm{Aut}\rvert = 120\), the largest automorphism group for any genus-\(4\) curve, though below the Hurwitz bound \(84(g-1) = 252\)) and Euler characteristic \(\chi(\Sigma_4) = 2 - 2g = -6\).

📄

Proposition 9.2 ∀ stated (Bring’s surface is a quantum observable universe). \(\forall\)

Bring’s surface \(\Sigma_4\) (Bring’s surface) gives rise to a quantum observable universe over \(R\) (with \(30 \in R^{\times}\)):

  1. Quantum universe. Set \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_{q}(2))\) over \(R\), \(A = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) with Frobenius form given by the Haar state, and \(\tau\) the forgetful functor to \(R\)-\(\mathrm{Mod}\). The differential calculus \(\Omega^1(A)\) is the Woronowicz \(3\)-dimensional calculus.

  2. Observability. \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1},\, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) by the quantum Schur lemma: \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) has no non-trivial invariants in the adjoint representation.

  3. Yekutieli lifting. The brane tower satisfies the Yekutieli lifting condition (Yekutieli lifting).

  4. Euler characteristic. By QU-to-QOU lifting, \(\chi(A) = \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) = 2 - 2g = -6\).

  5. Geometric descent (for \(n = 1\), \(\dim M_S = 3\)): \[M_S \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{Reeb}\;}\; \Sigma_4 \;\xrightarrow{\;\pi\;}\; \mathbb{P}(V) \;\xrightarrow{\;\mathrm{branch}\;}\; \{6\;\text{points}\}.\] The degree-\(4\) covering \(\pi\) has \(6\) branch points with total ramification \(R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 14\) (Riemann–Hurwitz), and the ramification profile is determined by the \(S_5\)-symmetry.

Proof of Bring’s surface is a quantum observable universe.

Item (1). The quantised coordinate ring \(A = \mathcal{O}_q(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) is a Hopf algebra over \(R[q, q^{-1}]\) with antipode \(S\), counit \(\varepsilon\), and the Haar state \(h_q \colon A \to R\) furnishing a non-degenerate Frobenius form \(\int_A = h_q\) (non-degeneracy follows from the faithfulness of the Haar state for compact quantum groups). The category \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) is \(R\)-linear, rigid monoidal (duals given by contragredient representations), and the forgetful functor \(\tau \colon \mathbf{C} \to R\text{-}\mathrm{Mod}\) is exact, faithful, and monoidal. The Woronowicz \(3D\)-calculus \(\Omega^1(A) = \ker(\varepsilon) / \ker(\varepsilon)^2\) is a \(3\)-dimensional \(A\)-bimodule in \(\mathbf{C}\), providing the differential calculus axiom.

Item (2). The adjoint representation \(\mathrm{Ad}(A)\) decomposes under \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) into irreducible representations of spin \(j \geq 1\) (the spin-\(0\) component vanishes because \(\mathrm{Ad} \cong V_1 \oplus V_2 \oplus \cdots\) with no trivial summand). Therefore \(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\) by the quantum Schur lemma.

Item (3). By jet prolongation, \(J^1(A)\) is Frobenius–Hopf, so the brane tower \(\{A_n\}\) is well-defined. Each transition \(A_n \hookrightarrow A_{n+1}\) gives a central extension of gerbes banded by the centre \(\mathcal{B} = Z(\mathrm{Aut}(A_n))\). The obstruction class \(\kappa_n \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathcal{B})\) exists by the standard gerbe classification theorem, verifying the Yekutieli lifting condition (Yekutieli lifting).

Item (4). The categorical trace of \(\mathrm{id}_A\) in \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) is the quantum dimension \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) = [N]_q \cdot [N-1]_q / [1]_q\) evaluated at \(N = 2\) (the rank of \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)). At generic \(q\), this recovers the topological Euler characteristic of \(\Sigma_4\): \(\chi(A) = 2 - 2g = 2 - 8 = -6\).

Item (5). The Reeb quotient \(M_S \to \Sigma_4\) collapses the \(\mathrm{U}(1)\)-orbits of the circle bundle (weight-\(0\) subalgebra \(A_0 = A^{\mathrm{U}(1)}\)). The covering \(\pi \colon \Sigma_4 \to \mathbb{P}(V)\) is the map to the projective line induced by the linear system \(|K_{\Sigma_4}|\); it has degree \(4\) and genus \(4\) source, so by Riemann–Hurwitz \(R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 2g(\Sigma_4) - 2 - 4(2g(\mathbb{P}^1) - 2) = 6 - 4(-2) = 14\). The \(S_5\)-symmetry of \(\Sigma_4\) forces the \(14\) units of ramification to be distributed over exactly \(6\) branch points (with ramification indices determined by the cycle types of \(S_5\)). ◻

📄

Remark 9.3 ✗ no Lean (Braid-group action on the resolvents).

The symmetric group \(S_5\) acts on Bring’s surface (Bring’s curve) by permuting \((x_0,\dots,x_4)\); this is the maximal automorphism group (order \(120\)) for genus \(4\). Three distinguished families of \(S_3\) subgroups govern the interplay between the base coordinates \(x_j\) and the spectral resolvents \(w_k\) (Lagrange resolvents). We describe each in terms of the (braid group), the resolvent coordinates, and the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)/\(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) matrices of SU(2) generators–SO(3) generators.

(i) Spacetime action (\(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) base). Fix the color coordinates \(x_2,x_3,x_4\) as internal fiber degrees of freedom. The constraint \(w_0=0\) forces \(x_0+x_1=C\) (constant), so the spacetime degrees of freedom collapse projectively to the ratio \(z=x_0/x_1\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). The transposition \(x_0\leftrightarrow x_1\) acts as the Mobius involution \(z\mapsto 1/z\), which is a \(\pi\)-rotation on \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) and embeds into \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) as \(\beta=\exp(\pi\,e_1)\). In the resolvent basis this acts as

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:spacetime-shift} w_k\;\longmapsto\; w_k+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\,(1-\zeta^k)(x_1-x_0), \qquad k=1,\dots,4, \end{equation}\]

an affine shift that fixes the color modes and translates the \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) fibre.

(ii) Spectral \(S_3\) (trefoil action). The frequency-coupled pairs \((w_1,w_4)\) and \((w_2,w_3)\) are permuted by the twist and flip involutions (braid twist-flip). The full \(S_3\) structure emerges on the projective ratios

\[\eta_1=\frac{w_1}{w_2},\qquad\eta_2=\frac{w_3}{w_4}:\]

\(\sigma_1\) inverts both ratios \((\eta_1\mapsto\eta_1^{-1},\; \eta_2\mapsto\eta_2^{-1})\), while \(\sigma_2\) exchanges them \((\eta_1\mapsto\eta_2^{-1},\;\eta_2\mapsto\eta_1^{-1})\). The \(2\)-cycle (reflection) swaps the pairs \((w_1,w_4)\leftrightarrow(w_2,w_3)\); the \(3\)-cycle (rotation) sends \((\eta_1,\eta_2)\mapsto(\eta_1,\,\zeta^j\eta_2)\) for \(j\in\{1,2,3\}\), permuting the three complex branches of the cubic constraint. The \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) representation assigns the \(3\)-cycle to \(\alpha\) and the reflection to \(\beta\); the \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) images act as the holonomy on the spectral energy distribution, with \(R_\alpha\) rotating the time-like resolvent pair \((\omega_2,\omega_3)\) and \(R_\beta\) reflecting the space-like axis \(\omega_1\).

(iii) Coordinate \(S_3\). Fixing any two coordinates (say \(x_0,x_1\)) as a spacetime base and permuting the remaining three \((x_2,x_3,x_4)\) gives a stabiliser \(\mathrm{Stab}(\{x_0,x_1\})\cong S_3\subset S_5\); there are \(\binom{5}{2}=10\) such subgroups. In the resolvent basis a permutation \(\sigma\in S_3\) of \((x_2,x_3,x_4)\) acts as

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:coord-s3-shift} w_k\;\longmapsto\; w_k+\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\sum_{j=2}^{4} \bigl(\zeta^{k\,\sigma(j)}-\zeta^{kj}\bigr)\,x_j, \end{equation}\]

so the \(w_k\) transform as vector fields over the \((x_0,x_1)\) plane and the \(S_3\) permutes how these fields couple to the base. The same \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) representation realises this action, now playing the role of the holonomy group on the internal fibre.

Geometric \(S_3\). When Bring’s curve is viewed as a branched cover \(\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{P}^1\), a third family of \(S_3\) subgroups arises: it permutes the three critical values of the covering map. These three families — spectral, coordinate, and geometric — correspond to the three copies of \(S_3\) inside \(S_5\) identified in chirality and trefoil.

Color tube coordinates

📄

Definition 9.4 ∀ stated (Color tube coordinates). \(\forall\)

Let \(z = x_0/x_1 \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) be the spacetime ratio (braid group action(i)) and let \(w_k\), \(k \in \{0,\dots,4\}\), be the Lagrange resolvents of Bring’s surface (Lagrange resolvents). The color tube coordinates are the shifted spectral coordinates

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:color-tube-coords} c_r = w_2 - z, \quad c_g = w_3 - z, \quad c_b = w_4 - z, \end{equation}\]

together with the space-like shift \(\sigma = w_1 - z\). The color vector is \(c = (c_r, c_g, c_b)\).

📄

Remark 9.5 ✗ no Lean (Interpretation of the color tube).

The terminology coral tube reflects two features of the geometry.

Color. The coordinates \(r, g, b\) label the three color degrees of freedom that correspond, via the \(S_3\) subgroups of \(S_5\) (braid group action(iii)), to the three colour charges of quantum chromodynamics. The color coordinates \(x_2, x_3, x_4\) of the QOU \(4\)-tuple (Bring’s QOU 4-tuple) descend to \(c_r = w_2 - z\), \(c_g = w_3 - z\), \(c_b = w_4 - z\) after shifting by the spacetime ratio \(z\).

Tube. For fixed \(z \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), the color vector \(c = (c_r, c_g, c_b)\) is constrained by the shifted quadric and cubic to lie on a curve inside the three-dimensional color space \(\mathbb{A}^3\). As \(z\) varies over the spacetime base, this curve sweeps out a tube — the total space of the color fibration over \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\).

Space-like coordinate. The shift \(\sigma = w_1 - z\) is distinguished: it measures the deviation of the \(C_5\)-fundamental resolvent \(w_1\) from the spacetime base, anchoring the \(U(1)\) longitudinal backbone (spectral dynamics) in the shifted frame.

Coral fibration and elliptic curves

📄

Proposition 9.6 ∀ stated (Coral fibre as an elliptic curve). \(\forall\)

Let \(z=x_0/x_1\in\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) be the projective spacetime ratio (braid group action(i)). Substituting the constraint \(x_0+x_1=C\) and eliminating \(x_0,x_1\) in favour of \(z\), the quadratic and cubic power-sum conditions on the coral variable \(X=(x_2,x_3,x_4)\) – so named because the geometry of the fibre resembles a coral reef: colorful twisted tubes with fractal boundary structure, capturing color, chirality, and rigidity in one image – reduce at each fixed \(z\) to the cubic

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:coral-elliptic} X^3+(z+1)\,X^2+(z^2+z+1)\,X+(z^3+z^2+z+1)=0. \end{equation}\]

For generic \(z\) this defines an elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_z\) in the coral fibre; its \(j\)-invariant varies as a rational function of \(z\). The monodromy of \(\mathcal{E}_z\) around the singular fibres (where the discriminant of the cubic vanishes) recovers the holonomy generators \(H_1,H_2\) of holonomy of trefoil.

Proof of Coral fibre as an elliptic curve.

Write \(x_0=z\,x_1\) and use \(x_0+x_1=C\) to eliminate both spacetime variables. The power-sum conditions \(\sum x_j^k=0\) for \(k=2,3\) then become polynomial in \(z\) and \(X=x_2+x_3+x_4\), \(X_2=\sum_{i<j}x_ix_j\), etc. Reducing by the Newton identities yields the cubic; its discriminant is a polynomial in \(z\) whose roots give the singular fibres. ◻

Remark 9.7 ✗ no Lean (Color tube cubic).

At fixed \(z \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), the three coral roots of the elliptic cubic (coral elliptic curve) each satisfy the cubic in the color tube coordinate \(\mathbf{c} \in \{\mathbf{r}_z, \mathbf{g}_z, \mathbf{b}_z\}\) obtained by substituting \(X = \mathbf{c} + z\) into the coral elliptic equation. Expanding gives the color tube cubic:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:color-tube-cubic} \mathbf{c}^3 + (4z+1)\,\mathbf{c}^2 + (6z^2+3z+1)\,\mathbf{c} + (4z^3+3z^2+2z+1) \;=\; 0. \end{equation}\]

This polynomial lies in \(\mathbb{Z}[z][\mathbf{c}]\) and defines a variety over \(\mathbb{Z}\). The leading \(z\)-coefficients \(4, 6, 4\) equal \(\binom{4}{1}\), \(\binom{4}{2}\), \(\binom{4}{3}\), and the constant term satisfies

\[4z^3 + 3z^2 + 2z + 1 \;=\; \frac{d}{dz}(z^4 + z^3 + z^2 + z).\]

Vieta’s formulas for the three roots give:

\[\begin{align} \mathbf{r}_z + \mathbf{g}_z + \mathbf{b}_z &\;=\; -(4z+1), \label{eq:vieta-sum}\\[4pt] \mathbf{r}_z\,\mathbf{g}_z + \mathbf{r}_z\,\mathbf{b}_z + \mathbf{g}_z\,\mathbf{b}_z &\;=\; 6z^2+3z+1, \label{eq:vieta-pairs}\\[4pt] \mathbf{r}_z\,\mathbf{g}_z\,\mathbf{b}_z &\;=\; -(4z^3+3z^2+2z+1). \label{eq:vieta-product} \end{align}\]

📄

Definition 9.8 ∀ stated (Color tube fibers). \(\forall\)

Let \(z \in \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). The coral tube at \(z\) is the affine curve defined over \(\mathbb{Z}[z]\) by the color tube cubic; we denote it \(R_z\), \(G_z\), or \(B_z\) according to which color tube coordinate \(\mathbf{r}_z\), \(\mathbf{g}_z\), or \(\mathbf{b}_z\) is used:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:color-tube-fiber-def} R_z \;:=\; \bigl\{\,\mathbf{r}_z \in \mathbb{A}^1 : \mathbf{r}_z^{\,3} + (4z+1)\,\mathbf{r}_z^{\,2} + (6z^2+3z+1)\,\mathbf{r}_z + (4z^3+3z^2+2z+1) = 0\,\bigr\}, \end{equation}\]

and \(G_z\), \(B_z\) are defined by the same equation with coordinates \(\mathbf{g}_z\) and \(\mathbf{b}_z\), respectively. The coordinates are related to the Lagrange resolvents by

\[\mathbf{r}_z = w_2 - z, \qquad \mathbf{g}_z = w_3 - z, \qquad \mathbf{b}_z = w_4 - z.\]

As varieties, \(R_z \cong G_z \cong B_z\) is isomorphic to the coral elliptic fiber \(\mathcal{E}_z\) of coral elliptic curve via the shift \(X = \mathbf{c} + z\).

Bundle structures and smoothness

📄

Remark 9.9 ✗ no Lean (Coral space as spectral curve and spinor bundle).

The spacetime–coral decomposition of Bring’s surface maps naturally onto three classical bundle structures over the \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) base \(z=x_0/x_1\).

Cotangent bundle. The three-sheeted cubic (coral elliptic curve) realises the coral variables \(X=(x_2,x_3,x_4)\) as a spectral curve \(\Sigma\subset T^{*}\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\): the base coordinate \(z\) parametrises spacetime position, and the three roots \(X_1,X_2,X_3\) of coral elliptic curve are eigenvalues of a Higgs-like field \(\Phi\) on the base. The six singular fibres (where the discriminant \(\Delta(z)\) vanishes) are the loci at which eigenvalues coincide and the differential \(dX\) degenerates in the cotangent fibre.

Spinor bundle. The spectral modes \(w_1,\dots,w_4\) (Lagrange resolvents) live in a rank-\(2\) complex vector bundle over \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). The coral doublet \(\Psi_L=(w_1,w_2)^T\) and its conjugate \(\Psi_R=(w_4,w_3)^T\) transform under the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) holonomy generators \(H_1,H_2\) of holonomy of trefoil, making \(\Psi_L\) a section of the spinor bundle \(\mathcal{S}^{+}\to\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\). The \(B_3\) monodromy equips this bundle with a flat connection whose holonomy is the trefoil-knot group.

Adjoint bundle. The \(\mathrm{SO}(3)\) images \(R_\alpha,R_\beta\) act on the triple \((\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3)\), which therefore spans a section of the adjoint bundle \(\mathrm{ad}\,P\to\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) associated to the principal \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle \(P\). The T-duality involution \(\iota\colon X\leftrightarrow z\) (T-duality on elliptic fibres) interchanges the fibre and base of the adjoint bundle, exchanging spectral eigenvalues with spacetime coordinates.

Proposition 9.10 ∀ stated (Smoothness of the Bring’s surface and intrinsic resolution of projection singularities). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{S}\) denote the Bring’s surface (Bring’s surface) and \(\pi \colon \mathcal{S} \to \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) the color projection.

  1. Smoothness. The three power-sum constraints are transverse in \(\mathbb{P}^4\), so \(\mathcal{S}\) is a smooth algebraic variety with no singular points.

  2. Intrinsic resolution. At each branch point \(z = z_c\) where two color sheets \(x_i, x_j\) collide, the local color coordinate \(\delta = x_i - x_j\) satisfies \(z - z_c \sim \delta^2\). The exceptional divisor of the blow-up at each ramification point is already embedded in the color coordinates: no external resolution is required.

  3. Regularity of the Briggs–Klein chart. The radial parameter \(r = \lvert w_1 \rvert^2\) is a regular function on \(\mathcal{S}\), and the \(C_5\) orbits \(w_k \mapsto \zeta^k w_k\) foliate the surface without fixed points for \(0 < r < \infty\).

Remark 9.11 ✗ no Lean (Smoothness of Bring’s surface and resolution of spacetime defects).

The Bring’s surface \(\mathcal{S}\) (Bring’s surface) is a smooth algebraic variety: the three power-sum constraints are transverse in \(\mathbb{P}^4\), so their intersection carries no singular points. The six topological defects identified in coral bundles—where the discriminant \(\Delta(z)\) vanishes and two color sheets \(X_i,X_j\) collide—are singularities of the projection \(\pi\colon\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\), not of the surface itself.

Resolution in the \(x_j\) coordinates. At a branch point \(z=z_c\) where, say, \(x_2=x_3\), define the local color coordinate \(\delta=x_2-x_3\). In a neighbourhood of the defect the spacetime ratio satisfies

\[z-z_c\;\sim\;\delta^2,\]

so while the projection map develops a ramification cusp, \(\delta\) passes smoothly through zero, carrying the geometry from one sheet to the other. The exceptional divisor of the blow-up at each branch point is therefore already embedded in the color coordinates \(x_2,x_3,x_4\): no external resolution is required.

Resolution in the \(w_k\) coordinates. The DFT mixes all five \(x_j\) into every resolvent \(w_k\) (Lagrange resolvents), so no single \(w_k\) vanishes at a branch point. The Briggs–Klein chart (Briggs–Klein chart) remains a smooth coordinate system throughout \(0<r<\infty\): the radial parameter \(r=\lvert w_1\rvert^2\) is a regular function on \(\mathcal{S}\), and the \(C_5\) orbits \(w_k\mapsto\zeta^k w_k\) foliate the surface without fixed points. The infinite torsion and eigenvalue crossings visible in the base \(\mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) are artefacts of projecting away the internal degrees of freedom that the \(w_k\) retain.

Definition 9.12 ∀ stated (Briggs–Klein affine chart). \(\forall\)

Let \(r=\lvert w_1\rvert^2\) denote the squared modulus of the first resolvent coordinate on (Bring’s surface). The Briggs–Klein affine chart is the coordinate system \((w_1,w_2)\) restricted to the open set \(0<r<\infty\), equipped with the Hermitian metric inherited from the Fubini–Study metric on \(\mathbb{P}^4\). In this chart the \(C_5\) action is the phase rotation \(w_k\mapsto\zeta^k\,w_k\), and the radial coordinate \(r\) is \(C_5\)-invariant.

Definition 9.13 ∀ stated (Quaternionic spectral resolvents). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{S}\) denote the (Bring’s surface). Let \(q\in\mathbb{C}\) with \(0<\lvert q\rvert\le 1\), and set \(r=-\ln\lvert q\rvert\) so that \(\lvert q\rvert=e^{-r}\). Write \(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k}\) for the standard basis of \(\mathrm{Im}\mathbb{H}\). Using the Lusztig \(q\)-exponential and \(q\)-logarithm,

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:q-exp} \exp_q(x)\;=\;\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{[n]_q!}, \qquad \ln_q(1+x)\;=\;\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}(-1)^{n+1}\frac{x^n}{[n]_q}, \end{equation}\]

we define the quaternionic spectral resolvents \(\omega_k\colon\mathcal{S}\to J^\infty E\) by

\[\begin{align} \omega_0 &\;=\; \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\!\sum_{j=0}^{4}x_j\Bigr)\, \ln_q(1+r) &&\text{(uncertainty),} \label{eq:omega-0}\\[4pt] \omega_1 &\;=\; \frac{\mathbf{i}}{\ln_q(1+r)}\, \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\!\sum_{j=0}^{4}\zeta^{j}\,x_j+i\Bigr) &&\text{(space-like),} \label{eq:omega-1}\\[4pt] \omega_2 &\;=\; \mathbf{j}\, \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\!\sum_{j=0}^{4}\zeta^{2j}\,x_j+i\Bigr)\, \bigl(\exp_q(r)-1\bigr) &&\text{(time-like),} \label{eq:omega-2}\\[4pt] \omega_3 &\;=\; \mathbf{k}\, \Bigl(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\!\sum_{j=0}^{4}\zeta^{3j}\,x_j+i\Bigr)\, \bigl(\exp_q(r)-1\bigr) &&\text{(time-like).} \label{eq:omega-3} \end{align}\]

By the first power sum, \(\omega_0=0\) in the balanced state; the remaining coordinates embed \(\mathcal{S}\) into the infinite jet shell \(J^\infty E\) (jet shell).

Proposition 9.14 ∀ stated (Abelianisation of the MI integral on exceptional divisors). \(\forall\)

Let \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) be the exceptional divisor at a branch point \(z_c\) (Bring’s surface smoothness), and let \((\nabla_A q,\; L \wedge F^+)\) be the connection–curvature pair of the (mass identity). Then for each vertical degree \(n \geq 0\) in the Reeb decomposition, the restriction of the nonabelian multiplicative integral to \(\mathcal{S}_c\) abelianises to the \(n\)-th prolonged Seiberg–Witten period:

\[\begin{equation} \label{eq:mi-sw-abelianisation} \bigl\lVert\, \mathrm{MI}\!\!\int_{\mathcal{S}_c} \bigl(\nabla_A q,\; L \wedge F^+\bigr) \,\bigr\rVert_{J^n} \;=\; \bigl\lvert a_D^{(n)}\bigr\rvert \;=\; \biggl\lvert\oint_{\mathcal{S}_c}\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)}\biggr\rvert, \end{equation}\]

where \(\lVert\cdot\rVert_{J^n}\) denotes the Killing-form norm projected onto the \(n\)-th jet component, and \(\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)}\) is the \(n\)-th prolonged Seiberg–Witten differential.

Proof of Abelianisation of the MI integral on exceptional divisors.

The proof proceeds in three steps.

Step 1: Abelianisation of the connection. On the exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) the principal \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle \(P\) trivialises (every \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)-bundle over \(S^2\) is classified by \(\pi_1(\mathrm{SU}(2)) = 0\)). The connection \(\nabla_A\) therefore reduces to a \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)-valued \(1\)-form \(A|_{\mathcal{S}_c}\). By the weight-space decomposition (weight space decomposition), the restriction splits as

\[A\big|_{\mathcal{S}_c} \;=\; A^0 \otimes H \;+\; A^+ \otimes E_+ \;+\; A^- \otimes E_-,\]

where \(H, E_\pm\) are the standard generators of \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\). The Cartan component \(A^0\) is a \(\mathrm{U}(1)\)-valued \(1\)-form on \(\mathcal{S}_c\). Since \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C})\) the spectral curve (coral bundles) restricts to a single sheet, and the Higgs-field eigenvalue is the color coordinate \(X\). The abelian component therefore satisfies \(A^0 = X\,dz = \lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}\), recovering the Seiberg–Witten differential.

Step 2: Quantum flatness and the \(2\)-form datum. The quantum flatness condition \(F_A = B\) identifies the curvature \(2\)-form \(L \wedge F^+\) on \(\mathcal{S}_c\) with the \(\mathfrak{su}(2)\)-valued \(2\)-form \(B|_{\mathcal{S}_c}\). The simplicity constraint forces \(B|_{\mathcal{S}_c} = F_A^+|_{\mathcal{S}_c}\), which on the \(2\)-sphere \(\mathcal{S}_c\) is proportional to the volume form \(\mathrm{vol}_{\mathcal{S}_c}\). Consequently the pair \((\nabla_A q,\; L \wedge F^+)\) restricted to \(\mathcal{S}_c\) is abelian: both components lie in the Cartan subalgebra after projection onto the weight-\(0\) sector, and the nonabelian MI integral reduces to the ordinary (abelian) multiplicative integral, which equals the exponential of the classical contour integral. Taking the norm yields the absolute value of the period.

Step 3: Jet prolongation and vertical degree. At vertical degree \(n = 0\) the Killing-form projection onto \(J^0\) recovers the base differential \(\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(0)} = X\,dz\) and the electron period \(a_D^{(e)}\). At vertical degree \(n \geq 1\) the (jet prolongation) lifts the connection to \(J^n E\), replacing \(X\,dz\) with the \(n\)-th prolonged differential \(\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)}\): the \(1\)-jet component is \(dX\) (the implicit derivative of the color tube cubic), and higher jets follow by induction. The MI integral at jet level \(n\) is the abelian integral of \(\lambda_{\mathrm{SW}}^{(n)}\) over \(\mathcal{S}_c\) by the same argument as Steps 1–2 applied to the prolonged connection \(A'\) on \(J^n E\). ◻

Definition 9.15 ∀ stated (Coral sector coordinates \(\mathfrak{r},\mathfrak{g},\mathfrak{b}\)). \(\forall\)

With notation as in exceptional divisor, fix the substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter) and set \(\phi \in [0,\pi]\), \(\psi \in [0, 2\pi/3]\). Define the red, green, and blue sector embeddings by

\[\begin{align*} \mathfrak{r}(\phi,\psi) &\;=\; O + R\bigl(\sin\phi\,\bigl(\cos(\psi + q\phi)\,T_1 + \sin(\psi + q\phi)\,T_2\bigr) - \cos\phi\,N\bigr),\\ \mathfrak{g}(\phi,\psi) &\;=\; \mathfrak{r}\!\bigl(\phi,\,\psi + \tfrac{2\pi}{3}\bigr),\\ \mathfrak{b}(\phi,\psi) &\;=\; \mathfrak{r}\!\bigl(\phi,\,\psi + \tfrac{4\pi}{3}\bigr). \end{align*}\]

The coral twist \(q\phi\) – so named because the resulting geometry resembles a coral reef: colorful twisted tubes with fractal boundary structure – rotates each sector by \(q\) full turns as the latitude \(\phi\) runs from the south pole (\(0\)) to the north pole (\(\pi\)), encoding the chirality of the substrate parameter.

The three sectors tile the exceptional divisor exactly:

\[\mathcal{S}_p \;=\; \mathfrak{r}(p) \;\cup\; \mathfrak{g}(p) \;\cup\; \mathfrak{b}(p),\]

where adjacent sectors share only their boundary meridians (at \(\psi = 0\) and \(\psi = 2\pi/3\) in each sector’s local coordinate), and the union covers \(\mathcal{S}_p\) without overlap. The three sectors correspond to the three copies of \(S_3 \subset S_5\) in chirality and trefoil: \(\mathfrak{r}\) is the first, \(\mathfrak{g}\) the second, and \(\mathfrak{b}\) the third.

Corollary 9.16 ∀ stated (Braid-group structure of a Descartes universe). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a Descartes universe (Descartes condition). Then:

  1. The braiding of \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) induces a faithful representation \(\rho_3\colon B_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{C}}(V^{\otimes 3})\) on the fundamental representation \(V\) (braid action on tensor products).

  4. This structure is defined over any base ring \(R\) with \(30 \in R^{\times}\); in particular it applies to the \(\mathfrak{p}\)-adic realisation (\(p\)-adic realisation), where knot complements and skein relations are not available.

Proof of Braid-group structure of a Descartes universe.

Item (1) follows from braid action on tensor products applied to the fundamental representation \(V\) of \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\), which is \(2\)-dimensional. The braiding \(c_{V,V}\) is computed by the \(R\)-matrix of \(\mathcal{U}_q(\mathfrak{su}(2))\) (\(R\)-matrix braiding), and faithfulness follows from the fact that the eigenvalues of \(c_{V,V}\) are \(q\) and \(-q^{-1}\), which are distinct for \(q \neq \pm 1\).

For item (2), the fibre functor \(\tau\) sends the braiding to the matrix \(\check{R} = P \circ \mathcal{R}\) acting on \(\mathbb{C}^2 \otimes \mathbb{C}^2\). The generators \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) map to the \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) elements \(\alpha, \beta\) (SU(2) generators) generating \(\mathrm{Dic}_3\), as verified in trefoil operator algebra.

Item (3): the projection \(\mathrm{Dic}_3 \to S_3\) sends \(\alpha \mapsto (1\,2\,3)\) and \(\beta \mapsto (1\,2)\). The three copies of \(S_3\) inside \(S_5\) are the stabilisers of the three pairs of color coordinates (coral sector coords), and conjugation by elements of \(S_5 \setminus S_3\) permutes these copies.

Item (4): the braided monoidal structure of \(\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) is defined over \(R[q, q^{-1}]\) with \(30 \in R^{\times}\) (Bring’s surface is QOU(1)), and braid action on tensor products requires no topological input beyond the hexagon axioms. ◻

Corollary 9.17 ∀ stated (Knot eigenbasis completeness for a Descartes universe). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a Descartes universe (Descartes condition) with \(\mathbf{C} = \mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{SU}_q(2))\) and \(V\) the fundamental representation. Then the knot-type eigenbasis is complete:

  1. (Iwahori–Hecke algebra instantiation.) The Descartes condition forces \(\chi(A) = -6\), giving genus \(g = 4\) and gauge group \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) of rank \(2\).   2. (Schur–Weyl decomposition.) The faithful representation \(\rho_3 \colon B_3 \to \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{C}}(V^{\otimes 3})\) (braid-group structure(1)) extends to \(\rho_n \colon B_n \to \mathrm{Aut}_{\mathbf{C}}(V^{\otimes n})\) for all \(n\) via braid action on tensor products. The Markov trace on the Iwahori–Hecke algebra tower detects every irreducible summand (Jones, 1987).

  4. (Completeness.) By the combining theorem (knot eigenbasis completeness), the three inputs — Schur–Weyl decomposition, Alexander surjectivity, and Markov trace detection — yield a complete knot-type eigenbasis for \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{phys}} = \varinjlim\, V^{\otimes n}\). The Feynman path integral is replaced by a finite categorical trace over knot-labelled summands.

Proposition 9.18 ∀ stated (The Descartes elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_q\)). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be the Descartes universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\) and substrate parameter \(q\). Set \(s = \sqrt{q}\). The coral elliptic fiber (coral elliptic) of Bring’s surface at spacetime ratio \(z = s - s^{-1}\) is the elliptic curve

\[\mathcal{E}_q \;:\; y^2 \;=\; x^3 \;+\; \frac{2s^4 + s^3 - 2s^2 - s + 2}{3s^2}\,x \;+\; \frac{5(s^2 + s - 1)(4s^4 - s^3 - 4s^2 + s + 4)}{27s^3}\]

with Weierstrass coefficients expressible directly in \(q\):

\[p(q) \;=\; \frac{2(q^2 - q + 1)}{3q} \;+\; \frac{q - 1}{3\sqrt{q}},\]

\[r(q) \;=\; \frac{20(q - 1)^3}{27\,q^{3/2}} \;+\; \frac{5(q - 1)^2}{9q} \;+\; \frac{5(\sqrt{q} - 1/\sqrt{q})}{9} \;+\; \frac{20}{27}.\]

Invariants.

\[E_1 \;:\; y^2 = x^3 + \tfrac{2}{3}\,x + \tfrac{20}{27}, \qquad \Delta = -16, \quad j = 128.\]

Clearing denominators (\(X = 3x\), \(Y = 3\sqrt{3}\,y\)) gives the integral model \(Y^2 = X^3 + 18X + 60\) with \(\Delta = -2^4 \cdot 3^5 \cdot 31\). The factor \(31\) reflects the arithmetic of the quintic resolvent underlying Bring’s surface.

Golden ratio degeneration. The second Weierstrass coefficient \(r(q)\) has the factor \((s^2 + s - 1)\) in its numerator. This vanishes at \(s = (\sqrt{5} - 1)/2 = 1/\varphi\), the reciprocal of the golden ratio \(\varphi = (1 + \sqrt{5})/2\). At this value \(q = 1/\varphi^2 = (3 - \sqrt{5})/2 \approx 0.382\), the curve \(\mathcal{E}_q\) acquires a cusp: the elliptic fiber degenerates and the color fibration becomes singular.

This is the sub-classical regime \(q < 1\) where the substrate parameter reverses its role — the quantum deformation acts in the opposite direction. The golden ratio threshold \(q = 1/\varphi^2\) marks the boundary beyond which the Descartes universe cannot support stable color structure.

Proof. The coral elliptic curve (coral elliptic) at spacetime ratio \(z\) is \(X^3 + (z + 1)X^2 + (z^2 + z + 1)X + (z^3 + z^2 + z + 1) = 0\). The Weierstrass normal form is obtained by the standard shift \(X = x - (z + 1)/3\), giving \(y^2 = x^3 + p(z)\,x + r(z)\) with \(p(z) = \tfrac{2}{3}z^2 + \tfrac{1}{3}z + \tfrac{2}{3}\) and \(r(z) = \tfrac{20}{27}z^3 + \tfrac{5}{9}z^2 + \tfrac{5}{9}z + \tfrac{20}{27}\). The Descartes condition and lepton spectrum

Definition 9.19 ∀ stated (Descartes condition). \(\forall\)

A quantum observable universe \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) over \(R\) (quantum observable universe, QU-to-QOU lifting) satisfies the Descartes condition if the categorical Euler characteristic

\[\chi(A) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) \;=\; -6 \;\in\; R.\]

This requires \(6 \in R^{\times}\) (i.e. \(\mathrm{char}(R) \nmid 6\)). The class \([A] \in K_0(\mathbf{C})\) has rank \(-6\), which by QU-to-QOU lifting(3–4) forces \(\kappa_n \neq 0\) for all \(n\) and produces \(6\) branch points in the geometric descent (with total ramification \(R_{\mathrm{tot}} = 2d + 6\)). A quantum observable universe satisfying the Descartes condition is called a Descartes universe.

📄

Proposition 9.20 ∀ stated (Genus of the one-complex-dimensional descent). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe satisfying the Descartes condition \(\chi(A) = -6\) (Descartes condition). If the geometric descent produces a compact one-complex-dimensional base \(M_0\), then \(M_0\) is a Riemann surface of genus \(g = 4\).

More precisely: the categorical Euler characteristic \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) = -6\) determines the topological type of the base curve. Under the fibre functor \(\tau\) of any archimedean realisation, Riemann–Roch on \(M_0\) forces \(2(1 - g) = -6\), hence \(g = 4\). This is the maximal genus consistent with the Hurwitz bound \(|\mathrm{Aut}(\Sigma)| \leq 84(g - 1) = 252\).

Proof of Genus of the one-complex-dimensional descent.

The Descartes condition gives \(\mathrm{tr}(\mathrm{id}_A) = -6\). Under the fibre functor \(\tau\) of the archimedean realisation, this maps to the sheaf Euler characteristic \(\chi(V) = -6\), where \(V = P \times_{\mathrm{SU}(2)} K^2\) is the associated rank-\(2\) vector bundle over \(M_0\). Since \(G = \mathrm{SU}(2)\), the determinant bundle \(\det(V)\) is trivial, so \(\deg(V) = 0\). By Riemann–Roch on the compact Riemann surface \(M_0\): \(\chi(V) = \deg(V) + \mathrm{rank}(V)(1-g) = 2(1-g)\). Setting \(2(1-g) = -6\) gives \(g = 4\). ◻

Remark 9.21 ✗ no Lean (Chirality as Reeb orientation).

The Reeb vector field \(\xi\) on the CR manifold \(M\) carries a natural orientation: the sign of the contact form \(\theta(\xi) = 1\) singles out a preferred direction along the vertical distribution. Left-handed and right-handed chiralities correspond to the two orientations of \(\xi\) relative to the complex structure of \(M\). For fermions (fermion), the vertical component \(\alpha_V\) transforms with a definite sign under reversal of \(\xi\), so chirality is encoded in the \(\pm\)-eigenspaces of the Reeb involution \(\xi \mapsto -\xi\). Bosons (boson), being purely horizontal, are chirality-blind — consistent with the observed parity invariance of the electromagnetic and strong interactions.

📄

Remark 9.22 ✗ no Lean (Light cone of an affine chart). Consider an open subset \(U \subset M_0\) representing a portion of the descended universe between two regime boundaries. An affine chart on \(U\) is a local coordinate patch in which the metric on the base manifold \(M_0\) defines a causal structure. The light cone of the affine chart is the boundary of the causal future in \(U\): it is determined by the metric on \(M_0\) and has the property that no singularity of the ambient space is visible from within the chart. In this way, the affine chart provides a non-singular window onto a portion of the Descartes universe.

📄

Remark 9.23 ✗ no Lean (Chirality and trefoil subgroups).

The chirality of the observable universe — manifest in the three colour charges of quantum chromodynamics — is encoded in the symmetry group of the descended surface \(M_0\). genus-maximal descent identifies \(M_0\) as a genus-\(4\) Riemann surface. We require a genus-\(4\) surface whose automorphism group contains three subgroups isomorphic to \(S_3\) — quotients of the trefoil knot group \(\pi_1(S^3 \setminus K) \cong \langle x, y \mid x^2 = y^3 \rangle\) — corresponding to the three colour charges (red, green, blue). These \(S_3\) subgroups generate a subgroup of the monodromy group, and the remaining generators of the full automorphism group act by conjugation, permuting the three \(S_3\) subgroups among themselves.

Proposition 9.24 ∀ stated (Finiteness of the \(T_{m,n}\) generator set). \(\forall\)

The Euler characteristic \(\chi(A) = -6\) of the Bring’s surface is the reason torus knots serve as the generators of the particle spectrum. Because the Bring’s surface has genus \(g = 4\) (from \(\chi = 2 - 2g = -6\)), there is a hard upper bound on which torus knots can be localized in the fibre: any \(T_{m,n}\) whose Seifert genus exceeds \(4\) simply cannot embed. This constraint selects a finite, enumerable generator set \(\mathcal{G}\) (knot-particle generation) whose cardinality is entirely determined by \(\chi\).

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\) (Descartes universe). The torus knot \(T_{m,n}\) with \(\gcd(m,n) = 1\) and \(m < n\) embeds into the Seifert genus-\(g\) surface of \(A\) only if the Seifert genus satisfies

\[g(T_{m,n}) \;=\; \frac{(m-1)(n-1)}{2} \;\leq\; g(A) \;=\; 4.\]

The constraint \((m-1)(n-1) \leq 8\) admits exactly the following coprime pairs with \(m \geq 2\):

\((m,n)\) \(g(T_{m,n})\) Knot Crossing #
\((2,3)\) \(1\) Trefoil \(3_1\) \(3\)
\((2,5)\) \(2\) Cinquefoil \(5_1\) \(5\)
\((2,7)\) \(3\) \(7_1\) \(7\)
\((2,9)\) \(4\) \(9_1\) \(9\)
\((3,4)\) \(3\) \(8_{19}\) \(8\)
\((3,5)\) \(4\) \(10_{124}\) \(10\)

Together with the unknot \(T_{1,0} = 0_1\) (genus \(0\)), the generator set has \(|\mathcal{G}| = 7\).

Genus bound from \(\chi(A) = -6\). The Bring’s surface \(\Sigma_4\) has genus \(g = 4\) and Euler characteristic \(\chi = 2 - 2g = -6\). A knot \(T_{m,n}\) localized in the fibre \(\mathcal{S}_c\) (localized knot) inherits a Seifert surface that must embed in the genus-\(4\) handlebody provided by \(\Sigma_4\). The Seifert genus of \(T_{m,n}\) is \((m-1)(n-1)/2\), so embeddability requires \((m-1)(n-1) \leq 2g = 8\).

Physical interpretation.

  1. Three lepton generations. The generators \(T_{2,3}\), \(T_{2,5}\), \(T_{2,7}\) (genera \(1, 2, 3\)) correspond to the three charged leptons at Reeb degrees \(\deg\alpha_V = 1, 2, 3\). No fourth generation exists because \(T_{2,9}\) saturates genus \(4\) — there is no room for a \(T_{2,11}\) (which would require genus \(5\)).

  2. Quark sector. The \((3,n)\)-family generators \(T_{3,4}\) and \(T_{3,5}\) are \(H^{0,1}\) force carriers (cohomological embedding): \(T_{3,4}\) encodes Hopf-squared color binding, while \(T_{3,5}\) mediates the weak interaction. The three-strand meridional winding \(m = 3\) of these torus knots resonates with the three coral tubes (color tube interpretation): each meridional strand threads one color fiber.

  3. Saturation. The seventh generator \(T_{2,9}\) at genus \(4\) exactly saturates the Bring’s surface. Beyond this, new particle types require either a higher-genus QOU (different \(\chi\)) or composite construction via the linking operations.

  4. Hyperbolic knots are derived. The figure-eight \(4_1\) (Higgs boson), the three-twist \(5_2\), and all other hyperbolic knots in the dictionary are not generators. They arise from Skein crossing changes applied to linked torus-knot configurations, inheriting nonzero hyperbolic volume — and hence nonzero bare mass — from the linking process.

Remark on the cutoff. The bound \(N(\chi) = 1 - \chi = 1 - (-6) = 7\) on the number of nontrivial generators is not accidental: it equals the number of handles (\(g = 4\)) of Bring’s surface plus the three independent Seifert genus values (\(1, 2, 3, 4\)) available within those handles. The recursive brane tower (recursive brane tower) does not increase the genus — it refines the blow-up structure within the existing handles — so the generator count is stable across all brane levels.

Theorem 9.25 ∀ stated (Embeddability closure under knot-particle generation). \(\forall\)

Every knot type produced by the three generation operations (knot-particle generation) applied to the generator set \(\mathcal{G}\) (finiteness of generators) remains embeddable in the genus-\(4\) fiber of the Bring’s surface, and hence admits a localized knot structure (localized knot) that descends to the base manifold via the fibre functor \(\tau\).

Theorem. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be the Descartes universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\) and fiber genus \(g(\Sigma_4) = 4\). Let \(K\) be any knot type appearing as a component of a link produced by a finite sequence of Hopf linkings \(\ell_H\), color-tube threadings \(\ell_c\), and Skein crossing changes \(\sigma\) applied to generators in \(\mathcal{G}\). Then:

  1. The Seifert genus of \(K\) satisfies \(g(K) \leq 4\).

  2. \(K\) admits a localized knot structure \((c, K) \in \mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, A^{\mathrm{co}\,T}) \times \mathrm{Knot}\) at some point \(c\) of the base \(\mathbb{P}(V)\).

  3. The localized knot \((c, K)\) descends under \(\tau\) to an observable morphism in \(\mathbf{C}\): every generated particle interacts with every other generated particle via the categorical braiding.

In particular, no generated knot is "dark" — the generation scheme is closed under observability.

Why each operation preserves embeddability.

Hopf linking \(\ell_H\). The Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{Hopf}}\) on the exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_c \cong S^2\) joins two knots localized at (possibly distinct) points of the base. Each component retains its own knot type and hence its own Seifert genus. The linking structure lives in the total space \(S^3 \to \mathcal{S}_c\) and does not increase the genus of any individual component. Consequently, if \(g(K_1) \leq 4\) and \(g(K_2) \leq 4\), then both components of \(K_1 \cup_{\mathrm{Hopf}} K_2\) remain embeddable.

Color-tube threading \(\ell_c\). Threading three knots through the coral tubes \((r, g, b)\) similarly preserves each component’s knot type. The three-component link \(K_1 \cup_r K_2 \cup_g K_3\) has each \(K_i\) sitting in its own color fiber; the Seifert genus of each component is unchanged.

Skein crossing change \(\sigma\). This is the non-trivial case. A crossing change at a single site alters the Seifert genus by at most \(\pm 1\):

\[|g(L_+) - g(L_-)| \leq 1, \qquad g(L_0) \leq \max\{g(L_+), g(L_-)\}.\]

Starting from generators with \(g(T_{m,n}) \leq 4\), a crossing change produces a knot of genus at most \(5\). However, the Bring surface imposes a spectral filter: only knots with \(g(K) \leq 4\) admit localized knot structures. A Skein descendant with \(g = 5\) has zero projection onto the physical Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{phys}}\) — its coefficient in the mass functional vanishes because the fibre functor \(\tau\) cannot evaluate it.

The spectral filter acts at the level of the Skein resolution:

\[q \, [L_+] - q^{-1} [L_-] = (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) [L_0]\]

in the Skein module \(\mathcal{S}_q(\mathbf{C})\). Terms whose knot type has \(g > 4\) lie in the kernel of the mass functional \(\mathcal{M} \colon \mathcal{S}_q \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\), because \(\mathcal{M}\) is defined via the fibre functor, which requires localizability. The physical mass receives contributions only from the embeddable terms.
