Physical consequence. The closure of embeddability under generation is the topological reason that all fundamental particles interact: they all descend to the same base manifold \(\mathbb{P}(V)\) and hence participate in the categorical braiding. A hypothetical particle corresponding to a genus-\(5\) knot would be unobservable — it could not be localized in the Bring’s surface fiber, could not descend to the base, and would have zero coupling to all other particles. The \(\chi = -6\) constraint of the Descartes universe therefore guarantees a self-consistent, fully interacting particle spectrum with no dark sectors arising from the generation scheme.

Proposition 9.26 ∀ stated (Genus-filtration ideal and the Chebyshev obstruction for \(T_{2,p}\)). \(\forall\)

The genus of the moduli surface is not assumed — it is determined by the Iwahori–Hecke algebra. The QOU axioms force \(g = 4\) through a completeness condition on the irreducible representations of \(H_2(q) \oplus H_3(q)\), and the genus-filtration ideal \(\mathfrak{I}_4 = (u^5)\) is the algebraic obstruction that kills \(T_{2,p}\) for all primes \(p \geq 11\).

Part 0: the genus is determined by the algebra

Proposition (Genus from Hecke completeness). Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a QOU with \(G = \mathrm{SU}_q(2)\). The braiding on \(V_1^{\otimes n}\) gives the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_n(q)\). The relevant strand counts are \(n = 2\) and \(n = 3\):

  • \(H_2(q)\) has \(2\) irreducible representations (partitions of \(2\): \((2)\) trivial, \((1,1)\) sign).

  • \(H_3(q)\) has \(3\) irreducible representations (partitions of \(3\): \((3)\), \((1,1,1)\), \((2,1)\)).

  • Total: \(5\) irreps.

At genus \(g\), the embeddable torus knots \(T_{r,s}\) with \((r-1)(s-1) \leq 2g\) and \(\gcd(r,s) = 1\) are the ones whose Jones polynomials can be evaluated on \(\Sigma_g\). Completeness (cohomological embedding) requires that these evaluations span all \(5\) irrep characters: the evaluation matrix \(M_{ij} = \chi_{\lambda_j}(T_i)\) must have rank \(5\).

The strand counts \(m \geq 4\) contribute no new knots: at genus \(g\), the constraint \((m-1)(s-1) \leq 2g\) with \(m \geq 4\) and \(m < s\), \(\gcd(m,s) = 1\), gives \(s \leq 2g/(m-1) + 1\), which for \(m = 4\) yields \(T_{4,3} = T_{3,4}\) (already counted) and for \(m \geq 5\) yields no valid \((m, s)\) pairs with \(m < s\). Therefore \(H_2(q) \oplus H_3(q)\) is the complete Hecke algebra of the QOU.

The genus scan.

\(g\) Embeddable torus knots Count Rank of \(M\) Complete?
\(2\) \(T_{2,3}\), \(T_{2,5}\) \(2\) \(\leq 2\) No
\(3\) \(T_{2,3}\), \(T_{2,5}\), \(T_{2,7}\), \(T_{3,4}\) \(4\) \(\leq 4\) No
\(4\) \(T_{2,3}\), \(T_{2,5}\), \(T_{2,7}\), \(T_{2,9}\), \(T_{3,4}\), \(T_{3,5}\) \(6\) \(5\) Yes
\(5\) \(+\; T_{2,11}\) \(7\) \(5\) Yes (redundant)

At \(g = 3\): only \(4\) knots are available, but \(5\) irreps must be spanned. Rank \(\leq 4 < 5\) — incomplete. Observability (\(\mathrm{Hom}(\mathbf{1}, \mathrm{Ad}(A)) = 0\)) would be violated: there would exist knot observables not determined by the generators.

At \(g = 4\): the two additional knots \(T_{2,9}\) (Chebyshev degree \(4\), saturates) and \(T_{3,5}\) (genus \(4\), saturates) bring the total to \(6\) knots spanning \(5\) irreps. Rank \(= 5\) — complete.

At \(g \geq 5\): \(T_{2,11}\) and further knots embed, but they add no new irreps (rank stays \(5\)). These extra knots predict unobserved particles — the redundancy violates minimality.

Therefore \(g = 4\) is the unique minimal genus where the Hecke completeness condition holds.

Part I: Chebyshev degree = Seifert genus

Why Chebyshev. The Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_2(q)\) is \(2\)-dimensional with basis \(\{1, T\}\) and the single relation \(T^2 = sT + 1\) where \(s = q - q^{-1}\). The generator \(T\) has two eigenvalues: \(q\) (symmetric channel) and \(-q^{-1}\) (antisymmetric channel). Computing \(T^p\) — the \(p\)-th power of the braid generator — reduces it via the relation:

\[T^p \;=\; a_p \cdot T \;+\; a_{p-1} \cdot \mathbf{1}\]

The coefficients \(a_n\) satisfy the recurrence \(a_{n+1} = s \cdot a_n + a_{n-1}\) with \(a_0 = 0\), \(a_1 = 1\). This is the Chebyshev recurrence: powers of a matrix with two eigenvalues are always Chebyshev polynomials. Precisely, \(a_p = U_{p-1}(s/2)\), the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind evaluated at \(s/2\), where \(U_n(\cos\theta) = \sin((n+1)\theta)/\sin\theta\).

For odd \(p\), only even powers of \(s\) appear, so writing \(u = s^2 = (q - q^{-1})^2\):

\[a_p(u) \;=\; U_{p-1}\!\left(\tfrac{s}{2}\right) \;=\; \sum_{j=0}^{(p-1)/2} c_j\, u^j\]

with leading coefficient \(c_{(p-1)/2} = 1\).

The degree–genus identity. The algebraic complexity of the Hecke coefficient (the polynomial degree \(\deg_u a_p\)) equals the topological complexity of the knot (the Seifert genus \(g(T_{2,p})\)):

\[\deg_u a_p \;=\; \frac{p-1}{2} \;=\; g(T_{2,p}).\]

Each monomial \(u^k\) in \(a_p\) represents the \(k\)-th independent \(1\)-cycle of the Seifert surface \(F_p\). To realise \(T_{2,p}\) as a localized knot on \(\Sigma_g\), each cycle needs a target class in \(H^1(\Sigma_g)\). When \(\deg_u a_p > g\), the polynomial encodes more topology than the surface can hold — the surplus monomials have no geometric home. This is the Chebyshev overflow: the Iwahori–Hecke algebra knows the knot doesn’t fit, before any surface is chosen.

The Chebyshev table

The Hecke recurrence \(a_{n+1} = s \cdot a_n + a_{n-1}\) with \(a_0 = 0\), \(a_1 = 1\) gives, for odd \(p\), the following polynomials in \(u = s^2 = (q - q^{-1})^2\):

\(p\) \(a_p(u)\) \(\deg_u\) genus status at \(g = 4\)
\(3\) \(u + 1\) \(1\) \(1\) embeds
\(5\) \(u^2 + 3u + 1\) \(2\) \(2\) embeds
\(7\) \(u^3 + 5u^2 + 6u + 1\) \(3\) \(3\) embeds
\(9^*\) \(u^4 + 7u^3 + 15u^2 + 10u + 1\) \(4\) \(4\) saturates
\(11\) \(u^5 + 9u^4 + 28u^3 + 35u^2 + 15u + 1\) \(5\) \(5\) overflow
\(13\) \(u^6 + 11u^5 + 45u^4 + 84u^3 + 70u^2 + 21u + 1\) \(6\) \(6\) overflow

(\(*\): \(9 = 3^2\) is not prime but \(T_{2,9}\) is the degree-\(2\) tower of the trefoil.)

The saturation at \(a_9\) (degree \(4\)) and the overflow at \(a_{11}\) (degree \(5\)) are not coincidences — they are the Chebyshev reflection of the Hecke completeness condition. The completeness scan (Part 0) shows that \(g = 4\) is the minimum genus where all \(5\) irreps are spanned. The Chebyshev degree at the boundary is \(\deg_u a_9 = 4 = g\), and \(\deg_u a_{11} = 5 = g + 1\) is the first overflow.

Part II: the genus-filtration ideal

Define the genus-\(g\) filtration ideal \(\mathfrak{I}_g \subset \mathbb{Z}[u]\) by

\[\mathfrak{I}_g \;=\; \bigl\{\, f(u) \in \mathbb{Z}[u] : \deg f > g \,\bigr\} \;=\; (u^{g+1}).\]

A torus knot \(T_{2,p}\) admits a localized knot structure on \(\Sigma_g\) if and only if \(a_p \notin \mathfrak{I}_g\), i.e., \(\deg_u a_p \leq g\).

For \(g = 4\) (as determined by Hecke completeness): \(\mathfrak{I}_4 = (u^5)\). Every \(T_{2,p}\) with \(p \geq 11\) has \(a_p \in \mathfrak{I}_4\) because \(\deg_u a_p \geq 5\). The ideal \((u^5)\) catches all of them simultaneously: \(u^k = u^{k-5} \cdot u^5 \in (u^5)\) for all \(k \geq 5\).

Part III: Yekutieli obstruction = leading coefficient

The Yekutieli obstruction class \(\kappa(T_{2,p}) \in H^2(\Sigma_g, \mathbb{Z})\) is the image of the leading monomial of \(a_p\) under the projection \(\pi_g \colon \mathbb{Z}[u] \to \mathbb{Z}[u]/(u^{g+1})\):

\[\kappa(T_{2,p}) \;=\; \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } (p-1)/2 \leq g \quad (\text{lifts: } a_p \text{ fits in } H^1(\Sigma_g)), \\[6pt] c_{(p-1)/2} \cdot [u^{(p-1)/2}] \neq 0 & \text{if } (p-1)/2 > g \quad (\text{obstructed: overflow}). \end{cases}\]

Since \(c_{(p-1)/2} = 1\) for all odd \(p\), the obstruction is nonzero for every prime \(p \geq 2g + 3 = 11\).

Proposition 9.27 ∀ stated (Completeness of torus knots embeddable in the Bring’s surface). \(\forall\)

The generator set \(\mathcal{G}\) (finiteness of generators) is not merely a convenient choice — it is the complete list of torus knots embeddable in the genus-\(4\) fiber of the Bring’s surface.

Proposition. Let \(T_{m,n}\) be a torus knot with \(\gcd(m,n) = 1\) and \(1 < m < n\). Then \(T_{m,n}\) embeds in the Seifert genus-\(4\) surface \(\Sigma_4\) of the Bring’s surface if and only if \((m,n)\) belongs to the set

\[\{(2,3),\;(2,5),\;(2,7),\;(2,9),\;(3,4),\;(3,5)\}.\]

Together with the unknot \(T_{1,0}\), these are the only torus knots that can appear as localized knots in the Descartes universe.

Proof. The Seifert genus of \(T_{m,n}\) is \(g(T_{m,n}) = (m-1)(n-1)/2\). Embeddability requires \(g(T_{m,n}) \leq g(\Sigma_4) = 4\), i.e., \((m-1)(n-1) \leq 8\). We enumerate all coprime pairs \((m,n)\) with \(1 < m < n\) satisfying this bound:

  • \(m = 2\): \((2-1)(n-1) = n-1 \leq 8\), so \(n \leq 9\). Odd coprime values: \(n \in \{3, 5, 7, 9\}\).

  • \(m = 3\): \((3-1)(n-1) = 2(n-1) \leq 8\), so \(n \leq 5\). Coprime to \(3\): \(n \in \{4, 5\}\).

  • \(m = 4\): \((4-1)(n-1) = 3(n-1) \leq 8\), so \(n \leq 3\). But \(m < n\) requires \(n \geq 5\); no solution.

  • \(m \geq 5\): \((m-1)(n-1) \geq 4 \cdot m > 8\) for \(n > m \geq 5\); no solution.

This exhausts all cases. The six nontrivial torus knots listed above, together with the unknot, form the complete set of torus knots embeddable in \(\Sigma_4\). No torus knot outside \(\mathcal{G}\) admits a localized knot structure in the Descartes universe. \(\square\)

Remark. The completeness is purely number-theoretic: it depends only on the Diophantine constraint \((m-1)(n-1) \leq 2g\) with a coprimality condition. For any QOU with fiber genus \(g'\), an analogous finite enumeration determines the torus knot generator set. The Descartes value \(g = 4\) is the smallest genus that accommodates all three lepton generations (requiring genera \(1, 2, 3\)) plus a non-trivial quark sector (requiring \(m = 3\) generators).

📄

Theorem 9.28 ∀ stated (Generation completeness: all embeddable knots are reachable). \(\forall\)

The embeddability closure (embeddability closure) shows that the generation scheme does not produce knots outside genus \(4\). The converse question is whether it produces all knots inside genus \(4\). The answer is yes: every knot embeddable in the Bring’s surface is reachable from \(\mathcal{G}\) by Skein operations alone.

Theorem (Generation completeness). Let \(K\) be any knot with Seifert genus \(g(K) \leq 4\). Then \(K\) is reachable from the generator set \(\mathcal{G}\) (finiteness of generators) by a finite sequence of Skein crossing changes. In particular, the generation scheme (knot-particle generation) applied to \(\mathcal{G}\) produces every knot type that admits a localized knot structure in the Descartes universe.

Proof. The argument proceeds in two steps.

Step 1: Reachability from the unknot. Every knot \(K\) has a finite unknotting number \(u(K)\) — the minimum number of crossing changes needed to convert \(K\) into the unknot \(0_1 = T_{1,0}\). Since crossing changes are involutions (each change is its own inverse), the same \(u(K)\) crossing changes applied to \(T_{1,0}\) produce \(K\). Because \(T_{1,0} \in \mathcal{G}\), the knot \(K\) is reachable from \(\mathcal{G}\) by at most \(u(K)\) Skein operations.

Step 2: The spectral filter selects genus \(\leq 4\). Not every knot reachable from \(T_{1,0}\) by crossing changes has genus \(\leq 4\) — intermediate steps may pass through arbitrarily high genus. However, the Bring’s surface imposes a spectral filter: in the Skein module \(\mathcal{S}_q(\mathbf{C})\), the mass functional \(\mathcal{M} \colon \mathcal{S}_q \to \mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\) annihilates any term whose knot type has \(g > 4\) (embeddability closure). The physical content of the Skein resolution is the projection onto the submodule spanned by knots with \(g(K) \leq 4\).

The composition of Steps 1 and 2 gives: for any knot \(K\) with \(g(K) \leq 4\), there exists a finite sequence of Skein crossing changes \(\sigma_1, \ldots, \sigma_r\) (with \(r \leq u(K)\)) such that \(K\) appears with nonzero coefficient in the Skein expansion of \(\sigma_r \circ \cdots \circ \sigma_1(T_{1,0})\), and \(K\) passes the spectral filter since \(g(K) \leq 4\). \(\square\)

Corollary. The Descartes particle spectrum is complete over embeddable knots: every knot type with \(g(K) \leq 4\) corresponds to a state in the physical Hilbert space \(\mathcal{H}_{\mathrm{phys}}\). No embeddable knot is excluded from the spectrum.

Counting embeddable knots. The number of distinct knot types with Seifert genus \(\leq g\) grows rapidly. For \(g \leq 4\), the knot tables give:

Genus Knots (prime, up to 16 crossings) Examples
\(0\) \(1\) \(0_1\)
\(1\) \(\geq 70\) \(3_1, 4_1, 5_2, 6_1, 6_2, 6_3, \ldots\)
\(2\) \(\geq 400\) \(5_1, 7_4, 8_1, \ldots\)
\(3\) \(\geq 2{,}000\) \(7_1, 8_{19}, 9_2, \ldots\)
\(4\) \(\geq 8{,}000\) \(9_1, 10_{124}, 11a_{367}, \ldots\)

The vast majority of these are hyperbolic (non-torus) knots. The generation scheme reaches all of them: the \(7\) torus knot generators are the seeds, and Skein crossing changes explore the full knot landscape within the genus bound.

Physical interpretation. The completeness theorem means the Descartes universe does not arbitrarily select which knots become particles. Every topologically admissible knot type is physically realizable — the \(7\) generators and the Skein algebra are sufficient to span the entire embeddable spectrum. The particle dictionary (knot formula table) names only the phenomenologically prominent knots (trefoil, figure-eight, etc.), but the theorem guarantees that the thousands of higher-crossing embeddable knots also populate the spectrum, appearing as massive, short-lived resonances in the Skein decomposition of hadronic processes.

Fundamental particles

📄

Definition 9.29 ∀ stated (Up quark). \(\forall\)

The up quark is an unknot (neutrino) localized in a color tube of the Bring’s surface with positive crossing orientation within the Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\) (Borromean quark conjecture).

\[u \;=\; \nu \,\big|_{\mathcal{B}_3,\, +} \qquad\text{(unknot, positive orientation in } \mathcal{B}_3\text{)}\]

The up quark is not a distinct knot type — it is the unknot \(K_{0_1}\) (neutrino) distinguished by its environment: threaded through a coral tube (color tube coordinates) and Borromean-linked with two other unknots.

📄

Definition 9.30 ∀ stated (Down quark). \(\forall\)

The down quark is an unknot (neutrino) localized in a coral tube with negative crossing orientation within the Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\) (Borromean quark conjecture).

\[\mathfrak{d} \;=\; \nu \,\big|_{\mathcal{B}_3,\, -} \qquad\text{(unknot, negative orientation in } \mathcal{B}_3\text{)}\]

The down quark differs from the up quark (up quark) only in crossing orientation: at each crossing point within \(\mathcal{B}_3\), the down quark’s strand passes under where the up quark passes over. This reversal contributes \(q^{-1}\) instead of \(q\) to the Skein polynomial, giving the down quark a Coulomb charge contribution of \(-1/3\) relative to the proton.

📄

Definition 9.31 ∀ stated (Electron). \(\forall\)

The electron is the trefoil \(T_{2,3}\) in the lepton sector — the same knot type as the up quark, but not localized in a coral tube.

\[e^- \;=\; T_{2,3} \qquad \text{(trefoil, solid ●)}\]

The electron and the up quark are the same knot \(T_{2,3}\). What distinguishes them is their environment: the up quark is threaded through a coral tube of the Bring’s surface (color tube coordinates), while the electron orbits the nucleus via Hopf linking without entering the coral tubes.

Visual convention. The electron is drawn as a solid trefoil (forward time direction), identical to the up quark. Context (coral tube vs. orbital) distinguishes quark from lepton.

📄

Definition 9.32 ∀ stated (Positron). \(\forall\)

The positron is the mirror trefoil \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) in the lepton sector — the antiparticle of the electron.

\[e^+ \;=\; T_{2,3}^{\sigma} \qquad \text{(mirror trefoil, outlined ○)}\]

The positron is the same knot as the down quark, distinguished by environment (orbital vs. coral tube). It carries reversed crossing chirality: where the electron has Coulomb charge \(Q = -1\), the positron has \(Q = +1\).

Visual convention. The positron is drawn as an outlined trefoil (reversed time direction).

Time reversal interpretation. The mirror operation \(\sigma\) reverses all crossings, which in the Reeb flow corresponds to reversing the direction of time (chirality remark). The positron is an electron travelling backward in time (Feynman–Stueckelberg interpretation).

📄

Definition 9.33 ∀ stated (Neutrino). \(\forall\)

The neutrino is the unknot \(K_{0_1}\) — the trivial knot with no crossings.

\[\nu \;=\; K_{0_1} \qquad \text{(unknot, circle ○)}\]

The unknot has Seifert genus \(0\), crossing number \(0\), and trivial Skein polynomial \(J_\nu(q) = 1\). It contributes no hyperbolic volume and hence no bare mass: the neutrino mass comes entirely from vacuum drag (mass identity), not from knot topology.

Visual convention. The neutrino is drawn as a simple circle, distinct from both the solid trefoil (forward-time fermion) and the outlined trefoil (backward-time fermion).

Properties.

  • Zero crossing chirality: \(Q(\nu) = 0\) (no crossings to be asymmetric). The neutrino is electrically neutral.

  • Trivial braiding: the \(R\)-matrix acts trivially on the unknot component. Neutrinos do not participate in the crossing-energy interactions that produce Coulomb repulsion.

  • Vacuum drag mass: the neutrino mass \(m_\nu \sim \mu_0 \cdot (q - 1)\) is proportional to the baseline vacuum drag, which vanishes at \(q = 1\).

📄

Definition 9.34 ∀ stated (Antineutrino as mirror unknot \(T_{1,0}^{\sigma}\)). \(\forall\)

The antineutrino is the mirror unknot \(T_{1,0}^{\sigma}\) — the antiparticle of the neutrino.

\[\nu^{\sigma} \;=\; T_{1,0}^{\sigma} \qquad \text{(mirror unknot, dashed circle ⊙)}\]

Since the unknot is amphichiral (\(T_{1,0} \cong T_{1,0}^{\sigma}\) as unoriented knots), the antineutrino has the same knot invariants as the neutrino:

  • Jones polynomial: \(J_{\nu^{\sigma}}(q) = 1\)

  • Alexander polynomial: \(\Delta_{\nu^{\sigma}}(t) = 1\)

  • Hyperbolic volume: \(\mathrm{Vol}(\nu^{\sigma}) = 0\)

  • Seifert genus: \(g = 0\)

  • Crossing number: \(c = 0\)

The distinction between \(\nu\) and \(\nu^{\sigma}\) is carried by orientation (framing), not by knot type. In the braid group, the neutrino is the identity braid \(e \in B_1\) with positive orientation; the antineutrino is \(e\) with negative orientation.

Visual convention. The antineutrino is drawn as a dashed circle (⊙), distinguishing it from:

  • Solid circle (○) = neutrino (forward time)

  • Solid trefoil (●) = electron (forward time)

  • Outlined trefoil (○) = positron (backward time)

Role in beta decay.

In \(\beta^-\) decay, the \(L_0^{-}\) smoothing of the \(\mathfrak{d} \to \mathfrak{u}\) crossing change produces:

\[L_0^{-} \;=\; T_{2,3} \;\sqcup\; T_{1,0}^{\sigma} \quad=\quad e^- \;+\; \nu_e^{\sigma}\]

The electron \(T_{2,3}\) carries the topological mass (\(\mathrm{Vol} = 0\) but crossing energy from the trefoil structure); the antineutrino \(T_{1,0}^{\sigma}\) carries zero topological mass and exits as a massless (or near-massless) particle.

Lepton number. The \(L_0^{\pm}\) smoothing always produces one fermion knot (\(T_{2,3}\) or \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\)) and one (anti)neutrino (\(T_{1,0}\) or \(T_{1,0}^{\sigma}\)). Lepton number is conserved because each smoothing creates exactly one lepton-antilepton pair.

Definition 9.36 ∀ stated (\(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-Value as Categorical Action Difference). \(\forall\)

The \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value of a nuclear transition is the \(q\)-deformed transition energy. It is NOT defined by classical energy conservation — it is defined directly from the categorical action.

Definition (categorical, primary)

For a beta decay $\{}mathcal{N}{\{}mathrm{par}} \{}to \{}mathcal{N}{\{}mathrm{dau}}

  • e + \{}nu^{\{}sigma}\(, the **\)\{}mathcal{Q}_q$-value** is the net change in categorical action at the Skein crossing change:

\[\mathcal{Q}_q \;:=\; S_q(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{par}}) \;-\; S_q(\mathcal{N}_{\mathrm{dau}}) \;-\; S_q(e) \;-\; S_q(\nu^{\sigma})\]

where \(S_q(K) = \mathrm{tr}_\tau(\rho(\beta_K))\) is the categorical action evaluated on the Gröbner–Shirshov normal form of each knot/link.

This is the primary definition. No conservation law is invoked. \(\mathcal{Q}_q\) is a computable function of \(q\) alone.

Crossing-level decomposition

The parent and daughter normal forms \(\mathcal{N}(p,n)\) and \(\mathcal{N}(p+1, n-1)\) differ at exactly \(|\delta p|\) crossings (the converting nucleon’s quarks). At each changed crossing:

\[\Delta \mathbf{E}_\times \;=\; \mathbf{E}_\times^{(\epsilon_{\mathrm{par}})}(q) - \mathbf{E}_\times^{(\epsilon_{\mathrm{dau}})}(q)\]

For a \(\mathfrak{d} \to \mathfrak{u}\) change (\(\sigma_k^{-1} \to \sigma_k\)): \(\Delta \mathbf{E}_\times = q - q^{-1}\).

\[\mathcal{Q}_q \;=\; \sum_{\text{changed crossings}} \Delta \mathbf{E}_\times \;-\; S_q(e)\]

(dropping \(S_q(\nu^{\sigma}) = 0\) since the unknot has trivial action).

Classical limit and the \(q\)-anomaly

⚠ WARNING: Classical energy conservation is NOT assumed.

In classical physics, the Q-value is defined via conservation of energy:

\[Q_{\mathrm{classical}} \;=\; T_e + T_{\nu^{\sigma}} + T_{\mathrm{recoil}} \;\stackrel{?}{=}\; M_{\mathrm{par}} - M_{\mathrm{dau}} - m_e\]

This equality uses \(E_{\mathrm{before}} = E_{\mathrm{after}}\) (first law of thermodynamics / Noether’s theorem for time translation). In the \(q\)-deformed framework, this conservation law may fail because the \(q\)-differential does not satisfy \(d_q^2 = 0\):

\[d_q f(x) \;=\; \frac{f(qx) - f(x)}{(q-1)x}\]

\[d_q(f \cdot g) \;=\; (d_q f) \cdot g \;+\; f(qx) \cdot (d_q g)\]

The \(q\)-Leibniz rule has a shift \(f(qx)\) rather than \(f(x)\). This means the \(q\)-differential of a product is NOT simply the sum of differentials. Squaring:

\[d_q^2 \;\neq\; 0 \quad \text{for } q \neq 1\]

Consequence: The total \(q\)-energy of the products need not equal the total \(q\)-energy of the parent. There is a \(q\)-anomaly:

\[\delta_q \;:=\; \mathcal{Q}_q \;-\; (T_e + T_{\nu^{\sigma}} + T_{\mathrm{recoil}})\]

This anomaly does NOT vanish in general. It is a genuine physical effect of the \(q\)-deformation, not a computational artefact.

Structure of the \(q\)-anomaly

The \(q\)-anomaly arises from the non-commutativity of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra. When the Skein crossing change converts one quark, the re-reduction to Gröbner–Shirshov normal form (nuclear Gröbner–Shirshov reduction) introduces R2 moves \(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\). Each R2 move shifts the local \(q\)-environment by:

\[q_{\mathrm{eff}} \;\mapsto\; q_{\mathrm{eff}} + \Delta q\]

where \(\Delta q \propto \hbar_q^2 = (1 - q^{-1})^2\).

The self-deformation (hadron self-correction) produces a net shift:

\[\Delta q_{\mathrm{eff}} \;=\; \frac{A - 1}{A^2} \cdot \hbar_q^2\]

This shift modifies \(\mathcal{Q}_q\) at second order:

\[\mathcal{Q}_q \;=\; \underbrace{\Delta S_q - S_q(e)}_{\text{leading (crossing change)}} \;+\; \underbrace{\frac{\partial S_q}{\partial q} \cdot \Delta q_{\mathrm{eff}}}_{\delta_q \text{ (q-anomaly)}}\]

At \(q = 1\): \(\delta_q = 0\) and \(\mathcal{Q}_q \to Q_{\mathrm{classical}}\) (classical conservation restored).

At the substrate parameter \(q\): \(\delta_q \neq 0\). For tritium (\(A = 3\)): \(\Delta q_{\mathrm{eff}} = 2/9 \cdot \hbar_q^2 \approx 0.0022\), giving a correction \(\delta_q / \mathcal{Q}_q \sim 5\%\). This is the same correction that brings the tritium half-life prediction from 13 yr to 12.4 yr (vs observed 12.32 yr).

\(\mathcal{Q}_q\) is NOT conserved

The \(q\)-anomaly \(\delta_q\) means that \(\mathcal{Q}_q\) defined as the action difference is NOT equal to the sum of kinetic energies. The "missing" energy goes into the \(q\)-deformation of the vacuum — it is absorbed by the change in the effective substrate parameter from \(q\) to \(q + \Delta q_{\mathrm{eff}}\).

This is not a violation of physics — it is the \(q\)-deformed version of the quantum anomaly. The conserved quantity is not \(\mathcal{Q}_q\) but the full categorical action \(S_q\) of the entire system (products + vacuum shift):

\[S_q(\mathrm{par}) \;=\; S_{q + \Delta q}(\mathrm{dau}) \;+\; S_q(e) \;+\; S_q(\nu^{\sigma}) \;+\; \text{kinetic terms}\]

Note: the daughter is evaluated at the shifted \(q\), not the original. This is the \(q\)-analogue of energy conservation.

Limits

\(q\) Regime \(\mathcal{Q}_q\) \(\delta_q\)
\(q = 1\) Classical \(0\) \(0\)
the substrate \(q\) Our universe \(\mathcal{Q}_{\exp} + \delta_q\) \(\neq 0\)
\(q \to \infty\) Deep-quantum \(\to \infty\) \(\to \infty\)

\(q\)-Momentum

The \(q\)-momentum (q-momentum) satisfies a similar non-conservation. Classically:

\[\vec{p}_{\mathrm{par}} = \vec{p}_{\mathrm{dau}} + \vec{p}_e + \vec{p}_{\nu^{\sigma}}\]

In the \(q\)-deformed case, the Iwahori–Hecke algebra non-commutativity means:

\[p_q(\mathrm{par}) \;=\; p_q(\mathrm{dau}) + p_q(e) + p_q(\nu^{\sigma}) \;+\; \delta p_q\]

where \(\delta p_q \propto \hbar_q\) is a \(q\)-anomaly in momentum. This is the braid-group analogue of the quantum anomaly in gauge theories.

Definition 9.37 ∀ stated (Proton (categorical)). \(\forall\)

The proton is the baryon with \(2 + 1\) crossing partition: two up quarks (positive orientation) and one down quark (negative orientation) in the Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\) (Borromean quark).

\[\mathfrak{p} \;=\; \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u},\, \mathfrak{u},\, \mathfrak{d}) \;\bowtie\; \mathcal{L}_H\]

where:

  • \(\mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d})\) is the Borromean link of three unknots threaded through coral tubes \((r, g, b)\) (color tube coordinates): two with positive crossing orientation (\(\mathfrak{u}\), up quark) and one with negative orientation (\(\mathfrak{d}\), down quark),

  • \(\mathcal{L}_H\) is the Hopf link binding the three constituents,

  • the \(S_3\) permutation symmetry of the coral tubes ensures the definition is independent of the color assignment.

Mass. The proton mass comes from the hyperbolic volume of the Borromean link:

\[m_{\mathfrak{p}} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(S^3 \setminus \mathcal{B}_3)}{\hbar_q^2} \cdot \lambda_{\mathrm{scale}} \;+\; \text{Skein corrections}\]

The Skein corrections arise from the crossing asymmetry between the \(\mathfrak{u}\) and \(\mathfrak{d}\) components. The pair Skein formula gives:

\[m_{\mathfrak{p}} \;=\; \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{u}}(q) + 2\,\mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{d}}(q)\]

At the CODATA value \(q_0\): \(m_{\mathfrak{p}}(q_0) \approx 938.272\) MeV, derived from the substrate parameter (local substrate).

Coulomb charge. The proton carries net positive crossing chirality: two positive-orientation unknots (\(\mathfrak{u}\)) outweigh one negative (\(\mathfrak{d}\)), giving a net Coulomb charge

\[Q(\mathfrak{p}) \;=\; 2 \cdot (+\tfrac{2}{3}) + 1 \cdot (-\tfrac{1}{3}) \;=\; +1.\]

📄

Definition 9.38 ∀ stated (Neutron (categorical)). \(\forall\)

The neutron is the baryon with \(1 + 2\) crossing partition: one up quark and two down quarks in the Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3\) (Borromean quark).

\[\mathfrak{n} \;=\; \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u},\, \mathfrak{d},\, \mathfrak{d}) \;\bowtie\; \mathcal{L}_H\]

Mass.

\[m_{\mathfrak{n}} \;=\; 2\,\mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{d}}(q) + \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{d}}(q)\]

At the CODATA value \(q_0\): \(m_{\mathfrak{n}}(q_0) \approx 939.565\) MeV, derived from the substrate parameter (local substrate). The proton–neutron mass splitting is

\[m_{\mathfrak{n}} - m_{\mathfrak{p}} \;=\; \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{d}\mathfrak{d}}(q) - \mathcal{S}_{\mathfrak{u}\mathfrak{u}}(q) \;\approx\; 1.293 \text{ MeV}\]

arising from the Skein resolution asymmetry between the \(\mathfrak{u}\text{-}\mathfrak{u}\) and \(\mathfrak{d}\text{-}\mathfrak{d}\) crossing pairs within \(\mathcal{B}_3\).

Coulomb charge.

\[Q(\mathfrak{n}) \;=\; 1 \cdot (+\tfrac{2}{3}) + 2 \cdot (-\tfrac{1}{3}) \;=\; 0.\]

The neutron is electrically neutral: its one positive-orientation unknot (\(\mathfrak{u}\)) is exactly cancelled by two negative-orientation unknots (\(\mathfrak{d}\)). Inter-neutron Hopf crossings pick up the coefficient \(q^{-1}\) (negative crossings), producing an attractive enhancement — the categorical expression of electric neutrality.

📄

Proposition 9.39 ✗ no Lean (Antiparticles from crossing reversal).

Let \(T_{2,3}\) be the left trefoil (the electron generator) and \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) its mirror image (all crossings reversed).

Statement.

  1. Crossing reversal defines antiparticles. The antihadron \(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma}\) of a composite hadron \(\mathfrak{H} = [K_1, \ldots, K_n]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}\) is obtained by replacing every constituent \(K_i\) with its mirror \(K_i^{\sigma}\). The braid word \(\beta\) representing the linking has all crossing signs reversed.

  2. Crossing energy sign reversal. If the crossing energy of \(\mathfrak{H}\) is \[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_{\text{crossings}} \epsilon_i, \qquad \epsilon_i \in \{q, -q^{-1}\},\] then the crossing energy of the antihadron satisfies \[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma}) = -\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) \bigg|_{q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}},\] i.e. positive crossings (\(+q\)) become negative (\(-q^{-1}\)) and vice versa.

  3. Coulomb charge reversal. The antisymmetric component of the crossing energy (the Coulomb channel) reverses sign: \(Q(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma}) = -Q(\mathfrak{H})\). In particular, \(Q(\mathfrak{p}^{\sigma}) = -1\) for the antiproton.

  4. Bare mass invariance. The mirror operation preserves the knot type (and hence hyperbolic volume), so the bare mass of a particle equals that of its antiparticle: \(m_{\mathrm{bare}}(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma}) = m_{\mathrm{bare}}(\mathfrak{H})\).

📄

Remark 9.40 ✗ no Lean (Left and right trefoils: electron and positron).

The left trefoil \(T_{2,3}\) and the right trefoil \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) are the electron and positron respectively. The choice of which chirality is assigned to which particle is arbitrary — it is a convention, not a physical distinction. What matters is that the two are mirror images: \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) is \(T_{2,3}\) with all crossings reversed.

Antiparticles from crossing reversal.

An antihadron is the hadron constructed from positrons instead of electrons: replace every \(T_{2,3}\) with \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) in the knot formula. The proton’s antiquark content is obtained by mirroring:

\[\mathfrak{p}^{\sigma} \;=\; [u^{\sigma}, u^{\sigma}, d^{\sigma}]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\]

where \(u^{\sigma} = T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) and \(d^{\sigma} = (T_{2,3}^{\sigma})^{\sigma} = T_{2,3}\). The crossing energy of \(\mathfrak{p}^{\sigma}\) has the opposite sign to that of \(\mathfrak{p}\): the Coulomb charge reverses, \(Q(\mathfrak{p}^{\sigma}) = -1\).

Time reversal and the exceptional divisor.

If a trefoil can change chirality — passing from \(T_{2,3}\) to \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) — while traversing the exceptional divisor of the brane tower, this would correspond to a particle travelling backward in time (in the Feynman–Stueckelberg sense: an electron moving forward in time is a positron moving backward).

The fiber adjoint involution (fiber adjoint involution) acts on the weight decomposition and reverses the sign of the Reeb flow direction. If this involution extends to the exceptional divisor, it could provide the mechanism for chirality reversal — the vortex tube of the electron reverses its winding orientation as it passes through the blow-up.

Open questions.

  1. Vortex inversion: can a vortex tube in the brane fluid reverse its circulation? Classical fluid dynamics has results on vortex reconnection and reversal — these should be translated to the categorical setting.

  2. Information transfer: if a trefoil reverses chirality twice (electron \(\to\) positron \(\to\) electron), this would constitute a round-trip through the time-reversed sector. Does the categorical algebra forbid this? The fiber adjoint involution is an involution (\(\sigma^2 = \mathrm{id}\)), so the double reversal returns to the original state — but whether information is preserved across the round-trip depends on the monodromy of the exceptional divisor.

  3. The imaginary part: in the Archimedean realisation over \(\mathbb{C}\), the substrate parameter \(q\) can be complex. The observability axiom (fibre functor) forces \(q\) to be real and positive (via the involutive structure), but the imaginary part of \(q\) — if it were nonzero — would contribute a phase to the crossing energy that distinguishes particles from antiparticles without requiring mirror reflection. This suggests that the full theory (before restricting to the observable sector) may have a richer structure in which chirality reversal is a continuous rotation, not a discrete flip.

  4. CPT from the categorical algebra: the combined operation C (charge conjugation = crossing reversal \(\sigma\)), P (parity = spatial reflection), T (time reversal = Reeb flow direction) should be derivable from the fiber adjoint involution and the Frobenius structure. The CPT theorem (CPT is always a symmetry) would then be a consequence of the involutive axiom on the QOU.

Definition 9.41 ∀ stated (Stable nucleus (Skein energy minimum)). \(\forall\)

A stable nucleus is a multi-nucleon Hopf link that extremizes the Skein binding Lagrangian (Skein binding Lagrangian).

Let \(\mathfrak{p}\) and \(\mathfrak{n}\) be the categorical proton and neutron (categorical proton, categorical neutron). A nucleus with \(Z\) protons and \(N\) neutrons is the iterated Hopf link. (Here \(Z\) is the atomic number — the standard nuclear physics notation for the proton count, freeing \(p\) for use as a brane point.)

\[\mathcal{N}(Z, N) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathfrak{p} \bowtie \cdots \bowtie \mathfrak{p}}_{Z} \;\bowtie\; \underbrace{\mathfrak{n} \bowtie \cdots \bowtie \mathfrak{n}}_{N}.\]

The nucleus \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\) is stable if \((Z, N)\) is a critical point of the Skein binding Lagrangian \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}}\) (Skein binding Lagrangian) under beta variation (exchange of \(\mathfrak{p} \leftrightarrow \mathfrak{n}\) at fixed \(A = Z + N\)):

\[\frac{\partial \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bind}}}{\partial Z} \bigg|_{A} = 0 \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad Z = \frac{A}{2 + a_C \, A^{2/3} / (2\,a_A)}\]

where \(a_C = (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_C\) and \(a_A\) is the Pauli coefficient (beta-stability).

A stable atom appends \(Z\) electrons:

\[\mathcal{A}(Z, N) \;=\; \mathcal{N}(Z, N) \;\bowtie\; Z \cdot T_{2,3}.\]

Restricting the hadron definition. The abstract hadron (hadron) permits arbitrary multi-component composites. The stability condition restricts the physically realised nuclei to the valley of stability: only configurations \((Z, N)\) satisfying the beta-stability equation above are long-lived. Nuclei outside this valley undergo beta decay (\(\mathfrak{n} \to \mathfrak{p} + e^- + \nu^{\sigma}\) or \(\mathfrak{p} \to \mathfrak{n} + e^+ + \nu\)) until the stable configuration is reached.

This is not an additional axiom — it is a consequence of the Skein binding Lagrangian. The parameter \(q\) determines both the strong binding (via \((q + q^{-1})/2\)) and the Coulomb repulsion (via \((q - q^{-1})/2\)), and their balance selects the unique stable \((Z, N)\) for each mass number \(A\).

Proposition 9.42 ∀ stated (Torus knot composites on Bring’s surface are stable hadrons). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be the Descartes universe with \(\chi(A) = -6\). Every baryon formed from torus knot generators \(\mathcal{G}\) (torus knot generators) linked by the Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_H\) satisfies the stability condition

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) \;<\; 0\]

and is therefore a hadron in the sense of Definition.

Proof sketch. The torus knot generators \(T_{m,n} \in \mathcal{G}\) have meridional winding \(m \in \{2, 3\}\) (forced by the genus-\(4\) bound). For any triple \([K_1, K_2, K_3]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\) drawn from \(\mathcal{G}\):

  1. The Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_H\) contributes a negative baseline crossing energy from the strong binding term \(\tfrac{1}{2}(n_+ + n_-)(q + q^{-1})\).

  2. The Coulomb correction \(Q(\mathfrak{H}) \cdot (q - q^{-1})\) (Coulomb charge) satisfies \(|Q(\mathfrak{H})| \leq 1\) for all generators in \(\mathcal{G}\), since the maximum crossing asymmetry between \(m = 2\) and \(m = 3\) strands is bounded by the genus constraint.

  3. Since \(\tanh(\ln q) \approx 0.104\), the Coulomb correction is at most \(\sim 10\%\) of the strong baseline, which is insufficient to overcome binding.

In particular:

  • Proton \(\mathfrak{p} = [T_{2,3}, T_{2,3}, T_{2,3}^{\sigma}]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\): Coulomb charge \(Q(\mathfrak{p}) = +1\) (proton). The positive Coulomb correction reduces binding but does not overcome it: \(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{p}) < 0\).

  • Neutron \(\mathfrak{n} = [T_{2,3}, T_{2,3}^{\sigma}, T_{2,3}^{\sigma}]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\): Coulomb charge \(Q(\mathfrak{n}) = 0\) (neutron). No Coulomb correction; the strong baseline binding is undiminished.

Both are stable hadrons. \(\square\)

Remark 9.44 ✗ no Lean (Force carriers from the involutive structure and saturating generators).

The three fundamental forces of the Standard Model arise from three distinct layers of the torus knot architecture on the Bring’s surface. Two are carried by the saturating genus-\(4\) generators \(T_{2,9}\) and \(T_{3,5}\) (unmapped torus knots); the third — electromagnetism — is not a knot at all but the involutive structure of the category itself.

I. Electromagnetism: the involutive structure.

The electromagnetic interaction does not require a dedicated torus knot generator. It is already present in the \(\dagger\)-structure on \(\mathbf{C}\) and the crossing-sign decomposition of the Skein algebra.

Recall that the crossing energy at each site decomposes into symmetric and antisymmetric channels (antiparticle crossing reversal):

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}} \;=\; \underbrace{E_{\mathrm{sym}}}_{\text{mass (strong)}} \;+\; \underbrace{E_{\mathrm{anti}}}_{\text{Coulomb (EM)}}.\]

The antisymmetric component — the Coulomb channel — reverses sign under the crossing reversal involution \(\sigma \colon K \mapsto K^{\sigma}\), which implements charge conjugation \(C\) at the categorical level. Electromagnetic charge is therefore the eigenvalue of the involution \(\sigma\) acting on the crossing energy:

\[Q(K) \;=\; \frac{1}{2}\bigl(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(K) - \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(K^{\sigma})\bigr).\]

This involution descends from three interlocking structures on the Bring’s surface:

  1. The \(\dagger\)-involution on \(\mathbf{C}\): the positive-definite contravariant endofunctor \(f \mapsto f^{\dagger}\) that defines observability. Every morphism carries a sign under \(\dagger\); the electromagnetic coupling is the component of the Skein pairing that is odd under this involution.

  2. The complex structure on the color elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_z\): the Bring’s surface admits a Kähler structure inherited from the embedding \(\Sigma_4 \hookrightarrow \mathbb{P}^4\). The complex structure \(J\) satisfies \(J^2 = -1\) and determines the phase of the crossing energy. Electromagnetic charge is the winding number of this phase around the \(\mathrm{U}(1)\) fiber of the Hopf map \(\mathrm{SU}(2) \to \mathbb{CP}^1\).

  3. The symplectic pairing on the coral tube coordinates: the T-duality involution \(\iota \colon (X, z) \mapsto (z, X)\) on the symmetric cubic \(F(X, z) = F(z, X)\) exchanges color and spacetime degrees of freedom. The symplectic form \(\omega = dX \wedge dz\) is preserved by \(\iota\), and the Coulomb interaction is the component of the crossing energy that transforms as a \((1,1)\)-form under the complex structure.

Electromagnetism is therefore intrinsic to any knot — it requires no special generator because it arises from the involutive fabric of the category. Every charged particle (every knot with nonzero antisymmetric crossing energy) automatically couples electromagnetically. This explains:

  • Universality of EM: all charged particles interact, regardless of knot type or genus.

  • Charge quantisation: \(Q\) is an eigenvalue of an involution, hence discrete (\(\pm 1\) for leptons, \(\pm 1/3, \pm 2/3\) for quarks in the Borromean decomposition).

  • Masslessness of the photon: EM is not carried by a knot (which would contribute topological mass) but by the algebraic structure itself — the \(\dagger\)-involution has no Seifert genus.

II. Strong force: \(T_{2,9}\) as gluonic binding.

The strong force binds by interpolation: \(T_{2,9}\) wraps through all three color fibers in a single closed curve, providing the topological rigidity that confines quarks into baryons. The three \(S_3\) subgroups of the automorphism group of Bring’s surface \(S_5\) — corresponding to the three color charges — are precisely the subgroups that leave one of the three \(T_{2,3}\) periods of \(T_{2,9}\) invariant.

Confinement has a natural interpretation: \(T_{2,9}\) cannot be continuously deformed to separate the three color copies without breaking the torus embedding. The three-fold cover structure means that extracting a single color strand would require cutting \(T_{2,9}\) into an open arc — topologically forbidden for a knot on the Bring surface.

Asymptotic freedom (weakening at short distances) corresponds to the local triviality of the torus embedding: at scales smaller than the coral tube radius, the three strands of \(T_{2,9}\) are locally parallel, and the binding provided by their global winding becomes negligible.

III. Weak force: \(T_{3,5}\) as flavor-changing mediator.

This cross-link enables flavor-changing processes: the weak interaction transmutes quarks between generations and converts quarks to leptons (and vice versa) because \(T_{3,5}\) topologically connects both sectors.

Parity violation follows from the Skein asymmetry at \(q \neq 1\): the Skein relation \(q[L_+] - q^{-1}[L_-] = (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2})[L_0]\) treats positive and negative crossings differently. The weak force, mediated by \(T_{3,5}\), inherits this asymmetry maximally because \(T_{3,5}\) has the highest crossing count (\(10\)) among generators — the \(q\)-vs-\(q^{-1}\) imbalance accumulates over more crossings, producing the maximal parity violation observed in weak decays.

Massive \(W^{\pm}\) and \(Z^0\) bosons. Unlike \(T_{2,9}\) (strong, massless), \(T_{3,5}\) contributes nonzero mass to the weak bosons. Although its hyperbolic volume is zero (torus knot), its \(10\) crossings generate crossing energy via the mass formula. The distinction: EM has no knot (zero mass), strong has a knot with \(9\) same-sign crossings (zero net crossing energy after color averaging), and weak has a knot with \(10\) crossings whose energy does not cancel — yielding the massive \(W\) and \(Z\).

Proposition 9.45 ∀ stated (Electromagnetic coupling from the antisymmetric braiding and force-carrier crossings). \(\forall\)

The electromagnetic fine structure constant \(\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}\) is not a free parameter in the Descartes universe. It is determined by three finite, combinatorial ingredients: the antisymmetric eigenvalue of the \(R\)-matrix, the \(q\)-deformed crossing numbers of the two force-carrier generators, and the substrate parameter \(q\). No contour integrals, no factors of \(2\pi i\), and no renormalisation-group running are required at the fundamental level.

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be the Descartes universe with substrate parameter \(q\) and force-carrier generators \(T_{2,9}\) (crossing number \(c_s = 9\)) and \(T_{3,5}\) (crossing number \(c_w = 10\)). Then the electromagnetic fine structure constant, defined as the \(\tau\)-trace of the antisymmetric braiding component normalised by the force-carrier crossing complexities, is

\[\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q) \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{[c_s]_q \cdot [c_w]_q} \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{[9]_q \cdot [10]_q}\]

where \([n]_q = (q^n - q^{-n})/(q - q^{-1})\) is the \(q\)-integer.

Derivation from three layers.

The electromagnetic coupling between two charged localized knots \((c_1, K_1)\) and \((c_2, K_2)\) factorises into three finite contributions:

Layer 1: Charge (discrete, from writhe). The electromagnetic charge of a knot \(K\) is its \(q\)-writhe, the antisymmetric crossing count under the crossing reversal involution \(\sigma\) (antiparticle crossing reversal):

\[Q_q(K) \;=\; [w(K)]_q \;=\; \frac{q^{w(K)} - q^{-w(K)}}{q - q^{-1}}\]

where \(w(K) = \sum_i \epsilon_i \in \mathbb{Z}\) is the writhe (signed crossing sum). For a torus knot \(T_{m,n}\), all crossings share the same sign, so \(w(T_{m,n}) = \pm m(n-1)\). This is purely combinatorial: a finite sum of \(\pm 1\) values, \(q\)-deformed.

Layer 2: Coupling strength (from the \(R\)-matrix). The categorical braiding \(\sigma_{K_1, K_2}\) decomposes into \(\dagger\)-eigenspaces:

\[\sigma = \sigma_{\mathrm{sym}} \oplus \sigma_{\mathrm{anti}}.\]

The antisymmetric eigenvalue of the \(R\)-matrix for \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) is \(-q^{-1/2}\), giving

\[|\mathrm{tr}_\tau(\sigma_{\mathrm{anti}})|^2 = q^{-1}.\]

This is the bare coupling: the probability amplitude for an electromagnetic interaction at a single crossing site, evaluated by the fibre functor \(\tau\). It is a rational function of \(q\) — no transcendental constants.

Layer 3: Normalisation by force-carrier complexity. The bare coupling \(q^{-1}\) must be normalised by the total crossing complexity of the force-carrying sector. The two genus-\(4\) saturating generators \(T_{2,9}\) and \(T_{3,5}\) (force identification) carry the strong and weak forces respectively. Their \(q\)-deformed crossing numbers \([9]_q\) and \([10]_q\) measure the total topological complexity available for non-electromagnetic interactions. The electromagnetic coupling is what remains after this complexity is factored out:

\[\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}} \;=\; \frac{|\mathrm{tr}_\tau(\sigma_{\mathrm{anti}})|^2}{[c_s]_q \cdot [c_w]_q} \;=\; \frac{q^{-1}}{[9]_q \cdot [10]_q}.\]

The denominator \([9]_q \cdot [10]_q\) is the product of the \(q\)-crossing complexities of the strong and weak sectors. The numerator \(q^{-1}\) is the antisymmetric braiding eigenvalue. The ratio gives the fraction of the total interaction that is electromagnetic.

Why this formula is finite.

Every ingredient is a finite algebraic expression in \(q\):

  • The charge \(Q_q = [w]_q\) is a ratio of \(q\)-powers — no integral.

  • The coupling \(q^{-1}\) is an eigenvalue of the \(R\)-matrix — no trace over infinite-dimensional spaces.

  • The normalisation \([9]_q \cdot [10]_q\) is a product of \(q\)-integers — no renormalisation group.

  • The spatial dependence (Coulomb \(1/r^2\)) is added by the Green’s function of the base manifold, which is external to \(\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}\) itself.

The formula makes sense over any completion of the base field: archimedean (\(\mathbb{R}\)), \(p\)-adic (\(\mathbb{Q}_p\)), or finite (\(\mathbb{F}_q\)). The fine structure constant is a \(q\)-arithmetic invariant of the Descartes universe, not a continuous parameter requiring measurement.

Remark on the classical limit. As \(q \to 1\), \([n]_q \to n\), and \(\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}} \to 1/(9 \times 10) = 1/90\). The observed value \(\alpha^{-1} \approx 137\) requires \(q > 1\); the departure from the classical limit is what makes the coupling weaker than \(1/90\).

Proposition 9.46 ∀ stated (Integer stability: the valley of stability as a Diophantine constraint). \(\forall\)

The beta-stability line (beta-stability) gives a continuous optimum \(p^*(A)\). Physical nuclei require integer proton and neutron numbers. The stable hadrons are integer solutions to a quadratic energy minimisation.

Proposition. Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be the Descartes universe with the substrate \(q\). At fixed mass number \(A = Z + N\), the nuclear binding energy is a convex quadratic in the proton number \(p\):

\[E(p, A) \;=\; \underbrace{\left(\frac{a_C}{A^{1/3}} + \frac{a_A}{A}\right)}_{\alpha(A)} p^2 \;-\; \underbrace{a_A}_{\gamma} p \;+\; \delta(A)\]

where \(a_C = (q - q^{-1}) \cdot \lambda_C\) is the Coulomb coefficient, \(a_A\) is the Pauli asymmetry coefficient, and \(\delta(A)\) collects terms independent of \(p\).

The continuous minimum is

\[p^*(A) \;=\; \frac{\gamma}{2\alpha(A)} \;=\; \frac{a_A \cdot A}{2(a_A + a_C \cdot A^{2/3})}.\]

Since \(E\) is strictly convex in \(p\), the integer minimiser is exact:

\[p_{\mathrm{stab}}(A) \;=\; \mathrm*{arg\,min}_{p \in \{0, 1, \ldots, A\}} E(p, A) \;\in\; \bigl\{\lfloor p^*(A) \rfloor,\; \lceil p^*(A) \rceil\bigr\}.\]

There is no approximation error — the integer minimiser of a convex quadratic is always one of the two nearest integers to the continuous minimum.

Even-odd selection. The pairing energy \(\pm \lambda_P / A^{1/2}\) breaks the \(p \leftrightarrow p + 1\) symmetry at the rounding boundary. Among the two integer candidates, the pair \((p, A - p)\) with both \(p\) and \(A - p\) even is preferred. This produces the observed even-even dominance: of the 254 stable nuclides, 166 have even \(p\) and even \(n\).

Regime transitions. The integer minimiser \(p_{\mathrm{stab}}(A)\) jumps by \(+1\) when \(p^*(A)\) crosses a half-integer. The critical mass numbers where the stable proton count increases from \(k\) to \(k + 1\) are

\[A_k \;=\; \left( \frac{a_C \cdot (2k + 1)}{2a_A} \right)^{3/2} \quad\text{(to leading order).}\]

These are the beta-decay thresholds: at \(A = A_k\), the nuclei \((k, A_k - k)\) and \((k + 1, A_k - k - 1)\) have equal binding energy, and beta decay is energetically neutral.

Remark 9.47 ✗ no Lean (The valley of stability as a Diophantine approximation problem).

The nuclear stability problem is a Diophantine problem on an algebraic curve. The stable hadrons — the nuclei that exist in nature — are precisely the integer solutions to an equation derived from the Skein binding Lagrangian.

The stability cubic. Substituting \(t = A^{1/3}\) into the continuous stability condition \(p^*(A) = a_A A / (2a_A + 2a_C A^{2/3})\) (integer stability) and clearing denominators gives the stability cubic

\[t^3 \;=\; 2p\,(1 + c\,t^2), \qquad c = \frac{a_C}{2\,a_A},\]

a plane curve \(\mathcal{S} \subset \mathbb{A}^2\) parametrising the locus of beta-stable nuclei in the \((p, t)\)-plane. The physical nuclei are the integer points of \(\mathcal{S}\): pairs \((p, A) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\) with \(t = A^{1/3}\) and \(A = t^3 \in \mathbb{Z}\).

Comparison with the color fibration. The coral elliptic curve of Bring’s surface (coral elliptic) is the cubic

\[X^3 + (z + 1)\,X^2 + (z^2 + z + 1)\,X + (z^3 + z^2 + z + 1) = 0\]

in the color variable \(X\) at spacetime ratio \(z\). The stability cubic (S) and the color cubic (C) are both cubics in one variable parametrised by another, arising from the same \(\chi = -6\) surface. The elliptic stability conjecture proposes that when the pairing energy lifts (S) to genus \(1\), the resulting elliptic curve is isogenous to the color fiber.

The \(n/p\) ratio. For each proton number \(p\), the stable neutron number \(n^*(p)\) satisfies

\[\frac{n^*(p)}{p} \;=\; \frac{A^*(p)}{p} - 1 \;=\; 1 + 2c \cdot {A^*}^{2/3} + O(1/p)\]

where \(A^*(p)\) is the mass number solving \(p = A/(2 + cA^{2/3})\). The ratio \(n/p\) is a slowly growing function of \(p\) whose integer-part transitions occur at specific elements:

\(n/p\) crosses Element \(p\) \(n\)
\(1.00\) Calcium 20 20
\(1.10\) Bromine 35 44
\(1.20\) Zirconium 40 50
\(1.30\) Tin 50 70
\(1.40\) Tungsten 74 110
\(1.54\) Lead 82 126
\(1.59\) Uranium 92 146

Stable hadrons as integer points on an algebraic curve. The central observation is that every stable nucleus in nature corresponds to a lattice point \((p, A) \in \mathbb{Z}^2\) on the stability cubic \(\mathcal{S}\). The nuclear chart is not a phenomenological fit — it is the set of integer solutions to an algebraic equation determined by the single parameter \(q\).

When the pairing correction lifts \(\mathcal{S}\) from genus \(0\) to genus \(1\) (elliptic stability conjecture), the stability pairs become rational points of an elliptic curve \(\mathcal{E}_p\) over \(\mathbb{Q}(q)\), and Mordell’s theorem constrains them to a finite set — potentially explaining why only finitely many stability pairs exist.

Connection to the substrate parameter. The curvature parameter \(c = (q - q^{-1})\lambda_C / (2a_A)\) is controlled entirely by \(q\). At \(q = 1\) the stability cubic degenerates to \(t^3 = 2p\) (a rational parametrisation with all nuclei symmetric, \(n = p\)). As \(q\) increases from \(1\), the \(ct^2\) term bends the curve, the integer solutions disperse, and the rich structure of the nuclear chart — neutron excess, stability pairs, even-odd staggering — emerges from a single deformation parameter.

Definition 9.49 ∀ stated (Beta decay as a Skein crossing change on the Gröbner normal form). \(\forall\)

Beta decay is a \(T_{3,5}\)-mediated crossing operation involving \(10\) crossings of the weak vertex (force identification).

The weak force in the Descartes universe (\(\chi(A) = -6\), the substrate \(q\)) is carried by the torus knot \(T_{3,5}\), which has \(10\) crossings — the highest crossing count among generators on the Bring surface. A beta transition inserts the \(T_{3,5}\) braid into the nuclear braid at the converting quark, then reduces the resulting word to obtain the daughter normal form plus the emitted lepton pair.

Setup. A nucleus \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\) is a satellite link of \(A = Z + N\) Borromean components (stable nucleus). Its braid word in \(B_{3A}\) reduces to a unique Gröbner–Shirshov normal form \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\) in the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_{3A}(q)\) (nuclear Gröbner–Shirshov reduction).

Each nucleon is a Borromean link \(\mathcal{B}_3(q_1, q_2, q_3)\) with quark strands:

  • Proton: \(\mathfrak{p} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d})\) (categorical proton)

  • Neutron: \(\mathfrak{n} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d})\) (categorical neutron)

The crossing type at each generator \(\sigma_i\) depends on the quark flavours of the two strands: \(\mathfrak{u}\text{-}\mathfrak{u}\) (positive), \(\mathfrak{d}\text{-}\mathfrak{d}\) (negative), or \(\mathfrak{u}\text{-}\mathfrak{d}\) (mixed).

The \(T_{3,5}\) weak vertex

The weak interaction is mediated by the torus knot \(T_{3,5}\) (force identification), whose braid word in \(B_3\) is:

\[\beta_{T_{3,5}} \;=\; (\sigma_1 \sigma_2)^5\]

This word has \(10\) crossings. In the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_3(q)\), the Hecke reduction of \((\sigma_1 \sigma_2)^5\) eliminates squares via \(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\), producing a polynomial in the reduced basis of \(H_3(q)\). The Markov trace of this polynomial is the weak vertex form factor:

\[\mathcal{W}(q) \;:=\; \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}\bigl((\sigma_1 \sigma_2)^5\bigr) \;\in\; \mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1/2}]\]

The single-crossing Skein amplitude \(s = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}\) appears as the coupling at each crossing of the \(T_{3,5}\) braid. The full vertex factor is not \(s^2\) (single crossing) but the Markov trace \(\mathcal{W}(q)\) of all \(10\) crossings.

The \(10\)-crossing budget

When the \(T_{3,5}\) braid is inserted at the converting quark, it introduces \(10\) crossings into the nuclear braid word. These \(10\) crossings are resolved by the Gröbner–Shirshov reduction into three components:

Crossings Destination Structure
\(3\) Electron \(T_{2,3}\) (trefoil) \(3\) positive crossings
\(0\) Antineutrino \(K_{0_1}\) (unknot) Trivial topology
\(7\) Nuclear re-reduction R2 moves absorbed into daughter normal form

The \(7\) re-reduction crossings change the R2 step count between parent and daughter normal forms. This is the dominant contribution to the \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value (transition energy) — the single-crossing approximation misses \(6\) of these \(7\) crossings.

Definition (\(\beta^-\) decay)

A \(\beta^-\) transition inserts the \(T_{3,5}\) braid at the converting \(\mathfrak{d}\)-quark crossing of the Gröbner–Shirshov normal form \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\), followed by re-reduction:

\[\mathcal{N}(Z, N) \cdot \beta_{T_{3,5}} \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{reduce}\;} \mathcal{N}(Z + 1, \, N - 1) \;\sqcup\; T_{2,3} \;\sqcup\; K_{0_1}\]

The \(10\) crossings of \(T_{3,5}\) are partitioned by the Gröbner–Shirshov reduction: \(3\) form the electron trefoil, \(0\) form the neutrino unknot, and \(7\) are absorbed as R2 moves into the daughter nuclear braid.

In the Skein relation at each of the \(10\) crossings:

\[q \, [L_+] \;-\; q^{-1} [L_-] \;=\; (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) \, [L_0]\]

The accumulated effect of \(10\) such relations (not \(1\)) determines the transition amplitude.

Definition (\(\beta^+\) decay)

A \(\beta^+\) transition is the mirror operation, inserting the conjugate \(T_{3,5}^{\sigma}\) braid (with \(q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}\)):

\[\mathcal{N}(Z, N) \cdot \beta_{T_{3,5}}^{\sigma} \;\xrightarrow{\;\text{reduce}\;} \mathcal{N}(Z - 1, \, N + 1) \;\sqcup\; T_{2,3}^{\sigma} \;\sqcup\; K_{0_1}\]

The \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) symmetry

\(\beta^-\) and \(\beta^+\) are related by the involution \(q \mapsto q^{-1}\) on the Iwahori–Hecke algebra, which acts as:

\(\beta^-\) \(\beta^+\)
\(\mathfrak{d} \to \mathfrak{u}\) via \(T_{3,5}\) \(\mathfrak{u} \to \mathfrak{d}\) via \(T_{3,5}^{\sigma}\)
\(q \, [L_+]\) \(q^{-1} [L_+]\)
electron \(T_{2,3}\) positron \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\)
antineutrino \(K_{0_1}^{\sigma}\) neutrino \(K_{0_1}\)
\(\mathcal{S}_{ab}(q)\) \(\mathcal{S}_{ba}(q) = \mathcal{S}_{ab}(q^{-1})\)

This \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) acts on the pair Skein mass formula:

\[\mathcal{S}_{ab}(q) = \frac{q \mu_a + q^{-1} \mu_b}{q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2}} \;\;\xrightarrow{\;q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}\;}\;\; \mathcal{S}_{ba}(q) = \frac{q \mu_b + q^{-1} \mu_a}{q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2}}\]

When \(\mu_a \neq \mu_b\) (i.e., \(\mu_{\mathfrak{u}} \neq \mu_{\mathfrak{d}}\)), the two are distinct: the asymmetry \(\mathcal{S}_{ab} - \mathcal{S}_{ba} = (q - q^{-1})(\mu_a - \mu_b)/(q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2})\) is the weak asymmetry that drives the \(Q\)-value.

The lepton pair from \(T_{3,5}\) decomposition

The \(T_{3,5}\) braid \((\sigma_1 \sigma_2)^5\) decomposes under Gröbner–Shirshov reduction into the lepton pair plus reduction residue. The electron trefoil \(T_{2,3} = (\sigma_1)^3\) accounts for \(3\) of the \(10\) crossings; the antineutrino unknot \(K_{0_1}\) accounts for \(0\). The remaining \(7\) crossings are the weak vertex residue — absorbed into R2 moves during re-reduction.

\[L_0^{-} \;=\; T_{2,3} \;\sqcup\; T_{1,0}^{\sigma} \qquad (\beta^- \text{ decay: } e^- + \nu_e^{\sigma})\]

\[L_0^{+} \;=\; T_{2,3}^{\sigma} \;\sqcup\; T_{1,0} \qquad (\beta^+ \text{ decay: } e^+ + \nu_e)\]

The \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value (10-crossing)

The transition energy is the difference in categorical actions between parent and daughter, now accounting for all \(10\) crossings of the \(T_{3,5}\) insertion:

\[\mathcal{Q}_q \;=\; \mathcal{S}_q[\mathcal{N}(Z, N)] \;-\; \mathcal{S}_q[\mathcal{N}(Z \pm 1, N \mp 1)] \;-\; m_e\]

The parent and daughter normal forms differ at all crossings affected by the \(T_{3,5}\) insertion and its subsequent re-reduction — not just the single converting crossing. The \(7\) re-reduction crossings from the weak vertex residue modify inter-nucleon crossing types at the converting quark’s strand, changing \(\binom{A-1}{1} \cdot 3\) inter-nucleon crossings (one per quark strand of each partner nucleon).

Re-reduction cost (10-crossing). After the \(T_{3,5}\) insertion at the converting quark, the braid word gains \(10\) crossings. The Gröbner–Shirshov reduction must:

  1. Extract the \(3\)-crossing electron trefoil from the \(T_{3,5}\) decomposition.

  2. Reduce the remaining \(7\) crossings via R2 moves (\(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\)) and R3/far-commutativity moves.

  3. Propagate the flavour change through all inter-nucleon crossings involving the converting quark’s strand.

The net R2 step count from all \(10\) crossings (not just \(1\)) determines the \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value:

\[\mathcal{Q}_q \;=\; \Delta(\text{R2 steps from 10 crossings}) \;\times\; (q - q^{-1}) \;\times\; (\text{pair Skein scale})\]

Why single-crossing was insufficient

The previous single-crossing approximation captured only \(1\) of the \(10\) crossings in the weak vertex. This explains:

  1. Systematic overshoot of \(10\)–\(17\%\) in heavy-nucleus half-life predictions: the missing \(9\) crossings contribute additional phase space that shortens the predicted half-life when properly included.

  2. Tritium accuracy (\(< 2\%\) error): for \(A = 3\), the nuclear braid is short enough that the \(7\) re-reduction crossings have limited room to propagate — the single-crossing approximation is accidentally good.

  3. Mass-dependent correction: heavier nuclei have more inter-nucleon crossings affected by the converting quark’s flavour change, so the \(7\) re-reduction crossings modify more transfer matrices.

Open computation: The exact weak vertex form factor \(\mathcal{W}(q) = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}((\sigma_1\sigma_2)^5)\) and the crossing budget (\(3 + 0 + 7\)) must be verified by explicit Iwahori–Hecke algebra computation of the \(T_{3,5}\) braid word reduction.

Definition 9.50 ∀ stated (Categorical Lepton Number). \(\forall\)

Lepton number is the count of Skein smoothings applied to the nuclear normal form.

Each beta decay (beta decay) applies the Skein relation at one crossing, producing a smoothing \(L_0^{\pm}\) that contains exactly one lepton–antilepton pair. Lepton number counts these smoothings.

Definition. Let \(\mathcal{N}\) be a nuclear link in Gröbner–Shirshov normal form and let \(\mathcal{N}'\) be obtained from \(\mathcal{N}\) by a sequence of \(k\) Skein crossing changes. The lepton number of the transition is \(L = k\).

Each smoothing \(L_0^{\pm}\) contributes:

  • One charged lepton (\(T_{2,3}\) or \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\)) with lepton number \(+1\)

  • One (anti)neutrino (\(K_{0_1}\) or \(K_{0_1}^{\sigma}\)) with lepton number \(-1\)

The net lepton number of each \(L_0^{\pm}\) pair is \(+1 + (-1) = 0\).

Conservation. Lepton number is conserved by construction:

  1. Skein smoothings produce lepton pairs with net lepton number \(0\). The nuclear sector loses one crossing (lepton number \(0\) for hadrons). Total: \(\Delta L = 0\).

  2. Gröbner–Shirshov re-reduction (R2, R3, far-commutativity) acts within the Iwahori–Hecke algebra and does not produce smoothings. \(\Delta L = 0\).

  3. Markov moves (conjugation, stabilisation) change the braid representative but not the link type. \(\Delta L = 0\).

Therefore: every process that can be expressed as a sequence of Skein relations and Hecke reductions conserves lepton number.

Lepton number is a \(\mathbb{Z}\)-grading on the Skein module. The Skein module \(\mathcal{K}(S^3; q)\) has a natural \(\mathbb{Z}\)-grading by the number of smoothings applied. Links in the nuclear sector have grade \(0\); each smoothing shifts the grade by \(+1\). The grade is preserved by the Hecke relations (which act within a fixed grade) and by Reidemeister moves (which do not change the smoothing count).

Individual lepton assignments.

Particle Knot type Lepton number \(L\) Origin
\(e^-\) \(T_{2,3}\) (trefoil) \(+1\) \(L_0^{-}\) charged component (\(\beta^-\))
\(e^+\) \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) (mirror trefoil) \(-1\) \(L_0^{+}\) charged component (\(\beta^+\))
\(\nu_e\) \(K_{0_1}\) (unknot) \(+1\) \(L_0^{+}\) neutral component (\(\beta^+\))
\(\nu_e^{\sigma}\) \(K_{0_1}^{\sigma}\) (mirror unknot) \(-1\) \(L_0^{-}\) neutral component (\(\beta^-\))

The charged lepton carries \(L = +1\) (or \(-1\) for the antiparticle) and the neutrino carries \(L = -1\) (or \(+1\)) so that each pair sums to zero.

The \(\chi = -6\) constraint. In the Descartes universe, the Euler characteristic \(\chi(A) = -6\) constrains the Bring’s surface. The torus knot generators \(T(2, n)\) with \(n\) odd and \(n \leq 7\) exhaust the fermion spectrum (torus knot generators). The electron (\(T_{2,3}\)) and neutrino (\(K_{0_1} = T_{2,1}\)) are the two lowest torus knots in this sequence. The smoothing \(L_0^{-}\) must decompose into exactly these knot types because they are the only single-component closures of a 2-arc resolution at a Borromean crossing.

Why lepton number is not broken. In the Standard Model, lepton number conservation is an accidental symmetry. In QOU, it is a structural invariant: the Skein relation is the unique operation that changes crossing type, and it always produces exactly one lepton pair. There is no mechanism in the Iwahori–Hecke algebra to produce an odd number of leptons — the smoothing is a topological operation on a single crossing, and each smoothing is binary (two arcs).

Lepton number violation would require a process that changes crossing type without going through the Skein relation — i.e., a process outside the Iwahori–Hecke algebra. In the \(\chi = -6\) universe, no such process exists.

Proposition 9.51 ∀ stated (Continuant recurrence for the lepton tower \(T_{2,n}\)). \(\forall\)

The charged lepton tower \(T_{2,n}\) (\(n = 3, 5, 7\) for \(e^-, \mu^-, \tau^-\)) has a closed-form normal form in \(H_2(q) \subset H_3(q)\) given by a Morgan–Voyce continuant recurrence.

Statement

Let \(h = q - q^{-1}\) be the Hecke parameter and \(T_{2,n} = \sigma_0^n\) the \((2, n)\)-torus knot braid in \(B_2\). The Gröbner–Shirshov normal form in \(H_2(q)\) is

\[\mathrm{NF}(\sigma_0^n) \;=\; a_n \cdot \mathbf{1} \;+\; b_n \cdot \sigma_0\]

where the sequences \(\{a_n\}\), \(\{b_n\}\) satisfy:

\[a_{n+1} = b_n, \qquad b_{n+1} = h \, b_n + b_{n-1}, \qquad b_0 = 0, \;\; b_1 = 1.\]

The second relation is the Morgan–Voyce continuant — a three-term recurrence with positive sign on \(b_{n-1}\), in contrast to the Chebyshev polynomials of the second kind \(U_n(\cos\theta)\) which have \(b_{n+1} = 2\cos\theta \cdot b_n - b_{n-1}\).

The net coefficient (sum of all NF terms) is \(\mathrm{net}(T_{2,n}) = a_n + b_n\).

Proof

The Hecke relation $\{}sigma_0^2 = (q - q^{-1}) \{}sigma_0

  • \{}mathbf{1}$ gives:

\[\sigma_0^{n+1} = \sigma_0 \cdot \sigma_0^n = \sigma_0 (a_n \cdot \mathbf{1} + b_n \cdot \sigma_0) = a_n \, \sigma_0 + b_n \, \sigma_0^2 = a_n \, \sigma_0 + b_n ((q - q^{-1}) \sigma_0 + \mathbf{1}) = b_n \cdot \mathbf{1} + (a_n + h \, b_n) \cdot \sigma_0.\]

Reading off: \(a_{n+1} = b_n\) and \(b_{n+1} = a_n + h\, b_n = b_{n-1} + h\, b_n\). The initial conditions \(a_0 = 1, b_0 = 0\) (identity) and \(a_1 = 0, b_1 = 1\) (single generator) complete the induction. \(\square\)

The lepton tower

At the substrate parameter \(q_0 \approx 1.1100\), the continuant yields the following NF data for the three charged lepton generations:

Lepton Torus knot \(n\) \(a_n\) \(b_n\) \(\mathrm{net}\)
\(e^-\) \(T_{2,3}\) \(3\) \(0.209\) \(1.044\) \(1.253\)
\(\mu^-\) \(T_{2,5}\) \(5\) \(0.427\) \(1.133\) \(1.560\)
\(\tau^-\) \(T_{2,7}\) \(7\) \(0.664\) \(1.272\) \(1.936\)

The recurrence is exact in \(\mathbb{Z}[q^{\pm 1}]\); the decimal values are evaluations at \(q = q_0\).

Structural content

Each additional factor of \(\sigma_0^2\) in \(T_{2,n+2}\) applies the Hecke relation once, adding exactly \((q - q^{-1}) b_n\) to the \(\sigma_0\) coefficient and shifting the identity coefficient by \(b_n\). The lepton generations are thus a discrete tower indexed by odd \(n\), with inter-generation spacing controlled by \(h = q - q^{-1}\).

Proposition 9.52 ∀ stated (Lepton universality from the \(T_{3,5}\) weak vertex). \(\forall\)

The tau lepton decays leptonically via the \(T_{3,5}\) weak vertex (beta decay). The factorized model — in which the squared matrix element is \(|\mathcal{M}|^2 = |\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5})|^2\), independent of the daughter lepton — predicts lepton universality directly from the Iwahori–Hecke algebra structure.

Statement

Let \(T_{3,5} = (\sigma_0 \sigma_1)^5\) be the weak vertex in \(H_3(q)\), and let \(f(x)\) denote the phase-space factor for \(\tau \to \ell \, \bar\nu_\ell \, \nu_\tau\) with \(x = (m_\ell / m_\tau)^2\):

\[f(x) = 1 - 8x + 8x^3 - x^4 - 12 x^2 \ln x.\]

Then the ratio of leptonic branching fractions is

\[\frac{\mathrm{BR}(\tau \to e\,\bar\nu_e\,\nu_\tau)} {\mathrm{BR}(\tau \to \mu\,\bar\nu_\mu\,\nu_\tau)} \;=\; \frac{|\mathcal{M}_e|^2 \cdot f(m_e^2/m_\tau^2)} {|\mathcal{M}_\mu|^2 \cdot f(m_\mu^2/m_\tau^2)}.\]

In the factorized model, the Markov trace of the weak vertex is the universal matrix element:

\[|\mathcal{M}_e|^2 \;=\; |\mathcal{M}_\mu|^2 \;=\; \bigl|\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5})\bigr|^2,\]

so the matrix-element ratio is exactly \(1\), and the branching ratio reduces to the pure phase-space ratio:

\[\frac{\mathrm{BR}(\tau \to e)}{\mathrm{BR}(\tau \to \mu)} \;=\; \frac{f(m_e^2 / m_\tau^2)}{f(m_\mu^2 / m_\tau^2)}.\]

Proof sketch

The \(T_{3,5}\) weak vertex acts as a mediator between the parent tau \(T_{2,7}\) and the daughter lepton \(T_{2,n_\ell}\). In the Iwahori–Hecke algebra \(H_3(q)\), one may form the product \(T_{2,n_\ell} \cdot T_{3,5} \cdot T_{2,7}\) and reduce to normal form. However, the correct physical amplitude is not this product trace.

The key observation is that the weak vertex creates the daughter lepton (topological quantum number conservation) rather than composing with it. The \(T_{3,5}\) braid mediates the crossing change; the daughter lepton \(T_{2,n_\ell}\) and the two neutrinos (\(\nu = \mathbf{1}\)) are produced as separate link components. The transition amplitude therefore factorises:

\[\mathcal{M}(\tau \to \ell\,\bar\nu\,\nu_\tau) \;=\; \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5}) \;\times\; (\text{kinematic factors depending on } m_\ell).\]

Since \(\mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}(T_{3,5})\) is independent of which daughter lepton is created, the matrix element \(|\mathcal{M}|^2\) cancels in the ratio, leaving only the phase-space factor \(f(m_\ell^2 / m_\tau^2)\).

Contrast with the product model. If one instead treats the amplitude as \(\mathrm{tr}_3(T_{2,n_\ell} \cdot T_{3,5} \cdot T_{2,7})\), the non-commutativity of \(H_3(q)\) introduces a daughter-dependent correction that breaks universality: \(|\mathcal{M}_e|^2 / |\mathcal{M}_\mu|^2 \approx 0.69 \neq 1\). The product model treats the daughter as composed with the vertex rather than created by it, violating the topological separation of link components in the Skein decomposition (lepton number). \(\square\)

Physical significance

Lepton universality — the statement that the weak interaction couples equally to all lepton generations — is here a consequence of the \(T_{3,5}\) braid being the unique cross-family mediator on the Bring surface (fivefold symmetry). Its Markov trace \(\mathcal{W}(q) = \mathrm{tr}_{\mathrm{Markov}}((\sigma_0 \sigma_1)^5)\) is a property of the weak vertex alone, not of the daughter channel. Universality is broken only by kinematics (the daughter mass entering through the phase-space integral), not by the vertex.

📄

Proposition 9.53 ∀ stated (Parity non-conservation from the Skein relation at \(q \neq 1\)). \(\forall\)

Parity is violated by the weak interaction if and only if \(q \neq 1\).

The parity operation \(\mathcal{P}\) on a link is the mirror: reverse all crossings (\(L_+ \leftrightarrow L_-\)). In the braid group \(B_n\), this is the involution \(\sigma_i \mapsto \sigma_i^{-1}\).

The Skein relation under parity.

The Skein relation at a single crossing:

\[q \, [L_+] \;-\; q^{-1} [L_-] \;=\; (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) \, [L_0]\]

Apply the mirror \(\mathcal{P}\): \(L_+ \mapsto L_-\), \(L_- \mapsto L_+\), \(L_0 \mapsto \mathcal{P}(L_0)\). The mirrored Skein relation reads:

\[q \, [L_-] \;-\; q^{-1} [L_+] \;=\; (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) \, [\mathcal{P}(L_0)]\]

Rearranging:

\[q^{-1} [L_+] \;-\; q \, [L_-] \;=\; -(q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) \, [\mathcal{P}(L_0)]\]

Compare with the original:

\[q \, [L_+] \;-\; q^{-1} [L_-] \;=\; (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2}) \, [L_0]\]

These are the same equation if and only if \(q = q^{-1}\), i.e., \(q = 1\).

Proposition. The Skein relation is invariant under parity \(\mathcal{P}: L_+ \leftrightarrow L_-\) if and only if \(q = 1\). For any \(q \neq 1\), the weak interaction (beta decay) violates parity.

Proof. The Skein relation assigns coefficient \(q\) to \([L_+]\) and \(q^{-1}\) to \([L_-]\). Parity exchanges \(L_+ \leftrightarrow L_-\) but does not change \(q\). The relation is \(\mathcal{P}\)-invariant iff \(q = q^{-1}\), which holds iff \(q^2 = 1\), hence \(q = 1\) (since \(q > 0\)). \(\square\)

Physical interpretation.

The Hecke relation \(T^2 = (q - q^{-1})T + 1\) breaks the symmetry between positive and negative crossings. At \(q = 1\): \(T^2 = 1\) (positive and negative crossings cancel — parity conserved). At the substrate parameter \(q\): \(T^2 = 0.209\,T + 1\) (the \(0.209\,T\) term distinguishes positive from negative — parity violated).

The degree of parity violation is controlled by:

\[q - q^{-1} = 0.209 \quad (\text{at } q = q_0)\]

This is the same quantity that appears in the Skein amplitude \((q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2})\) and the Hecke deformation. All parity violation traces back to \(q \neq 1\).

Maximal parity violation.

In the Standard Model, the weak force violates parity maximally — it couples only to left-handed particles. In the Descartes framework, this corresponds to the crossing chirality:

  • A positive crossing \(\sigma_i\) contributes weight \(q\) to the categorical action.

  • A negative crossing \(\sigma_i^{-1}\) contributes weight \(q^{-1}\).

The ratio \(q / q^{-1} = q^2 = 1.232\) measures the left-right asymmetry. At \(q = 1\): ratio \(= 1\) (no asymmetry). At \(q \to \infty\): ratio \(\to \infty\) (maximal asymmetry).

The Wu experiment (1957) measured the angular distribution of electrons from \({}^{60}\mathrm{Co}\) beta decay and found a strong forward-backward asymmetry. In the Descartes framework, this asymmetry is the crossing chirality of the nuclear link: the \({}^{60}\mathrm{Co}\) braid word has a specific writhe \(w \neq 0\), and the Skein crossing change at the substrate parameter \(q\) produces an asymmetric emission pattern determined by \(q^w\).

Connection to the \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) of beta decay.

The \(\mathbb{Z}/2\) symmetry \(q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}\) that exchanges \(\beta^- \leftrightarrow \beta^+\) (beta decay) is the combined \(\mathcal{CP}\) operation: parity \(\mathcal{P}\) (mirror all crossings) composed with charge conjugation \(\mathcal{C}\) (exchange particle \(\leftrightarrow\) antiparticle, i.e., \(T_{2,3} \leftrightarrow T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\)).

  • \(\mathcal{P}\) alone: violated (\(q \neq q^{-1}\))

  • \(\mathcal{C}\) alone: violated (electron \(\neq\) positron in mass ordering)

  • \(\mathcal{CP}\): the \(q \leftrightarrow q^{-1}\) involution, which IS a symmetry of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra

This gives the standard result: \(\mathcal{P}\) violated, \(\mathcal{C}\) violated, \(\mathcal{CP}\) conserved (to leading order in the Descartes framework).

📄

Proposition 9.54 ∀ stated (Nuclear spin is integral for even \(A\) and half-integral for odd \(A\)). \(\forall\)

The nuclear spin quantum number \(J\) is integral when \(A\) is even and half-integral when \(A\) is odd.

This is a topological consequence of the braid representation: each nucleon is a spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) fermion (a single-component knot), and the tensor product of \(A\) such representations has spin parity determined by \(A \bmod 2\).

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\) be a nucleus with mass number \(A = Z + N\). Then the total angular momentum \(J\) satisfies:

\[J \in \mathbb{Z} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad A \in 2\mathbb{Z}\]

\[J \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2} \quad \Longleftrightarrow \quad A \in 2\mathbb{Z} + 1\]

Proof. Each nucleon — proton \(\mathfrak{p} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d})\) or neutron \(\mathfrak{n} = \mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d})\) — is a knot (single-component link closure of the Borromean braid). By the fermion-boson correspondence (fermions are knots), knots carry half-integral spin and links carry integral spin.

The nuclear link \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\) is a satellite of \(A\) Borromean knots joined by Hopf links. In the \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) representation theory, the tensor product of \(A\) spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) representations decomposes as:

\[\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{\otimes A} \;=\; \bigoplus_{J = J_{\min}}^{A/2} V_J^{\oplus m_J}\]

where \(J_{\min} = 0\) if \(A\) is even and \(J_{\min} = \tfrac{1}{2}\) if \(A\) is odd. Every summand \(V_J\) has the same parity (\(J \bmod 1\)) as \(A/2 \bmod 1\). This is a standard result in \(\mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) representation theory and holds for all \(q > 0\) — the \(q\)-deformation does not change the spin parity of tensor products.

Explicitly: the \(q\)-Clebsch–Gordan decomposition \(V_{1/2} \otimes V_J = V_{J+1/2} \oplus V_{J-1/2}\) (for \(J \geq 1/2\)) adds \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) at each step, so after \(A\) tensor factors the spin parity equals \(A/2 \bmod 1\). \(\square\)

The braid group perspective.

In the braid group \(B_A\), the writhe \(w(\beta)\) of a braid word \(\beta\) (sum of crossing signs) has parity:

\[w(\beta) \equiv \binom{A}{2} \pmod{2}\]

for the standard nuclear braid representative (all pairs crossing once). The writhe parity determines the statistics:

  • \(w\) even \(\Leftrightarrow\) bosonic statistics \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(J \in \mathbb{Z}\)

  • \(w\) odd \(\Leftrightarrow\) fermionic statistics \(\Leftrightarrow\) \(J \in \mathbb{Z} + \tfrac{1}{2}\)

Since \(\binom{A}{2} = A(A-1)/2\), this is even iff \(A \equiv 0\) or \(1 \pmod{4}\). But the spin-statistics theorem in the \(q\)-deformed setting follows directly from the representation theory above, without reference to writhe.

The Jones–Wenzl projector.

In the Temperley–Lieb algebra \(TL_A(\delta)\) with \(\delta = -(q^{1/2} + q^{-1/2})\), the Jones–Wenzl projector \(p_A\) projects onto the highest-weight irreducible representation \(V_{A/2}\). The spin of the ground state is determined by the embedding of the nuclear link in the TL algebra and the action of \(p_A\).

For \({}^{14}\mathrm{N}\) (\(A = 14\), even): the ground state has \(J = 1\) (experimentally observed by molecular band spectroscopy). The Jones–Wenzl projector \(p_{14}\) projects onto \(V_7\), but the nuclear link’s embedding selects the \(J = 1\) subrepresentation via the coupling pattern of 7 protons and 7 neutrons.

\({}^{2}\mathrm{H}\) 2 even \(1\) \(\checkmark\)

The \({}^{14}\mathrm{N}\) case is historically significant: its integer spin (\(J = 1\)) was incompatible with the pre-1932 proton-electron nuclear model (which would give \(A = 14\) protons and 7 electrons \(= 21\) fermions, hence half-integer spin). The resolution — neutrons as spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) neutral particles — gives \(A = 14\) nucleons, hence integer spin.

In the Descartes framework, this is automatic: both the proton \(\mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d})\) and the neutron \(\mathcal{B}_3(\mathfrak{u}, \mathfrak{d}, \mathfrak{d})\) are spin-\(\tfrac{1}{2}\) knots (same Borromean topology, different quark colouring), and \(14\) half-integer spins couple to integer total spin.
