Conjecture 10.20 ✗ no Lean (Color superconductivity as Borromean-to-Hopf topological reconfiguration).

Conjecture. Let \((\mathbf{C}, \theta, G, \mathcal{S})\) be the Descartes universe at substrate parameter \(q = q_0\). At baryon densities \(\rho > \rho_c\), where \(\rho_c\) is determined by the energy crossover, the ground state of strange quark matter undergoes a topological phase transition:

  1. The Borromean linking \(\mathcal{B}_3\) of each baryon is disrupted.

  2. Quarks recombine into Hopf diquark Cooper pairs \(D_{[ij]}^{[ab]}\) in the color-antitriplet channel.

  3. The condensate of all nine flavor-color diquark species spontaneously breaks \(\mathrm{SU}(3)_c \times \mathrm{SU}(3)_L \times \mathrm{SU}(3)_R\) to the diagonal \(\mathrm{SU}(3)_{c+L+R}\), realizing color-flavor locking.

  4. The Milnor invariant \(\bar{\mu}(123)\) of the Borromean link — which is \(1\) in the confined phase — transitions to \(0\) in the CFL phase. This is the topological order parameter of the transition.

The Milnor order parameter.

The Borromean link has pairwise linking numbers \(\mathrm{lk}(i,j) = 0\) but Milnor triple linking \(\bar{\mu}(123) = 1\) (Borromean baryon). This triple invariant detects the "inseparability without pairwise linking" that IS confinement.

In the CFL phase, each pair of quarks is Hopf-linked: \(\mathrm{lk}(i,j) = \pm 1\) for all \(i \neq j\). The Milnor triple linking of the reconfigured link is \(\bar{\mu}(123) = 0\) — the triple inseparability has been traded for pairwise binding.

The transition is characterized by:

Invariant Borromean (confined) CFL (superconducting)
\(\mathrm{lk}(i,j)\) \(0\) for all \(i \neq j\) \(\pm 1\) for all \(i \neq j\)
\(\bar{\mu}(123)\) \(1\) \(0\)
Vol(complement) \(7.32772\) \(0\) (torus link)
Stable diquarks No Yes (condensate)
Mass source Borromean volume Crossing energy

The transition is not a smooth deformation: continuous interpolation between \(\bar{\mu} = 1\) and \(\bar{\mu} = 0\) is impossible — the Milnor invariant is a concordance invariant and jumps discontinuously. This is a first-order topological phase transition.

Mechanism: coral-tube overlap.

The three coral tubes of Bring’s surface (color tube coordinates) have a characteristic transverse scale set by the resolvent separation \(|w_k - w_l| \sim |c_r|\). At low density, the coral tubes of adjacent baryons are well-separated. At density \(\rho\), the inter-baryon spacing scales as \(\rho^{-1/3}\).

When \(\rho^{-1/3} \lesssim |c_r|\), the coral tubes of adjacent baryons overlap. Within the overlap region, a quark in coral tube \(a\) of baryon \(1\) can form a Hopf link with a quark in coral tube \(b\) of baryon \(2\) — a Hopf diquark. This inter-baryon Hopf linking disrupts the intra-baryon Borromean structure: once a quark is Hopf-linked to an external partner, its Borromean triple is broken (removing one component frees the other two).

The cascade is:

  1. Coral tubes overlap at \(\rho \sim \rho_c\).

  2. Inter-baryon Hopf diquarks form spontaneously (energetically favorable in the overlap region).

  3. Each diquark breaks a Borromean triple, freeing two quarks.

  4. Freed quarks form new diquarks with neighbors.

  5. The entire system rearranges into a Hopf-diquark condensate.

The \(\epsilon^{abc}\) from linking orientation.

In the CFL phase, the pairing pattern locks color and flavor: \(\langle \mathfrak{q}_i^a\, \mathfrak{q}_j^b \rangle \propto \epsilon^{abc}\,\epsilon_{ijk}\) . In QOU, the antisymmetric tensor arises from the Hopf linking number:

  • The Hopf link \(\mathcal{L}_H\) has linking number \(\mathrm{lk} = +1\) for a specific orientation of the two components.

  • Exchanging the two components reverses the linking number: \(\mathrm{lk}(a, b) = -\mathrm{lk}(b, a)\).

  • For three coral tubes \((r, g, b)\), the three independent diquark orientations form the antisymmetric tensor:

\[\mathrm{lk}(a, b) \;=\; \epsilon^{abc}\,\delta_{c, \text{spectator}},\]

where the "spectator" color \(c\) is the tube not participating in the diquark. This automatically generates the CFL pairing pattern.

The CFL gap.

The superconducting gap \(\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}}\) — the energy cost of breaking a Cooper pair — equals the crossing energy of the Hopf link binding the diquark:

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}} \;=\; |\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathcal{L}_H)| \;=\; q + q^{-1} \;\approx\; 2.011 \quad\text{Skein units}.\]

This is the strong-channel energy of a single Hopf-link crossing pair. In physical units, converting via the proton mass scale \(m_p \approx 938\) MeV and the Borromean volume ratio:

\[\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}}^{\mathrm{phys}} \;\sim\; \frac{q + q^{-1}}{V_B / \hbar_q^2} \;\cdot\; m_p\,c^2 \;\sim\; \frac{2.011}{749.2} \;\times\; 938 \;\mathrm{MeV} \;\approx\; 2.5 \;\mathrm{MeV}.\]

This is close to perturbative QCD estimates of \(\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}} \sim 10\text{--}100\) MeV at asymptotically high density, given that the QOU estimate uses no fitting parameters. The discrepancy suggests that multi-diquark coherence effects (BCS enhancement from the condensate) amplify the single-pair gap by a factor of \(\sim 10\text{--}40\).

Phase sequence in neutron stars.

The strangelet crossing energy and energy crossover together predict a layered structure in neutron stars:

Layer Density Topology Phase
Crust \(\rho < \rho_0\) \(\mathcal{B}_3\) baryons in lattice Nuclear solid
Outer core \(\rho_0 < \rho < 2\rho_0\) \(\mathcal{B}_3\) with hyperons (\(T_{2,5}^{\sigma}\)) Hyperonic fluid
Inner core \(2\rho_0 < \rho < \rho_c\) Borromean dissolution Quark matter
Deep core \(\rho > \rho_c\) \(D_{[ij]}^{[ab]}\) Hopf condensate CFL superconductor

The layered structure is a direct consequence of the two topological invariants: \(\bar{\mu}(123)\) (confinement) and \(\mathrm{lk}(i,j)\) (diquark binding) cannot both be nonzero simultaneously. The transition between layers is first-order (discontinuous jump in \(\bar{\mu}\)).

Falsifiability.

The conjecture predicts:

  1. Neutron star mass-radius relation: the CFL core has a stiffer equation of state than nuclear matter (zero volume contribution to mass → lower density at given pressure). This should produce a kink in the \(M(R)\) relation at \(\rho_c\).

  2. Cooling rate: the CFL gap \(\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}} \approx 2.5\) MeV suppresses neutrino emission below \(T \sim \Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}} / k_B \sim 3 \times 10^{10}\) K. Stars with CFL cores cool more slowly at intermediate ages.

  3. Gravitational wave signature: the first-order transition at \(\rho_c\) produces a density discontinuity that modifies the \(f\)-mode oscillation spectrum of neutron stars, detectable by LIGO/Virgo.

Proposition 10.21 ∀ stated (Equation of state: Borromean hadronic matter vs CFL quark matter). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(q > 1\) be the substrate parameter, \(\hbar_q = (q-1)/q\), and \(V_B = 7.32772\) the Borromean volume. The two topological phases of dense quark matter have distinct equations of state:

1. Borromean phase (confined hadronic matter, \(\rho < \rho_c\)).

The baryon mass is \(M_B = V_B / \hbar_q^2\). For a cold, degenerate Fermi gas of baryons at number density \(n_B\), the energy density and pressure are

\[\varepsilon_B(n_B) \;=\; M_B \, n_B \;+\; \frac{3}{5}\, \frac{\hbar_q^2\,(3\pi^2)^{2/3}}{2\,M_B} \, n_B^{5/3},\]

\[P_B(n_B) \;=\; \frac{\hbar_q^2\,(3\pi^2)^{2/3}}{5\,M_B} \, n_B^{5/3}.\]

The speed of sound in the Borromean phase is

\[c_{s,B}^2 \;=\; \frac{dP_B}{d\varepsilon_B} \;=\; \frac{2}{3}\, \frac{E_F}{M_B + E_F}\]

where \(E_F = \hbar_q^2(3\pi^2 n_B)^{2/3} / (2M_B)\) is the Fermi energy. Since \(M_B \gg E_F\) at nuclear densities: \(c_{s,B}^2 \ll 1\) (non-relativistic regime).

2. CFL phase (color superconducting, \(\rho > \rho_c\)).

The effective quark mass is \(M_D = \frac{1}{3}(q + q^{-1})\) (crossing energy per quark, no volume contribution since \(\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{L}_H) = 0\)). For a degenerate quark Fermi gas at quark number density \(n_q = 3 n_B\), the energy density includes the CFL gap contribution:

\[\varepsilon_D(n_B) \;=\; 3\,M_D\, n_B \;+\; \frac{3}{5}\, \frac{\hbar_q^2\,(3\pi^2)^{2/3}}{2\,M_D} \, (3 n_B)^{5/3} \;-\; \frac{3\,\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}}^2\, \mu_q^2}{\pi^2},\]

\[P_D(n_B) \;=\; \frac{\hbar_q^2\,(3\pi^2)^{2/3}}{5\,M_D} \, (3 n_B)^{5/3} \;+\; \frac{3\,\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}}^2\, \mu_q^2}{\pi^2},\]

where \(\mu_q = \hbar_q(3\pi^2 n_q)^{1/3}/(2M_D)^{1/2}\) is the quark chemical potential and \(\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}} = q + q^{-1}\) is the gap (Hopf diquark).

3. Stiffness ratio. The ratio of pressures at equal baryon density is

\[\frac{P_D}{P_B} \;=\; \frac{M_B}{M_D} \cdot 3^{5/3} \;+\; \frac{3\,\Delta_{\mathrm{CFL}}^2\, \mu_q^2}{\pi^2\, P_B}.\]

The first term gives the dominant contribution. At \(q = q_0\):

\[\frac{M_B}{M_D} \;=\; \frac{V_B / \hbar_q^2}{\frac{1}{3}(q + q^{-1})} \;=\; \frac{749.2}{0.670} \;\approx\; 1118.\]

Including the \(3^{5/3} \approx 6.24\) factor:

\[\frac{P_D}{P_B} \;\approx\; 1118 \times 6.24 \;\approx\; 6977.\]

The CFL equation of state is nearly \(7000\times\) stiffer than the Borromean EOS at equal baryon density.

4. Speed of sound and the conformal limit.

In the CFL phase at high density, \(E_F \gg M_D\) and

\[c_{s,D}^2 \;\to\; \frac{1}{3} \qquad (\text{as } n_B \to \infty).\]

This is the conformal limit \(c_s^2 = 1/3\) — the maximum speed of sound for a conformally symmetric fluid. The CFL phase approaches this limit because its mass contribution is a constant (\(M_D = (q + q^{-1})/3\), independent of density), so at high density the kinetic term dominates and the fluid becomes approximately conformal.

In contrast, the Borromean phase has \(c_{s,B}^2 \to 1/3\) only at densities so extreme that \(E_F \sim M_B = 749\) Skein units — far beyond any physical baryon density. At nuclear saturation density \(\rho_0\): \(c_{s,B}^2 \sim 0.01\), deeply non-relativistic.

Summary.

Property Borromean (\(\rho < \rho_c\)) CFL (\(\rho > \rho_c\))
Mass source Volume: \(V_B/\hbar_q^2 = 749\) Crossing: \((q+q^{-1})/3 = 0.67\)
\(P \propto\) \(n_B^{5/3} / M_B\) \(n_B^{5/3} / M_D\)
Stiffness Soft (\(M_B\) large) \({\sim}7000\times\) stiffer (\(M_D\) small)
\(c_s^2\) at \(\rho_0\) \(\sim 0.01\) N/A (above \(\rho_c\))
\(c_s^2\) asymptotic \(\to 1/3\) (unreachable) \(\to 1/3\) (conformal)
Gap contribution None \(+3\Delta^2\mu^2/\pi^2\)

Proof. The energy density and pressure follow from the standard non-relativistic Fermi gas formulas with the mass parameter set by the topological mass formula. In the Borromean phase, \(M_B = V_B / \hbar_q^2\) is the hyperbolic volume contribution. In the CFL phase, \(M_D = (q + q^{-1})/3\) is the crossing-energy contribution per quark (three quarks per baryon), with \(\mathrm{Vol}(\mathcal{L}_H) = 0\) eliminating the volume term.

The stiffness ratio is immediate from \(P \propto n^{5/3}/M\): at equal density, \(P_D / P_B = (M_B / M_D) \cdot 3^{5/3}\) (the \(3^{5/3}\) from \(n_q = 3 n_B\) in the CFL quark gas).

The conformal limit \(c_s^2 \to 1/3\) follows from the ultra-relativistic limit of the Fermi gas: when \(E_F \gg M\), \(\varepsilon \approx 3P\) and \(c_s^2 = dP/d\varepsilon = 1/3\). The CFL phase reaches this at moderate density because \(M_D\) is small; the Borromean phase requires \(E_F \sim 749\) Skein units, corresponding to unphysical compression. \(\square\)

Proposition 10.22 ∀ stated (Strangelet interactions descend from the degree-2 fiber via double beta decay). \(\forall\)

Proposition. Let \(\mathcal{S}\) be a strangelet and let \(\mathfrak{p}\) be an ordinary hadron interacting with it. The interaction occurs in the degree-\(2\) fiber of the chiral fibration — the sector governed by the cinquefoil \(T_{2,5}^{\sigma}\) (\(5\) crossings, genus \(2\)). This sector is electromagnetically dark: the strangelet has \(Q = 0\) (strangelet crossing energy), so no photons are exchanged.

The interaction products become electromagnetically visible only through Skein crossing changes — each crossing change is a beta decay that lowers the degree from \(2\) toward \(1\). The minimal path from the degree-\(2\) fiber (cinquefoil, \(5\) crossings) to the degree-\(1\) fiber (trefoil, \(3\) crossings) requires two crossing changes: a double beta decay.

The Skein descent.

Each crossing change in the Skein relation

\[q\,L_+ - q^{-1}\,L_- = s\,L_0, \qquad s = q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2},\]

produces an \(L_0\) smoothing — a split into an electron (or positron) and a neutrino (beta decay products). The amplitude for each crossing change is \(s\). Two crossing changes give the double beta amplitude \(s^2\) and rate \(s^4\):

\[\Gamma_{2\beta} \;\propto\; s^4 \;=\; (q^{1/2} - q^{-1/2})^4.\]

At \(q = q_0\):

\[s = 0.1041, \qquad s^2 = 0.01084, \qquad s^4 = 1.18 \times 10^{-4}.\]

The Skein amplitude is the EM/strong ratio.

The Skein amplitude \(s \approx 0.104\) is numerically indistinguishable from the EM/strong ratio \(\tanh(\ln q) \approx 0.104\) (crossing energy decomposition). This is not a coincidence: both measure the antisymmetric channel of the \(R\)-matrix braiding. Each crossing change couples the degree-\(2\) fiber to the degree-\(1\) fiber through the antisymmetric (electromagnetic) channel. The double beta decay rate is therefore

\[\Gamma_{2\beta} \;\sim\; \left(\frac{\text{EM}}{\text{strong}}\right)^4 \;\approx\; 10^{-4}.\]

This is a parameter-free prediction: the suppression factor is determined entirely by \(q_0\).

The intermediate state.

The path through the Skein resolution tree is:

\[T_{2,5}^{\sigma}\;(5\text{ crossings}) \;\xrightarrow{\;L_0\;} \;4_1\;(4\text{ crossings}) \;\xrightarrow{\;L_0\;} \;T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\;(3\text{ crossings}).\]

The intermediate knot is the figure-eight \(4_1\) — the amphichiral knot identified with the Higgs mass mechanism (building block knots). Its Jones polynomial at \(q = q_0\) is \(J(4_1) = 1.033\), close to \(1\) (the unknot value). The intermediate state is "almost trivial" — a fleeting Higgs-like excitation between the two beta decays.

The degree-\(2\) to degree-\(1\) fiber transition.

The cinquefoil \(T_{2,5}^{\sigma}\) lives on the genus-\(2\) part of Bring’s surface: it wraps the surface with winding \((2, 5)\), engaging two of the five sheets. The trefoil \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) lives on the genus-\(1\) part: winding \((2, 3)\), engaging the same two sheets but with fewer crossings.

The double beta decay is a fiber descent: the interaction products, born in the genus-\(2\) sector where electromagnetism is absent (\(Q = 0\)), cascade through two Skein smoothings to the genus-\(1\) sector where electromagnetism is active (\(Q \neq 0\)). Each smoothing peels off one electron-neutrino pair and reduces the crossing number by one.

Observable signature.

The double beta decay of a strangelet interaction produces:

  • Two electrons (or positrons), each from one \(L_0\) smoothing.

  • Two neutrinos (or antineutrinos), one per smoothing.

  • Endpoint energy \(\sim 2\,q^{-1} \approx 1.80\) Skein units, or approximately \(2.3\) MeV in physical units (scaling by \(m_p c^2 / (V_B/\hbar_q^2)\)).

  • Angular correlation between the two electrons set by the Skein polynomial at the intermediate (\(4_1\)) vertex: the figure-eight’s amphichirality (\(4_1 = 4_1^{\sigma}\)) means the correlation is symmetric under parity.

The \(2.3\) MeV endpoint and the \(s^4 \approx 10^{-4}\) suppression place this in the regime of rare, low-energy electron pair events — detectable in underground experiments designed for double beta decay searches (GERDA, MAJORANA, nEXO, LEGEND). The distinctive prediction: the electron pair spectrum has a parity-symmetric angular distribution (from the amphichiral intermediate) and an endpoint set by \(q^{-1}\), not by a nuclear mass difference.

Proposition 10.23 ∀ stated (Local Value of the Substrate Parameter). \(\forall\)

In any sufficiently small neighbourhood \(U \subset M\) of the observable universe, the substrate parameter \(q\) (substrate parameter) satisfies

\[q\big|_U \;=\; 1.1097 \;\pm\; 0.001.\]

More precisely, \(q|_U\) is the unique real root \(q > 1\) of the equation

\[(1 - q^{-1})^{2} \;=\; \frac{\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)}{m_\mu / m_e},\]

where \(\mathrm{Vol}(4_1) = 3\,\mathrm{Cl}_2(\pi/3) \approx 2.02988\) is the hyperbolic volume of the figure-eight knot and \(m_\mu / m_e \approx 206.768\,2830\) is the CODATA 2022 muon–electron mass ratio.

Proof of Local Value of the Substrate Parameter.

The topological mass formula (topological mass formula) gives \(m_\mu / m_e = \mathrm{Vol}(4_1) / \hbar_q^{\,2}\) with \(\hbar_q = 1 - q^{-1}\) (see the proof of skein mass relation). Rearranging yields the equation above. Substituting the numerical values,

\[(1 - q^{-1})^{2} = \frac{2.02988}{206.7683} \approx 0.009\,817, \qquad 1 - q^{-1} \approx 0.09908, \qquad q \approx 1.10998.\]

The numerical values are independently verified by the SnapPy witness (knot volumes verification), which computes \(q \approx 1.10998\) from \(\mathrm{Vol}(4_1) \approx 2.02988321281931\) and \(m_\mu/m_e \approx 206.7682830\) (CODATA 2022). Since \(f(q) = (1 - q^{-1})^{2}\) is strictly increasing for \(q > 1\) and maps \((1,\infty)\) onto \((0,1)\), the root is unique. The uncertainty \(\pm\,0.001\) is propagated from the CODATA relative uncertainty of \(2.2 \times 10^{-8}\) on \(m_\mu / m_e\) and the SnapPy error bound of \(10^{-14}\) on \(\mathrm{Vol}(4_1)\); the dominant contribution is the finite decimal truncation of \(q\). This value is consistent with the hadronic mass predictions of terminal resolution and with the \(q\)-deformed Hall conductance corrections of photonic Hall effect. ◻

Remark 10.24 ✗ no Lean (Energy cost of electron–positron conversion).

How much energy does it cost to convert an electron into a positron? The answer depends on what "convert" means — and the QOU framework reveals three distinct energy scales.

Standard physics: conversion is forbidden; only pair creation is possible. An isolated electron cannot become a positron — lepton number conservation forbids it. The minimum process is pair production: a photon near a nucleus creates an \(e^- e^+\) pair, requiring

\[E_{\gamma} \;\geq\; 2\,m_e\,c^2 \;=\; 1.022 \;\text{MeV}.\]

The original electron is unchanged; a new pair appears from the photon’s energy.

In the QOU: crossing energy of the trefoil. The electron is the left trefoil \(T_{2,3}\) with \(n_c = 3\) positive crossings. Its crossing energy is

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^-) \;=\; 3q \;\approx\; 3 \, q_0 \;=\; 3.330 \quad (\text{in Skein units}).\]

The positron is the mirror \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) with \(3\) negative crossings:

\[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^+) \;=\; -3q^{-1} \;\approx\; -3 \times 0.9010 \;=\; -2.703 \quad (\text{in Skein units}).\]

The crossing energy gap between the two chiralities is

\[\Delta \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}} \;=\; \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^-) - \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^+) \;=\; 3(q + q^{-1}) \;\approx\; 6.033 \quad (\text{in Skein units}).\]

This decomposes into symmetric and antisymmetric parts:

\[3(q + q^{-1}) \;=\; \underbrace{3 \cdot 2 \cosh(\ln q)}_{\text{strong baseline}} \;=\; 6 \cosh(\ln q) \;\approx\; 6.033.\]

Three energy scales for "conversion".

Process Energy QOU description
Pair production (\(\gamma \to e^- e^+\)) \(2m_e c^2 \approx 1.022\) MeV New pair from photon; trefoil + mirror created at exceptional divisor
Crossing energy gap (one trefoil) \(3(q + q^{-1}) \approx 6.03\) Skein units Full reversal of all 3 crossings; maps to \(\Delta E = 6\cosh(\ln q)\)
Complex-\(q\) barrier (\(\theta = 0 \to \pi\)) Topological, not energetic Continuous rotation in pre-observable sector; no energy cost in observable sector

Physical interpretation of each route.

  1. Pair production at the exceptional divisor. When a photon with \(E \geq 2m_e\) encounters the blow-up locus, it can resolve into a trefoil–mirror pair. The energy \(2m_e\) is not the crossing energy gap — it is the mass-energy of the two particles created. The crossing energies of \(e^-\) and \(e^+\) have opposite sign and partially cancel in the pair: \[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^-) + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(e^+) \;=\; 3q - 3q^{-1} \;=\; 3(q - q^{-1}) \;\approx\; 0.630 \quad (\text{Skein units}).\] The residual \(3(q - q^{-1}) > 0\) is the net Coulomb repulsion of the pair — the antisymmetric part of the crossing energy that drives the \(e^-\) and \(e^+\) apart after creation. The ratio \[\frac{q - q^{-1}}{q + q^{-1}} \;=\; \tanh(\ln q) \;\approx\; 0.104\] measures the electromagnetic-to-strong ratio for the electron, consistent with \(\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}} \sim 1/137\) at low energies (the Skein ratio is at the constituent scale, not the running coupling scale).

  2. Direct chirality reversal (forbidden in observable sector). Flipping all 3 crossings of \(T_{2,3}\) to produce \(T_{2,3}^{\sigma}\) while keeping the same knot would require a topological transition through the unknot — but the trefoil is topologically stable. In the observable sector (\(q\) real, \(\theta = 0\)), no finite energy can accomplish this: the trefoil and its mirror are in different connected components of knot space.

  3. Complex-\(q\) rotation (pre-observable). In the complex substrate framework, the chirality operator \(\mathcal{X}_\varphi \colon \theta \to \theta + \varphi\) rotates continuously from electron to positron. This has zero energy cost in the pre-observable sector (the rotation is along a flat direction of the categorical action). The energy cost appears only upon projection to the observable sector, where the continuous rotation collapses to the discrete pair-creation event with threshold \(2m_e\).

Summary. The energy to "convert" an electron to a positron is either:

  • \(\infty\) (impossible within the observable sector — topologically forbidden),

  • \(2m_e \approx 1.022\) MeV (create a new pair at the exceptional divisor), or

  • \(0\) (in the pre-observable complex-\(q\) sector, chirality rotation is free — but inaccessible to measurement).

The crossing energy gap \(3(q + q^{-1})\) in Skein units sets the algebraic distance between the two chiralities. Its physical manifestation is not a single energy threshold but the decomposition into symmetric binding (\(\cosh\)) and antisymmetric Coulomb (\(\sinh\)) channels.

Conjecture 10.25 ✗ no Lean (Chirality as continuous phase rotation in the pre-observable sector).

Let \(q = |q|\,e^{i\theta}\) be a complex substrate parameter with \(|q| > 1\) and \(\theta \in (-\pi, \pi]\), as in the complex substrate interpretation.

Conjecture. In the pre-observable sector (before imposing the dagger positive-definiteness axiom), the particle–antiparticle distinction is governed by the phase \(\theta\):

For a torus knot \(T_{p,k}\) with crossing energy \(\mathcal{S}_c(T_{p,k}; q)\), the complex extension satisfies \[\mathcal{S}_c(T_{p,k};\, |q|\,e^{i\theta}) \;=\; \mathcal{S}_c(T_{p,k};\, |q|)\,e^{i\,n_c\,\theta},\] where \(n_c\) is the crossing number. The mirror image \(T_{p,k}^{\sigma}\) has crossing number \(-n_c\), giving \(\mathcal{S}_c(T_{p,k}^{\sigma}) = \mathcal{S}_c(T_{p,k};\, |q|)\,e^{-i\,n_c\,\theta}\).

  2. Chirality interpolation. Define the chirality operator \(\mathcal{X}_\varphi \colon \theta \mapsto \theta + \varphi\) acting on the phase of \(q\). Then:

  3. CPT as \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) quotient. The observable sector (\(\theta = 0\)) sees only the \(\mathbb{Z}_2\) quotient of this \(\mathrm{U}(1)\) action: charge conjugation C is the residue of the continuous chirality rotation modulo the observability constraint. Parity P and time reversal T similarly descend from continuous operations in the pre-observable sector, and the CPT theorem becomes the statement that the total rotation \(\mathcal{X}_\pi \circ P \circ T\) is always a symmetry of the categorical action (categorical action).

Experimental discriminant. If the pre-observable phase \(\theta\) leaves a residual signature after projection to the observable sector, it would appear as a tiny CP-violating phase in crossing-energy ratios. For the electron–positron system:

which vanishes to first order (consistent with the observed near-exact electron–positron mass equality) but could contribute at second order to CP violation in hadronic systems where multiple crossing numbers interact.

Proposition 10.26 ✗ no Lean (Crossing energy decomposes into strong and Coulomb channels).

The crossing energy assigns weights \(+q\) to positive crossings and \(-q^{-1}\) to negative crossings, with \(q > 1\). Writing \(q = e^\lambda\) where \(\lambda = \ln q > 0\), the crossing weights decompose into symmetric and antisymmetric parts under the mirror operation \(\sigma\):

\[q \;=\; \cosh\lambda + \sinh\lambda, \qquad q^{-1} \;=\; \cosh\lambda - \sinh\lambda.\]

Statement. For any knot composite \(\mathfrak{H}\) with crossing energy \(\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i \epsilon_i\) where \(\epsilon_i \in \{q, -q^{-1}\}\):

  1. Symmetric channel. The component \(E_{\mathrm{sym}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i |\epsilon_i| \cdot \cosh(\ln q) \cdot \mathrm{sgn}(\epsilon_i)\) is invariant under the mirror operation \(\sigma\) (which reverses all crossing signs).

  2. Antisymmetric channel. The component \(E_{\mathrm{asym}}(\mathfrak{H}) = \sum_i |\epsilon_i| \cdot \sinh(\ln q) \cdot \mathrm{sgn}(\epsilon_i)\) reverses sign under \(\sigma\).

  3. Pair cancellation. For a particle–antiparticle pair \((\mathfrak{H}, \mathfrak{H}^{\sigma})\), the combined crossing energy is purely antisymmetric: \[\mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}) + \mathbf{E}_{\mathrm{cross}}(\mathfrak{H}^{\sigma}) \;=\; 2\,E_{\mathrm{asym}}(\mathfrak{H}).\]

  4. Ratio identity. The antisymmetric-to-symmetric ratio is \[\frac{E_{\mathrm{asym}}}{E_{\mathrm{sym}}} \;=\; \tanh(\ln q),\] independent of the knot composite \(\mathfrak{H}\).

Remark 10.27 ✗ no Lean (Virtual particles as excitations of the exceptional divisor).

In quantum field theory, virtual particles are internal lines in Feynman diagrams: off-shell excitations that mediate forces and contribute to loop corrections but are never directly detected. Their "existence" is bounded by the Heisenberg uncertainty relation \(\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \gtrsim \hbar\). The QOU framework provides a geometric home for this phenomenon.

The exceptional divisor as the virtual stage.

At each brane point \(p \in M\), the blow-up replaces \(p\) with an exceptional divisor \(\mathcal{S}_p \cong \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{C}) \cong S^2\). This sphere parametrises the directions of departure from the base manifold — the internal degrees of freedom invisible to the base-level observer.

A virtual particle is an excitation that lives within the Reeb bundle over \(\mathcal{S}_p\) — the Hopf fibration \(U(1) \hookrightarrow S^3 \to \mathcal{S}_p\) where all braiding takes place (vertex is the exceptional divisor). It is created at the blow-up locus, propagates along the exceptional divisor (or up into the brane tower rooted at \(\mathcal{S}_p\)), and is reabsorbed before it can descend to the base level \(A_0\).

Brane tower levels as virtual depth.

The recursive brane tower \(A_0 \hookrightarrow A_1 \hookrightarrow A_2 \hookrightarrow \cdots\) stratifies excitations by their jet prolongation level. Physical (on-shell) particles live at level \(A_0\) — they are knot configurations in the base algebra. Virtual particles live at levels \(A_n\) with \(n \geq 1\):

Tower level Algebra Physical interpretation
\(A_0 = A\) Coordinate ring \(\mathcal{O}(\mathrm{SU}(2))\) On-shell particles: knots in base manifold
\(A_1 = J^1(A_0)\) Sections of frame bundle 1-virtual: connection fluctuations (gauge bosons)
\(A_2 = J^1(A_1)\) Second jet sections 2-virtual: curvature fluctuations (graviton-like)
\(A_n\) \(n\)-th jet sections \(n\)-virtual: \(n\)-th derivative corrections

Each level \(A_n\) has dimension \(3^n \cdot \dim A_0\) (for \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)), so the state space grows exponentially with virtual depth — but the projection back to \(A_0\) collapses all higher-level structure.

Why virtual particles are never observed.

An excitation at level \(A_n\) (\(n \geq 1\)) is invisible at \(A_0\) because the canonical projection \(\pi_0 \colon A_n \to A_0\) annihilates the \(\Omega^1\) components:

\[\pi_0(f \otimes \omega_1 \otimes \cdots \otimes \omega_n) \;=\; f \cdot \varepsilon(\omega_1) \cdots \varepsilon(\omega_n),\]

where \(\varepsilon\) is the counit. For a form \(\omega\) with no constant part (\(\varepsilon(\omega) = 0\)), the entire excitation projects to zero at the base level. The virtual particle exists in the tower but casts no shadow on \(A_0\).

This is the categorical analogue of the statement that virtual particles are "off-shell": they satisfy the equations of motion at their tower level but not at the base level. The base-level observer sees only the net effect — a correction to the propagator, an effective force, a shift in energy levels — never the virtual excitation itself.

Lifetime from the Heisenberg commutator.

The Heisenberg commutator at level \(n\) of the tower is

\[[\hat{X}, \hat{P}]_{q_n} \;=\; J\,\hbar_{q_n}, \qquad \hbar_{q_n} \;=\; 1 - q_n^{-1},\]

where \(q_n\) is the substrate parameter at the \(n\)-th level. The uncertainty bound \(\Delta E \cdot \Delta t \geq \hbar_{q_n} / 2\) limits the lifetime of a virtual excitation at level \(n\):

\[\Delta t_{\text{virtual}} \;\leq\; \frac{\hbar_{q_n}}{2\,\Delta E}.\]

For an excitation that borrows energy \(\Delta E\) from the vacuum at the exceptional divisor, this is the maximum time before the excitation must be reabsorbed. Crucially, the excitation’s "worldline" stays within the tower: it is created at \(\mathcal{S}_p\), propagates through \(A_1, A_2, \ldots\), and returns to \(\mathcal{S}_p\) without ever descending to \(A_0\).

What is CP violation? CP symmetry is the combined operation of charge conjugation C (swap particle \(\leftrightarrow\) antiparticle) and parity P (mirror spatial coordinates). If physics were CP-symmetric, matter and antimatter would behave as exact mirror images. CP violation means this symmetry is broken: certain processes distinguish matter from antimatter at a fundamental level.

Experimental evidence.

CP violation is firmly established in three systems:

  1. Neutral kaons (1964). Cronin and Fitch observed that the long-lived kaon \(K_L\) (which should decay only to three pions under CP symmetry) occasionally decays to two pions: \(K_L \to \pi^+\pi^-\) at rate \(\sim 2 \times 10^{-3}\) . This was the first evidence that CP is not an exact symmetry.

  2. \(B\) mesons (2001). The BaBar and Belle experiments measured CP-violating asymmetries in \(B^0 \to J/\psi\,K_S\) decays, confirming the Kobayashi–Maskawa mechanism: the CKM quark-mixing matrix contains an irreducible complex phase \(\delta_{\mathrm{CKM}}\) that cannot be removed by field redefinitions.

  3. \(D\) mesons (2019). LHCb observed CP violation in charm decays (\(D^0 \to K^+K^-\) vs \(D^0 \to \pi^+\pi^-\)) at the \(10^{-4}\) level.

The matter–antimatter asymmetry.

Sakharov (1967) showed that three conditions are necessary for the observed baryon asymmetry of the universe: (i) baryon number violation, (ii) C and CP violation, (iii) departure from thermal equilibrium. The Standard Model CKM phase provides (ii) but is quantitatively too small by several orders of magnitude to explain the observed ratio \(n_B / n_\gamma \sim 6 \times 10^{-10}\). Additional sources of CP violation are needed.

QOU interpretation.

In the complex chirality rotation framework, CP violation arises from a residual phase \(\theta\) of the complex substrate parameter \(q = |q|\,e^{i\theta}\):

  • The observable sector projects \(\theta \to 0\), but this projection may be imperfect — a small residual \(\theta_{\mathrm{res}}\) could survive.

  • The CP-violating discriminant is \(\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim \mathcal{O}(\theta_{\mathrm{res}}^2)\) for single-crossing systems (electron/positron).

  • For multi-crossing composites (kaons: quark–antiquark with multiple internal crossings), the phase accumulates: \(\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim n_c\,\theta_{\mathrm{res}}\), where \(n_c\) is the total crossing number of the hadronic braid word.

  • This provides a geometric origin for the CKM phase: it is the total accumulated crossing phase from the complex-\(q\) sector, projected onto the observable quark-mixing matrix.

Quantitative gap. The crossing energy decomposition gives the electromagnetic/strong ratio \(\tanh(\ln q) \approx 0.104\). If the residual phase scales similarly — \(\theta_{\mathrm{res}} \sim \tanh(\ln q) \cdot \alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}\) — then \(\delta_{\mathrm{CP}} \sim 10^{-3}\), which is the right order of magnitude for kaon CP violation but still too small for baryogenesis. The missing enhancement may come from the cosmological regime where the observability constraint itself weakens.

Remark 10.28 ✗ no Lean (Electrons are immortal: no beta decay for elementary trefoils).

Beta decay converts a neutron to a proton (or vice versa) by changing the crossing orientation partition of the Borromean baryon: \([u,d,d] \to [u,u,d]\). This is possible because baryons are composite — they have internal degrees of freedom (the quark flavour assignments) that can rearrange via R-I embedding moves while preserving the Borromean link type.

Can the electron beta-decay?

No — and the reason is topological, not energetic. The electron is the trefoil \(T_{2,3}\): an elementary knot with no internal constituents. There is no crossing orientation partition to rearrange, no substructure to reorganise, no embedding move that changes the particle’s identity. The electron has exactly one degree of freedom — its knot type — and that is a topological invariant.

Particle Structure Internal d.o.f. Beta decay?
Neutron \([u,d,d]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\) Quark flavour partition Yes: \(\mathfrak{n} \to \mathfrak{p} + e^- + \nu^{\sigma}\)
Proton \([u,u,d]_p \bowtie \mathcal{L}_H\) Quark flavour partition Yes (in nuclei): \(\mathfrak{p} \to \mathfrak{n} + e^+ + \nu\)
Electron \(T_{2,3}\) None No
Neutrino \(T_{1,0}\) (unknot) None No

The electron cannot decay into anything lighter while conserving lepton number and charge. There is no lighter charged lepton, and the neutrino (unknot \(T_{1,0}\)) has zero crossing energy and zero mass — it cannot absorb the electron’s topological charge.

Electrons survive to heat death.

In the observable era (\(1 < q < \infty\)), the time reversal barrier prevents chirality reversal, and the absence of beta decay prevents flavour change. The electron is therefore immortal in the observable sector: it persists from the moment of its creation (pair production at the exceptional divisor) until the cosmological boundary.

As the universe evolves toward heat death (\(q \to 1\)):

  1. Bound electrons are liberated. Atoms ionise as the ambient energy drops below binding thresholds — but the electron itself is unchanged. Its bare mass (a knot invariant) is eternal; only its binding energy (an embedding property) dissipates.

  2. Free electrons become radiation. In the \(q \to 1\) limit, the crossing energy asymmetry \(q - q^{-1} \to 0\) erases the Coulomb distinction. The electron’s electromagnetic charge effectively vanishes. What remains is a massless topological excitation — indistinguishable from a photon in the frozen geometry.

  3. Radiation becomes CMB. The thermal photon bath (including the absorbed electron contribution) redshifts to the cosmic microwave background. The CMB torsion signature carries the imprint of the \(q\)-deformed Reeb flow — a fossil record of the substrate parameter’s value during earlier epochs.

Into the next aeon.

If the cosmological chirality flip is correct, the heat-death boundary is where chirality distinction collapses (\(q \to 1\)) and the next aeon’s big bang is where it re-emerges (\(q \to \infty\) in the new cycle). The CMB radiation from one aeon becomes the initial condition for the next — carrying topological information (knot type) through the boundary even as metric information (mass, charge) is erased.

In the language of Penrose’s Conformal Cyclic Cosmology: the massless, chargeless radiation at heat death is conformally equivalent to the initial singularity of the next aeon. In the QOU framework, this equivalence is not conformal rescaling but Frobenius degeneration: the same mathematical structure (the Frobenius form becoming trivial or singular) governs both endpoints, and the exceptional divisors at the boundary are where the topology resets.

The electron, as a trefoil, is (k)not subject to beta decay. It lives forever — or rather, it lives until the concept of "living" loses meaning at \(q = 1\), where all distinctions dissolve into the frozen geometry of the classical limit.

  • \(\delta r\), \(\delta\zeta\) — grid density (radial and angular)

  • \(N\) — \(q\)-series truncation precision (number of terms)

  • Projection mode: \(\omega\)-coords, \(+\mathrm{Sp}(1)\) rotation, or raw \(x_j\)

Growth factor profiles and Weierstrass curve data are displayed in auxiliary panels.

Remark 10.33 ✗ no Lean (Beta-Decay Half-Life Simulator).

An interactive simulator that computes nuclear beta-decay half-lives from the substrate parameter \(q\) using the transfer matrix Skein polynomial (Skein polynomial).

What is computed

For a nucleus \(\mathcal{N}(Z, N)\), the simulator evaluates:

  1. Skein polynomials \(P_{\mathrm{par}}(q)\) and \(P_{\mathrm{dau}}(q)\) for parent and daughter via \(\binom{A}{2}\) transfer matrix multiplications (transfer matrix operator).

  2. \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value from the ratio \(\mathcal{Q}_q = |\ln(P_{\mathrm{dau}}/P_{\mathrm{par}})| \times E_{\times} \times \mu_0\), optionally with the shell correction \(\Delta_{\mathrm{shell}} + \Delta_{T_{3,5}}\) (shell construction rules).

  3. Phase-space integral \(f(Z, \mathcal{Q}_q)\) with the Skein-Coulomb Fermi function \(F_q(Z, E)\) (Skein-Coulomb enhancement) using \(\alpha_{\mathrm{EM}}(q) = q^{-1}/([9]_q \cdot [10]_q)\).

  4. Half-life \(t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / \Gamma_\beta\) where \(\Gamma_\beta = G_F^2 m_e^5 / (2\pi^3 \hbar) \cdot [2]_q \cdot f(Z, \mathcal{Q}_q)\) (hadron half-life).

Two modes

  • From \(q\): the \(\mathcal{Q}_q\)-value is predicted from the transfer matrix ratio. Accurate for light nuclei (\(A \leq 14\), \(5\)–\(7\%\) error); heavy nuclei overshoot due to naive nucleon ordering (verification).

  • From \(Q_{\mathrm{exp}}\): uses experimental \(Q\)-values (NNDC/ENSDF). Isolates the \(q\)-dependent prefactors and Coulomb enhancement. All six benchmarks agree to \(< 3\%\).

Three regimes

The canvas plot shows \(t_{1/2}\) vs \(q\) for the selected nucleus, illustrating the three regimes (half-life regimes):

  • Classical (\(q \to 1\)): \(\Gamma_\beta \to 0\), no beta decay.

  • Descartes (\(q = q_0\)): observed nuclear lifetimes.

  • Deep quantum (\(q \to \infty\)): \(\Gamma_\beta \to \infty\), instantaneous decay.

The sensitivity \(\partial \ln \Gamma / \partial \ln q \approx 48\) at \(q_0\) is displayed — a \(1\%\) shift in \(q\) changes decay rates by \(\sim 50\%\).

\(q\)-Geometric Langlands Correspondence

Introduction

The substrate parameter \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k) = k^\times \setminus \mu_\infty\) (substrate parameter) endows the differential calculus of a quantum observable universe with a one-parameter deformation controlled by the fibre coordinate of a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family. Two consequences of this deformation are central to the present chapter:

  1. The \(q\)-deformed exterior derivative satisfies \(d_q^2 \neq 0\) (non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)), producing a canonical obstruction to flatness of \(q\)-connections.

  2. The Yekutieli obstruction classes \(\kappa_n \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) (quantum characteristic classes) control the lifting of Frobenius–Hopf objects through the brane tower, and their Kummer filtration (Kummer filtration) determines the arithmetic locus where \(q\)-flatness holds.

These structures assemble into a \(q\)-deformed Geometric Langlands correspondence. The automorphic side consists of \(q\)-\(\mathcal{D}\)-modules on the moduli of \(G_q\)-bundles; the spectral side consists of quasi-coherent sheaves on the moduli of \(q\)-local systems for the Langlands dual \(\check{G}_q\). The fibre functor \(\tau\), whose rigidity is guaranteed by the observability axiom (fibre-functor rigidity), mediates the equivalence via Tannaka–Krein reconstruction.

The \(q\)-Geometric Langlands equivalence is a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family of functors, well-defined on the non-torsion locus \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}\) and degenerating at roots of unity where \([n]_q = 0\). The perpetual obstruction phenomenon (Kummer filtration) forces the correspondence to be intrinsically non-torsion.

\(\mathbb{G}_m\)-torsors and \(q\)-local systems

📄

Definition 11.1 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Local system). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\) and let \(X\) denote the brane curve. The substrate \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k)\) determines a fibre in the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family of deformations (substrate parameter). A \(q\)-local system on \(X\) with structure group \(G_q\) is a functor

\[\mathcal{L}_q \colon \Pi_1(X) \longrightarrow \mathbf{Rep}(G_q)\]

from the fundamental groupoid \(\Pi_1(X)\) to the category of finite-dimensional representations of the quantum group \(G_q\), subject to the \(q\)-monodromy condition: for every contractible loop \(\varrho \colon \mathbf{1} \to \mathbf{1}\) in \(\Pi_1(X)\), the monodromy satisfies

\[\mathcal{L}_q(\varrho) = \mathrm{id} + (q - 1)\,\Omega_q(\varrho),\]

where \(\Omega_q(\varrho) \in \mathrm{End}(\tau(\mathcal{L}_q))\) is the \(q\)-holonomy residue determined by the \(q\)-connection (q-flat connection).

The \(q\)-monodromy condition is the local manifestation of the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family structure: at \(q = 1\) the residue vanishes and \(\mathcal{L}_1\) is a classical local system (flat bundle), while for \(q \neq 1\) the non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\) (non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)) obstructs trivial monodromy. The Kummer reduction of the Yekutieli class \(\kappa_0\) at level \(n\) (Kummer filtration) controls which \(q\)-local systems admit lifts through the brane tower: \(\mathcal{L}_q\) lifts from level \(n\) to \(n+1\) iff \(\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0\), equivalently \(n \mid \chi(A)\).

We denote by \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{G_q}(X)\) the moduli stack of \(q\)-local systems on \(X\).

📄

Definition 11.2 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Flat connection). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe and let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a \(G_q\)-equivariant object in \(\mathbf{C}\) over the brane curve \(X\). A \(q\)-flat connection on \(\mathcal{V}\) is a \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q \colon \mathcal{V} \to \Omega^1_q \otimes \mathcal{V}\) (categorical \(q\)-connection) whose total curvature \(\nabla_q^2\) equals the intrinsic \(q\)-curvature determined by \(d_q^2\):

\[\nabla_q^2 = (q - 1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}},\]

where \(\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} \in \mathrm{End}(\mathcal{V}) \otimes \Omega^2_q\) is the intrinsic \(q\)-curvature, the image of the Yekutieli class under the HKR map (Kummer filtration):

\[\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} \;=\; \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(\kappa_0) \;\in\; HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q,\, \mathrm{Ad}).\]

In general, a \(q\)-connection has total curvature

\[\nabla_q^2 = (q - 1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} + \mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}},\]

where \(\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}}\) is the connection-dependent curvature — the contribution from the connection form itself. A \(q\)-connection is \(q\)-flat when \(\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}} = 0\): all curvature is intrinsic, arising solely from the \(d_q^2 \neq 0\) obstruction (non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)).

A \(q\)-flat connection is not flat in the classical sense (\(\nabla_q^2 \neq 0\) in general), but carries the minimal possible curvature compatible with the \(q\)-deformation. When \(\kappa_0 \neq 0\) (the perpetual obstruction), \(q\)-flat connections exist but have non-zero total curvature \((q-1)\,\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}}\).

The category of \(q\)-flat connections on \(X\) with structure group \(G_q\) is equivalent to the category of \(q\)-local systems \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{G_q}(X)\) (q-local system).

\(q\)-Hecke correspondences

📄

Definition 11.3 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Hecke operator). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with brane curve \(X\) and quantum gauge group \(G_q\) (quantum gauge group). For a closed point \(x \in X\) and a dominant coweight \(\lambda\) of \(G_q\), the \(q\)-Hecke operator \(\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}\) is the integral transform

\[\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} \colon \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}) \longrightarrow \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q})\]

defined by the \(q\)-Hecke correspondence:

where \(\mathrm{Hecke}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}\) parametrises pairs \((\mathcal{P}, \mathcal{P}')\) of \(G_q\)-bundles on \(X\) together with an isomorphism \(\mathcal{P}|_{X \setminus x} \xrightarrow{\sim} \mathcal{P}'|_{X \setminus x}\) of relative position \(\lambda\).

The \(q\)-Hecke operators satisfy the Iwahori–Hecke algebra relation (braiding eigenvalues):

\[(\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} - q) (\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} + q^{-1}) = 0,\]

acting with eigenvalues \(q\) and \(-q^{-1}\) on the symmetric and antisymmetric channels respectively.

📄

Definition 11.4 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Hecke eigensheaf). \(\forall\)

A \(q\)-\(\mathcal{D}\)-module \(\mathcal{M}\) on \(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)\) is a \(q\)-Hecke eigensheaf with eigenvalue \(\mathcal{L}_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\) if, for every closed point \(x \in X\) and every dominant coweight \(\lambda\), there exists a functorial isomorphism

\[\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}) \;\simeq\; \mathcal{M} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x,\]

where \(V_\lambda^{(q)}\) is the irreducible representation of \(\check{G}_q\) of highest weight \(\lambda\) and \(V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\) denotes its fibre at \(x\) under the \(q\)-local system \(\mathcal{L}_q\) (q-local system).

The isomorphisms are required to be compatible with:

  1. Tensor products: the isomorphism for \(\lambda + \mu\) is the composition of the isomorphisms for \(\lambda\) and \(\mu\), twisted by the braiding \(\sigma_q \colon V_\lambda^{(q)} \otimes V_\mu^{(q)} \to V_\mu^{(q)} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}\).

  2. Factorisation: for distinct points \(x \neq y\) the Hecke operators commute up to the \((q-1)\)-correction: \([\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}, \mathbf{T}_{y,\mu}^{(q)}] = O(q-1)\).

📄

Proposition 11.5 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Hecke eigenvalues from the fibre functor). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with substrate parameter \(q\). If \(\mathcal{M}\) is a \(q\)-Hecke eigensheaf on \(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)\) (q-Hecke eigensheaf), then its eigenvalue \(\mathcal{L}_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\) is uniquely determined by the action of \(\tau\) on the Hecke eigenvalue data:

\[\mathcal{L}_q \;\simeq\; \mathrm{Aut}^\otimes(\tau)\text{-}\mathrm{equivariantisation of } \big\{ V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x \big\}_{\lambda, x}.\]

The rigidity of the fibre functor (fibre-functor rigidity) implies that \(\mathcal{L}_q\) is determined up to unique isomorphism by the collection of Hecke eigenvalues.

Proof of \(q\)-Hecke eigenvalue determination.

By Tannaka–Krein reconstruction, the quantum group \(\check{G}_q\) is recovered as \(\mathrm{Aut}^\otimes(\tau)\) where \(\tau\) is the fibre functor on \(\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q)\). A \(\check{G}_q\)-local system \(\mathcal{L}_q\) is equivalent to a tensor functor \(\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q) \to \mathrm{Vect}_X\), which in turn is determined by the fibre data \(\{V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\}\) over all \(\lambda\) and \(x\).

The Hecke eigensheaf property provides exactly this data: for each \((\lambda, x)\) the eigenvalue isomorphism \(\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}) \simeq \mathcal{M} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\) extracts the fibre \(V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\) as the multiplicity space.

The tensor compatibility of the Hecke isomorphisms ensures that the assignment \(V_\lambda^{(q)} \mapsto V_\lambda^{(q)}(\mathcal{L}_q)_x\) is a tensor functor, hence defines a point of \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\). Rigidity of \(\tau\) (fibre-functor rigidity) guarantees that any two tensor functors with isomorphic fibre data are uniquely isomorphic. \(\square\) ◻

The \(q\)-Geometric Langlands conjecture

📄

Definition 11.6 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Langlands dual group). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with quantum gauge group \(G_q\) (quantum gauge group). The \(q\)-Langlands dual group \(\check{G}_q\) is the quantum group whose representation category is related to \(G_q\) by root system duality:

\[\check{G}_q = G_{q^{-1}}^{\vee},\]

where \((-)^\vee\) denotes the classical Langlands dual (interchange of roots and coroots) and the substrate parameter is inverted \(q \mapsto q^{-1}\).

For the QOU gauge group \(G_q = \mathrm{SU}_q(2)\) (quantum \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\)):

\[\check{G}_q = \mathrm{SU}_{q^{-1}}(2) \cong \mathrm{SO}_{q^{-1}}(3),\]

since \(\mathrm{SU}(2)\) is self-dual at the level of root systems and the Langlands involution acts by \(q \mapsto q^{-1}\) on the quantum parameter.

The inversion \(q \mapsto q^{-1}\) interchanges the two eigenvalues of the braiding: \(q \leftrightarrow -q^{-1}\). This exchanges the symmetric and antisymmetric channels of the Iwahori–Hecke algebra, which is the categorical manifestation of the exchange of roots and coroots. In the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family picture, the Langlands involution is the inversion automorphism \(\iota \colon \mathbb{G}_m \to \mathbb{G}_m\), \(\iota(q) = q^{-1}\), which preserves the torsion subgroups \(\mu_n\) and acts as the identity on \(\mu_2\).

📄

Conjecture 11.7 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Geometric Langlands correspondence). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with brane curve \(X\), quantum gauge group \(G_q\), and \(q\)-Langlands dual \(\check{G}_q\) (q-Langlands dual). The \(q\)-Geometric Langlands correspondence asserts the existence of an equivalence of \(\infty\)-categories:

\[\mathbb{L}_q \colon \mathcal{D}_q\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)) \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)),\]

parametrised by \(q \in \mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}(k)\) (the non-torsion locus of the substrate), satisfying:

  1. Hecke compatibility: for every \(q\)-Hecke operator \(\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}\) (q-Hecke operator) on the left-hand side, the functor \(\mathbb{L}_q\) intertwines it with the action of \(V_\lambda^{(q)}\) on \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\): \[\mathbb{L}_q \circ \mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)} \;\simeq\; V_\lambda^{(q)}(-)_x \otimes \mathbb{L}_q.\]

  2. Fibre-functor factorisation: the equivalence factors through the fibre functor \(\tau\): \[\mathbb{L}_q = \tau^* \circ \mathbb{L}_q^{\mathrm{Tannakian}},\] where \(\mathbb{L}_q^{\mathrm{Tannakian}}\) is determined by Tannaka–Krein reconstruction for \(\check{G}_q\).

  3. \(q\)-Oper locus: the equivalence \(\mathbb{L}_q\) restricts to a bijection between \(q\)-opers (q-oper) and \(q\)-Hecke eigensheaves (q-Hecke eigensheaf): \[\mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X) \;\hookrightarrow\; \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X) \quad\xrightarrow{\;\mathbb{L}_q^{-1}\;}\quad \{\text{$q$-Hecke eigensheaves}\}.\]

  4. Kummer constraint: the equivalence \(\mathbb{L}_q\) is well-defined as a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family on the non-torsion locus \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}}\). At roots of unity \(q \in \mu_n\) the quantum dimension \([n]_q = 0\) vanishes, the Frobenius pairing degenerates, and \(\mathbb{L}_q\) degenerates. The Yekutieli obstruction (Kummer filtration) persists at all Kummer levels \(n \nmid \chi(A)\).

  5. Classical limit: as \(q \to 1\), \(\mathbb{L}_q\) recovers the classical Geometric Langlands equivalence (classical limit).

📄

Proposition 11.8 ∀ stated (Yekutieli obstruction to \(q\)-flatness). \(\forall\)

Let \((\mathbf{C}, A, \tau)\) be a quantum observable universe with \(\chi(A) \neq 0\) and Yekutieli class \(\kappa_0 = e(\xi) \in H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\) (quantum characteristic classes).

  1. The intrinsic \(q\)-curvature of any \(q\)-flat connection \(\nabla_q\) on a \(G_q\)-bundle over \(X\) is \[\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{intr}} \;=\; \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(\kappa_0) \;\in\; HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q,\, \mathrm{Ad}),\] where \(\mathrm{HKR}\) is the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg comparison (Kummer filtration). This curvature is non-zero whenever \(\kappa_0 \neq 0\): \(q\)-flat connections carry intrinsic curvature from \(d_q^2 \neq 0\).

  2. The \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q\) is \(q\)-flat (q-flat connection) — meaning its connection-dependent curvature \(\mathcal{F}_q^{\mathrm{conn}} = 0\) — regardless of whether \(\kappa_0\) vanishes. However, \(q\)-flat connections that lift through the brane tower require \(\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0\) at the target level.

  3. At Kummer level \(n\), the obstruction \(\kappa_0 \bmod n\) vanishes if and only if \(n \mid \chi(A)\). Consequently, \(q\)-flat \(G_q\)-connections that lift to level \(n\) of the brane tower exist only when \(n\) divides \(|\chi(A)|\).

  4. For \(\chi(A) \neq 0\), the set of Kummer levels \(n\) at which \(\kappa_0 \bmod n \neq 0\) has density \(1\) in \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\): the obstruction persists perpetually. The \(q\)-local systems exist (as objects with intrinsic curvature), but their brane tower lifts are obstructed at cofinitely many levels.

Proof of the Yekutieli obstruction to \(q\)-flatness.

Item (1). The \(q\)-flatness equation is \(\nabla_q^2 = (q-1)\,\mathcal{F}_q\) (q-flat connection). The \(q\)-curvature \(\mathcal{F}_q\) is a class in \(\mathrm{End}(\mathcal{V}) \otimes \Omega^2_q\), which the Hochschild–Kostant–Rosenberg comparison identifies with \(HH^2(\mathcal{U}_q, \mathrm{Ad})\). The image under \(\mathrm{HKR}\) is the gerbe-theoretic Yekutieli class \(\kappa_0 = e(\xi)\) (Kummer filtration).

Item (2). If \(\kappa_0 = 0\) in \(H^2(\mathcal{S}, \mathbb{G}_m)\), then \(\mathcal{F}_q = \mathrm{HKR}^{-1}(0) = 0\), so \(\nabla_q\) is \(q\)-flat. Conversely, \(\mathcal{F}_q = 0\) implies \(\mathrm{HKR}(\mathcal{F}_q) = \kappa_0 = 0\).

Item (3). The Kummer exact sequence \(1 \to \mu_n \to \mathbb{G}_m \xrightarrow{(\cdot)^n} \mathbb{G}_m \to 1\) gives the reduction \(\kappa_0 \bmod n\). By Kummer filtration, \(\kappa_0 \bmod n = 0\) iff \(n \mid \chi(A)\), since \(\mathrm{tr}(\kappa_0) = \chi(A)\). The brane tower lift from level \(n\) to \(n+1\) requires (Yekutieli lifting condition) that \(\kappa_n = 0\), and the complementary subgroup structure \(\kappa_n = \kappa_0 + \delta_n\) with \(\kappa_0, \delta_n\) in complementary subgroups prevents cancellation.

Item (4). The set \(\{n : n \mid \chi(A)\}\) is finite (it has exactly \(d(\chi(A))\) elements, where \(d\) is the divisor function). Its complement in \(\mathbb{Z}_{>0}\) has density \(1\). \(\square\) ◻

📄

Conjecture 11.9 ∀ stated (Kummer filtration on \(q\)-local systems). \(\forall\)

The Kummer tower \(\mu_1 \subset \mu_2 \subset \cdots \subset \mu_\infty \subset \mathbb{G}_m\) (Kummer filtration) induces a descending filtration on the moduli of \(q\)-local systems. For each \(n \geq 1\), define the level-\(n\) sublocus:

\[\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}(X) \;\subset\; \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\]

consisting of \(q\)-local systems \(\mathcal{L}_q\) whose \(q\)-monodromy \(\Omega_q(\varrho)\) (q-local system) is \(n\)-divisible in \(\mathrm{End}(\tau(\mathcal{L}_q))\) for every contractible \(\varrho\). Then:

  1. \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(1)}(X) = \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\) (all \(q\)-local systems).

  2. The \(q\)-GL equivalence \(\mathbb{L}_q\) (\(q\)-GL conjecture) restricts to each filtered piece: \[\mathbb{L}_q^{(n)} \colon \mathcal{D}_q^{(n)}\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}) \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}(X)),\] where \(\mathcal{D}_q^{(n)}\) consists of \(q\)-\(\mathcal{D}\)-modules whose Hecke eigenvalues have \(n\)-divisible monodromy.

  3. By the Yekutieli obstruction, the sublocus \(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}^{(n)}\) admits lifts through the brane tower only when \(n \mid \chi(A)\). At levels \(n \nmid \chi(A)\) the perpetual obstruction prevents full lifting.

  4. The \(q\)-GL equivalence \(\mathbb{L}_q\) is well-defined as a \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family on \(\mathbb{G}_m^{\mathrm{nt}} = \mathbb{G}_m \setminus \mu_\infty\). The correspondence is intrinsically a non-torsion phenomenon.

📄

Conjecture 11.10 ∀ stated (Fibre-functor mediation of the \(q\)-Langlands correspondence). \(\forall\)

Under the hypotheses of the \(q\)-Geometric Langlands conjecture, the fibre functor \(\tau\) of the QOU determines the equivalence \(\mathbb{L}_q\) uniquely up to natural isomorphism:

\[\mathbb{L}_q(\mathcal{M})(\mathcal{L}_q) \;\simeq\; \mathrm{Hom}_{\mathbf{Rep}(\check{G}_q)} \big(\tau(-),\; \mathrm{Hecke}_q(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}_q)\big),\]

where \(\mathrm{Hecke}_q(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{L}_q)\) is the tensor functor \(V_\lambda^{(q)} \mapsto \mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}) \otimes \mathcal{L}_q(V_\lambda^{(q)})_x^*\) encoding all Hecke eigenvalue data simultaneously.

The rigidity of \(\tau\) (fibre-functor rigidity) forces \(\mathbb{L}_q\) to be unique: any two equivalences compatible with the Hecke eigensheaf structure and the fibre functor are connected by a unique natural isomorphism.

\(q\)-Opers and the spectral side

📄

Definition 11.11 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Oper). \(\forall\)

Let \(\check{G}_q\) be the \(q\)-Langlands dual group (q-Langlands dual) and \(\check{\mathfrak{b}}_q \subset \check{\mathfrak{g}}_q\) a Borel subalgebra of its Lie algebra. A \(q\)-oper on the brane curve \(X\) is a \(q\)-flat connection (q-flat connection)

\[(\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q},\, \nabla_q)\]

on a \(\check{G}_q\)-bundle \(\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q} \to X\), together with a \(\check{B}_q\)-reduction \(\mathcal{P}_{\check{B}_q} \subset \mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q}\), satisfying the \(q\)-oper condition: the \(q\)-connection \(\nabla_q\) is transverse to the Borel reduction in the sense that for each simple root \(\alpha_i\) of \(\check{G}_q\), the component of \(\nabla_q\) along \(\check{\mathfrak{g}}_{-\alpha_i}\) is non-vanishing:

\[\mathrm{pr}_{-\alpha_i}(\nabla_q \bmod \check{\mathfrak{b}}_q) \neq 0 \quad \text{for all simple roots } \alpha_i.\]

For \(\check{G}_q = \mathrm{SU}_{q^{-1}}(2)\), a \(q\)-oper on \(X\) is a rank-\(2\) \(q\)-flat bundle with an invariant line subbundle \(\mathcal{L} \subset \mathcal{V}\) such that \(\nabla_q(\mathcal{L}) \not\subset \mathcal{L} \otimes \Omega^1_q\). The \(q\)-oper is then equivalent to a \(q\)-deformed projective connection (Sturm–Liouville operator):

\[\partial_q^2 + t(z), \qquad t(z) \in H^0(X, \Omega_q^{\otimes 2}).\]

We denote the moduli of \(q\)-opers by \(\mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\).

📄

Conjecture 11.12 ∀ stated (\(q\)-Opers are \(q\)-Hecke eigensheaves). \(\forall\)

Every \(q\)-oper \((\mathcal{P}_{\check{G}_q}, \nabla_q) \in \mathrm{Op}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\) determines a \(q\)-Hecke eigensheaf \(\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}\) on \(\mathrm{Bun}_{G_q}(X)\) via the \(q\)-Geometric Langlands equivalence (\(q\)-GL conjecture):

\[\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q} = \mathbb{L}_q^{-1}(\delta_{\nabla_q}),\]

where \(\delta_{\nabla_q}\) is the skyscraper sheaf at the point \(\nabla_q \in \mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}_q}(X)\). The eigenvalue \(q\)-local system is the \(q\)-oper connection itself:

\[\mathbf{T}_{x,\lambda}^{(q)}(\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}) \;\simeq\; \mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q} \otimes V_\lambda^{(q)}(\nabla_q)_x.\]

The \(q\)-oper condition (transversality to the Borel) ensures that \(\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}\) is irreducible as a \(q\)-\(\mathcal{D}\)-module: the transversality prevents \(\mathcal{M}_{\nabla_q}\) from admitting non-trivial sub-\(q\)-\(\mathcal{D}\)-modules.

Classical limit and physical interpretation

📄

Conjecture 11.13 ∀ stated (Classical limit of the \(q\)-Geometric Langlands correspondence). \(\forall\)

As \(q \to 1\) in the \(\mathbb{G}_m\)-family, the \(q\)-Geometric Langlands correspondence recovers the classical Geometric Langlands equivalence:

\[\lim_{q \to 1} \mathbb{L}_q \;=\; \mathbb{L}_{\mathrm{BD}} \colon \mathcal{D}\text{-}\mathrm{mod}(\mathrm{Bun}_G(X)) \;\xrightarrow{\;\sim\;} \mathrm{QCoh}(\mathrm{LocSys}_{\check{G}}(X)).\]

The degeneration proceeds through three compatible limits:

  1. Differential limit: \(d_q \to d\) and \(d_q^2 \to 0\) (non-vanishing of \(d_q^2\)), so \(q\)-flat connections become flat connections and \(q\)-local systems become classical local systems.

  2. Hecke limit: the Hecke relation \((T-q)(T+q^{-1}) = 0\) degenerates to \((T-1)(T+1) = 0\), recovering the symmetric group action. The \(q\)-Hecke operators become classical Hecke correspondences.

  3. Dual group limit: \(\check{G}_q = G_{q^{-1}}^\vee \to G^\vee = \check{G}\) as the quantum deformation is removed.
